<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36437v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.36437-concur/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-928962c2c93fbd5b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:concur" data-paper-title="CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-aebcbcd2e1c9e89d">Why sort by primary then auxiliary before PAVA without averaging all equal primary scores?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aconcur">CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Monotonicity only constrains strictly higher primary levels, not equal non-ceiling primary values. Sorting ties by auxiliary lets PAVA fix cross-primary violations only. Equal outputs are required at the ceiling only when that tie is enabled.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Primary [0.3,0.3,0.7], auxiliary [-1,0,1] is already feasible. Replacing the two first values with −0.5 adds a constraint.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地结果与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36437v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.36437-concur/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aebcbcd2e1c9e89d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:concur" data-paper-title="CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-2b9aaf1497f68e59">Does CONCUR-A exceeding two standard errors prove auxiliary reliability at the ceiling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aconcur">CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It measures concordance of passing pairs with different primary values, releasing ties after at least 61 valid readings and mean greater than two standard errors. The evolving distribution is not IID, and ceiling pairs are not directly measured. This is not a significance level or universal guarantee.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Concordance can reverse later and drop below the threshold; rebind the ceiling rather than treating the first release as permanent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与实现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36437v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.36437-concur/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2b9aaf1497f68e59">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swim" data-paper-title="SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a40912dd5fb29c9d">Why not gate the current state, and why require true mismatched discrimination?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswim">SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Boston University / Unity Technologies</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The current state is full action context; the paper gates only future displacement. Fitting positives alone can predict actions from current context and ignore displacement. A cyclic mismatch changes the future while holding current state/action fixed, encouraging behavior-relevant displacement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keep the current position and move-right action. For a negative, take the next batch row&#x27;s future minus this position. Replacing the current state gives a spurious context cue.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36662v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36662-swim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a40912dd5fb29c9d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swim" data-paper-title="SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0989a9f5d8371bbd">How do tests distinguish L1 shrinkage from learning behavior, and prevent future state leakage?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswim">SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Boston University / Unity Technologies</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Check gate gradients from the behavioral term alone, then real optimizer updates; parameter change alone is insufficient. In stage two state distance is stop-gradient. Future state constructs offline displacements only and must not be available to deployed planning. Constant-distance Pearson is undefined and should be rejected, not declared valid via arbitrary epsilon.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: λsum(g) shrinks gates even with actions ignored, so also test λ=0. If all frame distances are zero, reject the zero-denominator correlation rather than report success 1.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36662v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36662-swim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0989a9f5d8371bbd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swim" data-paper-title="SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c1b394272419a8ac">Are multiplying state by g or sqrt(g), or standardizing again afterward, equivalent?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswim">SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Boston University / Unity Technologies</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Square root scaling yields coefficient g in squared distance; scaling by g gives g². Gates weight already-standardized coordinates; re-standardization cancels scaling. Overall gate scale cancels from Pearson correlation and can be absorbed by the inverse model, so absolute gate magnitudes are not uniquely identifiable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Difference 2 with g=0.25 should give 0.25×4=1. Multiplying by sqrt(g)=0.5 before squaring gives 1; multiplying by g gives 0.25. Rescaling the standard deviation afterward cancels the 0.5.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36662v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36662-swim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c1b394272419a8ac">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swim" data-paper-title="SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-swim-9da395d5" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-300d76e6b7918837">Does SWIM learn a robot policy or which state coordinates matter for distance?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswim">SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Boston University / Unity Technologies</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It learns continuous coordinate weights from recorded actions and uses them for world-model geometry. Inverse action prediction only trains the weights. Deployment still needs image encoding, latent dynamics and planning such as CEM. Local coverage is the gate objective and metric, not a robot policy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Block position can receive more weight than background light color. That changes distance, not the robot&#x27;s grasp trajectory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36662v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36662-swim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-300d76e6b7918837">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:merlin" data-paper-title="Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e291827c8e0288f6">Why does Eq. 7 distinguish the second moment from covariance?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amerlin">Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It stores mean(kkᵀ), without centering, then computes variance qᵀΣq−(qᵀμ)². Passing covariance and subtracting again double-centers; treating the raw moment as variance includes mean strength. The local reference directly measures dot-product variance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keys [1,3] have mean 2, moment 5 and variance 1. Using 5 overcounts by 4; subtracting 4 from centered 1 yields the invalid −3.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37645v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.37645-merlin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e291827c8e0288f6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:merlin" data-paper-title="Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d276140dff602bb">Why only expose completed segments to local queries?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amerlin">Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Full-segment means and moments include future tokens for queries inside that segment. A full model could maintain prefix moments and recurrent state; the local path does not. It exposes completed segments only and rejects calls with none visible, rather than leaking future statistics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Segment start 4 length 4 covers positions 4–7. It is not visible at 6, only at 7; reading all keys at 4 leaks positions 5–7.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37645v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.37645-merlin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d276140dff602bb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:merlin" data-paper-title="Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-6a6cbfe669675cd8">Why not mix logits then apply one softmax instead of mixing two softmax distributions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amerlin">Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Softmax is nonlinear. MERLIN normalizes mean and variance routes separately and mixes probabilities with gamma. Mixing logits first changes competition and normalization even though both outputs sum to one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Mean logits [4,0], variance logits [0,0], gamma 0.5 yield [0.741,0.259]; softmax of mixed logits [2,0] gives [0.881,0.119].</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37645v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.37645-merlin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6a6cbfe669675cd8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:merlin" data-paper-title="Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-merlin-4afaa9c4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8c1c0aafb3dafdad">Why can two key segments with the same mean require different attention routing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amerlin">Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mean alignment can hide strong key matches canceled by others. MERLIN also retains raw second moments and recovers query-direction alignment variance, mixing it with mean routing. It enriches segment routing without reconstructing full per-token attention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keys [-2,2] and [0,0] both average zero. Query 1 gives alignment variances 4 and 0, invisible to mean routing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37645v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.37645-merlin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8c1c0aafb3dafdad">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fold-bias" data-paper-title="Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4c1c6936de7640a0">Why rescale a ridge direction to μᵀu=1 rather than use unconstrained least squares?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afold-bias">Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Unconstrained LS trades mean offset against projection spread and may shrink all biases. The paper rescales a ridge-stabilized inverse covariance direction to force mean projection one and minimize spread under that constraint. Covariance divides by N and ridge uses its trace; replacing N with N−1 changes the objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: With one-dimensional μ=2, variance 1 and no ridge, unconstrained LS gives 2/5 and mean projection 0.8. The constrained direction 1/2 gives exactly 1.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36520v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36520-fold-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4c1c6936de7640a0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fold-bias" data-paper-title="Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-09d707e834f73aa9">Why actually cast keys to BF16 before refitting values?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afold-bias">Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Least squares must see attention from the rounded keys. Fitting with high-precision keys then rounding changes the matrix and invalidates the intended normal equations. The local path casts before building A and returns fit-precision coefficients; cache installation, value rounding and backend correctness need separate validation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: BF16 maps 1.003 to 1.0. Fitting attention with 1.003 compensates an attention table that deployment will not see.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36520v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36520-fold-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-09d707e834f73aa9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fold-bias" data-paper-title="Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-20b2acd190796a3b">Why is FoldBias more informed than deleting bias, but not better for every query?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afold-bias">Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Deletion multiplies bias by zero; folding multiplies by q·u and can be closer to one if future queries resemble calibration. Drift can be worse. The bound also needs bias range and value diameter and compares unrounded keys at fixed values, not a refitted serving stack.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: q·u=0.9 leaves 10% bias error; q·u=−2 gives coefficient 3 vs deletion&#x27;s 1. This is not LLM accuracy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式, 论文离线与线上效果. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36520v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36520-fold-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-20b2acd190796a3b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fold-bias" data-paper-title="Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-fold-bias-1b8893e9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e4fe32856525b65d">Why can&#x27;t a static bias folded into a key be exact for every future query?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afold-bias">Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A key shift contributes a linear function of query, whereas nonzero bias is query-independent. FoldBias fits a direction u so q·u is near 1 on context queries; future drift can increase error. It is distribution-dependent, not an identity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A zero query produces zero logit change from any key shift, not bias 0.8. A query satisfying q·u=1 can express that bias exactly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36520v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36520-fold-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e4fe32856525b65d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evalalloc" data-paper-title="Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-19ec74cd1e637afe">Why aren&#x27;t equally sized independent random item sets equivalent to a shared core?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevalalloc">Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · The University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Common items supply paired covariance, helping when candidates agree on most items and set difficulty varies. Frozen item model and prior put successive generations on one scale. Refitting per candidate breaks comparability. This benefit depends on candidate correlation, not guaranteed variance reduction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A faces hard items and B easy ones. A common informative core is more comparable than merely requiring 60 items each.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与实现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37276v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.37276-evalalloc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-19ec74cd1e637afe">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evalalloc" data-paper-title="Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-evalalloc-e28d06aa" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-475561c032d4eedb">If cheap search feedback is sufficient, why spend extra on final confirmation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevalalloc">Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · The University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Search needs comparable low-cost guidance; final selection must separate near-tied candidates. EvalAlloc uses sparse shared-core search and paired confirmation that reuses cache, with real observations for the final prefix rather than perpetual imputation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A predicted difference of 0.01 can guide exploration but should not decide the champion by itself.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37276v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.37276-evalalloc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-475561c032d4eedb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evalalloc" data-paper-title="Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-acbbb6ce4a3b415b">Can partial credit 0.9 add 0.9 to an item&#x27;s acquisition success count?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevalalloc">Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · The University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Acquisition counts only full credit a_i and uses a Beta posterior for conservative p(1−p) informativeness. Partial grades are not full successes there but remain scores for the response model. Mixing the stages changes the shared core.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Ten 0.9 scores yield a=0, n=10, not a=9; 0.9 still enters model fitting and final scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地结果与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37276v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.37276-evalalloc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-acbbb6ce4a3b415b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evalalloc" data-paper-title="Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cd62ca40b7b37d16">Why retain the search-cache union and check candidate IDs in cross-fitting?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevalalloc">Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · The University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Already executed cells need not be paid for again; fill missing common-prefix items and retain candidate-specific observations. Separate two-fold refit predictions prevent candidates from training their own correction. The correction is zero when all items are observed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keep A&#x27;s cached item 4 even if prefix is 0/1/2. If a round needs four new cells and only three remain, reject the round; never read hidden complete scores to select a winner.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与实现边界, 本地结果与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37276v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.37276-evalalloc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cd62ca40b7b37d16">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:emma" data-paper-title="EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-628c21208d8098ea">Why treat context overflow differently from missing capability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aemma">EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · University of California San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Overflow can mean a step is too broad. Split incomplete steps and resume without discarding finished work. A new specialist needs evidence of missing capability or repeated overflow; repeated overflow calls for changing the decomposition, not simply changing prompts/skills.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: If steps one and two already produced a table and step three is too large, keep the table and subdivide step three among existing agents.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式, 代码映射. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35966v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.35966-emma/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-628c21208d8098ea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:emma" data-paper-title="EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c81e84114c9000a3">Why require one edited entry and retain at least 60% of old prompt lines?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aemma">EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · University of California San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Single-entry and ownership scope bound location; retention, length and pool capacity bound magnitude. Only agents involved in the failed attempt may change. New entries must actually be used in the next plan. Structural validity is not better task performance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keeping two of five lines and replacing the role is rejected. Keeping three and adding a local check reaches 60%, but still needs an external rerun.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地结果与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35966v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.35966-emma/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c81e84114c9000a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:emma" data-paper-title="EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-emma-e2de2da1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b5bc65c5db3ad6e9">Why doesn&#x27;t EMMA turn every failure into a new skill?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aemma">EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · University of California San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Ownership depends on the error. Use task-local plan guidance for one execution slip, agent prompts for general habits, skills for missing procedures and controller changes for routing. Experience at the wrong scope can fail to trigger or interfere elsewhere.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Checking units can be reusable. One misclick does not require a permanent unit-check skill or a new agent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35966v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.35966-emma/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b5bc65c5db3ad6e9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:emma" data-paper-title="EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c89ecfb26059fd12">Do passing local guards prove no memory leakage and a stronger agent?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aemma">EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · University of California San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The code checks ownership, capacity, retention, rotation, lifecycle and concatenation. Independent external services judge semantic deduplication, real specialization and leakage; the component cannot prove those judgments correct. No evaluated actor, LLM reflection or real task traces.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A service may incorrectly mark an answer-bearing proposal safe. A Boolean interface cannot detect that; local rejection counts are not AppWorld success rates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 数据协议与实现边界, 本地结果与负控, 高成本完整实验. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35966v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.35966-emma/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c89ecfb26059fd12">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinger" data-paper-title="PinGER: Token-Efficient Generative Retrieval with Semantic IDs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-29956241de9aa37e">Why isn&#x27;t prefix diversity just subtracting a constant for duplicate next tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinger">PinGER: Token-Efficient Generative Retrieval with Semantic IDs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Penalty depends on longest common prefix depth between parent beams and accumulated chosen slots, including the same parent. Deeper shared prefixes penalize repeated subtrees more. The next token alone drops hierarchy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Parents (1,2) and (1,3) share depth one; (1,2) with itself shares depth two. After picking its child, penalties differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33435v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../recommendation-components/2610.33435-pinger/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-29956241de9aa37e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinger" data-paper-title="PinGER: Token-Efficient Generative Retrieval with Semantic IDs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a40d6e62f3c4f3a9">Why does PinGER DPO accumulate every prefix and retain an NTP anchor?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinger">PinGER: Token-Efficient Generative Retrieval with Semantic IDs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Per-level loss gives earlier SID decisions preference signal; using only full IDs changes the objective. NTP limits drift. Reference margin offsets the logistic input, not a hard stop-gradient for correct ranking. Local checks are formula-only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: For three levels sum losses for prefixes 1, 1–2 and 1–3, then add NTP. Tripling only the final loss differs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<h2 id="qa-f9327d3b5e34e40b">Why keep SIDs during PinGER training but remove historical SIDs at serving?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinger">PinGER: Token-Efficient Generative Retrieval with Semantic IDs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Asymmetric masking sends historical item information forward only through dense tokens. Historical SID positions are not read by other items or dense states, so removing those positions does not alter retained dense states. Dense input can still incorporate SID features.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A historical item occupies three SID positions and one dense position during training. Keeping only the dense position can preserve its attention output if inputs match.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<h2 id="qa-029893dfd176215d">How does local selection avoid test data or a final unevaluated prompt, and what do callbacks establish?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acrop">CROP: Token-Efficient Reasoning in Large Language Models via Regularized Prompt Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Selection requires fixed validation revision/IDs matching the frozen CoT length baseline, disjoint training IDs, and no train/test scoring for selection. Each round validates the current prompt before proposing the next, so the final unevaluated one cannot win. Deterministic model/critic fixtures verify gating, concatenation and selection, not real LLM improvement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Measured A=0.8 and B=0.9; last proposal C has no validation. Return B, not newest C.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 数据协议与实现边界, 本地结果与负控, 高成本完整实验. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It adds length feedback and selection by output-token cost. Table 3 includes accuracy drops: Gemini2Flash on ObjectCounting goes 96.0%→94.8% while mean tokens go 101.2→19.6. Report both sides of the tradeoff, not universal losslessness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: At equal 0.9 accuracy a 50-token prompt can beat a 100-token one. If the short prompt is less accurate, do not report only length.</p>

<h2 id="qa-1abbf5985f2cce1c">Does CROP optimize model parameters, individual answers or the system prompt?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acrop">CROP: Token-Efficient Reasoning in Large Language Models via Regularized Prompt Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It freezes model weights and iterates the system prompt offline. The model generates; task and length critics identify accuracy and redundancy problems; a meta-optimizer rewrites the prompt. Deployment uses the selected prompt for one generation. This is neither hard truncation nor RL weight updates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Iteratively changing “explain every step” to “keep the combined calculation and remove repetition” is prompt optimization; cutting any reply after 50 tokens is not.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 原论文关键图. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<h2 id="qa-8032636210dd476d">Why does Sample–Beam separate sampled reasoning from item beam generation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apailitao-mmsearch2">PailitaoMMSearch2.0 Technical Report: Scaling Generative Retrieval to Unified End-to-End Multimodal Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Taobao &amp; Tmall Group of Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Serving returns an item set; sampling one response does not match that structure. Sample reasoning, then beam-expand the SID to train RL on a serving-like candidate set. Intent rewards and trajectories are still needed; beam search alone is not the full method.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Expand ten product codes under one rationale instead of sampling ten unrelated rationale–ID pairs.</p>

<h2 id="qa-191febc5125e9909">Can a 0.58 percentage-point CTR gain be reported as 0.58% relative?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apailitao-mmsearch2">PailitaoMMSearch2.0 Technical Report: Scaling Generative Retrieval to Unified End-to-End Multimodal Search</a></p>

<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Percentage points are absolute; relative change depends on baseline CTR. The paper&#x27;s result is from full deployment. This repository records the work only, without model, private-data training or A/B; don&#x27;t attribute production lift to a local stub.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: 10%→10.58% is +0.58 points but +5.8% relative. This illustrates units, not the paper baseline.</p>

<h2 id="qa-ba1eaa41311ff0a8">Does more reasoning always improve PailitaoMMSearch2.0 retrieval?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apailitao-mmsearch2">PailitaoMMSearch2.0 Technical Report: Scaling Generative Retrieval to Unified End-to-End Multimodal Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Taobao &amp; Tmall Group of Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The 0.8B No-think variant has highest macro ER; 2B Low-think better balances overall quality and latency, and 4B varies by intent. Consider scale, intent and serving cost rather than generalizing a single optimum.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A clearly visible exact-match attribute may need no rationale, while a match with several constraints can benefit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 论文离线与线上效果. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6ad4ec1f2700540d">Does PailitaoMMSearch2.0 rewrite queries or directly generate items?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apailitao-mmsearch2">PailitaoMMSearch2.0 Technical Report: Scaling Generative Retrieval to Unified End-to-End Multimodal Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Taobao &amp; Tmall Group of Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It consumes the original image and free text and generates three-level SIDs that map to products. Decoding produces candidates. Some deployments still mix them with incumbent retrieval results; end-to-end generation does not remove every production module.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Upload a shirt and request matching pants; outputs are product IDs, not just a rewritten query for another engine.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式, 论文离线与线上效果. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
