<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:kl-mopd" data-paper-title="KL-MOPD: Discrepancy-Aware Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-dd274eb36d8c0d0d">Does KL-MOPD compute alpha from the current student or the frozen initial student?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Akl-mopd">KL-MOPD: Discrepancy-Aware Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Calibrate once before training using the frozen initial student&#x27;s own sampled prefixes. Training loss uses current student prefixes but does not recalculate alpha from current gaps. Dynamic weights would define a different objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Initial gaps 1 and 3 produce fixed weights 1/4 and 3/4. Later gaps of 2 and 1 do not swap them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36973v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../recommendation-components/2610.36973-kl-mopd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dd274eb36d8c0d0d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:kl-mopd" data-paper-title="KL-MOPD: Discrepancy-Aware Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f943ef4c424b8aa8">Why doesn&#x27;t a gradient-tested tensor loss establish on-policy recommender training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Akl-mopd">KL-MOPD: Discrepancy-Aware Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Logits alone don&#x27;t tell the kernel who sampled a prefix. Initial calibration, current student generation, frozen teacher scoring, SID decoding and real splits require external integration. Only the loss component and small CPU/CUDA mechanism evidence are present.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: The kernel accepts cached old-policy prefixes, but that does not make them samples from the current student.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36973v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../recommendation-components/2610.36973-kl-mopd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f943ef4c424b8aa8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:kl-mopd" data-paper-title="KL-MOPD: Discrepancy-Aware Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e1b61ee586eb6c08">Is weighting two reverse KL losses equivalent to averaging teacher probabilities and computing one KL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Akl-mopd">KL-MOPD: Discrepancy-Aware Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Not in general. Weight the separate student-to-teacher KL losses, not an arithmetic mixture of teacher probabilities, and keep KL(student||teacher), not forward KL. Negative controls distinguish the computations without establishing recommendation gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Teachers favor different tokens. An arithmetic mixture keeps mass on both modes; weighted reverse KL involves log teacher probabilities and yields different gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36973v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../recommendation-components/2610.36973-kl-mopd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e1b61ee586eb6c08">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:kl-mopd" data-paper-title="KL-MOPD: Discrepancy-Aware Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-kl-mopd-35d8ffea" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-225530c49babcf34">Why estimate each teacher&#x27;s difficulty at each SID position in KL-MOPD?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Akl-mopd">KL-MOPD: Discrepancy-Aware Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An item ID needs several correct tokens. The click teacher may be easy to imitate early and the value teacher later. Fixed half weights ignore this; KL-MOPD upweights the harder teacher based on each initial student-to-teacher KL gap.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A three-part code starts with category and ends with attributes. If a teacher diverges only on category, one sequence-wide weight obscures that difference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36973v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../recommendation-components/2610.36973-kl-mopd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-225530c49babcf34">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:select-ttt" data-paper-title="Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0936a469597e97bb">Why average the lowest-CE positions in a chunk rather than the highest?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aselect-ttt">Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>CE is mean negative log probability of question tokens under the current hidden state&#x27;s vocabulary distribution. Lower values mean the position predicts question words better. Averaging the lowest k preserves local relevance more robustly than a single minimum. Reversing it reinforces irrelevant positions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: For CE 1 and 6, select 1 as more relevant. Repeated question tokens count as many times as they appear.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36794v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36794-select-ttt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0936a469597e97bb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:select-ttt" data-paper-title="Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f70c34eaf358e479">Why emit the current chunk before writing its keys and values?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aselect-ttt">Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Its outputs read the pre-update state; only later chunks use the new information. Writing first leaks the current update into an earlier output and changes causal order. The local reference tests tensor-state transitions, not real NTP-aligned features, backbone integration or long-dialogue evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Start with W=0. Chunk one outputs 0 then writes W=1. Chunk two can read 1; an output of 1 in chunk one would use its write prematurely.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36794v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36794-select-ttt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f70c34eaf358e479">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:select-ttt" data-paper-title="Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-aa77181e9a488912">Why isn&#x27;t Select-TTT a strictly conserved write-budget allocation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aselect-ttt">Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Softmax multiplied by chunk count sums to that count before clipping. An upper cap can lower the sum. Approximate mean learning-rate preservation is not strict conservation. Renormalization changes Eq. 10 and can violate the per-chunk cap.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Three chunks can start near [3,0,0]. A cap of 1.2 gives total about 1.2, not 3; this is a formula example, not a QA result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36794v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36794-select-ttt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aa77181e9a488912">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:select-ttt" data-paper-title="Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-select-ttt-1dc0ac0a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-99cdb22b8325ac12">Does Select-TTT change retrieval or the strength of writes to fast weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aselect-ttt">Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It keeps In-Place TTT chunk writes and scales each chunk&#x27;s learning rate with question relevance. Scores come from question-token negative log probabilities under the frozen LM head. It neither trains a retriever nor discards all low-scoring chunks. Different questions can induce different multipliers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A long conversation may favor different passages for a moving date and food preferences, without labels telling the model where the answer is.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36794v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36794-select-ttt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-99cdb22b8325ac12">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gui-jepa" data-paper-title="GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-012814975154e4eb">Why route action and ROI through the residual predictor rather than directly to the structured scoring head?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agui-jepa">GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The paper forces candidate-conditioned visual information through the JEPA predictor rather than a shortcut. Action and ROI condition a query; a three-layer Transformer creates a residual latent, followed by ROI and global pooling. Training with a decision loss does not prove accurate future-screen prediction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two click candidates with different ROI content and positions should give different latents. A bypass from raw ROI to the scorer cannot demonstrate predictor utility.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36877v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36877-gui-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-012814975154e4eb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gui-jepa" data-paper-title="GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3b5a93ef5e4fcae4">Does a verified three-layer predictor and gradient path mean the repository can operate Android?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agui-jepa">GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It receives external screen/condition latents and verifies the residual head, candidate masking and weighted listwise loss. It has no encoder, a11y enumeration, MiniLM ranker or executor. Positive labels are loss-only, not forward inputs. A GPU tensor check is not AndroidControl success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Backpropagating on two valid candidate latents only checks gradients. Launching an app also requires screen encoding, candidate discovery, execution and observing the next screen.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 检查与负控, 高成本完整实验. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36877v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36877-gui-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3b5a93ef5e4fcae4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gui-jepa" data-paper-title="GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e4c26d5506f18c85">How does GUI-JEPA scoring differ from predicting a next state and choosing the one closest to a goal?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agui-jepa">GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Latents are decision features trained by listwise action loss; distance to a goal latent is not the value. A randomly initialized predictor can match a dynamics-pretrained one in the paper, so useful decision features are not necessarily good dynamics predictions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Confirming may finish a task with little visual change, while an animation looks closer to a target image but is wrong. Action score is not image or latent similarity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式, 论文离线与线上效果. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36877v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36877-gui-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e4c26d5506f18c85">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gui-jepa" data-paper-title="GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-gui-jepa-f231a89e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d61dbbeb9e00d39">Why doesn&#x27;t GUI-JEPA generate actions token by token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agui-jepa">GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It enumerates actions from the accessibility tree and conditions visual latents on each candidate, then scores the batch. The action space comes from observations rather than free-form text generation. Speed depends on candidate count and a11y input, which pixel-only agents may lack, so not all GUI systems are directly comparable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Score three valid button actions and choose the best, instead of generating JSON and parsing coordinates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36877v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.36877-gui-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d61dbbeb9e00d39">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:ruharness" data-paper-title="When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-503b195db49bbbcd">Does better rubric compliance automatically promote the next harness?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aruharness">When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Harbin Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Rubrics diagnose weaknesses and guide proposals, not task outcomes. Candidates must pass external verification and compete with the current harness on independent validation. Only the top-scoring candidate whose improvement strictly clears the threshold replaces it. Final test is excluded.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A candidate adds many evidence-check lines but does not improve validation success. Keep the current harness rather than promote prettier self-check logs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与实现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36826v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.36826-ruharness/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-503b195db49bbbcd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:ruharness" data-paper-title="When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3ad4f868d9fa0da1">Does outcome-blind judging conflict with later use of success/failure labels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aruharness">When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Harbin Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The judge sees behavior only when assigning rubric labels, avoiding hindsight. A separate statistical layer then joins those labels with outcomes to form the six-cell table. The component accepts both inputs but cannot prove an external judge was blinded or claim full evaluation integration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Seal the label for whether the target file was checked before revealing test success; don&#x27;t reinterpret an ambiguous check after learning the run failed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 数据协议与实现边界, 本地结果与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36826v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.36826-ruharness/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3ad4f868d9fa0da1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:ruharness" data-paper-title="When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-ruharness-cecd9850" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-2e575e0803773eb3">If an agent can already edit its harness, why update the rubric too?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aruharness">When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Harbin Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A repaired harness changes its failure distribution. Fixed criteria may track resolved faults and miss new ones. RuHarness reevaluates criteria against current trajectories while keeping the task objective fixed, then uses criteria that still diagnose weaknesses to guide edits.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Initially it forgot search; later it searches but submits with insufficient evidence. Rewarding any search call misses the new failure.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36826v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.36826-ruharness/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2e575e0803773eb3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:ruharness" data-paper-title="When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8cfddc49739eda77">Why compute discrimination, coverage and predictiveness from one six-cell posterior?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aruharness">When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Harbin Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>They are correlated because they come from the same success/failure × Violated/Satisfied/N/A table. Add 0.5 to each cell, draw 2,000 joint Dirichlet samples, recompute all three for each draw and take the 0.2 utility quantile. Independent draws would discard correlations. Trajectory-set N and Red are fixed during sampling.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two observed violations both fail, giving a high point estimate. A lower posterior quantile reflects that two hits are not hundreds of stable observations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与实现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36826v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.36826-ruharness/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8cfddc49739eda77">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:discernmem" data-paper-title="Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3fc0461b8244cb89">Why can&#x27;t a new memory body inherit the parent&#x27;s success evidence?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adiscernmem">Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · East China Normal University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Effects are tied to the body actually used. The new body has not shown the same reliability. Keep identity, owner and compliant correction history, but clear previous effect evidence and mark the new version provisional. This versioning component is not evidence of LLM repair or multi-agent ability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: v2 worked on ten tasks. If v3 adds a stopping condition, keep v2 records but start v3&#x27;s effects empty; do not say v3 passed the ten tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与实现边界, 本地结果与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36652v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.36652-discernmem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3fc0461b8244cb89">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:discernmem" data-paper-title="Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-79284be821911bd5">Why compare a proposed repair to both its parent memory and a no-memory baseline?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adiscernmem">Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · East China Normal University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The parent may already be harmful. Merely beating it can still underperform injecting nothing. For each task in the fixed trigger and history sets, the proposal must match the better reference minus tolerance, without adding outright failures. This protects tested behavior, not every unseen task.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Parent 0.2, no memory 0.8, proposal 0.7. The proposal beats its parent by 0.5 but misses the 0.79 threshold with default tolerance 0.01; reject it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36652v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.36652-discernmem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-79284be821911bd5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:discernmem" data-paper-title="Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ceac2d055153b0af">How does testing only on the triggering failure differ from DiscernMem&#x27;s cross-task validation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adiscernmem">Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · East China Normal University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A local fix can harm past capabilities. DiscernMem fixes a set of triggers, previous positive-effect tasks and related tasks, then applies thresholds per task, not to the mean. Related tasks must not regress; they need not improve. Origin tasks are excluded from history validation so the original example cannot repeatedly validate its own memory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Trigger improves 0.4→0.9 and an old task drops 0.8→0.5. Reject even though the mean improves.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与实现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36652v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.36652-discernmem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ceac2d055153b0af">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:discernmem" data-paper-title="Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-discernmem-43739873" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-208331253abf4012">Why not rewrite every memory used after a team failure?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adiscernmem">Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · East China Normal University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Another role, a tool or an out-of-scope scenario may have caused the failure. DiscernMem compares replay with just the suspect memory against no-memory replay on the same task, seed and configuration. It then asks whether the rule body is defective or a useful rule was used out of scope. A negative effect alone does not prove a defective body.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Repair the source before running tests may help with code bugs. If the test environment is broken, more source edits can harm. Add an avoid scope rather than delete a useful source-repair rule.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36652v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.36652-discernmem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-208331253abf4012">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rescom" data-paper-title="ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f90806934ea200c7">Why does ResCom decompose whitened output cross-statistics rather than truncate the original weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arescom">ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rank should go to residual directions that occur on calibration data and affect outputs. The Gram matrix measures residual scale and correlations; error–residual cross-statistics measure output impact. Cholesky whitening then truncated SVD solves a ridge-regularized output-reconstruction objective. Direct weight truncation ignores residual distribution and solves a different problem.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A large residual may have little output effect while a small one is amplified. Allocate rank by output error, not residual size alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35955v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.35955-rescom/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f90806934ea200c7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rescom" data-paper-title="ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-823e70895c07a37a">Why not attach each layer&#x27;s compensation as soon as its statistics are collected?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arescom">ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Early compensation changes the activations at later layers, so statistics no longer describe the same frozen model. Collect every target layer first, then install branches. Streaming merges only data from the same frozen mapping. G and C are sums: averaging without adjusting ridge changes the solution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Doubling samples doubles G and C, changing a fixed ridge&#x27;s relative strength. Dividing them by sample count is a different objective unless ridge is adjusted.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35955v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.35955-rescom/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-823e70895c07a37a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rescom" data-paper-title="ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ec528a42e7e51e74">What changes when a low-rank branch sees rounding residuals rather than quantized input?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arescom">ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A branch reading quantized input cannot distinguish two inputs on the same grid point. A residual branch reads the discarded component. ResCom leaves the original path frozen, unlike approaches that remove high-precision weights before quantizing the remainder.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Removing weights before quantization changes calibration; adding UVd+b beside a frozen path does not change its quantization settings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35955v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.35955-rescom/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ec528a42e7e51e74">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rescom" data-paper-title="ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-rescom-f00947a9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8dfbcbd312870357">How can a quantized model recover information from the current activation&#x27;s rounding residual?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arescom">ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Quantization maps a range of continuous inputs to one grid value. The forward pass can access both pre-rounding and rounded activations, so their difference retains information the quantized value lost. ResCom reads that residual through a fixed low-rank branch rather than retraining the quantizer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: 1.01 and 1.04 both round to 1.0. Residuals of 0.01 and 0.04 let compensation differ. This is not a model accuracy result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35955v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.35955-rescom/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8dfbcbd312870357">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rpl" data-paper-title="Learning to Program Retrievals: Composing Search Primitives via Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-rpl-95ce1341" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-908c2d6b9d2abe39">Does Meta&#x27;s release of full RPL code automatically make the local typed-program component a full reproduction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arpl">Learning to Program Retrievals: Composing Search Primitives via Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · KAIST AI / Meta Superintelligence Labs</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Release improves provenance, not local fidelity. Local work still omits neural retrievers, cross-turn Python state, policy generation, GRPO, and distillation. The main project&#x27;s CC-BY-NC and vendored licenses still apply. Public code is not permission to copy or upgrade evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Having factory blueprints does not mean a small pipe simulator makes the same product. The real execution path and costs still need verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 论文信息, 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:embedding-gemma2" data-paper-title="EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6a5d62a51c0cdd94">The formal paper pools before projection, but the local path pools official last_hidden_state. Is a layer missing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Aembedding-gemma2">EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The pinned official implementation applies a bias-free embedding_projection before returning its 768-dimensional token states. Equal-weight masked mean commutes with linear projection, so pooling those outputs matches the paper; projecting again would be incorrect. The formal paper does not upgrade the existing 16-image GPU run to seven full benchmarks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Averaging two tokens after multiplying each by the same matrix equals averaging first and then multiplying. Nonlinearity or token-dependent transformations break this equivalence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 结果与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37364v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/embeddinggemma2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6a5d62a51c0cdd94">Question link</a></p>
</details>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hope-hilbert" data-paper-title="Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-868a387e39220c9a">Why is an input function times an output vector a rank-one operator?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahope-hilbert">Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A neuron returns a scalar activation, which only changes the magnitude along one output-weight vector. The input function maps into one output direction, forming a rank-one tensor. Neuron inner products multiply an activation kernel by the output-vector inner product, not input-weight cosine alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Activation 0.2→0.8 changes 0.2w→0.8w, still along w. Changing the output vector changes functional similarity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 原论文关键图. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2607.21366-hope-hilbert/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-868a387e39220c9a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hope-hilbert" data-paper-title="Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-aa4684949b6038fc">Why freeze initial parameter savings and adjust downstream BN mean during pruning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahope-hilbert">Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The pruning priority divides distortion by initial parameter savings; recomputing from shrinking neighbor shapes changes the criterion. Remove the deleted activation&#x27;s mean contribution from dense consumers&#x27; BN running means to avoid an extra shift. This does not preserve every prediction, and exact undo does not prove lossless accuracy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Mean activation 0.8 and output weights [1,2] imply subtracting [0.8,1.6] from the consumer&#x27;s BN mean, not adding it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议、结果与负控, 高成本完整实验与复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2607.21366-hope-hilbert/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aa4684949b6038fc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hope-hilbert" data-paper-title="Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-16be87c74267c415">Is HOPE Hilbert compression the same as the Hope network in Sleep?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahope-hilbert">Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding analyzes frozen-network functional capacity and compresses with PRUNE, MERGE and EVICT. Sleep&#x27;s Hope is a multi-frequency memory network updated in learning and offline consolidation. Local coverage is the former&#x27;s kernel, pruning and one-step restoration components.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Scoring a frozen ResNet&#x27;s neurons for removal is not teaching a language model during sleep.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 保留机制与接口, 高成本完整实验与复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2607.21366-hope-hilbert/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-16be87c74267c415">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hope-hilbert" data-paper-title="Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-hope-hilbert-ad1735c1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-678a615e93864162">Why doesn&#x27;t HOPE simply remove neurons with small weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahope-hilbert">Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Scaling a ReLU neuron&#x27;s input and BN scale up and its output weights down can leave the function unchanged. Raw weight magnitude is therefore unreliable. HOPE compares Hilbert-operator capacity from activation functions and output vectors under a Gaussian surrogate, not proven importance on real data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Multiply the hidden activation by seven and divide output weights by seven. Predictions and functional capacity stay unchanged, although weight magnitude falls.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2607.21366-hope-hilbert/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-678a615e93864162">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:sleep-lti" data-paper-title="Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-357fc7df50a38180">Does LTI&#x27;s edit-distance threshold cap edit count or a similarity ratio?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asleep-lti">Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It caps the absolute number of token edits, inclusively. For accepted pairs the literal reward is one minus distance divided by the longer completion length. A fixed similarity-ratio threshold differs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Threshold 1 admits one substitution in both 6- and 60-token completions, with rewards 5/6 and 59/60.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03979v2">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2606.03979-sleep-lti/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-357fc7df50a38180">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:sleep-lti" data-paper-title="Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
