<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30951v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.30951-openattention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b733e66f95bcc284">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:openattention" data-paper-title="OpenAttention: One Percent Is Enough with Tail Proxies" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6de51fcd1292a9c7">Why not read only a few important KV entries?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aopenattention">OpenAttention: One Percent Is Enough with Tail Proxies</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Sogang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A low read rate can leave substantial total mass in the tail. Counted residual-cluster averages supplement exact reads instead of treating the tail as zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Many individually weak tokens can jointly affect the output.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30951v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.30951-openattention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6de51fcd1292a9c7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lazyflash" data-paper-title="LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-lazyflash-43455fcb" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-73f4f2504e86cd44">Why does LazyFlash save backward work rather than visibility?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alazyflash">LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Forward stays dense. Output-gradient block norms set backward retention probabilities, and inverse-probability weighting estimates dense gradients. A tiled backward kernel must skip actual work; masking afterward does not. A single random draw need not equal dense gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A low-contribution query block can be skipped in backward even though forward reads all evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31911v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.31911-lazyflash/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-73f4f2504e86cd44">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lazyflash" data-paper-title="LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-360bcff30d297860">Why isn&#x27;t masking gradients after dense backward a LazyFlash kernel?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alazyflash">LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compute and memory traffic have already occurred. Skip tiles inside FlashAttention backward. No local operator or GPU receipt is claimed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Discarding half the results after computing all blocks saves no backward execution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31911v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.31911-lazyflash/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-360bcff30d297860">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lazyflash" data-paper-title="LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-67cc8c10b70561d5">Is importance backward equivalent to fixed top-k gradient truncation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alazyflash">LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Inverse-probability reweighting targets an unbiased dense-gradient estimate in expectation; fixed truncation generally does not. Individual draws still differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A block kept with probability 0.5 is upweighted when sampled, not permanently dropped.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lazyflash" data-paper-title="LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1694bf608c608052">Why preserve dense forward but compress backward?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alazyflash">LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Forward determines visible context. Uneven gradient contributions let training sample/reweight backward blocks without making inference forward sparse.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Read the whole document, then sample only some backward blocks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31911v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.31911-lazyflash/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1694bf608c608052">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-dlc" data-paper-title="Jev-DLC: Decision-Level Continual Learning from Typed Feedback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/adaptive-decisions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/adaptive-decisions/">Structured Decisions / Decisions on Demand: Selective Reasoning, Transfer, and Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-06eefc2e388ae998">Why assess Jev-DLC reliability before updates and apply feedback only later?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-dlc">Jev-DLC: Decision-Level Continual Learning from Typed Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reliability measures prediction before feedback, not after learning the answer. The conservative state tracks repeated semantic experience, the responsive state tracks current correction, and reliability mixes them. Feedback must bind a committed decision; no forgery/replay or reading current gold before prediction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A user undo can update both channels for the next request, not retroactively turn this choice into a success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 双通道、PA-I与可靠性. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31521v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.31521-jev-dlc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-06eefc2e388ae998">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-dlc" data-paper-title="Jev-DLC: Decision-Level Continual Learning from Typed Feedback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/adaptive-decisions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/adaptive-decisions/">Structured Decisions / Decisions on Demand: Selective Reasoning, Transfer, and Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cfa09967908de8b9">Why reject feedback on forged, replayed or stale Jev-DLC Decisions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-dlc">Jev-DLC: Decision-Level Continual Learning from Typed Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Feedback must refer to a committed decision from this instance; otherwise arbitrary targets or duplicated experience can alter state. Release the current public cache after update. Adaptation never overrides hard safety masks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Sending the same undo event twice must not count as two corrections.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 双通道、PA-I与可靠性. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31521v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.31521-jev-dlc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cfa09967908de8b9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-dlc" data-paper-title="Jev-DLC: Decision-Level Continual Learning from Typed Feedback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/adaptive-decisions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/adaptive-decisions/">Structured Decisions / Decisions on Demand: Selective Reasoning, Transfer, and Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d6fc3fb543805f86">Why separate conservative and responsive Jev-DLC channels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-dlc">Jev-DLC: Decision-Level Continual Learning from Typed Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The conservative one builds a stable prior from repeated behavior; the responsive one tracks recent corrections. Reliability mixing balances long-term patterns and change; one state struggles to express both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A long-standing preference for A and temporary switch to B can be recorded separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 双通道、PA-I与可靠性. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31521v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.31521-jev-dlc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d6fc3fb543805f86">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-dlc" data-paper-title="Jev-DLC: Decision-Level Continual Learning from Typed Feedback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/adaptive-decisions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/adaptive-decisions/">Structured Decisions / Decisions on Demand: Selective Reasoning, Transfer, and Feedback</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-jev-dlc-8eed7f0b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-58e39b989e85825c">Does Jev-DLC continual adaptation need to retain complete histories?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-dlc">Jev-DLC: Decision-Level Continual Learning from Typed Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A frozen scorer has two compact states: semantic counts/direction for the conservative channel and a current correction direction for the responsive channel. Feedback enters state, not an ever-growing conversation prefix.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Repeated routing corrections update counts and directions rather than append every old ticket.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 双通道、PA-I与可靠性. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31521v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.31521-jev-dlc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-58e39b989e85825c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:inside-jepa" data-paper-title="Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-inside-jepa-840eadf0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-098a3adf3f209998">Why use a differentiable online future encoding in the inverse-dynamics head instead of EMA?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ainside-jepa">Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Australian Institute for Machine Learning, Adelaide University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The inverse objective must send action-explanation gradients into relationship representations on the future side. JEPA prediction can still use a stable EMA target. Entity-only and shuffled-action controls test whether relations truly supply action information.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Predict the action from changes in cup–box relations; the future relation encoder needs gradients to learn such changes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与五臂. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31194v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.31194-inside-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-098a3adf3f209998">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:inside-jepa" data-paper-title="Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-37cda28a2170cf1f">Why is the four-entity K=8 state 256-dimensional, not 224 after removing diagonals?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ainside-jepa">Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Australian Institute for Machine Learning, Adelaide University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Entity latents occupy 4×32 and ordered pair slots occupy 4×4×8. Padding and diagonals stay present but zero. JEPA uses detached EMA future targets; inverse dynamics needs differentiable online future state. Mixing them cuts a defining gradient.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Zeroing diagonal relationships does not delete their 32 slots or shrink the predictor interface.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式与五臂, 本地复现与操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31194v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.31194-inside-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-37cda28a2170cf1f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:inside-jepa" data-paper-title="Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-eec426b4717383d2">What do INV-S, INV-R, and shuffled-label controls isolate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ainside-jepa">Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Australian Institute for Machine Learning, Adelaide University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>INV-S reads relations only for inverse dynamics; INV-R reads entity latents only. Shuffling changes only inverse labels, while prediction still reads true actions. These controls isolate supervision sources rather than treating any auxiliary gain as relation grounding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Similar gains with random action labels suggest regularization rather than learned action–relation correspondence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与五臂. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31194v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.31194-inside-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eec426b4717383d2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:inside-jepa" data-paper-title="Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c81bf3ff739be368">Why does Inside-JEPA want latent states to encode relationships?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ainside-jepa">Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Australian Institute for Machine Learning, Adelaide University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Latent forecasts need not expose contact or relative position. Inside-JEPA models entities and relations and studies how action supervision shapes them. A relation channel or low prediction loss does not establish learned relational semantics; controls are needed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two unchanged-looking objects can transition from separated to touching, altering the right action despite unchanged categories.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与五臂. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31194v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.31194-inside-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c81bf3ff739be368">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:finesid" data-paper-title="Progressive Learning from Content to Relevance to Personalization for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-finesid-1b73a633" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f378d3166750e8f2">Why does FineSID need more than SID embeddings when transferring relevance pretraining to CTR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afinesid">Progressive Learning from Content to Relevance to Personalization for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Relevance pretraining teaches ordered content fusion and HiFormer interactions across embeddings, dense layers, and normalization state. Copying only the vocabulary loses much of that learning. Change the CTR head and handle optimizer state explicitly. Full experiments were excluded for cost; random-token fixtures are not substitutes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Copying codes without the layers that match query uses to image details transfers a dictionary but not how to read it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 三阶段结构, 成本判定：不执行复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29138v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../recommendation-components/2610.29138-finesid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f378d3166750e8f2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:finesid" data-paper-title="Progressive Learning from Content to Relevance to Personalization for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1f9ddee4a7682fef">Why explicitly handle optimizer and normalization state at FineSID stage transitions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afinesid">Progressive Learning from Content to Relevance to Personalization for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Full transfer includes interaction layers and normalization statistics beyond SID embeddings. Keeping or resetting optimizer state changes training dynamics and must follow the stage contract, as must conversion to the CTR head. These requirements are documented; no local training validates performance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Copying weights without their normalization can change scale abruptly, and old task momentum should not silently enter a new CTR head.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 三阶段结构, 成本判定：不执行复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29138v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../recommendation-components/2610.29138-finesid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1f9ddee4a7682fef">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:finesid" data-paper-title="Progressive Learning from Content to Relevance to Personalization for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a81772613dcdad3d">How does full FineSID predictor transfer differ from freezing a content encoder and adding a CTR head?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afinesid">Progressive Learning from Content to Relevance to Personalization for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A frozen encoder mainly transfers content features; FineSID also retains cross-token fusion, interaction networks, and state learned on relevance, then adapts to personalized CTR. This costs more and requires matched interfaces. The repository completed cost review, not a reduced-model performance run.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Transfer the matching network that relates query conditions to item details, not just a content vocabulary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 三阶段结构, 成本判定：不执行复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29138v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../recommendation-components/2610.29138-finesid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a81772613dcdad3d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:finesid" data-paper-title="Progressive Learning from Content to Relevance to Personalization for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e9710414fc4bd3e4">Why keep fine-grained visual and text tokens rather than a single product code in FineSID?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afinesid">Progressive Learning from Content to Relevance to Personalization for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A single code can discard local texture, regions, and text details that drive relevance and clicks. Discrete local tokens support richer interactions through relevance pretraining but cost more in training and serving. More granularity does not guarantee better recommendations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two coats differ mainly in cuffs or pockets; a single summary code may lose the deciding detail.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 三阶段结构, 成本判定：不执行复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29138v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../recommendation-components/2610.29138-finesid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e9710414fc4bd3e4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:minimal-edit-opd" data-paper-title="Edit, Don&#x27;t Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c91dbc6c4760e464">Why skip correction for successes and select only some tokens from failures?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aminimal-edit-opd">Edit, Don&#x27;t Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Preserve successful student behavior with task reward. Compare teacher and old student only for errors, correcting less teacher-supported tokens. Full group advantage precedes split. Reference solution and full reply are teacher training inputs only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A misread geometry label can receive focused suppression without reworking a successful alternative response.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30231v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.30231-minimal-edit-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c91dbc6c4760e464">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:minimal-edit-opd" data-paper-title="Edit, Don&#x27;t Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-66ee5b0fc573399b">Compute ME-OPD group advantages before or after splitting successes and failures?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aminimal-edit-opd">Edit, Don&#x27;t Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use all K rewards before splitting. A success-only group has constant reward. Use frozen old student for strict-greater mask and divide by selected correction tokens across the minibatch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teacher and old student ties are not selected; do not remake mask from updated scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30231v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.30231-minimal-edit-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-66ee5b0fc573399b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:minimal-edit-opd" data-paper-title="Edit, Don&#x27;t Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-1965d1730d240a81">How do ME-OPD and Projected Distillation produce corrections differently?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aminimal-edit-opd">Edit, Don&#x27;t Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>ME-OPD teacher-forces and suppresses chosen original error tokens. Projected Distillation generates a verified revision and compares edited spans via DPO. Scoring existing tokens and producing paired text differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Only the latter needs a newly written answer aligned to the original.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30231v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.30231-minimal-edit-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1965d1730d240a81">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:minimal-edit-opd" data-paper-title="Edit, Don&#x27;t Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-minimal-edit-opd-97f1b5ed" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-622a1fc443b1a5c7">Why skip teacher correction for correct ME-OPD replies?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aminimal-edit-opd">Edit, Don&#x27;t Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Successful traces retain task reward without stylistic interference. Failures alone select original tokens the teacher supports less. The teacher scores existing responses instead of writing new ones.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not rewrite a valid alternative solution just because its style differs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30231v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.30231-minimal-edit-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-622a1fc443b1a5c7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cord" data-paper-title="CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1ebcba12aeca3711">Why project one gradient relative to a chosen protected gradient?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acord">CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Minimally change the conflicting other vector to preserve the selected objective. Swapping protection changes updates. Conflict-only and always differ; project after full-batch accumulation. This is pre-optimizer first-order geometry, not guaranteed finite AdamW descent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Task reward and imitation may push a parameter oppositely; changing which is protected changes what survives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29965v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.29965-cord/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1ebcba12aeca3711">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cord" data-paper-title="CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-096a6edd2e82c442">Why aggregate a full CORD optimizer batch before projecting once?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acord">CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Projection is nonlinear, so per-microbatch projection and summation usually differ. After fixed aggregation apply objective weight λ first. Skip projection if protected gradient is zero; λ=0 returns first objective direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Conflicts in two microbatches can cancel in the aggregate; early projection changes the result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29965v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.29965-cord/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-096a6edd2e82c442">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cord" data-paper-title="CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-05b2cde4b0ffd64b">How do CORD conflict-only and always-project variants differ?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acord">CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Conflict gating keeps helpful aligned components and projects only for negative dot product. Always projecting removes even helpful parallel components. The resulting direction is different; no finite adaptive-optimizer descent guarantee.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Aligned gradients add directly under conflict gating; always-project still removes a parallel component.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29965v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.29965-cord/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-05b2cde4b0ffd64b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cord" data-paper-title="CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-cord-0b4a5d25" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a09f25b1ef523765">Why does CORD select a protected objective first?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acord">CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Adding conflicting task and teacher gradients can cancel them. The protected direction states whose first-order progress must not be harmed; modify the other minimally. It is a tradeoff.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Protecting task reward versus teacher imitation defines different projections.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29965v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.29965-cord/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a09f25b1ef523765">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:aw0" data-paper-title="Agentic World Action Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<span id="paper-multimodal-models-aw0-c41ecc38" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b0c5a8e2785d041b">Why allow bidirectionality within AW-0 experts but enforce code→video→action across them?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Aaw0">Agentic World Action Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Bidirectionality organizes representations inside a modality; block causality preserves conditioning from plan to scene prediction to control. Code must not see later videos or actions, while action can use earlier code and predicted scenes. Full mutual visibility changes inference order and available information.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Generate a cup-grasp program, predict the scene, then output controls; do not give the planner future ground-truth actions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30136v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/2610.30136-aw0/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b0c5a8e2785d041b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:aw0" data-paper-title="Agentic World Action Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-09ecab1ee5f08245">Can flow targets and masked code diffusion use one noise and supervision mask?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Aaw0">Agentic World Action Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Video and action use continuous noising and velocity regression. Code uses an independent Bernoulli mask and loss only on masked program tokens. Action noise and code masking are not determined by video noise. Mixed video sampling also needs separate clipped and normalized importance weights.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Low video noise does not imply lightly masked code; one shared mask changes the paper&#x27;s independent sampling.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地收录与复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30136v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/2610.30136-aw0/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-09ecab1ee5f08245">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:aw0" data-paper-title="Agentic World Action Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-80ec646f7634554a">How do separate expert projections, normalization, and FFNs differ from fully shared transforms?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Aaw0">Agentic World Action Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate transforms serve code, video, and action while joint attention exchanges information at prescribed boundaries. They add parameters and interfaces, not guaranteed improvement. The paper combines bidirectional intra-expert and block-causal cross-expert attention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Discrete code and continuous actions can use separate FFNs and still interact, without being isolated or freely bidirectional.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30136v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/2610.30136-aw0/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-80ec646f7634554a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:aw0" data-paper-title="Agentic World Action Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-63a711c06d27630b">Why combine composable programs, future vision, and robot action in one AW-0 model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Aaw0">Agentic World Action Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Programs provide reusable steps, video anticipates scenes, and continuous actions control the robot. Three experts jointly link plan to physical consequences; generated code plans by default rather than being executed. Local work reviews evidence only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Generate “grasp then place,” forecast the scene, and produce controls without running arbitrary Python.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30136v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/2610.30136-aw0/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-63a711c06d27630b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:right-on-q" data-paper-title="Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-right-on-q-5ed3d308" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fbeed3269c200615">Why distill on the quantized student&#x27;s prefixes with per-candidate KL mixing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aright-on-q">Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Michigan, Ann Arbor</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Quantization changes visited states, so score the student&#x27;s own prefixes. Teacher/student probability ratios mix forward and reverse KL per candidate to treat over- and underestimation differently. Detach mixture weights and retain a residual mass bucket.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A correct number underweighted and a connective overweighted at one position need different coefficients, not ideal teacher prefixes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29378v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.29378-right-on-q/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fbeed3269c200615">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:right-on-q" data-paper-title="Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-68065f2c5d2ee242">Can OnQ renormalize only the union of teacher and student top-20?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aright-on-q">Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Michigan, Ann Arbor</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Keep a remainder bucket with student residual gradients and teacher smoothing. Truncation would erase tail differences. OPD updates latent weights and scales, with fixed zero point.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the union covers 90%, the remaining 10% stays a class.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29378v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.29378-right-on-q/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-68065f2c5d2ee242">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:right-on-q" data-paper-title="Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-dcd2b6d622a04412">How does candidate Dynamic KL differ from one fixed mixture per response?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aright-on-q">Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Michigan, Ann Arbor</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>At a prefix, some candidates are underweighted and others overweighted. α_v adapts to p_v/q_v per candidate and is detached to avoid optimizing the weight itself.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Increasing support for one candidate and suppressing another need not share a mixture.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29378v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.29378-right-on-q/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dcd2b6d622a04412">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:right-on-q" data-paper-title="Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-015ce5e8dc05282d">Why let the quantized student generate training prefixes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aright-on-q">Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Michigan, Ann Arbor</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Quantization changes visited reasoning states. Query the frozen teacher on the student&#x27;s actual states rather than fixed full-precision answers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the student takes a wrong turn, the teacher still scores the same prefix.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29378v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.29378-right-on-q/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-015ce5e8dc05282d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:moezip" data-paper-title="MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-moezip-03b66820" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-88eb9936565008cf">Why reserve routing anchors in a normal MoE KV compression budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amoezip">MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>KV deletions can change attention and subsequent routing. Propagate Fisher sensitivity from observed instruction positions through attention, reserve anchors, then fill with the base compressor. Sensitivity is a proxy, not a route-flip guarantee or permission to read gold.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An older low-attention token can still affect expert choice and merit retention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30206v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.30206-moezip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-88eb9936565008cf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:moezip" data-paper-title="MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-86fa47a3c2433cb6">Can the base compressor select anchors again when filling budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amoezip">MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Exclude already selected anchors and fill with distinct positions. Gather real KV in original temporal order. Use prefill instruction only, never future gold diagnostics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With 64 slots and 16 anchors, add 48 distinct non-anchor positions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30206v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.30206-moezip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-86fa47a3c2433cb6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:moezip" data-paper-title="MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e1475de3e0254894">Is Fisher trace an exact top-k router flip criterion?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amoezip">MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It averages distribution curvature over directions and omits the router-to-hidden Jacobian. High trace does not imply a flip.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal trace at two positions can yield different routing changes under different perturbation directions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30206v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.30206-moezip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e1475de3e0254894">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:moezip" data-paper-title="MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ed92465526edc741">Why connect KV error to MoE routing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amoezip">MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Eviction perturbs attention outputs seen by the router. Attention quality alone can miss route-sensitive positions, so estimate anchors from observed instruction gates and attention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A nonmaximal KV can move a token across an expert boundary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30206v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.30206-moezip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ed92465526edc741">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-multicorrect" data-paper-title="When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/candidate-invariance">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/candidate-invariance/">Structured Decisions / Candidate Invariance: Order, Competitors, and Calibration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f127e2b1238febde">Why can exact-set recovery fail even when every correct option outranks distractors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-multicorrect">When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One correct choice can absorb most listwise mass, leaving another below threshold or the uniform baseline. Correct ranking differs from exact-set recovery, and shares are not independent probabilities. Fit deployment thresholds on validation only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two correct options rank first and second, but uneven shares cause thresholding to keep only one. A top-one hit misses the incomplete set.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 方法与本地协议. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29217v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.29217-jev-multicorrect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f127e2b1238febde">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-multicorrect" data-paper-title="When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/candidate-invariance">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/candidate-invariance/">Structured Decisions / Candidate Invariance: Order, Competitors, and Calibration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-8028e759e705e072">May the threshold be reselected from the test exact-set curve?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-multicorrect">When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Deployment selects thresholds on a validation grid and freezes them for test. A same-data threshold curve is retrospective. The predictor does not see the correct set.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Picking the best point after seeing test is a hindsight upper bound, not unseen-data performance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 方法与本地协议. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29217v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.29217-jev-multicorrect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8028e759e705e072">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-multicorrect" data-paper-title="When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/candidate-invariance">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/candidate-invariance/">Structured Decisions / Candidate Invariance: Order, Competitors, and Calibration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-fa4dc8b32ee9fc84">Why calibrate listwise shares differently from independent binary probabilities?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-multicorrect">When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Listwise shares depend on other options and sum to one; multiple binary probabilities may be simultaneously high. One threshold or calibration meaning confuses competition with correctness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Adding another correct option can reduce one item&#x27;s listwise share without reducing its binary probability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 方法与本地协议. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29217v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.29217-jev-multicorrect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fa4dc8b32ee9fc84">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-multicorrect" data-paper-title="When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/candidate-invariance">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/candidate-invariance/">Structured Decisions / Candidate Invariance: Order, Competitors, and Calibration</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-jev-multicorrect-937628d2" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b551d438465d2f51">Does a multicorrect task require one answer or the entire correct set?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-multicorrect">When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Recover all correct candidates; there may be more than one. One correct choice can miss others; choosing everything can include distractors. Interpret ranking, thresholding and exact-set metrics using a set rather than a winner.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Correct {A,B} is not recovered by {A} or {A,B,C}.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 方法与本地协议. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29217v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.29217-jev-multicorrect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b551d438465d2f51">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:detector-scope" data-paper-title="Building Auditable AI Text Detectors with Sparse Autoencoders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-detector-scope-a45f37d9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-cf2ae2f87e6ebcb4">Why is zeroing a DetectorScope concept exact in logit space but not equivalent to editing text?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adetector-scope">Building Auditable AI Text Detectors with Sparse Autoencoders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Pennsylvania</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sparse pooled features feed a linear head, so each weight times activation is an exact contribution. Text edits can change several features and contexts. Automatic descriptions are imperfect; local head excludes the full SAE/explanation pipeline.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Zero one feature to verify its score change; deleting a word can alter several concepts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
