<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>MLP input outputs and MLP output inputs represent corresponding hidden channels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21808">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.21808-roleq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7153f53110d125bc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:remote-kv-tiers" data-paper-title="When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-remote-kv-tiers-30f3c03e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a402f43cbcb16963">Why can a remote KV hit be slower than re-prefill?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aremote-kv-tiers">When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Multiverse Computing</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fetch has fixed request latency and volume-dependent transfer; recompute depends on prefill throughput. Break-even depends on length and bandwidth, and asynchronous shards must avoid head-of-line blocking. Hit rate is not latency. No local remote implementation or GPU results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A short hit can spend more time opening the connection than local recompute takes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21500">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.21500-remote-kv-tiers/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a402f43cbcb16963">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:remote-kv-tiers" data-paper-title="When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-4f0347ac1da13fce">Why use per-PCP-rank remote instances and async loading?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aremote-kv-tiers">When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Multiverse Computing</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MLA cache is sharded by rank; independent instances and async loads reduce head-of-line blocking. Validation needs the multi-node service and workload, not a single A100/A30 fixture.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A large request on one rank should not hold a small load on another.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 成本判断. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21500">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.21500-remote-kv-tiers/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4f0347ac1da13fce">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:remote-kv-tiers" data-paper-title="When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b9793c53dde08a50">Does B&gt;sR with fixed T0 guarantee fetch is faster at every length?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aremote-kv-tiers">When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Multiverse Computing</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It gives asymptotic bandwidth advantage. Compare T0+sn/B against n/R for finite requests; fixed cost can dominate short ones.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Fast per-token transfer does not erase first-packet latency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21500">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.21500-remote-kv-tiers/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b9793c53dde08a50">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:remote-kv-tiers" data-paper-title="When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-3e527c1e282435f7">Why analyze fetch versus re-prefill break-even first?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aremote-kv-tiers">When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Multiverse Computing</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Remote hits pay request and transfer costs; GPU recompute can be fast. Compare both paths by length and bandwidth, not only hit rate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Fetching a short cached prefix can be slower than recreating KV.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21500">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.21500-remote-kv-tiers/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3e527c1e282435f7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:prism-1" data-paper-title="Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/candidate-invariance">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/candidate-invariance/">Structured Decisions / Candidate Invariance: Order, Competitors, and Calibration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f8589f6603d77f11">Why combine isolated attention and equal starting positions in Prism-1?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aprism-1">Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The score may depend only on shared state, question and its own option. Isolation prevents cross-reading; equal positions remove order effects. Joint softmax may change the denominator but should preserve old odds. This does not suit cross-option choices such as &#x27;none of the above&#x27; or prevent injection in shared state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A new tool can win and lower old shares but insertion position alone should not swap the old tools&#x27; ranking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22066">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22066-prism-1/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f8589f6603d77f11">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:prism-1" data-paper-title="Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/candidate-invariance">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/candidate-invariance/">Structured Decisions / Candidate Invariance: Order, Competitors, and Calibration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-19cf1c2f49d33384">Can Prism-1 option blocks read each other or start at different positions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aprism-1">Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Each reads shared context and attends causally within its own block; all start at the same position. Otherwise independent scoring breaks. This isolation does not block injection in shared context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Inserting a longer option must not shift later options&#x27; position IDs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22066">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22066-prism-1/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-19cf1c2f49d33384">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:prism-1" data-paper-title="Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/candidate-invariance">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/candidate-invariance/">Structured Decisions / Candidate Invariance: Order, Competitors, and Calibration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-48222e52dee00817">Why doesn&#x27;t Prism-1&#x27;s option independence suit &#x27;none of the above&#x27;?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aprism-1">Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent scores see shared state, question and the option itself. &#x27;None of the above&#x27; depends on the validity of other options and needs interaction, so imposing the same Luce constraint is inappropriate. This is a structural boundary, not a routine training error.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Adding a correct answer should invalidate &#x27;none of the above&#x27;, which an isolated option cannot determine.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22066">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22066-prism-1/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-48222e52dee00817">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:prism-1" data-paper-title="Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/candidate-invariance">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/candidate-invariance/">Structured Decisions / Candidate Invariance: Order, Competitors, and Calibration</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-prism-1-45b3ae20" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-746ef6fbeaffa986">Must Prism-1&#x27;s original probabilities stay numerically unchanged after a third option?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aprism-1">Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The denominator can increase and both shares can fall. Preserve their relative odds and order; the new option may win. The consistency constraint does not require ignoring additions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Original 2:1 odds can become probabilities 0.4 and 0.2 after adding C, still 2:1.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22066">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22066-prism-1/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-746ef6fbeaffa986">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:novelty-patching" data-paper-title="Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-novelty-patching-3454dd1e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b724f96d1642e069">Why use matching length offline but a two-byte lookup online?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Anovelty-patching">Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent Researcher, Chile</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Longer recent matches define offline novelty labels. Deployment uses a prefix-indexed table and low-count fallback instead of reading a future span. Offline labels are not available when deciding a boundary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Train with full template matches, then estimate from the two already generated bytes online.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22100">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22100-novelty-patching/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b724f96d1642e069">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:novelty-patching" data-paper-title="Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">

<h2 id="qa-a1021385673b04f4">How does Novelty Patching handle rare byte pairs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Anovelty-patching">Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent Researcher, Chile</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Below 20 observations, back off to one-byte means, then the global mean. Calibrate τ on training bytes and reset history at document boundaries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One observed match should not determine online boundaries for a rare pair.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22100">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22100-novelty-patching/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a1021385673b04f4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:novelty-patching" data-paper-title="Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-320494967794fa3e">How does a two-byte table differ from recomputing future match length online?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Anovelty-patching">Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent Researcher, Chile</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Future match lengths are offline labels. Deployment uses already generated bytes and a frozen threshold; looking past the current position leaks future information.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not inspect whether the next 16 unseen bytes occurred before generating them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22100">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22100-novelty-patching/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-320494967794fa3e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:novelty-patching" data-paper-title="Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d5a318b9dcdf5183">Why use recent repetition to choose byte patches?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Anovelty-patching">Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent Researcher, Chile</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Byte patches reduce global calls. Recent match length captures repeatability, and a cheap two-byte predictor estimates novelty instead of relying only on entropy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A recently seen span may be reusable, whereas a novel span may need finer boundaries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22100">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22100-novelty-patching/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d5a318b9dcdf5183">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>

<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-01050f98565ed331">Why doesn&#x27;t lower Muon loss at equal steps prove superiority at equal compute or tuning cost?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amuon-paired-budget">When Does Muon Actually Win? A Paired Data-, Time-, and Tuning-Budget Benchmark</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文未列一作机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Step latency, throughput, and tuning can differ. Pair initialization, data order, and candidates; compare processed data, elapsed training time, and fixed tuning budget separately. Freeze selection before test.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Twice-slower steps can win at 100 steps but lose at ten minutes; retuning for time confounds the comparison.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<h2 id="qa-d0920c3cb6a09d74">Why sample the same seed indices in paired bootstrap?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amuon-paired-budget">When Does Muon Actually Win? A Paired Data-, Time-, and Tuning-Budget Benchmark</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文未列一作机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Paired trajectories share initialization and data order. Mismatching seeds loses correlation. Integrate AUC over common measurement support and freeze validation-selected settings for all budget axes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Sample seed 42 for both optimizers, not 42 for one and 44 for the other.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 结果与独立对照. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<h2 id="qa-4682ad997eed076f">Why isn&#x27;t random-access regret on a fixed candidate pool prospective adaptive HPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amuon-paired-budget">When Does Muon Actually Win? A Paired Data-, Time-, and Tuning-Budget Benchmark</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文未列一作机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It studies random order within precomputed candidates. Adaptive HPO uses prior results to propose or choose new trials, with different information and time costs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Randomly inspect 23 existing settings versus inventing a 24th from feedback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<h2 id="qa-9a0c27dfaf4180bd">Why report data, elapsed time, and tuning costs separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amuon-paired-budget">When Does Muon Actually Win? A Paired Data-, Time-, and Tuning-Budget Benchmark</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文未列一作机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Per-step and per-second quality and the cost of finding parameters differ. Equal-data gains need not hold at equal time or search budget.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Lower loss for equal tokens can still lose after one hour if steps are slower.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mjev-spatial" data-paper-title="MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/typed-readout">

<h2 id="qa-8616ff0ec0b4fbe8">Why read options using final attention Q/K rather than a separate classifier head?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amjev-spatial">MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未注明（论文未列一作机构；公开发布主体为 MindLab）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use the decision marker as query and candidate end markers as keys in the backbone&#x27;s own projections. This shares a readout for options, numeric buckets and regions. Position encoding and grouped-query mapping matter. Points still need staged selection and crops from the original image; classification alone does not ensure spatial precision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Select a coarse region, then crop it from the original image. Repeatedly cropping the last resized image changes coordinates and detail.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22276">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22276-mjev-spatial/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8616ff0ec0b4fbe8">Question link</a></p>

<h2 id="qa-91604612ac3aa076">Why average multistage spatial losses within each original question first?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amjev-spatial">MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未注明（论文未列一作机构；公开发布主体为 MindLab）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Otherwise questions with more refinement stages receive more weight. Average stage cross-entropies per question, then average questions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Three localization choices should not automatically count three times as much as one choice.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<h2 id="qa-00f044551c2eb364">How does two-stage counting differ from one class per integer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amjev-spatial">MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未注明（论文未列一作机构；公开发布主体为 MindLab）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Two smaller candidate sets compose the result as 32a₁+a₂, covering 0–1023. A large head directly scores each integer. Reusing finite-choice readout is useful, but first-stage errors affect the result; matching output spaces do not imply equivalent training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: a₁=2 and a₂=3 represent 67, not the sum of two independent counts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<h2 id="qa-ef409a28d227d518">How does MJev-Spatial express a 2D point as classification?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amjev-spatial">MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未注明（论文未列一作机构；公开发布主体为 MindLab）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Treat image regions as candidates and select progressively finer regions. Quantities such as counts also use buckets or staged readout. The output is typed choice, not free-form coordinate parsing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Pick the upper-right region, then one cell in its next 3×3 grid.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mirror-moe" data-paper-title="Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">

<span id="paper-foundation-models-mirror-moe-43695dbb" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2750f3a34fee37eb">Should MirrorMoE use mixed mirror probabilities to weight outputs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amirror-moe">Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ETH Zurich</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Mix forward and negated-logit distributions for exploratory selection only, annealing back to standard routing. Selected outputs retain original probabilities. Track actual dispatch separately; mixing or renormalizing output weights changes the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A low-probability expert can run for exposure without receiving a larger output coefficient.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22353">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22353-mirror-moe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2750f3a34fee37eb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mirror-moe" data-paper-title="Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-dde9c8ec3f02b8fe">Which probabilities and frequencies enter MirrorMoE&#x27;s load term?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amirror-moe">Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ETH Zurich</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use actual dispatch frequencies and original ξ, not mixed p. Aggregate outputs with original weights and Z=1 without renormalizing selected experts. Selection, load, and aggregation differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Mirror probability can change whether an expert runs, but not its original output weight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mirror-moe" data-paper-title="Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ccb0ea3c337d2306">How does mirror selection differ from arbitrary router noise?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amirror-moe">Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ETH Zurich</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Apply softmax to negated logits and mix with original probabilities using an annealing coefficient. Arbitrary noise does not reproduce its distribution or endpoint.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>At ρ=0, selection returns to ordinary top-k.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22353">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22353-mirror-moe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ccb0ea3c337d2306">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mirror-moe" data-paper-title="Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cd36506392655d60">Why select near-boundary experts early?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amirror-moe">Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ETH Zurich</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Dominant shared experts and many fine-grained combinations can obscure alternatives. Mirror routing temporarily suppresses some usual winners to train other combinations, then anneals back.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Avoid always giving the same winners every early token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22353">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22353-mirror-moe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cd36506392655d60">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lct" data-paper-title="LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-lct-f385814a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-74b7ca86cd3c25c0">Why retain rare exponents and overflow rather than drop them in LCT?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alct">LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Bit-exact recovery requires escape codes with raw rare exponents and raw overflow after stream exhaustion. Sign/fraction remain separate and a fixed codebook avoids relearning. This is lossless compression, not quantization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A rare exponent uses escape plus eight original bits; overflow stays raw rather than becoming zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22179">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22179-lct/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-74b7ca86cd3c25c0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lct" data-paper-title="LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-549e6e120af7ef04">Why compare raw bits in LCT round trips?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alct">LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Preserve signed zeros, subnormals, infinities, and NaN payloads. Numeric equality can miss these. Test all exponents, centers, and overflow paths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>+0 and −0 compare equal numerically but have different bits.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与运行. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22179">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22179-lct/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-549e6e120af7ef04">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lct" data-paper-title="LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-95b48be5b7b4f2f3">How does bounded exponent coding differ from zlib on a tensor?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alct">LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>LCT specifies a fixed table, length cap, escapes, stream budget, and raw overflow tail. General compression does not provide that layout. Count codebooks and metadata in total bytes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Smaller payload may still produce larger total output after metadata.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 结果与独立对照. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22179">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22179-lct/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-95b48be5b7b4f2f3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lct" data-paper-title="LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8f32908d4070ebe7">Why store exponents separately from sign and mantissa?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alct">LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Exponents are often concentrated and compressible. Preserve sign/fraction verbatim, use a fixed bounded code, and handle runtime center shifts without losing bits.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Shared exponent patterns can compress while fraction bits remain intact.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22179">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22179-lct/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8f32908d4070ebe7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:langdit" data-paper-title="Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-langdit-ba73a77f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-999cd9aaee6ecf4c">Why detach only the explicit codebook shortcut, not the entire noisy input?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alangdit">Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dots Studio, Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Both paths share a codebook. Detaching shortcut gradient still lets the codebook learn through noisy input; detaching everything breaks it. Training uses entropy-gated self-conditioning while inference uses unweighted posterior mean.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Freeze one shortcut multiplication, not the same table&#x27;s input construction path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22330">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22330-langdit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-999cd9aaee6ecf4c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:langdit" data-paper-title="Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a19870609b8abb9b">Why initialize calibration aψ to one and constrain it to [0.5,2]?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alangdit">Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dots Studio, Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One preserves initial shortcut scale. Bounded exponential calibration avoids extreme amplification or suppression, with 5000 warmup steps. Verify ranges and gradient paths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Large calibration outputs must not make the shortcut dominate the vocabulary head.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22330">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22330-langdit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a19870609b8abb9b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:langdit" data-paper-title="Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-11b5da4d78a813dc">Should training entropy gating also weight inference posterior means?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alangdit">Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dots Studio, Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Training bootstrap confidence-attenuates and detaches feedback. Inference uses unweighted pC and no extra bootstrap. Training heuristics are not posterior guarantees.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not discount inference probability mass a second time because training suppressed low-confidence feedback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22330">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22330-langdit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-11b5da4d78a813dc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:langdit" data-paper-title="Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e37db734cbc08d6b">Why add a likelihood shortcut besides noisy embeddings?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alangdit">Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dots Studio, Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Codebook-to-noisy-state relations supplement token posterior with noise-conditioned backbone and bounded calibration. This is more than a normal head and needs correct gradients and self-conditioning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>At low noise, nearby codebook vectors help identify the underlying token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22330">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22330-langdit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e37db734cbc08d6b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lamp" data-paper-title="LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-lamp-52f612c4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d272f3c9d6e7debd">Why mix LAMP&#x27;s layer predictions in class-score space rather than concatenate features?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alamp">LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Taizhou Institute of Science and Technology, Nanjing University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different layers have different widths and similarity geometry. Concatenation would introduce projection assumptions. Each LAMP branch fits support-set residuals relative to CLIP, then mixes scores in common class space. If text prototypes change, the residuals must change as well.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A shallow texture branch and a deeper semantic branch each score cat versus dog before their scores are combined.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22182">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22182-lamp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d272f3c9d6e7debd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lamp" data-paper-title="LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-35cf268cc640f6cd">Why must LAMP-F update the cached response when text prototypes change?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alamp">LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Taizhou Institute of Science and Technology, Nanjing University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Updating prototypes changes both query priors and support residuals. The cached linear response represents how the kernel solution changes and allows exact updates without a complete solve. Updating just the query prior omits a term. Kernel statistics and mixture weights remain frozen.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Moving the prototype toward cat images raises the prior for support cats, so their residual should shrink. Keeping the old correction double counts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 代码映射与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22182">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22182-lamp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-35cf268cc640f6cd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lamp" data-paper-title="LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7084f5f48e922c1a">How does a support-bank regional kernel differ from including evaluation queries in its centering statistics?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alamp">LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Taizhou Institute of Science and Technology, Nanjing University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Both m(x) and b use the support set as the reference; queries are scored against the fixed reference. Adding test queries would make an individual result depend on the evaluation batch. Test labels must not select mixing weights.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With fixed support, query A uses the same calibration alone or with query B; B does not redefine the support mean.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22182">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22182-lamp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7084f5f48e922c1a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lamp" data-paper-title="LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f533d9685d57ba72">Relative to what does LAMP compute its label residuals?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alamp">LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Taizhou Institute of Science and Technology, Nanjing University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Subtract the original CLIP text-prototype scores from true support labels. Each layer&#x27;s kernel predictor corrects the prior rather than relearning all classes. If prototypes change, the residual must follow or the correction no longer matches its target.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If a cat support image has a low CLIP cat score, the kernel branch learns the difference rather than retraining the vision encoder.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22182">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.22182-lamp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f533d9685d57ba72">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hardware-diversity" data-paper-title="Architecting for Hardware Diversity: Meta&#x27;s End-to-End Co-Design for High-Performance AI Training on AMD GPUs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-hardware-diversity-2c171dec" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1a1c64a8f0514de8">Why doesn&#x27;t CUDA-to-HIP compatibility establish performance portability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahardware-diversity">Architecting for Hardware Diversity: Meta&#x27;s End-to-End Co-Design for High-Performance AI Training on AMD GPUs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Running code does not align compute units, memory hierarchy, tiles, and parallelism. The work co-designs model, memory, parallel strategy, and kernels and estimates tail stalls. Hardware constants and optima vary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A tile filling one GPU&#x27;s compute units can be limited by shared memory or tail imbalance on another.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<h2 id="qa-752b38d08848c516">Can one A100 or A30 reproduce the MI350X/B200 production system?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahardware-diversity">Architecting for Hardware Diversity: Meta&#x27;s End-to-End Co-Design for High-Performance AI Training on AMD GPUs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The original uses matching clusters and private workloads. This is a literature and cost review, not a reproduction. A public operator would need its own hardware and acceptance protocol.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A small A100 GEMM cannot verify another cluster&#x27;s end-to-end training throughput.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The analytical model estimates compute, hierarchical memory, pipelines, and idle tail work. End-to-end results include actual workload and system effects. Neither constants nor local optima transfer automatically.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A faster GEMM tile may be offset by synchronization or other stages.</p>
