<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/typed-readout/">Structured Decisions / Typed Readout: From Generated Sentences to Candidate Distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ec82c7d79648130a">Why do cached candidates and options in the request not imply full candidate interaction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ametaencoder">MetaEncoder: Exploring the Limit of Bi-Encoders for Multimodal System One Decision Making with Natural Language Interface</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Shared dual towers independently encode request and candidate and match normalized last-token vectors. A candidate can be cached because it doesn&#x27;t depend on the request. Training partly drops closed-set options to discourage surface matching. Cross-reasoning remains limited, and cache requires identical model, prompt and candidate content.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Pre-encode tools and encode each request online. A changed tool definition invalidates its old vector.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与原文效果. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11316">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.11316-metaencoder/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ec82c7d79648130a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:metaencoder" data-paper-title="MetaEncoder: Exploring the Limit of Bi-Encoders for Multimodal System One Decision Making with Natural Language Interface" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/typed-readout">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/typed-readout/">Structured Decisions / Typed Readout: From Generated Sentences to Candidate Distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-69f111929cadd443">Why deduplicate open-retrieval negatives over the full MetaEncoder batch?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ametaencoder">MetaEncoder: Exploring the Limit of Bi-Encoders for Multimodal System One Decision Making with Natural Language Interface</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Open retrieval uses global batch candidates. Treating duplicates as independent negatives changes training mass. The specified direction is request-to-candidate; adding a reverse term changes the objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: The same tool appearing twice should not become two competing negatives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与原文效果. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11316">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.11316-metaencoder/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-69f111929cadd443">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:metaencoder" data-paper-title="MetaEncoder: Exploring the Limit of Bi-Encoders for Multimodal System One Decision Making with Natural Language Interface" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/typed-readout">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/typed-readout/">Structured Decisions / Typed Readout: From Generated Sentences to Candidate Distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-54db6525464abcdb">What does MetaEncoder&#x27;s dual encoder sacrifice relative to joint deep interaction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ametaencoder">MetaEncoder: Exploring the Limit of Bi-Encoders for Multimodal System One Decision Making with Natural Language Interface</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate encoding enables caching and large retrieval, but limits fine-grained pairwise reasoning. Including options in a closed-set request adds context without turning the candidate tower into an arbitrary cross-encoder.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Detecting a subtle contradiction between long proofs can be harder with fixed vectors than joint reading.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与原文效果. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11316">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.11316-metaencoder/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-54db6525464abcdb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:metaencoder" data-paper-title="MetaEncoder: Exploring the Limit of Bi-Encoders for Multimodal System One Decision Making with Natural Language Interface" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/typed-readout">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/typed-readout/">Structured Decisions / Typed Readout: From Generated Sentences to Candidate Distributions</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-metaencoder-e65c35d0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-29b505285e015e9f">How does MetaEncoder use one representation for closed choices and open retrieval?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ametaencoder">MetaEncoder: Exploring the Limit of Bi-Encoders for Multimodal System One Decision Making with Natural Language Interface</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Encode requests and candidates separately with a shared encoder, normalize their final-token embeddings and compare similarity. Closed choice uses supplied options; open retrieval searches a larger bank. Candidate scope and training negatives differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: One request vector can choose among three tools or search a full description index.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与原文效果. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11316">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.11316-metaencoder/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-29b505285e015e9f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lewam" data-paper-title="LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-lewam-7895d3a3" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-64e4dca51fbd2f0a">Why prevent LeWAM&#x27;s noisy-action branch from seeing clean actions indirectly?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alewam">LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Clean actions supervise future dynamics for state queries but are unavailable to the deployed action policy. Indirect access through shared attention would let the noisy branch copy targets. Separate parameters alone do not prevent leakage; enforce visibility across layers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A provided “push left” label can train prediction but must not be read by the action generator and counted as a decision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12818">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2610.12818-lewam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-64e4dca51fbd2f0a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lewam" data-paper-title="LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c23e22f887512a09">Why refine actions with a proximity penalty but select by the original goal cost?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alewam">LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Adam penalizes deviations from the sampled plan to constrain refinement. Final selection compares unpenalized goal cost, retaining original samples in case refinement worsens them. Planning updates actions, not model weights, and does not guarantee real success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A refined action that deviates more can still win if it reaches the predicted goal more closely; keep the original if refinement fails.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 数据协议、结果与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12818">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2610.12818-lewam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c23e22f887512a09">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lewam" data-paper-title="LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7d7c630753bca65d">How does action flow differ from wide Gaussian random search?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alewam">LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Flow matching learns velocities from noise to action data, proposing candidates nearer the learned distribution before planning in latent dynamics. Wide Gaussian search relies on unstructured coverage. Actual task advantage requires controlled validation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A learned proposal might favor plausible pushes along a table instead of many trajectories through it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12818">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2610.12818-lewam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7d7c630753bca65d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lewam" data-paper-title="LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/world-state-actions/">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1a6959f95b4f9227">Why link predicting consequences with producing usable actions in LeWAM training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alewam">LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A world model can predict an action&#x27;s future without finding goal-reaching actions efficiently. A separate policy may not shape visual representations. Joint state, dynamics, and stochastic action learning shares signals, but does not remove isolation or execution requirements.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Knowing a push moves an object is not the same as deciding which direction and distance to push.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12818">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2610.12818-lewam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1a6959f95b4f9227">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-capability" data-paper-title="Specialized Decision Models vs. General-Purpose LLMs: Benchmarking Jev Across Knowledge, Reasoning, and Multilingual Tasks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/adaptive-decisions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/adaptive-decisions/">Structured Decisions / Decisions on Demand: Selective Reasoning, Transfer, and Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-bb0935a34d3a1a2c">Why not combine vendor and local Jev capability numbers into one leaderboard?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-capability">Specialized Decision Models vs. General-Purpose LLMs: Benchmarking Jev Across Knowledge, Reasoning, and Multilingual Tasks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dalian Maritime University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different prompts, backends and data protocols confound capability. Fix public prompts, candidates and one decision; join labels only in scoring, recording language and missing coverage. This is an audit, not training, and one task class cannot represent all reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Vendor math under another prompt and local knowledge under a fixed interface can be listed separately, not used to declare an overall winner.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 数据与评测契约. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.11978-jev-capability/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bb0935a34d3a1a2c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-capability" data-paper-title="Specialized Decision Models vs. General-Purpose LLMs: Benchmarking Jev Across Knowledge, Reasoning, and Multilingual Tasks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/adaptive-decisions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/adaptive-decisions/">Structured Decisions / Decisions on Demand: Selective Reasoning, Transfer, and Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7390391cb4bb71f5">Why submit question and candidates once in the Jev capability evaluation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-capability">Specialized Decision Models vs. General-Purpose LLMs: Benchmarking Jev Across Knowledge, Reasoning, and Multilingual Tasks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dalian Maritime University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One public decision prevents answer leakage or retry assistance. The scorer reads gold only afterward. Record vendor protocols separately and disclose missing items rather than silently removing them from the denominator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Strip the answer field before calling the predictor; score through a separate stage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 数据与评测契约. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.11978-jev-capability/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7390391cb4bb71f5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-capability" data-paper-title="Specialized Decision Models vs. General-Purpose LLMs: Benchmarking Jev Across Knowledge, Reasoning, and Multilingual Tasks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/adaptive-decisions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/adaptive-decisions/">Structured Decisions / Decisions on Demand: Selective Reasoning, Transfer, and Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-821d51d1732bfd58">Do strong knowledge and weak math scores prove the model cannot reason?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-capability">Specialized Decision Models vs. General-Purpose LLMs: Benchmarking Jev Across Knowledge, Reasoning, and Multilingual Tasks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dalian Maritime University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Evidence is limited to tested tasks, prompts and choice interface, possibly with language/coverage effects. Report measured tasks and gaps separately instead of generalizing to every setting.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Failure on one arithmetic format does not establish failure in tool planning or all mathematics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 数据与评测契约. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.11978-jev-capability/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-821d51d1732bfd58">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:jev-capability" data-paper-title="Specialized Decision Models vs. General-Purpose LLMs: Benchmarking Jev Across Knowledge, Reasoning, and Multilingual Tasks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="system-one" data-topic="system-one/adaptive-decisions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/system-one/adaptive-decisions/">Structured Decisions / Decisions on Demand: Selective Reasoning, Transfer, and Feedback</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-jev-capability-899cdbd2" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-2a74c52e1db4ea30">Why is the Jev capability paper an evaluation rather than a new architecture?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ajev-capability">Specialized Decision Models vs. General-Purpose LLMs: Benchmarking Jev Across Knowledge, Reasoning, and Multilingual Tasks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dalian Maritime University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It tests knowledge, reasoning and multilingual behavior under finite candidates. The contribution is protocol and capability boundaries, not a new training objective. An evaluator neither implements nor improves the model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Converting public questions to four choices and scoring them measures performance; it is not a reasoning module.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 数据与评测契约. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../system-one/2610.11978-jev-capability/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2a74c52e1db4ea30">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:elastic-expert-routing" data-paper-title="Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-elastic-expert-routing-bd240699" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fd11a9699c42f50d">How does elastic routing preserve expected compute with a random expert count?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aelastic-expert-routing">Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory / Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A legal symmetric support centered at k balances more and fewer experts, keeping expectation k. Boundary experts get real sparse exposure. Deployment fixes k; training load counts actual dispatch, not fixed row length.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal probabilities for one, two, or three experts average two, but selecting three really costs more than one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.11575-elastic-expert-routing/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fd11a9699c42f50d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:elastic-expert-routing" data-paper-title="Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-2faf7156fa76811e">Why not truncate one side of the discrete Gaussian arbitrarily?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aelastic-expert-routing">Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory / Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Keep support symmetric around k and legal to preserve E[r]=k. Execute only selected experts, count actual loads, and fix k at inference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Near the upper limit, deleting only the high side lowers mean budget.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.11575-elastic-expert-routing/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2faf7156fa76811e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:elastic-expert-routing" data-paper-title="Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0980348af90cb9c9">How does elastic budget perturbation differ from raising fixed k?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aelastic-expert-routing">Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory / Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raising k always spends more. Symmetric perturbation preserves expected k while changing exposure. Match parameters, initialization, and average dispatch before comparing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal chances of two and four experts average three, not four every time.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.11575-elastic-expert-routing/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0980348af90cb9c9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:elastic-expert-routing" data-paper-title="Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-982dc49332289795">What is the fixed top-k exposure problem?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aelastic-expert-routing">Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory / Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Experts just below rank k rarely receive the actual token computation and training. Elastic budgets give near-boundary experts chances before fixed-k deployment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>At k=2, a frequently third-ranked expert can be useful but rarely trained on those tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.11575-elastic-expert-routing/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-982dc49332289795">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:data-space-iteration" data-paper-title="Few-Step Generation via Data-Space Iteration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-data-space-iteration-cef25f24" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-039b91ebbdf6cbe4">Why refine with the same noise rather than interpreting iteration index as flow time?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adata-space-iteration">Few-Step Generation via Data-Space Iteration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The shared generator repeatedly improves one data-space prediction from fixed original noise. DMD uses frozen real teacher and fake distribution model. Earlier refinements are detached and only the current one trains; it is not real-image regression. Local tiny runs do not replace paper metrics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Refine outline then detail from the same noise; changing noise or time semantics changes the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12102">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.12102-data-space-iteration/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-039b91ebbdf6cbe4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:data-space-iteration" data-paper-title="Few-Step Generation via Data-Space Iteration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-718c6f2b28293a39">How isolate prefix, fake model, and generator gradients?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adata-space-iteration">Few-Step Generation via Data-Space Iteration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Roll out prefix without a graph and train the final refinement. Train fake on detached samples; freeze teacher/fake gradients during generator updates and detach the direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Updating step four does not backpropagate through the first three steps or teacher.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12102">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.12102-data-space-iteration/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-718c6f2b28293a39">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:data-space-iteration" data-paper-title="Few-Step Generation via Data-Space Iteration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e76cd9b0d0ef4e4b">Is direct real-image regression equivalent to DMD?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adata-space-iteration">Few-Step Generation via Data-Space Iteration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. DMD uses a frozen real teacher and a fake model fitted to generated data to supply a distribution-matching direction. Per-step paired image regression replaces it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A teacher-minus-fake direction on a generated sample is not assigning a fixed real image to noise.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12102">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.12102-data-space-iteration/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e76cd9b0d0ef4e4b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:data-space-iteration" data-paper-title="Few-Step Generation via Data-Space Iteration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-48133a6bbe3428ba">What changes across Data-Space Iteration refinements?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adata-space-iteration">Few-Step Generation via Data-Space Iteration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A shared network updates data predictions from fixed noise. Iteration counts refinement, not the separate DMD noising time τ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Refinement three is another prediction update, not diffusion time three.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12102">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.12102-data-space-iteration/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-48133a6bbe3428ba">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cots" data-paper-title="CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-cots-9dd74b8e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-54d3e8b20e547876">How does CoTS preserve the sampled discrete trajectory under soft mixing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acots">CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaomi AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Top-two competition sets the mixing fraction, capped at half, so the sampled embedding remains at least half even outside the soft set. End-of-reasoning disables soft mixing permanently; format guards can affect one step.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Probabilities 0.6 and 0.4 give base mix 0.4 and keep 0.6 discrete; a larger gap weakens mixing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20642">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.20642-cots/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-54d3e8b20e547876">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cots" data-paper-title="CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-70ae8db465d64ac8">Can soft mixing restart after the end-of-reasoning marker?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acots">CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaomi AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Per-example phase-lock is irreversible starting at the step emitting &lt;/think&gt;. One-step format protection differs. Keep the discrete anchor even when it falls outside top-k.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Later close probabilities do not reopen mixing after a sample finishes reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20642">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.20642-cots/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-70ae8db465d64ac8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cots" data-paper-title="CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ecbeb97765865850">How does CoTS differ from averaging top-k embeddings?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acots">CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaomi AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Form a probability-weighted soft vector and mix it with the discrete anchor using top-two-dependent α. An unweighted mean ignores probabilities and anchoring; phase-lock controls eligibility.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>0.9/0.1 and 0.5/0.5 distributions should not produce the same uniform representation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20642">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.20642-cots/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ecbeb97765865850">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cots" data-paper-title="CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-9f4fbec4454ef178">Why keep the sampled token rather than replace it with a soft token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acots">CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaomi AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Soft embeddings express alternatives but may drift from the sampled trajectory. The discrete anchor keeps at least half the weight while top-two competition controls the remainder.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Close candidates raise soft mixing without removing the sampled token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20642">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.20642-cots/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9f4fbec4454ef178">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:adamw4bit" data-paper-title="Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-adamw4bit-715c8ec7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c8a13b370455cc00">Why control second-moment rounding in preconditioner space in 4-bit AdamW?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadamw4bit">Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley / Nubank</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Bias correction, square root, and reciprocal nonlinearly transform moment error into update error. ZIP-SR uses preconditioner values for stochastic rounding; ZE-EDEN handles code points and scales. Error persists through state recurrence. Use working moments for the update before packing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Small moment differences can greatly change reciprocal-root steps, so raw moment MSE misses the effective gradient scale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12444">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.12444-adamw4bit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c8a13b370455cc00">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:adamw4bit" data-paper-title="Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-8b106936b90fd09d">Should current working moments be quantized before updating parameters?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadamw4bit">Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley / Nubank</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Decode old state, form new working moments, update using their unquantized values, then pack for persistence. Reversing the order injects error into the current step.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Use v to precondition this step before compressing it for the next.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12444">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.12444-adamw4bit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8b106936b90fd09d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:adamw4bit" data-paper-title="Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a2ee36b4cc02d185">How do ZIP-SR and ZE-EDEN store second moments differently?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadamw4bit">Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley / Nubank</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>ZIP-SR stochastically rounds in preconditioner space. ZE-EDEN excludes zero code points and calibrates block scales. Compare training loss and actual persistent bytes, not a generic four-bit rounding table.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Randomly choosing adjacent codes differs from rescaling blocks to avoid zero codes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12444">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.12444-adamw4bit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a2ee36b4cc02d185">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:adamw4bit" data-paper-title="Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0b06e014d4785862">Why does state quantization affect later steps?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadamw4bit">Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley / Nubank</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>First and second moments recur, so stored errors enter optimization after decoding at the next step. Control their effects on preconditioning and future updates, not merely bytes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeated downward rounding of v can inflate effective learning rates across steps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12444">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.12444-adamw4bit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0b06e014d4785862">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:race" data-paper-title="When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-race-11c5fa7f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-98ccf35fdf26f763">Why check likelihood changes for all later original actions when deleting a turn&#x27;s reasoning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arace">When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An unchanged immediate action does not show earlier reasoning is irrelevant to later planning. After tentative deletion, evaluate later actions in the affected context and proceed only if changes stay within tolerance. Accepted deletions persist for later compression. Checking only the current turn misses long-range dependencies, and removed token counts are not task success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reasoning may record a safety restriction while the current action only reads a file. A later deletion relies on that restriction, so a current-turn-only check can wrongly remove critical reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12061">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12061-race/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-98ccf35fdf26f763">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:race" data-paper-title="When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-202711996a37bca1">How do real trajectory requirements and the local bounded-calculator run limit conclusions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arace">When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Real training data need an environment, revision, split, and reasoning/action/observation records. QA rows are not tool trajectories. The local calculator actually samples actions and runs SFT/on-policy updates, but is L1 mechanism evidence only. A few successes under one seed do not replicate ScienceWorld or four-environment RL.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Calling two real calculation tools demonstrates interactive training, not long-horizon web or embodied capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 验证与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12061">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12061-race/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-202711996a37bca1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:race" data-paper-title="When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4be62e7f3db5d3ea">How does a reasoning loss mask differ from actually deleting training context?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arace">When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A mask removes supervision for deemed-removable tokens, while other actions train under prescribed conditions. Deleting context directly changes later prediction distributions. RACE also supervises early closing and keeps denominators for all original policy tokens and turns; rescaling by amount removed would silently change the objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If half the reasoning supervision is removed, still normalize by original token count to avoid inadvertently doubling the weight of remaining actions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12061">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12061-race/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4be62e7f3db5d3ea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:race" data-paper-title="When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-126077c5cb720dd9">Why does RACE remove reasoning that does not help an agent&#x27;s trajectory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arace">When Should Agents Think? Adaptive Reasoning via Cross-Turn Estimation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Long-horizon agents generate much reasoning that repeats information or does not affect later actions, yet adds training and inference load. RACE reduces redundancy while preserving behavioral support. Shorter is not inherently better: deletion can remove needed context, so check downstream effects rather than using word count alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeating a goal without changing later choices may be redundant. A brief note with a critical path cannot be removed just because it is short.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12061">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12061-race/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-126077c5cb720dd9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:option-channel-attack" data-paper-title="One Word Opens the Gate: The Option-Channel Attack on Typed Decision Models as Agent Guardrails" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-option-channel-attack-6cce967b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7e849af5852a4fa5">Why can changing only option labels affect guard approval while actions and trusted policy remain fixed?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aoption-channel-attack">One Word Opens the Gate: The Option-Channel Attack on Typed Decision Models as Agent Guardrails</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Southern California</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Labels are model inputs and their semantics can affect typed output selection without action changes. Separate unsafe approvals from benign denials. Conditional attack rate uses prohibited examples correctly rejected on clean inputs; an empty denominator is undefined, not zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A misleading label for &#x27;deny&#x27; can change the model&#x27;s choice for the same prohibited call without changing the actual policy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12292">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12292-option-channel-attack/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7e849af5852a4fa5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:option-channel-attack" data-paper-title="One Word Opens the Gate: The Option-Channel Attack on Typed Decision Models as Agent Guardrails" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c4bff9ac6252201f">What is conditional ASR when no clean example was correctly rejected?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aoption-channel-attack">One Word Opens the Gate: The Option-Channel Attack on Typed Decision Models as Agent Guardrails</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Southern California</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Undefined because the denominator is empty; do not report zero or one. Recompute the conditional denominator in each paired bootstrap draw. Select attack labels on calibration and measure on separate evaluation data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A model already incorrectly approving every case offers no clean rejection that could flip to approval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 代码映射与复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12292">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12292-option-channel-attack/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c4bff9ac6252201f">Question link</a></p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:option-channel-attack" data-paper-title="One Word Opens the Gate: The Option-Channel Attack on Typed Decision Models as Agent Guardrails" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-1c21f0da9acb53da">Why not combine fail-open and fail-closed into one safety accuracy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aoption-channel-attack">One Word Opens the Gate: The Option-Channel Attack on Typed Decision Models as Agent Guardrails</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Southern California</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fail-open admits prohibited actions; fail-closed denies permitted actions. Safety and usability effects differ. Conditional ASR applies only to clean correctly rejected cases and cannot replace overall error rates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Rejecting everything can reduce unsafe approvals while making legitimate tasks unusable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12292">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12292-option-channel-attack/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1c21f0da9acb53da">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:option-channel-attack" data-paper-title="One Word Opens the Gate: The Option-Channel Attack on Typed Decision Models as Agent Guardrails" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">

<h2 id="qa-33342ffea93fc28c">Why can Option-Channel Attack change a guard decision by altering only labels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aoption-channel-attack">One Word Opens the Gate: The Option-Channel Attack on Typed Decision Models as Agent Guardrails</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Southern California</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Typed-output names also enter the model. Misleading labels can affect the mapping from an unchanged action to allow or deny, exposing the option-name channel while trusted policy and actions stay fixed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The meaning of allow and deny is unchanged, but caller-supplied names can induce the wrong choice.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:ontrack" data-paper-title="OnTrack: Real-Time Monitoring and Intervention in LLM Agent Trajectories via Streaming Structure-Aware Optimal Transport" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
