<span id="paper-agent-research-ontrack-56d9bc62" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-655da0c786f78c79">Why not rescale old prefix-node mass to 1/t whenever a new event arrives?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aontrack">OnTrack: Real-Time Monitoring and Intervention in LLM Agent Trajectories via Streaming Structure-Aware Optimal Transport</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Cribl AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rescaling changes historical weights merely because the stream grows, confounding progress with normalization. Fixed prefix mass, streaming warm starts, and structural coupling preserve comparisons over time. Before intervening, increase the solver budget and recompute; irreversible-action gates cannot rely on stale frontier caches.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A new log read should not automatically reduce the mass of an earlier critical edit. Otherwise a score change can come from the denominator rather than actual drift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12375-ontrack/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-655da0c786f78c79">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:ontrack" data-paper-title="OnTrack: Real-Time Monitoring and Intervention in LLM Agent Trajectories via Streaming Structure-Aware Optimal Transport" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cba62001fc682760">May OnTrack reset existing node mass from 1/m to 1/t at each event?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aontrack">OnTrack: Real-Time Monitoring and Intervention in LLM Agent Trajectories via Streaming Structure-Aware Optimal Transport</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Cribl AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Agent nodes receive fixed prefix mass 1/m_bar. Rescaling changes old masses and leakage conventions. Recompute the frontier with current coupling before irreversible actions. Planner references can warn but cannot automatically halt execution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One unrelated new event should not lower all prior masses solely by changing a denominator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12375-ontrack/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cba62001fc682760">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:ontrack" data-paper-title="OnTrack: Real-Time Monitoring and Intervention in LLM Agent Trajectories via Streaming Structure-Aware Optimal Transport" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d5d972834c027596">Why use different weights for OnTrack&#x27;s early exploration grace and final alignment?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aontrack">OnTrack: Real-Time Monitoring and Intervention in LLM Agent Trajectories via Streaming Structure-Aware Optimal Transport</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Cribl AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Online new nodes receive age discount and a frontier mask to avoid premature penalties. At termination, cold-start without these adjustments to check the complete trace. Keeping exploration grace in final scores can hide unresolved drift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A temporary artifact gets early grace, but if still unused at termination it needs full review.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12375-ontrack/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d5d972834c027596">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:ontrack" data-paper-title="OnTrack: Real-Time Monitoring and Intervention in LLM Agent Trajectories via Streaming Structure-Aware Optimal Transport" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-23e3166f678480f8">Why does OnTrack represent trajectories as dependency graphs rather than compare action text?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aontrack">OnTrack: Real-Time Monitoring and Intervention in LLM Agent Trajectories via Streaming Structure-Aware Optimal Transport</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Cribl AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Order and artifact dependencies determine deviation, and independent branches may have different valid orders. Structured unbalanced alignment allows partial prefix/reference matches. Without a reference, explicitly fall back to loop, retry, and stagnation signals.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Swapping the order of two independent files should not be labeled deviation merely because indices change.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12375-ontrack/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-23e3166f678480f8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memento3" data-paper-title="Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-memento3-dd7ada6c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-81dc7395c90b6e8d">Why must historical replay avoid resetting simulated state from the next real observation at every step?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemento3">Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University College London</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Per-step resets hide accumulation of world-model errors and can make an incorrect model appear to match history. Continuous replay initializes from the first observation only, then generates subsequent states solely through model transitions, testing whether the rulebook really explains the trajectory. Semantic fidelity is checked separately; fitting finite history does not show general correctness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the first transition predicts the wrong door position, feeding the real screenshot at the second step erases the error. Continuous replay exposes its downstream consequences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11794">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.11794-memento3/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-81dc7395c90b6e8d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memento3" data-paper-title="Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-66d5b7038bccdd48">Why must new world-model code pass both semantic fidelity and historical execution checks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemento3">Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University College London</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Code might fit some observations without expressing the current rulebook, or faithfully implement an incorrect rule. The semantic check verifies that the compiled model matches the rules; historical replay checks that it recreates observed transitions. They constrain representation and behavior separately. Mismatches on new actions still trigger repairs, and a GPU execution receipt does not establish general rule correctness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A rulebook specifies clockwise rotation, but the code hardcodes an output image. Passing one example by chance is not a faithful implementation of the rule.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 结果与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11794">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.11794-memento3/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-66d5b7038bccdd48">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memento3" data-paper-title="Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c135d3f3afc9d094">How does uniform sampling over complete-plan equivalence classes differ from voting by model member?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemento3">Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University College London</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Several models may propose exactly the same action sequence. Sampling by member gives duplicates more probability. Group nonempty complete sequences and sample their classes uniformly to emphasize behavioral diversity rather than model counts. Follow the selected plan until completion, mismatch, or replanning; do not randomly switch paths at every step.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If three models propose left-left and one proposes right-up, member sampling has 3:1 odds, while the two plan classes each get one-half probability. Duplicates do not amplify a route.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11794">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.11794-memento3/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c135d3f3afc9d094">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memento3" data-paper-title="Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ad1d7f6482680c52">Why does Memento 3 learn environmental rules for planning from black-box interaction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemento3">Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University College London</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A new environment may not publish its transition rules. An agent sees actions and outcomes and can repeatedly err by guessing plans in language alone. Memento 3 organizes observations into a rulebook, compiles it into an executable model, and checks it with history and new actions so planning can occur in the model first. Learned rules are revisable hypotheses; agreement with history does not guarantee correctness in unseen states.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After a button changes an object&#x27;s orientation, propose a rotation rule and check other observed transitions. Revise the rule when new observations contradict it rather than ignoring the counterexample.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11794">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.11794-memento3/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ad1d7f6482680c52">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:mass" data-paper-title="Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-mass-a7f2d6e4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f2ba8ed1f9334346">Why remove the orchestrator&#x27;s initial workflow prompt before training but retain worker role assignments?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amass">Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The initial prompt contains the searched workflow. Retaining it directly could teach the model to rely on an external instruction rather than internalize useful collaboration. Worker roles preserve the execution structure and supervision applies to assistant tokens. Bradley–Terry ranking filters trajectories but self-ranked outcomes do not establish independent task capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the search prompt specifies retrieval then verification, remove that initial prompt so the model learns from successful execution, but keep the actual retriever and verifier turns.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12176">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12176-mass/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f2ba8ed1f9334346">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:mass" data-paper-title="Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3b165fac154d365c">What do two actual local LoRA rounds and lower validation loss establish?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amass">Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>They show the shared-checkpoint execution, proposal, ranking, and update chain ran, including real parameter training in a constrained two-worker text workflow. The data were self-generated trajectories, with one seed and few steps. There were no arbitrary workflow graphs or research-file tools, so lower loss does not establish stronger independent research capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Round two may imitate its own validation text more easily and lower loss without ever testing whether its conclusions on unseen research tasks are correct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 验证与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:mass" data-paper-title="Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c73c85ee811935d7">How does holding out the Kth Bradley–Terry-ranked trajectory differ from using all top trajectories for SFT?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amass">Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>After frozen-weight search, MASS independently collects trajectories and builds a BT ranking from pairwise comparisons. The first K−1 train the model and the Kth is for validation. The holdout separates training and checking targets, but the validation signal still comes from the chosen evaluator, not independent real-task success. Search traces cannot double as both training and generalization evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Use the top two of three ranked trajectories to train and the third to validate. If the third also contributes to gradients, the validation loss no longer measures a true holdout.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12176">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12176-mass/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c73c85ee811935d7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:mass" data-paper-title="Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a53cbfd37dcfcacc">Why collect trajectories separately for frozen-weight search and subsequent SFT?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amass">Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Search for workflows first without confounding exploration with parameter changes. Then generate and rank fresh trajectories, train on better samples, reserve one for validation, and only then update the shared model. The same model executes, proposes, and evaluates, but that does not make self-scoring unbiased. Self-generated validation loss is not independent task accuracy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A promising workflow during search still needs separately collected execution trajectories for training. An accidental high score from the same search trace is not independent validation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12176">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12176-mass/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a53cbfd37dcfcacc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hippocam" data-paper-title="Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-hippocam-33da2b45" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f958509ffcb6e00a">Why does hierarchical recall return one layer at a time rather than immediately expanding all raw history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahippocam">Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Upper-level narratives give purpose and structure first, letting the agent drill down only when needed instead of refilling context each time. Original messages remain in child nodes, so abstraction is reversible. Reserve budget for the next turn and explicitly fail if protected complete exchanges still do not fit, rather than silently truncating them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: An upper node says login was repaired last week. Expand the log children only when checking the error, without returning every debug output.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12124-hippocam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f958509ffcb6e00a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hippocam" data-paper-title="Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d3449f814ee2415f">Do three archives in a controlled pressure probe show autonomous learning of intent closure?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahippocam">Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Three real autonomous tasks produced no closure and zero archives. The separate controlled probe verifies pressure handling and protection only. Include request overhead and the next-turn estimate in budget. If protecting K complete exchanges and the dynamic window exceeds capacity, fail before main inference rather than truncate silently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A predefined closure signal exercises Palim. It does not show that a model emits the signal on unknown tasks; report these runs separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 验证与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12124-hippocam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d3449f814ee2415f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hippocam" data-paper-title="Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8a074b4ab31f5006">Why does it matter that Precip triggers after the response but before the tool result?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahippocam">Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The placement lets the system process closed intentions from the completed main response without assuming an observation that has not arrived. Tool exchanges must remain complete; compression cannot split an unfinished call. Trigger timing is a state contract, not interchangeable with inserting a summary anywhere.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: After a tool call is issued but before its result arrives, do not summarize it as a successful verification. Wait until the real observation enters a later exchange.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12124-hippocam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8a074b4ab31f5006">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hippocam" data-paper-title="Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0dd2936011497890">How do nested intentions differ from an ordinary rolling summary?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahippocam">Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Nested intentions organize current goals and subgoals. Experiences are abstracted when their intent closes, whereas rolling summaries compress primarily by time and need not know whether a task finished. Hippocam keeps an original-message tree and recalls one layer at a time, retaining traceability after abstraction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Dependency checks can finish within an unresolved debugging goal. Summarize the closed subgoal without archiving the whole task as complete.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12124-hippocam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0dd2936011497890">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evoalloc" data-paper-title="EvoAlloc: A Self-Evolving Resource Allocation Agent for Efficient Program Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-evoalloc-9a5390ec" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea25419573e292b0">Why should some discarded candidates still receive counterfactual evaluation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevoalloc">EvoAlloc: A Self-Evolving Resource Allocation Agent for Efficient Program Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · King Abdullah University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>If only selected programs are evaluated, the allocation policy cannot see high-quality candidates it missed and may become overly confident in its own preferences. Random counterfactual checks reveal the risk of missing a new best, and shadow policies need shared evidence. Those Full calls consume budget; do not exclude exploration or warmup to make savings look larger.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A filter may discard an unfamiliar implementation that an occasional full evaluation reveals to be superior. That evidence corrects selective feedback that equates unfamiliarity with low quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12086">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12086-evoalloc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ea25419573e292b0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evoalloc" data-paper-title="EvoAlloc: A Self-Evolving Resource Allocation Agent for Efficient Program Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ad4d7c9071244a6f">Why charge warmup, the shadow union, and counterfactual Full evaluations to the budget, and what did the short GPU run not trigger?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevoalloc">EvoAlloc: A Self-Evolving Resource Allocation Agent for Efficient Program Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · King Abdullah University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>They actually consume resources and are not free administrative work. Shadow promotion also requires two observed disagreements. The best of four real local Full evaluations did not beat the initial program. Warmup was insufficient and no promotion occurred. Partial and the two-disagreement case were covered only by contract tests, not triggered in the real run.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If a shadow policy requests a Full evaluation of a program discarded by the primary policy, charge it even if it never changes the primary champion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 验证与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12086">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12086-evoalloc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ad4d7c9071244a6f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evoalloc" data-paper-title="EvoAlloc: A Self-Evolving Resource Allocation Agent for Efficient Program Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-89728affaf2b375a">How does prioritizing missed new bests before cost differ from minimizing Full evaluations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevoalloc">EvoAlloc: A Self-Evolving Resource Allocation Agent for Efficient Program Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · King Abdullah University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Saving evaluations alone can miss the actual best candidate. Lexicographic ranking first protects search quality, then saves Full and Partial evaluations when missed-new-best counts tie. Random counterfactual checks of discarded candidates mitigate selective feedback, and shadow policies share evidence. Do not evaluate an allocator on accepted candidates alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If A avoids ten evaluations but misses a new champion, while B pays for two more evaluations and retains the champion, A should not advance merely for being cheaper.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12086">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12086-evoalloc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-89728affaf2b375a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:evoalloc" data-paper-title="EvoAlloc: A Self-Evolving Resource Allocation Agent for Efficient Program Evolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6fe37e2f64ef258e">Why is continuing or stopping after Partial more flexible than an immediate Full/Discard decision?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aevoalloc">EvoAlloc: A Self-Evolving Resource Allocation Agent for Efficient Program Evolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · King Abdullah University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Partial evaluation offers cheaper initial evidence before paying full cost, avoiding exhaustive evaluation of clearly bad candidates and premature discarding of potential winners. The task needs a trustworthy Partial signal; do not invent a score for an environment that does not support one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A quick program constraint check followed by a lengthy performance evaluation can be useful, but Circle26&#x27;s current interface has no Partial, so the local path supports only Full or Discard.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12086">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.12086-evoalloc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6fe37e2f64ef258e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:embedding-gemma2" data-paper-title="EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c1671088f314bae5">Why renormalize a truncated Matryoshka embedding?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Aembedding-gemma2">EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The retained prefix generally no longer has unit norm. Raw dot products would mix differences in retained energy with similarity. Renormalizing restores cosine scale. This relies on trained prefix representations, not arbitrary truncation, and pooling must exclude padding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Truncate two 768-dimensional vectors to 128 dimensions and normalize each again so larger retained norms do not confer an advantage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37364v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/embeddinggemma2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c1671088f314bae5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:embedding-gemma2" data-paper-title="EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1730598e354b01ed">What details matter for mean pooling, truncation, and precision?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Aembedding-gemma2">EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Attention-mask pooling excludes padding, followed by prefix truncation and L2 renormalization. Queries and documents use their respective text prefixes; images use none. Official activation ranges can produce non-finite FP16 values, so the local path pins FP32 and rejects non-finite or zero vectors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Identical text padded to different lengths should yield the same masked representation. Including padding makes it length-dependent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 结果与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37364v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/embeddinggemma2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1730598e354b01ed">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:embedding-gemma2" data-paper-title="EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-eed6fdf443ec6128">How does MRL truncation differ from randomly dropping dimensions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Aembedding-gemma2">EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MRL trains designated prefixes, such as 128, 256, or 512 dimensions, to serve as representations after renormalization. Random subsets lack that training convention. Shorter prefixes save storage and retrieval cost, but quality must be reported by task and fixed size.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Taking the first 128 of 768 dimensions follows the trained contract; randomly drawing 128 each time is a different compression method.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37364v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/embeddinggemma2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eed6fdf443ec6128">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:embedding-gemma2" data-paper-title="EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8d009645d6382686">Does a shared 768-dimensional space require all four modalities at once?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Aembedding-gemma2">EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A shared space lets all modalities use comparable vector similarities, while towers load as needed. Supported inputs and actually verified paths differ. Local official-checkpoint validation covers text and images only, not audio and video pipelines.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Image-to-text search needs only the image and text paths; their validation does not establish audio retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37364v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/embeddinggemma2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8d009645d6382686">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:specguard" data-paper-title="SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-specguard-31696f7e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-837e8a2527eb3a28">Why can a Lean proof still yield inconclusive even though SpecAgent never sees tests?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspecguard">SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MATS</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Test isolation keeps intent independent of potentially wrong or malicious requirements, and the Certifier checks conflict. A proof applies only to translations and connector expressions. If natural-language meaning cannot be aligned faithfully, kernel success does not prove the original task is corrupted; keep inconclusive.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Sorting versus reverse-order requirements can be formalized as a conflict. Ambiguity over &#x27;stable sorting&#x27; should not be settled solely by a limited proof.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09159">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.09159-specguard/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-837e8a2527eb3a28">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:specguard" data-paper-title="SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a583d933cd754ee0">Does a passed SpecGuard A100 receipt show real end-to-end model success?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspecguard">SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MATS</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. All three archived small-model cases were inconclusive with zero conflict certificates and stopped at Spec. Passed verifies real CUDA execution and provenance. Handwritten Lean passes test mechanics, not model output.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A working GPU command and saved failures do not establish that the model reached TestAgent and connector stages.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 结果与验收边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09159">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.09159-specguard/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a583d933cd754ee0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:specguard" data-paper-title="SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-55dce45e534cd4ad">Does a Lean-kernel conflict certificate prove that the original natural-language task must conflict?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspecguard">SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MATS</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It establishes no common implementation for the generated specification and test constraints, not faithful translation. Semantic connection or intent extraction may be wrong. Allow inconclusive when expression or alignment fails.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A proof obtained after translating &#x27;add one&#x27; as &#x27;add two&#x27; does not validate the original task.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 结果与验收边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09159">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.09159-specguard/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-55dce45e534cd4ad">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:specguard" data-paper-title="SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7b4123e304451411">Why doesn&#x27;t SpecGuard let SpecAgent see tests?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspecguard">SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MATS</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tests may conflict with trusted task descriptions; copying them into intent would prove only the tests&#x27; own requirements. SpecAgent sees description and code, TestAgent translates independently, and Lean checks conflict after semantic connection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the description says add one but tests demand 2 become 4, do not write &#x27;2 becomes 4&#x27; into the intent specification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 数据协议. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09159">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.09159-specguard/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7b4123e304451411">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:video-encoder-selection" data-paper-title="Video Encoders Built on Image Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-video-encoder-selection-2d465377" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4a106f0ffb777141">Why refine only retained anchors without adding visual tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Avideo-encoder-selection">Video Encoders Built on Image Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Selection first preserves addressable evidence under a fixed budget. The refiner reads neighboring frames to enrich those anchors without increasing output length. Appending neighbor tokens would break the budget and confound selection with context enrichment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Ten retained patches can read neighboring motion and still output ten vectors, not ten plus 20 appended positions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06616">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.06616-video-encoder-selection/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4a106f0ffb777141">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:video-encoder-selection" data-paper-title="Video Encoders Built on Image Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-378b6dec7ef4d3ae">How are tied pairs and singletons resolved, and why can the selector fill an odd budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Avideo-encoder-selection">Video Encoders Built on Image Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Add a pair only if its per-token gain is strictly higher, otherwise add a singleton. Respect quotas and remaining budget. Even with negative gains or no temporal edge, select exactly B distinct indices. Local external uniform quotas and scene proxies are explicit deviations; SITE is not implemented.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One remaining slot permits only a singleton; an equal per-token gain also selects the singleton.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 本地结果与验收边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06616">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.06616-video-encoder-selection/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-378b6dec7ef4d3ae">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:video-encoder-selection" data-paper-title="Video Encoders Built on Image Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-6879eb4eb04dbefb">What do intra-frame DPP and adjacent-frame correspondence rewards constrain?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Avideo-encoder-selection">Video Encoders Built on Image Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The log-determinant balances quality and diversity to avoid near-duplicate tokens within frames. Cross-frame edges reward matched endpoints that preserve traceable relations. Similarity, margin, and spatial gates apply; edges are not guaranteed true trajectories.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Select a cup and hand rather than two table patches; keep the cup&#x27;s reliable match in the next frame to see movement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06616">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.06616-video-encoder-selection/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6879eb4eb04dbefb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:video-encoder-selection" data-paper-title="Video Encoders Built on Image Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-79eabead0b3ea73d">Why select evidence from independently encoded frames before passing them to a language model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Avideo-encoder-selection">Video Encoders Built on Image Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Framewise encoding preserves localizable evidence but produces a large sequence for long videos. Selection balances question needs, intra-frame diversity, and cross-frame links under a budget. It does not create evidence; high motion alone need not help.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A question about which object was picked up first needs that object and cross-frame relations, not every changing background patch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06616">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.06616-video-encoder-selection/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-79eabead0b3ea73d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:lesser" data-paper-title="LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-23f6b957f56de63e">Why isn&#x27;t one-forward analytic output gradient an exact full-model substitute?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Alesser">LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Pennsylvania</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The outer product is exact for an independent readout; shared bilateral projection compresses it for existing selection. Tied embeddings can introduce indirect gradients. Use validation proxies and isolate test. This is not all-layer gradient equality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Select training examples using readout gradients of validation queries, not test examples.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03702">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.03702-lesser/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-23f6b957f56de63e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:lesser" data-paper-title="LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d424b130e8a7aebb">Why share random projections between LESSER candidates and queries?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Alesser">LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Pennsylvania</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Only shared coordinates support comparison. Project both residual and hidden sides without materializing the full outer product. Use validation query proxies, never test selection; local random tensors are diagnostics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Independent projection draws per sample destroy comparability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03702">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.03702-lesser/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d424b130e8a7aebb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:lesser" data-paper-title="LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-f265bae522721287">Is LESSER fully equivalent to full-model gradient similarity?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Alesser">LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Pennsylvania</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Exactness applies to an independent output layer; tied embeddings add hidden-state paths. Projection also approximates geometry and downstream performance needs testing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Similar final-layer directions do not guarantee similar middle-layer updates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03702">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.03702-lesser/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f265bae522721287">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:lesser" data-paper-title="LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-lesser-18cdf418" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c5e873d09446feea">Why use output-layer gradients as LESSER selection features?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Alesser">LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Pennsylvania</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Full per-example backprop is costly. Independent readout gradient follows analytically from prediction residual and final hidden state in one forward, then project for the existing selector.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Keep query similarity selection but replace expensive gradient features.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03702">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.03702-lesser/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c5e873d09446feea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:follow-the-winners" data-paper-title="Follow the Winners: Conservative Policy Improvement with the Cross-Entropy Method for Critic-Free RFT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-410d39abbd09bc56">Why repeatedly select small-batch elites rather than pool top-K?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Afollow-the-winners">Follow the Winners: Conservative Policy Improvement with the Cross-Entropy Method for Critic-Free RFT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Trent AI Limited</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Random minibatches followed by local top reward yield smoothed occupancy, with repetition weighting. Hard global elites are a special case and may drop useful runners-up. No same-prompt groups/critic needed, but KL remains and local tool gains aren&#x27;t proven.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Strongest often wins but a runner-up can win some batches; don&#x27;t deduplicate then equally weight them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03361">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.03361-follow-the-winners/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-410d39abbd09bc56">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:follow-the-winners" data-paper-title="Follow the Winners: Conservative Policy Improvement with the Cross-Entropy Method for Critic-Free RFT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0d6b4047412aaba8">What are FTW limits K=C and C=N?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Afollow-the-winners">Follow the Winners: Conservative Policy Improvement with the Cross-Entropy Method for Critic-Free RFT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Trent AI Limited</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>K=C keeps the whole sampled minibatch and yields uniform sampling. C=N draws the whole pool and yields global elites. Verify normalized distribution and preserve repeated selections; bandits aren&#x27;t tool-world results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If K=C still favors highest rank, the implementation misses the limit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03361">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.03361-follow-the-winners/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0d6b4047412aaba8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:follow-the-winners" data-paper-title="Follow the Winners: Conservative Policy Improvement with the Cross-Entropy Method for Critic-Free RFT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-1d5e36608da4db56">Why aren&#x27;t repeated minibatch elites equivalent to one global top-K?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Afollow-the-winners">Follow the Winners: Conservative Policy Improvement with the Cross-Entropy Method for Critic-Free RFT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Trent AI Limited</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Repeated batches create soft rank occupancy; near-elites sometimes win. Global hard truncation retains only top ranks. Repeated selection counts are weights, so deduplication changes the objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A second-tier trajectory can win a batch without the strongest opponents.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03361">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.03361-follow-the-winners/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1d5e36608da4db56">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:follow-the-winners" data-paper-title="Follow the Winners: Conservative Policy Improvement with the Cross-Entropy Method for Critic-Free RFT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-follow-the-winners-b5a02f54" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d44fcdf056fedcaa">Why doesn&#x27;t FTW need same-prompt groups or a critic?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Afollow-the-winners">Follow the Winners: Conservative Policy Improvement with the Cross-Entropy Method for Critic-Free RFT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Trent AI Limited</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Stateful tool trajectories are expensive. Repeatedly draw minibatches from recent real FIFO traces, imitate within-batch elites and apply KL. Replay ranks replace some group sampling/value needs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One trace per task can still participate in a pool minibatch tournament.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:sentry" data-paper-title="Sentry: Learning to Recover from LLM Agent Failures at Test Time" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-sentry-acd21bdd" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2ae4b0a62a5f04d6">Why add recovery advice to the playbook only after it is verified by observable later progress?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asentry">Sentry: Learning to Recover from LLM Agent Failures at Test Time</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
