<h2 id="qa-b4a2e2a2808d8743">Why give teacher textual coordinates while student receives only image and question?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Awhere-opd">Where-OPD: Spatially Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation of MLLMs with Synthetic Scenes</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Valeo.ai</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Exact synthetic object/location metadata gives privileged scoring on student prefixes. Deployment lacks that metadata, so keep student inputs clean. Preserve spatial mask; random-logit tests don&#x27;t prove spatial ability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teacher can correct left-of-box relationships, but test students cannot be told coordinates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02117">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.02117-where-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b4a2e2a2808d8743">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:where-opd" data-paper-title="Where-OPD: Spatially Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation of MLLMs with Synthetic Scenes" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d953d9a8ea49d645">Does local Where-OPD generate scenes and load an MLLM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Awhere-opd">Where-OPD: Spatially Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation of MLLMs with Synthetic Scenes</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Valeo.ai</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It checks teacher KL under a spatial mask aligned to generated student positions, with frozen teacher. Random logits aren&#x27;t visual evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two hand-built left/right logits don&#x27;t constitute image reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02117">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.02117-where-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d953d9a8ea49d645">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:where-opd" data-paper-title="Where-OPD: Spatially Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation of MLLMs with Synthetic Scenes" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a6e6be5151119ef4">How does spatial privileged text differ from ordinary text distillation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Awhere-opd">Where-OPD: Spatially Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation of MLLMs with Synthetic Scenes</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Valeo.ai</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The method needs matching actual scene images and spatial annotations. Random text distributions don&#x27;t verify visual integration; privilege doesn&#x27;t prove student reliance on images.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A correct description paired with the wrong image still yields a computable loss but meaningless guidance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02117">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.02117-where-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a6e6be5151119ef4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:where-opd" data-paper-title="Where-OPD: Spatially Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation of MLLMs with Synthetic Scenes" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-where-opd-73f1d45e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c0798f7dbc5e175d">Why use synthetic scene coordinates as privileged Where-OPD input?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Awhere-opd">Where-OPD: Spatially Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation of MLLMs with Synthetic Scenes</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Valeo.ai</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Generated scenes provide exact objects/positions for teacher while student sees image/question. Internalize spatial hints without coordinate access at deployment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teacher knows positions; student learns left/right from pixels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02117">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.02117-where-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c0798f7dbc5e175d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tvrl" data-paper-title="Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-52574986269291c8">Why interpret high VLM-reward gradient as sensitivity rather than correct credit?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atvrl">Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It measures local response of the current reward function. Mean-normalized token reweighting controls scale, but shortcut-driven sensitivities need not be causal. Local checks neither train videos nor prove perception gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A corner watermark can receive a large gradient without being a route to better video quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01973">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01973-tvrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-52574986269291c8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tvrl" data-paper-title="Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7e0532299250133a">Does local TVRL train a video diffusion model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atvrl">Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It computes gradient-based credits and mean normalization. Real video, frozen VLM gradients and policy training remain; handle all-zero norms explicitly. Random inputs are not video capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Hand-supplied gradient sizes validate weighting without generating videos.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01973">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01973-tvrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7e0532299250133a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tvrl" data-paper-title="Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-344d709eb000f913">How does TVRL sensitivity differ from uniformly broadcasting advantage?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atvrl">Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Normalized gradient norms emphasize sensitive positions while uniform credits ignore them. Quality depends on the frozen VLM; gradients alone are not causal evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Evaluator sensitivity to a word can be a shortcut.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01973">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01973-tvrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-344d709eb000f913">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tvrl" data-paper-title="Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-tvrl-0c541634" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-017b1a45c76fbcfd">Why use gradient sensitivity for video-token credit in TVRL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atvrl">Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Terminal video reward is coarse. Sensitivity through a frozen evaluator localizes group advantage. Sensitivity means response to perturbations, not verified correctness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Action terms may affect video reward more than connective words.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01973">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01973-tvrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-017b1a45c76fbcfd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpening-tax" data-paper-title="Sharpening Tax in Post-Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7fe59e1e2e6de973">Why measure fixed-budget task coverage even when pass@1 improves?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpening-tax">Sharpening Tax in Post-Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sharper distributions hit familiar solutions more often but may lose rare solutions accessible with several draws. Compare base/post coverage under equal budget and adapt temperature by difficulty. First-hit accuracy, entropy and task coverage are not interchangeable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Better common-item answers can hide lost rare correct solutions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01509">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01509-sharpening-tax/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7fe59e1e2e6de973">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpening-tax" data-paper-title="Sharpening Tax in Post-Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cdbe2496774f9c56">Why hold K and task inputs fixed when computing Tax_K?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpening-tax">Sharpening Tax in Post-Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Coverage changes with samples and tasks. Match both and retain the sign of base minus post-training coverage. Local code is a metric only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Many base samples against one post-training sample confound the estimated tax.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01509">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01509-sharpening-tax/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cdbe2496774f9c56">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpening-tax" data-paper-title="Sharpening Tax in Post-Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4b1a6a6ef598e60f">How does posterior-conditioned temperature differ from uniformly raising temperature?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpening-tax">Sharpening Tax in Post-Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Allocate temperature by estimated difficulty to balance exploitation and coverage. Global heating treats all tasks alike. Bad estimates may misallocate, so recovery isn&#x27;t guaranteed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Mastered problems may need little exploration while difficult problems benefit from branching.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01509">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01509-sharpening-tax/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4b1a6a6ef598e60f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpening-tax" data-paper-title="Sharpening Tax in Post-Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-sharpening-tax-09653801" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b1670c70f32180f7">Why measure both first-attempt success and fixed-budget coverage in Sharpening Tax?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpening-tax">Sharpening Tax in Post-Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Training may raise probability of familiar successes while making other solutions or tasks unreachable. Fixed-budget coverage exposes this tradeoff.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One problem becomes usually correct while another never yields a correct sample, reducing coverage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01509">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01509-sharpening-tax/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b1670c70f32180f7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcpr" data-paper-title="RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-524181a96eb45723">Why penalize relative length only if all answers are long and posteriors concentrated?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlcpr">RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Similar posteriors indicate limited distinction from reasoning length; widespread long replies support compressing redundant ones. Penalize relatively only after both gates. Equality and quantile rules matter; real entropy/posteriors must come from a model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Favor shorter among equally supported long replies, not a long reply that clearly increases answer support.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01458">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01458-rlcpr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-524181a96eb45723">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcpr" data-paper-title="RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-2deca80ebb108f1b">Do exact length or posterior thresholds activate RLCPR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlcpr">RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Minimum length must strictly exceed its threshold and posterior range must be strictly below its bound. Entropy CDF also uses strict less-than on ties. Handcrafted numbers test formulas, not RL gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Minimum length exactly at threshold is not penalized.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01458">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01458-rlcpr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2deca80ebb108f1b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcpr" data-paper-title="RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-89ed669827603c39">Are RLCPR entropy strata and length gating the same choice?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlcpr">RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Entropy strata shape examples before sampling. Length/posterior gates adjust rewards inside generated groups. Different inputs and stages, not one global length threshold.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Deciding which tasks to sample precedes checking whether current replies are all redundant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01458">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01458-rlcpr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-89ed669827603c39">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcpr" data-paper-title="RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rlcpr-dde5901c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f17b3c74251f3a07">Why not apply a uniform length penalty to all long replies in RLCPR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlcpr">RLCPR: Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Long reasoning can be necessary. Enable relative penalty only when all group replies are long and answer posteriors concentrated, where length may add little distinction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeated explanation after agreement differs from exploring uncertain critical branches.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01458">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01458-rlcpr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f17b3c74251f3a07">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:range-grpo" data-paper-title="Range-GRPO: Policy Optimization via Pairwise Relations among Reward Intervals" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-58d186d40a148b8d">Why not rank replies with overlapping reward intervals?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arange-grpo">Range-GRPO: Policy Optimization via Pairwise Relations among Reward Intervals</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yonsei University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Small point differences may be judge noise. Use determinate calibrated interval relations and aggregate relative group advantage without inventing directions. Degenerate intervals recover point rewards. The kernel is not judge calibration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not favor one broad overlapping interval merely because its center is higher.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01548">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01548-range-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-58d186d40a148b8d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:range-grpo" data-paper-title="Range-GRPO: Policy Optimization via Pairwise Relations among Reward Intervals" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-50dbc843fd89d3de">Does local Range-GRPO calibrate a conformal judge?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arange-grpo">Range-GRPO: Policy Optimization via Pairwise Relations among Reward Intervals</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yonsei University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It consumes intervals and tests comparisons and the point limit. Coverage needs real calibration data/judging. Degenerate intervals should recover the DR-GRPO limit, not arbitrary smoothing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A wide interval passing an interface test doesn&#x27;t establish coverage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01548">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01548-range-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-50dbc843fd89d3de">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:range-grpo" data-paper-title="Range-GRPO: Policy Optimization via Pairwise Relations among Reward Intervals" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e90be0ef0d21656e">How does treating overlap as uncertain differ from midpoint ranking?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arange-grpo">Range-GRPO: Policy Optimization via Pairwise Relations among Reward Intervals</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yonsei University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Midpoints always impose order even inside large uncertainty. Interval comparison discards dubious direction, at the cost of sparser supervision. It does not prove faster/better training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Different midpoints with overlap needn&#x27;t imply a clear preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01548">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01548-range-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e90be0ef0d21656e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:range-grpo" data-paper-title="Range-GRPO: Policy Optimization via Pairwise Relations among Reward Intervals" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-range-grpo-b66c385f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a15f72e3b4bd2e6e">Why use reward intervals instead of point scores in Range-GRPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arange-grpo">Range-GRPO: Policy Optimization via Pairwise Relations among Reward Intervals</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yonsei University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A point hides judge uncertainty. Intervals identify pair orderings that can be justified and avoid treating tiny noise as preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Strongly overlapping score ranges need not produce a winner.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01548">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01548-range-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a15f72e3b4bd2e6e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:my-fault" data-paper-title="My FAULT: Self-Diagnosis as Credit Assignment in Self-Evolving Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8a0aa95a3d7af3e5">Why verify diagnostic claims before error pricing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amy-fault">My FAULT: Self-Diagnosis as Credit Assignment in Self-Evolving Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Hindsight explanations can rationalize. Evidence-verified location and class drive relative online prices and conserved terminal credit redistribution. No invented success reward or jointly trained local diagnosis model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If search was correct but summary dropped a fact, don&#x27;t penalize search merely because the model blames it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01161-my-fault/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8a0aa95a3d7af3e5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:my-fault" data-paper-title="My FAULT: Self-Diagnosis as Credit Assignment in Self-Evolving Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-22cc52b5d633b695">What conservation invariant should My FAULT check?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amy-fault">My FAULT: Self-Diagnosis as Credit Assignment in Self-Evolving Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Valid-step credits sum to original return. Mean cost and step count use the same mask. Local screening/cost/conservation does not jointly train a policy and diagnosis model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Including padding in mean cost breaks conservation on valid steps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01161-my-fault/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-22cc52b5d633b695">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:my-fault" data-paper-title="My FAULT: Self-Diagnosis as Credit Assignment in Self-Evolving Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ad19140e9b0328c6">How does conserved redistribution differ from an extra error penalty?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amy-fault">My FAULT: Self-Diagnosis as Credit Assignment in Self-Evolving Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Conservation preserves total terminal return and changes only allocation. Extra penalties change the objective and incentives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Lower one step&#x27;s credit and offset elsewhere rather than deduct from the entire return twice.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01161-my-fault/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ad19140e9b0328c6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:my-fault" data-paper-title="My FAULT: Self-Diagnosis as Credit Assignment in Self-Evolving Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-my-fault-cefa1f11" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-3e739d97e21fc937">Why verify My FAULT self-diagnoses before pricing errors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amy-fault">My FAULT: Self-Diagnosis as Credit Assignment in Self-Evolving Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Self-explanations can invent causes. Only evidence-supported categories/locations enter online pricing; relative costs allocate terminal credit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A claim that the tool failed needs trace evidence before penalizing tool steps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01161-my-fault/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3e739d97e21fc937">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gmc-grpo" data-paper-title="Asynchronous LLM Post-Training: Group-Mass Capping and Convergence Analysis" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c6f729f6a888dc53">Why rescale an entire group instead of clipping trajectories one by one?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agmc-grpo">Asynchronous LLM Post-Training: Group-Mass Capping and Convergence Analysis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent clipping changes relative weights. A shared factor limits total ratio mass and retains relative contributions. Sampling and moment assumptions remain; a formula test is not an asynchronous training system.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Uniformly scale stale trajectories when total mass is too large; separate caps can flatten differences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01896">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01896-gmc-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c6f729f6a888dc53">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gmc-grpo" data-paper-title="Asynchronous LLM Post-Training: Group-Mass Capping and Convergence Analysis" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1610e7e0c7bb3600">How do GMC weights behave below the total cap?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agmc-grpo">Asynchronous LLM Post-Training: Group-Mass Capping and Convergence Analysis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use multiplier one until total exceeds cap; then multiply by cap divided by sum. Check nonnegative weights and group boundaries. Local kernel does not measure asynchronous cluster throughput.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not pool two prompts: a large weight in one should not scale the other.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01896">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01896-gmc-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1610e7e0c7bb3600">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gmc-grpo" data-paper-title="Asynchronous LLM Post-Training: Group-Mass Capping and Convergence Analysis" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4eea76d90300a7b0">What does a group cap preserve that per-trajectory clipping may not?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agmc-grpo">Asynchronous LLM Post-Training: Group-Mass Capping and Convergence Analysis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Common scaling retains ratios between weights. Independent caps change them. Theory still requires conditions such as common second moments; it does not repair arbitrary staleness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Clipping may make large and medium weights equal, while group scaling preserves their ratio.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01896">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01896-gmc-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4eea76d90300a7b0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gmc-grpo" data-paper-title="Asynchronous LLM Post-Training: Group-Mass Capping and Convergence Analysis" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-gmc-grpo-1030f809" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4530e4fc6872ebb5">Why cap total group importance mass in GMC-GRPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agmc-grpo">Asynchronous LLM Post-Training: Group-Mass Capping and Convergence Analysis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Asynchronous stale policies can produce huge ratios. Apply one multiplier to the group to cap mass while preserving within-group proportions, unlike independent clipping.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Scale the whole inflated group instead of cutting only its largest member.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01896">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01896-gmc-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4530e4fc6872ebb5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gaw-po" data-paper-title="GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0307c820f34c8286">Why penalize rejected-response tokens less if they support the preferred direction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agaw-po">GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A whole response&#x27;s rejection does not condemn all tokens. Smaller negative weights for aligned gradients avoid suppressing shared useful steps. This changes credit, not factual verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If both openings are right and only the rejected conclusion is wrong, an aligned opening needn&#x27;t receive the same penalty.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01511">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01511-gaw-po/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0307c820f34c8286">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gaw-po" data-paper-title="GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-92390bc26a92b79e">How does GAW-PO&#x27;s positive-part cosine handle aligned, orthogonal and opposite gradients?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agaw-po">GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Weight is one minus positive cosine. Perfect alignment approaches zero; orthogonal/opposite directions keep weight one; partial positive alignment reduces penalty. Actual gradients are required. Local evidence is only the weight kernel.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A negative cosine is first set to zero, so the weight does not exceed one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01511">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01511-gaw-po/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-92390bc26a92b79e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gaw-po" data-paper-title="GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-013be2268305c60d">How does GAW-PO gradient alignment differ from weighting by token likelihood?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agaw-po">GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Likelihood measures how often the current model produces a token. Alignment measures whether penalizing it conflicts with preferred updates. Common tokens can be irrelevant and rare tokens helpful; this is a mechanism comparison, not an empirical ranking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not punish a rare term merely for low probability if it supports a correct explanation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01511">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01511-gaw-po/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-013be2268305c60d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gaw-po" data-paper-title="GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-gaw-po-bf9dde22" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7bb97a727465c23f">Does GAW-PO label complete replies or each token as preferred/rejected?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agaw-po">GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Labels compare two replies to one prompt; there is no per-token annotation. Rejected replies can contain good steps or shared wording. Gradient alignment supplies credit at a finer granularity, not additional human token truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If both answers start with the correct equation and differ only at the end, the rejection does not label the shared equation wrong.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01511">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01511-gaw-po/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7bb97a727465c23f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dars" data-paper-title="Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-644835722eac59bb">Why decay nearby credit rather than reset every completed step?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adars">Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Invalid prerequisites affect dependent branches, not independent work. Graph-distance decay and potential differences encode breakage/repair. Valid predicates and edges are prerequisites; local transitions aren&#x27;t agent gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Ticket failure weakens hotel credit but not independent reimbursement materials.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01207">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01207-dars/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-644835722eac59bb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dars" data-paper-title="Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-985f17937ae96c42">Does DARS repair change only immediate reward?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adars">Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Update dependency state/potential and derive reward from differences. Otherwise later credit uses stale breakage. Local state kernel doesn&#x27;t train paper model; upstream interfaces aren&#x27;t released training code.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repaired flights restore downstream state rather than add an isolated bonus.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01207">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01207-dars/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-985f17937ae96c42">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dars" data-paper-title="Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-680896d0dd51adf2">How does dependency-distance decay differ from global failure penalty?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adars">Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Decay depends on relation to the broken prerequisite; global penalty ignores it. Wrong graph or predicates still misassign credit, so validate them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Flight-dependent hotels are affected, not unrelated account verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01207">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01207-dars/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-680896d0dd51adf2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dars" data-paper-title="Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-dars-eb9dd187" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f737fb5a8ac8ba71">Why represent DARS progress as a dependency predicate graph?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adars">Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Completed steps can rely on later-invalid conditions. Graph validation, invalidation and repair update related credit without clearing independent branches.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Canceling a booking can affect itinerary but not unrelated document preparation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01207">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.01207-dars/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f737fb5a8ac8ba71">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:carm" data-paper-title="CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8bd0cdb80dceafcc">Why take absolute log ratios before response averaging?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acarm">CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Moore Threads AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Opposing probability shifts can cancel in a normal sequence mean. Absolute averaging detects magnitude and masks large mismatch. It measures policy shift, not answer quality, with a detached gate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Opposite shifts across sentence halves produce near-zero total signed drift but large mean absolute drift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02039">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.02039-carm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8bd0cdb80dceafcc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:carm" data-paper-title="CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5e16cfa5082016de">Should CARM differentiate through the response gate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acarm">CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Moore Threads AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Freeze selection, measure valid response tokens only and apply the specified threshold. No Qwen3.5 training or measured stability improvement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Don&#x27;t add gradients through a threshold recomputed from updated probabilities.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02039">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.02039-carm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5e16cfa5082016de">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:carm" data-paper-title="CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5c46d61ebc67a055">How does CARM differ from filtering on geometric ratio near one?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acarm">CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Moore Threads AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Geometric ratios allow signed cancellation; CARM measures unsigned change and can reject internally shifted responses near ratio one. This is not quality scoring.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A balanced ledger can still hide large cash movements.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02039">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.02039-carm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5c46d61ebc67a055">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:carm" data-paper-title="CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-carm-c2bacd93" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4d62623fa8b57200">Why take absolute token log ratios in CARM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acarm">CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Moore Threads AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Signed shifts can cancel across positions and conceal severe drift. Average absolute magnitude and use a response-level gate to detect cancellation risk.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A sharp rise at one token and equal fall at another can average to zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02039">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.02039-carm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4d62623fa8b57200">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:veto" data-paper-title="VETO: Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-veto-75da8cb3" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ffd7d671be8de7d4">Why merge within frames before removing cross-frame redundancy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aveto">VETO: Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National Taiwan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Intra-frame merging shrinks per-frame candidates, lowering temporal matching cost. Matching all raw patches first already pays that search cost and can yield different correspondences. The order is part of the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Compress 100 patches per frame to 20 before matching adjacent frames; the reverse does not save the same work.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01785">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.01785-veto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ffd7d671be8de7d4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:veto" data-paper-title="VETO: Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-45257d5781bda87f">What does the local farthest-point representative test preserve, and what does it omit?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aveto">VETO: Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National Taiwan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Deterministic farthest-point representatives test the space-first, time-second sequence and budget, and execute compression on GPU. There is no paper 7B VLM or real video benchmark. The heuristic does not reproduce semantic merging, and author throughput is not a local result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Meeting the token cap confirms both stages ran, not that small-object movement remains recognizable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01785">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.01785-veto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-45257d5781bda87f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:veto" data-paper-title="VETO: Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-29587d13df18756f">At fixed token budget, what do more frames versus more positions per frame preserve?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aveto">VETO: Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National Taiwan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>More frames favor temporal coverage; more positions favor spatial detail. The local tensor is frames × positions × dimensions, with each keep count bounded by its source axis and output position count equal to their product. No allocation is universally proven optimal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four frames × 16 positions and 16 frames × four both use 64 tokens; the former sees more detail, the latter may catch brief events.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01785">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.01785-veto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-29587d13df18756f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:veto" data-paper-title="VETO: Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-893d97b86bd46781">Why are there both intra-frame and cross-frame redundancies in video?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aveto">VETO: Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National Taiwan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Nearby patches can depict one background, and adjacent frames can repeat one scene. VETO removes duplication along space and time. Each compression axis risks losing different details, so total rate alone does not show required motion or local cues survived.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A wall repeats within and across frames, but a fleeting hand movement needs both temporal coverage and spatial detail.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01785">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.01785-veto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-893d97b86bd46781">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:tess" data-paper-title="TESS: Scalable, Transferable Meta-network for Data Selection Requires a Different Loss (and Why the Obvious Choice is Problematic)" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-tess-5d7b0b3c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b2d1ae7150fa0a51">Why train TESS on loss-gap pseudolabels instead of directly optimizing selection?</h2>
