<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:gear" data-paper-title="Generative End-to-end Ad Retrieval at Douyin" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-779db58082983dba">Why do GEAR BasisVQ and BasisRQ represent codes in a shared orthogonal basis?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agear">Generative End-to-end Ad Retrieval at Douyin</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A common basis coordinates updates; orthogonality constrains rotation so codewords do not drift independently. Hierarchical generation supplies addresses and context reranks collisions. Orthogonality does not guarantee semantic independence or collision-free coding; test quantization and ranking separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two similar items can still share a bucket despite a stable coordinate system.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39327">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.39327-gear/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-779db58082983dba">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:t2spo" data-paper-title="T2SPO: Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-32febe1027d78f23">Why set successor distance to zero at success but directly zero progress at failure?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3At2spo">T2SPO: Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Success reaches the goal; failure only stops execution, so treating it as distance zero creates false progress. Score before updating successful history to avoid leakage. Handle time truncation according to GRPO/PPO.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A tool-exhaustion exit is not zero steps to success and must not reward the final failure.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00388">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.00388-t2spo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-32febe1027d78f23">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:t2spo" data-paper-title="T2SPO: Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1808ae2cbc70dbb5">Does T2SPO optimizer=ppo provide a full PPO trainer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3At2spo">T2SPO: Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It changes truncation semantics only, no critic/GAE. GRPO zeroes truncated credit; PPO uses predicted real successor. Fit standardization/SVD only on historical supports.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Changing an option string does not create a value network.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00388">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.00388-t2spo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1808ae2cbc70dbb5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:t2spo" data-paper-title="T2SPO: Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-dfa8733b74c8bb46">How does distance-improvement credit complement terminal success?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3At2spo">T2SPO: Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Distance differences guide intermediate steps; terminal reward still measures outcome. Mask/scale imperfect forecasts. TabPFN prediction errors don&#x27;t establish task success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An action can move toward the goal without completing it; still verify terminal result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00388">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.00388-t2spo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dfa8733b74c8bb46">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:t2spo" data-paper-title="T2SPO: Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-t2spo-3a6c006a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-140748fa5efbfd50">Why use remaining steps in successful traces as T2SPO distance?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3At2spo">T2SPO: Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Successful history offers state/remaining-step support examples for a frozen in-context predictor, giving denser progress than terminal success. Failure cannot be relabeled as close to success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A state three steps from completion provides a support label.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00388">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.00388-t2spo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-140748fa5efbfd50">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpo" data-paper-title="SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-eb132069cbbc6f92">Why use bounded scaling after rescoring segments against a successful path?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpo">SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Same-group success supplies extra context at the actual prefix. Segment logp gaps express local support. Bounded factors limit amplification and preserve original GRPO direction. Success context remains training-only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Retrieval in a failed trace may resemble a successful path while synthesis diverges, so weight the two segments differently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00838">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.00838-sharpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eb132069cbbc6f92">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpo" data-paper-title="SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c8a64e5d92aa765a">What constraints apply to SHARPO segments and gold plans?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpo">SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Average teacher–student gaps within matching interaction segments and broadcast there, excluding tool observations. Local segments use no gold plan or 7B training; fixtures aren&#x27;t capability evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Mixing a tool call with a different turn&#x27;s answer gives the wrong segment mean.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00838">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.00838-sharpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c8a64e5d92aa765a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpo" data-paper-title="SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a8453c1cebfd958d">How does bounded SHARPO multiplication differ from adding teacher advantage?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpo">SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Twice sigmoid lies between zero and two, so scaling preserves sign and cannot turn zero nonzero. Additive terms can flip credit. The teacher modulates intensity rather than rewriting outcomes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A failed segment can be penalized less but not rewarded merely by teacher preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00838">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.00838-sharpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a8453c1cebfd958d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sharpo" data-paper-title="SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-sharpo-de267e69" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f14e021dde614f5f">Why give SHARPO a successful same-group trajectory as teacher context?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asharpo">SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An in-task success guides rescoring student logp within interaction segments and scales original GRPO advantage. Teacher context is training credit, not a deployment gold plan.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Use a successful path to strengthen related behavior without pasting it into the inference prompt.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00838">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2610.00838-sharpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f14e021dde614f5f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hawk" data-paper-title="HAWK: Rethinking Multimodal Drafting for Speculative Decoding" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-hawk-938adaa0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a6e2431346cfbada">Why train the HAWK drafter on shifted trajectories after its own proposals?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahawk">HAWK: Rethinking Multimodal Drafting for Speculative Decoding</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Proposed tokens put the system on drafter-generated prefixes. Training only on teacher prefixes hides that shift. Shifted trajectories align supervision with actual proposal states, and a mix of teacher layers conveys visual information. The target must still verify acceptance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the first draft token chooses different wording, the second should learn the target distribution under that actual prefix.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00623">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.00623-hawk/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a6e2431346cfbada">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hawk" data-paper-title="HAWK: Rethinking Multimodal Drafting for Speculative Decoding" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1e1157c08ff9a8f8">Does local HAWK validation include a specialized decoding kernel?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahawk">HAWK: Rethinking Multimodal Drafting for Speculative Decoding</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It checks softmax-weighted target hidden states, shifted-target supervision, and target isolation. It does not run a complete speculative verification loop or specialized kernel, so cannot demonstrate end-to-end lossless speedup.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Checking that three weights sum to one does not measure accepted tokens or saved generation time.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00623">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.00623-hawk/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1e1157c08ff9a8f8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hawk" data-paper-title="HAWK: Rethinking Multimodal Drafting for Speculative Decoding" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-08951b88c5bc06ae">How does HAWK&#x27;s learned layer mix differ from using only the final target layer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahawk">HAWK: Rethinking Multimodal Drafting for Speculative Decoding</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Softmax-normalized trainable weights combine hidden states from multiple layers; final-only is a fixed choice of one source. Weights sum to one but need not be equal. Mixing alone proves neither acceptance-rate gains nor speed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A high layer weight increases its share in the mixed representation rather than concatenating layers as extra tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00623">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.00623-hawk/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-08951b88c5bc06ae">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hawk" data-paper-title="HAWK: Rethinking Multimodal Drafting for Speculative Decoding" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-969c6e9709068ac4">What are the target and drafter roles in HAWK speculative decoding?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahawk">HAWK: Rethinking Multimodal Drafting for Speculative Decoding</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The cheaper drafter proposes tokens; the target verifies them and preserves the output distribution. HAWK compresses multiple target layers for a shallow drafter to improve proposals, not to bypass verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A shallow model proposes several words, then the larger model checks how many can be accepted.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00623">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2610.00623-hawk/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-969c6e9709068ac4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rule-evolve" data-paper-title="Self-Evolving Coding Rules for AI Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-rule-evolve-f1ced1e2" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e4060e8043015f09">Why can&#x27;t a mutator write back a coding rule based only on its own assessment?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arule-evolve">Self-Evolving Coding Rules for AI Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A plausible rule may fit only a few examples or damage old behavior. An isolated validation evaluator measures the candidate pool and variants consistently and selects what to write back, separating proposals from acceptance evidence. Selection data are development feedback; do not expose final tests to repeated mutator tuning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A new rule that retries every function sounds robust but can repeat non-idempotent operations. Independent validation can reveal this regression.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00650">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00650-rule-evolve/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e4060e8043015f09">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rule-evolve" data-paper-title="Self-Evolving Coding Rules for AI Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0dd59670d06cd928">Does local selection after mutation establish that LLM rule evolution ran?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arule-evolve">Self-Evolving Coding Rules for AI Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It checks validation selection among mutated candidates but does not call an LLM mutator or full coding agent. Correct argmax over supplied scores is control-flow evidence; if scores come from fixtures, they do not indicate code quality. Retain old rules and failed candidates for audit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Choosing the largest of three preset scores verifies the selector. Without a model proposing rules and actually fixing code, it does not verify the whole self-evolution path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00650">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00650-rule-evolve/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0dd59670d06cd928">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rule-evolve" data-paper-title="Self-Evolving Coding Rules for AI Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5c0648898c9a12dc">How does retaining a rule candidate pool differ from immediately overwriting the only rule, for search and rollback?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arule-evolve">Self-Evolving Coding Rules for AI Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A pool compares multiple versions under one evaluation protocol and retains old rules as baselines or candidates. Immediate overwrite makes the proposal active and can lose a usable baseline after failure. A pool does not supply a correct judge by itself; it still needs an isolated evaluator. Candidate counts are not actual performance on tool tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Keep both a retrieval-focused rule and a testing-focused rule for comparison. If each generation immediately overwrites the rule, it is hard to tell which change caused a regression.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00650">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00650-rule-evolve/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5c0648898c9a12dc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rule-evolve" data-paper-title="Self-Evolving Coding Rules for AI Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-846804b9a08fcd6a">Why does RuleEvolve treat coding rules as development experience that can be tested and revised?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arule-evolve">Self-Evolving Coding Rules for AI Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Coding-agent rules affect recurring search, editing, and testing behavior, and one manually written tip might not fit the task distribution. RuleEvolve selects variants with behavioral evidence so experience can be revised. More detailed wording is not better execution; use isolated validation rather than the generator&#x27;s confidence to update rules.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After adding &#x27;check callers before editing,&#x27; test whether it helps repair the same development tasks, not just whether it sounds sensible.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00650">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00650-rule-evolve/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-846804b9a08fcd6a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memfit" data-paper-title="MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-memfit-d14853dc" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b9ff61056b142ab1">Why store append-only raw turns separately from searchable segment summaries?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemfit">MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Summaries make compact indexes but can omit details. Keeping raw records unchanged gives later close reading traceable evidence. Writes avoid expensive model rewrites of all history; reads combine lexical, semantic, and reranking signals. An index hit is only an entry point, and an omitted summary detail may still exist.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A segment summary says payment API discussion. Read the original turn to find the exact timeout; keeping only the summary might lose it permanently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00872-memfit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b9ff61056b142ab1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memfit" data-paper-title="MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-499b4408c327aeaf">Does the local hybrid retrieval hook mean embedding and cross-encoder inference ran?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemfit">MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The hook accepts lexical, semantic, and reranking signals but does not call a real embedder or cross-encoder. It tests append-only behavior and score combination. Fixture semantic scores cannot establish real long-conversation retrieval quality or paper latency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Correctly sorting three records with preset semantic scores tests fusion, not whether a model derives reliable scores from natural language.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00872-memfit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-499b4408c327aeaf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memfit" data-paper-title="MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e107e4a047780dea">What does inexpensive append-only writing trade off against LLM memory rewriting every turn?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemfit">MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Append-only avoids repeated generation and irreversible rewriting, but raw storage grows and retrieval and indexing do more filtering. LLM writes can abstract early but lose details. Compare writing, storage, and final retrieval quality together, not just call counts in one stage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Saving a thousand raw turns is cheap, but a later query must quickly locate one address change. Inexpensive writes do not guarantee cheap reads.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00872-memfit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e107e4a047780dea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memfit" data-paper-title="MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4b853f8ead5db496">Why does MemFit focus on write costs for high-frequency conversations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemfit">MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A long-lived assistant continually receives turns. Rewriting all memory with a costly model on every turn incurs cost before retrieval and can erase details. MemFit keeps writes lightweight and originals traceable, moving query-specific filtering to reads while facing the growing index size.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A support system gains hundreds of turns per day, many never queried. Complex semantic rewriting of each turn can cost more than useful future queries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00872-memfit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4b853f8ead5db496">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:jev-spawn" data-paper-title="JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-jev-spawn-dc827975" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-03aec54a5d1918af">Why keep several action branches rather than immediately selecting the highest score from the first distribution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ajev-spawn">JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Early probabilities can be wrong. Keeping multiple composite branches leaves room to recover after contradictory evidence. New feedback reweights priors and guides future exploration; it does not rewrite past success labels. Branches consume budget, so parallel retention trades compute for lower decision risk rather than searching all possibilities.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keep both searching and inspecting local files. If search fails, switch to the retained inspection branch without rebuilding the plan from scratch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00437">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00437-jev-spawn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-03aec54a5d1918af">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:jev-spawn" data-paper-title="JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e7e9f27b9bbfb974">Why do p(a)·exp(feedback) updates still need normalization and a branch budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ajev-spawn">JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multiplication yields unnormalized weights. Divide by their total to obtain a distribution, then retain branches within budget. Multiplication cannot recover a branch with zero prior mass, and extreme feedback can cause numerical instability. The local test verifies a finite posterior and top-branch retention without calling a Jev checkpoint.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two branches begin at one half with feedback 0 and 1. Their weight ratio becomes 1:e; e/2 is not a valid probability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00437">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00437-jev-spawn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e7e9f27b9bbfb974">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:jev-spawn" data-paper-title="JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-089d2009fb0016d1">How does branch retention differ from independently resampling plans every round?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ajev-spawn">JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retention preserves the probabilities and states of earlier unchosen options for reuse after feedback. Independent resampling can repeat old errors or lose progress. Retention also consumes compute and memory, so more retained candidates do not prove lower cost; compare at equal budgets.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: After search fails, switch to the existing file-inspection branch. Resampling may suggest the same failed search again.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00437">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00437-jev-spawn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-089d2009fb0016d1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:jev-spawn" data-paper-title="JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5a841ad22d666429">What options does JevSpawn preserve when one agent execution path fails?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ajev-spawn">JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Early judgments in long tasks can be wrong. Spending the entire budget on one action makes contradictory evidence costly. JevSpawn allocates reasoning adaptively by organizing optional actions into retainable composite branches and shifting effort after execution feedback. This preserves alternatives without promising exhaustive search.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Inspecting local data and searching online can both be reasonable. If the first path is blocked, continue the other prepared path rather than starting from a blank plan.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00437">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2610.00437-jev-spawn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5a841ad22d666429">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:recap-ctr" data-paper-title="Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-recap-ctr-8a9efe0a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d48a3ea0b094184">Why share recursive blocks in RECAP-CTR yet average routes and retain a training-trajectory EMA?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arecap-ctr">Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different routes through shared blocks produce multiple logits without independent models. Averaging reduces route fluctuations; EMA smooths weights over training time. Correlated routes limit benefit. Local evidence verifies state and operator invariants only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Two recursive routes yield slightly different click scores; average those while separately smoothing neighboring training checkpoints.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37905">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37905-recap-ctr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d48a3ea0b094184">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:recap-ctr" data-paper-title="Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ec50d7a4585aae79">Why checkpoint RECAP-CTR EMA state separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arecap-ctr">Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>EMA accumulates parameter history across steps, so losing it changes the estimator on resume. Match route count and averaging denominator rather than treating missing routes as zero. Verify recurrence, EMA updates, and export separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Resetting EMA to current parameters after interruption loses thousands of smoothed steps even if training resumes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37905">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37905-recap-ctr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ec50d7a4585aae79">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:recap-ctr" data-paper-title="Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e72f1a396b8fee34">Why can&#x27;t route averaging replace trajectory EMA in RECAP-CTR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arecap-ctr">Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Route averaging combines simultaneous outputs; EMA smooths parameters over time. Shared routes can remain correlated and EMA can lag drift. Local invariants do not show CTR lift from smoothing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: All routes can share a high bias, and EMA can smooth an unusual step without adding a missing feature.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37905">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37905-recap-ctr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e72f1a396b8fee34">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:recap-ctr" data-paper-title="Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5aaae777d05508db">Is averaging RECAP-CTR route logits equivalent to averaging click probabilities?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arecap-ctr">Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Sigmoid is nonlinear. The source averages logits first, which does not turn shared routes into independent complete models.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: With logits 0 and 4, sigmoid of their mean is about 0.88; mean sigmoid is about 0.74.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37905">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37905-recap-ctr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5aaae777d05508db">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:helix" data-paper-title="HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-helix-94ed43e6" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fdc7e424eea56b8a">Why does HELIX forbid candidate tokens from writing back to shared sequence state?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahelix">HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One-way dependence keeps expensive user-history encoding candidate-independent and reusable within a request while candidates repeatedly read it for deep interaction. Writes back would make history candidate-dependent. Local checks cover sensitivity and cache invariance, not production throughput or gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A shoe can reuse the history read by a camera only if the camera did not modify that state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37183">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37183-helix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fdc7e424eea56b8a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:helix" data-paper-title="HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d081140a6218cc83">Why check candidate deltas, invariant user caches, and finite gradients in HELIX?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahelix">HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Candidate changes should alter scores without changing public user state. Missing either indicates ignored candidates or cache pollution; finite loss and gradients test trainability. These are diagnostics, not quality metrics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Identical scores suggest candidate insensitivity; changing scores and cache together breaks sharing despite successful forward execution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37183">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37183-helix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d081140a6218cc83">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:helix" data-paper-title="HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-63277b17cffa622f">How do HELIX one-way communication and WHALE-style bidirectional exchange differ in cacheability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahelix">HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>HELIX blocks candidate-conditioned writes into public sequence state. Bidirectional exchange allows deeper co-evolution but creates candidate dependence. Both can use cross-attention without equivalent dependencies, and no universal quality ordering follows.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After a camera reads shared history, shoes can read the same cache only if the camera state never wrote back.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37183">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37183-helix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-63277b17cffa622f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:helix" data-paper-title="HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-21fa62a2c298c656">Why does HELIX expand both sequence modeling and heterogeneous feature interaction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahelix">HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>History and feature combinations supply distinct information. Interleaved modules let candidate states read history at multiple depths while preserving user-only state. This is not late concatenation, and caching constrains direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Layers can combine travel history with price and device features; enlarging either path alone cannot provide the other&#x27;s evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37183">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37183-helix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-21fa62a2c298c656">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:grp" data-paper-title="GRP v0.1 Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-grp-12c5e416" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c1a13612a425df6">Why activate GRP&#x27;s one-sided logged-target margin only when original-target retrieval suffers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agrp">GRP v0.1 Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reward optimization can move mass to a few high-reward outputs and lower logged-target probability. Penalize decreases past tolerance while permitting other improvements. Freeze and stop gradients through the ranking reward head to prevent co-adaptation. Local objectives and gradients do not verify production funnel replacement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Improve new candidates without a penalty if the original target remains competitive; penalize shifting all mass to one high-reward category.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36688">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.36688-grp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c1a13612a425df6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:grp" data-paper-title="GRP v0.1 Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5ccd8a0812b61c8e">Why does GRP&#x27;s MHP ranking head read detached generator representations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agrp">GRP v0.1 Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Ranking gradients through shared encoding and SID paths can damage existing retrieval. Stop-gradient trains the ranker without changing the generator from this loss. Version it when frozen as RL reward and verify actual gradient separation rather than only registration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Updating ranking BCE should change the head but not send gradients into the SID-generation backbone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36688">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.36688-grp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5ccd8a0812b61c8e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:grp" data-paper-title="GRP v0.1 Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-094cd821bb640a1f">What freedom does GRP&#x27;s one-sided margin retain compared with symmetric probability constraints?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agrp">GRP v0.1 Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Only a logged-target drop beyond reference tolerance incurs penalty, leaving other preference improvements free. Symmetric constraints may suppress beneficial changes too. Target preservation does not validate the new reward, and local checks only cover surrogate objectives and gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Raise better candidates while preserving the logged target without penalty; a large abandonment of that target activates the guard.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36688">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.36688-grp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-094cd821bb640a1f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:grp" data-paper-title="GRP v0.1 Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e4195cdb964d413c">Why migrate GRP&#x27;s recommendation funnel gradually instead of replacing all stages at once?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agrp">GRP v0.1 Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Established systems serve several goals and risks. Introduce an additional retrieval source, replace weak sources, increase quota, and then bypass ranking progressively. Keep original recall protections and separate evidence and permissions per stage; a unified design is not a finished rollout.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Start with a small candidate share and expand only after validation rather than removing retrieval and fine ranking on one offline win.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36688">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.36688-grp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e4195cdb964d413c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cohortmix-ts" data-paper-title="Challenges and Solutions for Bandits in the Wild: Warm-Started Mixture Bandits for Cross-Cohort Slate Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-cohortmix-ts-f84d0507" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a52b737be11c2a3b">Why does CohortMix-TS use a mixed Beta prior with fixed strength instead of inheriting all cohort counts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acohortmix-ts">Challenges and Solutions for Bandits in the Wild: Warm-Started Mixture Bandits for Cross-Cohort Slate Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DFKI / RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Similar cohorts can warm-start a new user, but copying their sample sizes would make personal observations ineffective for too long. Mix cohort means, use controlled pseudocounts, and update on individual exposure feedback. Thompson sampling retains exploration, and local evidence only checks the posterior mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With 100,000 cohort events and three personal events, full inheritance drowns out the new user. Fixed prior strength allows personal preference to take over gradually.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37800">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37800-cohortmix-ts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a52b737be11c2a3b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cohortmix-ts" data-paper-title="Challenges and Solutions for Bandits in the Wild: Warm-Started Mixture Bandits for Cross-Cohort Slate Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-dc1bab4e714e15fa">Why keep independent Beta counts per new user and exclude previously exposed slate items in CohortMix-TS?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acohortmix-ts">Challenges and Solutions for Bandits in the Wild: Warm-Started Mixture Bandits for Cross-Cohort Slate Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DFKI / RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The cohort prior only initializes state. Subsequent success and failure belong to that user&#x27;s arm, not every new user. Select from unseen items each round for sequential exploration; unexposed arms do not receive invented failures.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A comedy click updates only the viewing user&#x27;s success count. An action movie not shown receives no feedback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37800">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37800-cohortmix-ts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dc1bab4e714e15fa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cohortmix-ts" data-paper-title="Challenges and Solutions for Bandits in the Wild: Warm-Started Mixture Bandits for Cross-Cohort Slate Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea291b7996f80080">How does CohortMix-TS explore differently from always choosing the highest posterior mean?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acohortmix-ts">Challenges and Solutions for Bandits in the Wild: Warm-Started Mixture Bandits for Cross-Cohort Slate Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DFKI / RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Greedy selection ignores uncertainty. Thompson sampling draws from each posterior, giving uncertain but promising arms a chance; more evidence naturally reduces uncertainty. It does not improve every round, and the local three-seed state-transition diagnostic is not recommendation capability evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A slightly lower-mean, rarely observed arm can sometimes beat a well-known arm in sampled scores, while greedy selection may never try it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37800">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37800-cohortmix-ts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ea291b7996f80080">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cohortmix-ts" data-paper-title="Challenges and Solutions for Bandits in the Wild: Warm-Started Mixture Bandits for Cross-Cohort Slate Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-75004509b0ab288c">Why does CohortMix-TS construct a mixed cohort prior before sufficient personal data arrive?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acohortmix-ts">Challenges and Solutions for Bandits in the Wild: Warm-Started Mixture Bandits for Cross-Cohort Slate Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DFKI / RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Few personal observations give unstable success estimates. Infer cohort memberships from metadata and mix historical item-arm means to guide initial exploration. Fixed strength limits borrowed confidence so individual feedback can gradually revise it. Shared membership does not imply identical preferences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Initialize a new user&#x27;s movie success rates from two cohorts, then let a few personal outcomes move the posterior away from the group average.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37800">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.37800-cohortmix-ts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-75004509b0ab288c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:weakest-link" data-paper-title="The Weakest Link: Distilling LLM Reasoning with Worst-Case Constrained Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
