<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37725">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.37725-context-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1b83f4d20e64d534">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:branch-mixture" data-paper-title="Mixture of Self-Improving Branches for Agent Harness Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-branch-mixture-203f2124" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-aabf9fb0b40ae634">Why remove development examples solved by every branch while retaining examples that distinguish branches?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abranch-mixture">Mixture of Self-Improving Branches for Agent Harness Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Shared solved examples provide little information about branch differences and can dilute weaknesses while consuming budget. Each branch retains a discriminating subset and proposal strategy, and a deployment router picks a development champion by input. An adaptive development set is not an independent final test; routing cannot use test labels to choose a winner.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If all branches solve simple sorting but graph search distinguishes two strategies, devote more curriculum budget to the latter rather than repeatedly testing common strengths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37834">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.37834-branch-mixture/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aabf9fb0b40ae634">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:branch-mixture" data-paper-title="Mixture of Self-Improving Branches for Agent Harness Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6112ff8a7f4f4deb">May a deployment router read branches&#x27; true scores on the current test item to pick the winner?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abranch-mixture">Mixture of Self-Improving Branches for Agent Harness Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Use input features to select a development champion without test labels or future execution scores. The local implementation provides subset diversification and linear routing, not LLM-generated harnesses or SWE-bench runs. Correct branch choice on fixtures does not show real mixture gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Running all branches and selecting the hidden judge&#x27;s best result is an oracle ensemble, not deployment routing based on request inputs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37834">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.37834-branch-mixture/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6112ff8a7f4f4deb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:branch-mixture" data-paper-title="Mixture of Self-Improving Branches for Agent Harness Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-9a69ceef4c84d93f">What assumption differs between routing across specialist branches and always running one global champion?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abranch-mixture">Mixture of Self-Improving Branches for Agent Harness Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A global champion assumes one harness covers all inputs. Branch mixtures allow workflows to specialize and choose among them from public input features. Specialization may improve fit but adds routing errors and maintenance cost. Routing must use deployment-visible information, not current test gold scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Code and browsing tasks can have different development champions. Routing by task features is deployable; reading both branches&#x27; gold scores on the current test before choosing is not.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37834">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.37834-branch-mixture/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9a69ceef4c84d93f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:branch-mixture" data-paper-title="Mixture of Self-Improving Branches for Agent Harness Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d71231e390a01996">Why should branches maintain different development subsets and proposal policies?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abranch-mixture">Mixture of Self-Improving Branches for Agent Harness Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>When all branches see the same examples and use the same proposals, they can converge to redundant harnesses. Distinct subsets and strategies preserve specialization that the router can select by input. Additional branches also increase development cost; do not hide total search budget when comparing with one branch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One branch can specialize in tool formats and another in long-horizon verification, giving routing meaningful alternatives rather than copies under different names.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37834">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.37834-branch-mixture/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d71231e390a01996">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:promptshift" data-paper-title="Measuring and Mitigating Identity-Cue Preference Drift in LLM-based Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-promptshift-7e539145" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-27ec4d2dd288c79e">Why hold history fixed and vary only identity prompts in PromptShift, then measure Drift and SliceShift separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apromptshift">Measuring and Mitigating Identity-Cue Preference Drift in LLM-based Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Electronic Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Changing both confounds actual preference and identity cues. Drift measures overlap/rank changes and SliceShift measures cohort popularity direction; mainstreamness conditions relevance and inverse-popularity blending. This is a controlled sensitivity diagnostic, not causal discrimination proof.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Use the same movie history with and without identity text to see whether rankings shift toward cohort-popular films.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34229">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.34229-promptshift/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-27ec4d2dd288c79e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:promptshift" data-paper-title="Measuring and Mitigating Identity-Cue Preference Drift in LLM-based Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cc6ed8a8ddc8268a">What must stay fixed between PromptShift&#x27;s reference and identity-prompt lists?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apromptshift">Measuring and Mitigating Identity-Cue Preference Drift in LLM-based Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Electronic Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Keep history, candidates, model, and decoding as consistent as possible and vary the identity cue only. Handle shared item ranks and set changes as defined; do not pair disjoint items artificially. Do not choose mitigation on test.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If one arm also has recent clicks, drift may come from the extra behavior rather than identity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34229">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.34229-promptshift/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cc6ed8a8ddc8268a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:promptshift" data-paper-title="Measuring and Mitigating Identity-Cue Preference Drift in LLM-based Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-2fd0165111d28e58">Where does user conditioning enter adaptive inverse-popularity blending versus a uniform tail bonus?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apromptshift">Measuring and Mitigating Identity-Cue Preference Drift in LLM-based Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Electronic Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mainstreamness m changes the mix of relevance and inverse popularity, unlike a uniform bonus. Both can hurt relevance. Diagnostics do not establish real fairness or satisfaction and do not belong on formal capability leaderboards.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A mainstream user and a niche user may need different corrections; pushing even more obscurity can be unhelpful for the latter.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34229">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.34229-promptshift/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2fd0165111d28e58">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:promptshift" data-paper-title="Measuring and Mitigating Identity-Cue Preference Drift in LLM-based Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-12d0a4e2ffd1606c">Does high PromptShift Drift directly imply lower accuracy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apromptshift">Measuring and Mitigating Identity-Cue Preference Drift in LLM-based Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Electronic Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Drift measures list change, not relevance of old and new items. SliceShift adds popularity direction, not quality. Independent relevance or feedback is needed; do not relabel sensitivity as accuracy loss.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Swapping two equally suitable films changes rank drift without necessarily hurting the user.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34229">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.34229-promptshift/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-12d0a4e2ffd1606c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:evoskillrec" data-paper-title="EvoSkillRec: Skill-Genome Evolution for Recommender Architecture Discovery" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-evoskillrec-7ef949da" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-11fbd5c6574e563d">Why type-check adjacent skills in a genome instead of chaining high-scoring modules arbitrarily?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aevoskillrec">EvoSkillRec: Skill-Genome Evolution for Recommender Architecture Discovery</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · City University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Individually good modules may have incompatible shapes and semantics. Check input/output contracts, construct executable candidates, evaluate validation, and store only promoted combinations. Names and types alone do not integrate a skill; three local seeds check composition and state transitions, not capability rankings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An item-vector producer cannot feed a full-history consumer without a suitable adapter and semantic validation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34552">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.34552-evoskillrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-11fbd5c6574e563d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:evoskillrec" data-paper-title="EvoSkillRec: Skill-Genome Evolution for Recommender Architecture Discovery" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-aaaed1d71fd23064">Why is matching final tensor width insufficient for skill type checks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aevoskillrec">EvoSkillRec: Skill-Genome Evolution for Recommender Architecture Discovery</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · City University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>B×d user vectors, B×C×d candidate tensors, and B×T×d sequence states have distinct roles. Check batch, candidate, and time semantics, then execute and evaluate. Local state-transition diagnostics do not rank capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Broadcasting one user vector over all candidates can run but loses candidate differences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34552">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.34552-evoskillrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aaaed1d71fd23064">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:evoskillrec" data-paper-title="EvoSkillRec: Skill-Genome Evolution for Recommender Architecture Discovery" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b51a0203ac02a2fe">How does validation promotion protect EvoSkillRec&#x27;s reuse library versus keeping every skill?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aevoskillrec">EvoSkillRec: Skill-Genome Evolution for Recommender Architecture Discovery</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · City University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Only innovations exceeding a baseline threshold become reusable, reducing propagation of untested or harmful modules. The threshold is still bounded by budget and data, and neither type checks nor repeated test selection establish quality. Keep failures as failures.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Record a shape-correct module that lowered validation, but do not promote it as a default skill.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34552">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.34552-evoskillrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b51a0203ac02a2fe">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:evoskillrec" data-paper-title="EvoSkillRec: Skill-Genome Evolution for Recommender Architecture Discovery" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-3735285efdd844ab">Why require executable skill I/O contracts in EvoSkillRec?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aevoskillrec">EvoSkillRec: Skill-Genome Evolution for Recommender Architecture Discovery</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · City University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Natural-language names do not ensure composability. Types make genomes executable and uniformly evaluable but are only the first check; semantics and recommendation quality need validation and promotion separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A sequence encoder can feed a vector head, but a candidate-set consumer needs an explicit conversion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34552">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.34552-evoskillrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3735285efdd844ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ross" data-paper-title="ROSS: Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9faad04c9357c685">Why retain full context but supervise selected continuation only?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aross">ROSS: Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · AllSpark Team（原文以团队署名，未列机构）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>History determines what state the continuation addresses. Masked supervision avoids imitating mistakes/redundancy while keeping context visible. Fixed local masks do not implement the paper selector.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An early error can remain visible while only a later successful repair is learned.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35954">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35954-ross/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9faad04c9357c685">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ross" data-paper-title="ROSS: Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-18dbcba85610e737">Is the local ROSS selector learned?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aross">ROSS: Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · AllSpark Team（原文以团队署名，未列机构）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A fixture mask verifies full-context/selective-loss boundaries, not autonomous selection of useful historical steps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Marking the last two sentences manually tests adherence, not discovery.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35954">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35954-ross/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-18dbcba85610e737">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ross" data-paper-title="ROSS: Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-138dd71554ebd473">How does ROSS differ from deleting unselected spans before SFT?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aross">ROSS: Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · AllSpark Team（原文以团队署名，未列机构）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Deletion changes conditional state, while full context plus masked loss preserves the trace. Selector quality still matters; mask correctness is not selector implementation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Removing a wrong prefix can change meaning/likelihood of a corrective sentence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35954">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35954-ross/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-138dd71554ebd473">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ross" data-paper-title="ROSS: Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-ross-56261390" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-53158c924443c142">Why reuse historical self-rollout in ROSS without imitating all of it?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aross">ROSS: Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · AllSpark Team（原文以团队署名，未列机构）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Old traces contain mistakes/redundancy. Full context conditions later behavior; selective continuation labels retain only valuable segments. Visible text need not be target.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Read the failure history but supervise only its selected correction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35954">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35954-ross/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-53158c924443c142">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:roft" data-paper-title="Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fa5d3a606524d353">Why supervise only retrospection tokens, not actions or feedback?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aroft">Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>History conditions the lesson, but the target is the later reflection. Separate input and loss masks and globally average reflection tokens. Local fixtures/registry aren&#x27;t a complete agent/Evolve loop.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Read a bad call and error, but learn the parameter-check lesson, not the bad call or tool error text.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35741">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35741-roft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fa5d3a606524d353">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:roft" data-paper-title="Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d3fe3fffdba6ba97">How normalize losses across differently sized ROFT retrospections?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aroft">Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Average all valid reflection tokens globally. Keep tasks/actions/observations/feedback as context but mask their loss. Per-reflection means change length weights. No full agent data/Evolve loop.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Short and long reflections contribute different total mass under token vs example means.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35741">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35741-roft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d3fe3fffdba6ba97">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:roft" data-paper-title="Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-dd724cac5d5c8bf5">How does ROFT differ from cloning original actions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aroft">Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Cloning repeats recorded behavior; reflection supervision can teach avoiding it. Different labels and reflection quality still matters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After deleting a wrong file, learn to check paths rather than repeat deletion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35741">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35741-roft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dd724cac5d5c8bf5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:roft" data-paper-title="Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-roft-6e694561" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7af0302d79d9d6da">Why turn environment feedback into retrospection before ROFT learning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aroft">Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Terminal reward rarely expresses reusable lessons. Text reflections summarize useful experience from successes/failures. The reflection is the target, not every historical action.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A permission mistake can teach checking access before next time.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35741">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35741-roft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7af0302d79d9d6da">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:olive" data-paper-title="Learning from Teacher Continuations at Student States" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4d5768797235694a">Why don&#x27;t OLIVE prefixes receive supervised loss?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aolive">Learning from Teacher Continuations at Student States</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The teacher continues the student&#x27;s actual prefix, giving useful next-step examples without treating student mistakes as correct labels. Apply CE only to teacher tokens. Teacher quality and full-model experiments remain separate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Read a repairable wrong expression and learn only the corrected teacher continuation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36246">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.36246-olive/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4d5768797235694a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:olive" data-paper-title="Learning from Teacher Continuations at Student States" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-af1bd061756a9659">Can OLIVE remove prefixes from input because they have no loss?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aolive">Learning from Teacher Continuations at Student States</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Prefix remains conditioning for continuation and student supervision; mask targets only. Handle concatenation, EOS and padding. Local tests verify masks without a closed teacher.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Retain three mistaken steps as context without training to imitate them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36246">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.36246-olive/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-af1bd061756a9659">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:olive" data-paper-title="Learning from Teacher Continuations at Student States" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-648e9cd502b8ce7a">How does teacher continuation CE differ from scoring original student tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aolive">Learning from Teacher Continuations at Student States</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Continuation adds newly generated teacher text as target; rescoring evaluates existing sampled actions/states. A scoring kernel doesn&#x27;t produce new teacher continuations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Writing the next steps differs from rating the old steps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36246">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.36246-olive/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-648e9cd502b8ce7a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:olive" data-paper-title="Learning from Teacher Continuations at Student States" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-olive-4870752f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-be7936ba40a16330">Why let OLIVE teacher continue from student-visited states?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aolive">Learning from Teacher Continuations at Student States</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Student mistakes differ from ideal teacher paths. Real prefixes supply deployment-like supervision for continuation/recovery instead of memorizing complete solutions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Continue from an unusual intermediate expression the student reached.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36246">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.36246-olive/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-be7936ba40a16330">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:mas-opd" data-paper-title="MAS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Agent Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f1042ce3ff30e42a">Why put conflict attribution in teacher view instead of changing every role&#x27;s reward?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amas-opd">MAS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Agent Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One team score doesn&#x27;t identify corrections. Privileged teacher distinguishes target and other contributions. Extra attribution is training-only and local mask/advantage does not establish multi-model collaboration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A sound planner and an executor using the wrong tool shouldn&#x27;t receive the same blame.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34234">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.34234-mas-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f1042ce3ff30e42a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:mas-opd" data-paper-title="MAS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Agent Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6a2f647ebe9aace5">Does local MAS-OPD jointly train real models?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amas-opd">MAS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Agent Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It tests role advantage and conflict masks. Align roles, traces and valid generated positions. Registry labels or misassigned signals don&#x27;t establish team training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Swapping role order can keep arrays valid while assigning credit to the wrong member.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34234">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.34234-mas-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6a2f647ebe9aace5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:mas-opd" data-paper-title="MAS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Agent Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0ff64018a557f657">How does teacher-only conflict information differ from giving full attribution to all roles?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amas-opd">MAS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Agent Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Students act on their own public histories; only teacher sees extra conflict explanation. Giving hindsight to students changes deployment inputs and hides whether learning internalized it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teacher may know who misunderstood after failure; deployed members cannot start with that diagnosis.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34234">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.34234-mas-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0ff64018a557f657">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:mas-opd" data-paper-title="MAS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Agent Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-mas-opd-e3c3be86" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0ff54511f31821a3">Why add role-specific advantage in MAS-OPD?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amas-opd">MAS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Agent Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Terminal team outcomes hide member responsibility. Target vs other-role teacher signals supply local collaboration credit. Verify attribution rather than punish everyone equally.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Good retrieval and faulty summarization call for different credit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34234">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.34234-mas-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0ff54511f31821a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:lspd" data-paper-title="An RL View of OPD: Least Square Policy Distillation for Sample-Efficient LLM Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-940f981ab925625c">Why use a quadratic center with Huber tails instead of squared loss throughout?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Alspd">An RL View of OPD: Least Square Policy Distillation for Sample-Efficient LLM Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Quadratic shrinks small logp gaps while linear tails bound outlier influence and retain correction direction. Average responses equally. Reused old traces are not fresh current-policy samples.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One teacher-improbable token can dominate squared loss; robust tails curb it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35505">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35505-lspd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-940f981ab925625c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:lspd" data-paper-title="An RL View of OPD: Least Square Policy Distillation for Sample-Efficient LLM Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5ef6042f7787ae37">How handle teacher gradients and lengths in LSPD?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Alspd">An RL View of OPD: Least Square Policy Distillation for Sample-Efficient LLM Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Freeze teacher logp. Average differentiable student gaps over valid tokens per response, then responses equally, with specified entropy subtraction. Registry presence doesn&#x27;t prove executable Evolve.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Long replies do not automatically receive twice the weight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35505">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35505-lspd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5ef6042f7787ae37">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:lspd" data-paper-title="An RL View of OPD: Least Square Policy Distillation for Sample-Efficient LLM Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-6facb14ce3c65e7b">How does robust LSPD behave in tails compared with reverse KL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Alspd">An RL View of OPD: Least Square Policy Distillation for Sample-Efficient LLM Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It explicitly limits residual slope; KL is defined through distribution/probability weights. Clipping KL isn&#x27;t equivalent. Replay also changes state provenance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Doubling tail residual changes linear and unbounded quadratic gradients differently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35505">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35505-lspd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6facb14ce3c65e7b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:lspd" data-paper-title="An RL View of OPD: Least Square Policy Distillation for Sample-Efficient LLM Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-lspd-3161a2b9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d188b7e250db6eeb">Why treat teacher–student logp gaps as robust residuals in LSPD?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Alspd">An RL View of OPD: Least Square Policy Distillation for Sample-Efficient LLM Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Squared loss shrinks ordinary gaps; Huber-like linear tails limit gradients from extreme ones. Residual regression can reuse older trajectories.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A rare token&#x27;s huge log gap should not dominate a batch indefinitely.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35505">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.35505-lspd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d188b7e250db6eeb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:telescopic-lm" data-paper-title="Telescopic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-telescopic-lm-c2ab9fe1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ede6a79b9ddd5bb5">Why train multiple depth prefixes instead of truncating a finished deep model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atelescopic-lm">Telescopic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Standard training supervises the full path, not necessarily viable intermediate exits. Telescopic trains sampled prefixes with next-token supervision plus a full-depth anchor. Evaluate shallow and deep capabilities separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Running eight versus 24 layers is supported only if the eight-layer exit was explicitly trained.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35769">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2609.35769-telescopic-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ede6a79b9ddd5bb5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:telescopic-lm" data-paper-title="Telescopic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5ba76aef5a3a17ce">How check that random prefixes do not replace the full-depth anchor?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atelescopic-lm">Telescopic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Verify full-depth loss and gradients on every specified step and record the sampled depth. Local diagnostics do not reproduce 20B-token pretraining.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Even when sampling a shallow exit, confirm full-depth parameters still receive their signal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35769">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2609.35769-telescopic-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5ba76aef5a3a17ce">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:telescopic-lm" data-paper-title="Telescopic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-37256dd8e30f5391">How do sampled prefixes differ from training all depths every step?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atelescopic-lm">Telescopic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sampled training gives prefix supervision to selected depths plus the full anchor; all depths cost more per step. Match compute rather than only parameter count.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One three-layer exit is not equivalent in cost to every exit from one to 12.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35769">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2609.35769-telescopic-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-37256dd8e30f5391">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:telescopic-lm" data-paper-title="Telescopic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cafa935d4f4aefa8">Why support multiple depths in one Telescopic checkpoint?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atelescopic-lm">Telescopic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Budgets and inputs can need different depths. Supervise prefixes and full depth so shallow execution is an explicit trained option.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Choose a shorter prefix rather than train one checkpoint per depth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35769">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2609.35769-telescopic-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cafa935d4f4aefa8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ms-gla" data-paper-title="MS-GLA: Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention for Addressing Representational Bottlenecks via Multi-Temporal Resolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-ms-gla-a1875a93" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea64391758996402">How does MS-GLA avoid leaking later tokens when pooling a block?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ams-gla">MS-GLA: Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention for Addressing Representational Bottlenecks via Multi-Temporal Resolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each coarse branch masked-averages nonoverlapping blocks and runs GLA. A summary becomes visible only at the block end; causal hold restores token resolution without broadcasting into earlier positions. Input-conditioned weights fuse scales.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>In a four-token block, position two cannot see the average including positions three and four.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35664">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2609.35664-ms-gla/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ea64391758996402">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ms-gla" data-paper-title="MS-GLA: Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention for Addressing Representational Bottlenecks via Multi-Temporal Resolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-97483a5c9b1dce32">When may tokens access scale-four pooled state?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ams-gla">MS-GLA: Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention for Addressing Representational Bottlenecks via Multi-Temporal Resolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>At or after the block&#x27;s final token. Use causal hold and input softmax fusion rather than broadcasting full means to every token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Token one cannot use the average of words one through four before word four arrives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35664">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2609.35664-ms-gla/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-97483a5c9b1dce32">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ms-gla" data-paper-title="MS-GLA: Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention for Addressing Representational Bottlenecks via Multi-Temporal Resolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8d3d6b392df03331">Why is multiscale GLA more than a larger window?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ams-gla">MS-GLA: Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention for Addressing Representational Bottlenecks via Multi-Temporal Resolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each scale pools at a different nonoverlapping granularity before GLA, changing temporal update resolution. Extending a window still updates at the original rate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Updating once per four words differs from updating every word while looking farther back.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35664">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2609.35664-ms-gla/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8d3d6b392df03331">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ms-gla" data-paper-title="MS-GLA: Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention for Addressing Representational Bottlenecks via Multi-Temporal Resolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-95933f677c9061f9">Why give MS-GLA heads different temporal scales?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ams-gla">MS-GLA: Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention for Addressing Representational Bottlenecks via Multi-Temporal Resolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One resolution can bottleneck representations. Some heads preserve token-level variation, others use pooled history, and their outputs combine.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Phrase detail and trends across phrases can use different update rates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35664">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2609.35664-ms-gla/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-95933f677c9061f9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:frac-ssm" data-paper-title="Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-frac-ssm-9d35422b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-70c0b6310e5e85f1">How do finitely many recurrent states approximate long fractional-order power-law memory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afrac-ssm">Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei Noah&#x27;s Ark Lab, Montreal Research Center</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One exponential has one decay timescale. Log-spaced modes approximate a power-law tail: fast modes handle recent changes and slow ones keep older influence. Finite capacity and approximation range do not give unlimited exact memory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Fast, medium, and slow channels combine into a longer tail than one decay.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36314">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2609.36314-frac-ssm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-70c0b6310e5e85f1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:frac-ssm" data-paper-title="Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea7bf61d830b801b">What should finite-mode recurrence tests verify besides shape?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afrac-ssm">Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei Noah&#x27;s Ark Lab, Montreal Research Center</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Verify equivalence to the finite-mode calculation, long-tail invariants, and state propagation. Operator checks are not reproduction of 1.3B training or model quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Inject an early impulse and compare combined decay over time with the defined approximation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36314">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2609.36314-frac-ssm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ea7bf61d830b801b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:frac-ssm" data-paper-title="Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4881d67379b8f1c5">Why do multiple decay rates approximate a long tail better?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afrac-ssm">Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei Noah&#x27;s Ark Lab, Montreal Research Center</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Log-spaced modes span recent and distant timescales, unlike a single exponential. Their finite combination approximates a bounded range, not infinite exact history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Fast modes track fluctuations while slow ones retain trends.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
