<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:harness-bandit" data-paper-title="HarnessBandit: Joint Learnability-Transferability Scheduling for Multi-Harness Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-harness-bandit-ffd58529" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ab71656976360ab1">Why schedule multi-harness training using both learnability and transferability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aharness-bandit">HarnessBandit: Joint Learnability-Transferability Scheduling for Multi-Harness Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harbin Institute of Technology / Alibaba Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An easy harness may teach only its specific interface; a transferable but currently hard one may need exploration. Combining both signals and a bonus allocates limited budget and avoids overfitting to easy scores. Scheduling weights are training decisions; a reference function or multi-seed diagnostics are not cross-harness ability evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A provides many hints and B resembles deployment. Do not give A all budget for faster near-term gains without checking whether the learning transfers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13739">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.13739-harness-bandit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ab71656976360ab1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:harness-bandit" data-paper-title="HarnessBandit: Joint Learnability-Transferability Scheduling for Multi-Harness Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-2437ebba3b51eb5c">Do local online harness-selection counts establish completed multi-harness LLM RL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aharness-bandit">HarnessBandit: Joint Learnability-Transferability Scheduling for Multi-Harness Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harbin Institute of Technology / Alibaba Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The reference runs gates, allocation, and state updates, without real LLM RL, full rollouts, or transfer benchmarks. Synthetic learnability and transferability check weight response, not portable capability. Three-seed scheduling statistics cannot establish training effects.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>More allocations to an arm with a supplied high transfer score verify the scheduler. A manually set score does not measure model transfer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13739">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.13739-harness-bandit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2437ebba3b51eb5c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:harness-bandit" data-paper-title="HarnessBandit: Joint Learnability-Transferability Scheduling for Multi-Harness Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0750ff4e3195da29">What trade-offs distinguish uniform multi-harness allocation from bandit scheduling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aharness-bandit">HarnessBandit: Joint Learnability-Transferability Scheduling for Multi-Harness Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harbin Institute of Technology / Alibaba Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Uniform allocation does not adapt to changing payoffs. A bandit can sample more from environments worth learning or uncertain at the current stage. It may favor short-term proxies and spend budget on exploration, so assess scheduling cost and transfer rather than only within-harness efficiency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After one harness saturates, shift budget to paths with transferable gains, while occasionally revisiting it to guard against stale estimates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13739">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.13739-harness-bandit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0750ff4e3195da29">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:harness-bandit" data-paper-title="HarnessBandit: Joint Learnability-Transferability Scheduling for Multi-Harness Agentic Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b961ccb8ddc0f357">Why might learning in one harness fail to improve performance under other interfaces?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aharness-bandit">HarnessBandit: Joint Learnability-Transferability Scheduling for Multi-Harness Agentic Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harbin Institute of Technology / Alibaba Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tool protocols, prompts, and workflows change which states and actions are encountered. Some learning is specific to that organization. Harness Bandit allocates budget across harnesses for both learning and transfer. In-training gains are not cross-interface generalization; report evaluation conditions separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A model familiar with one edit command may face different arguments elsewhere. More practice on the known interface can improve its score without improving transfer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13739">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.13739-harness-bandit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b961ccb8ddc0f357">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mima" data-paper-title="MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-mima-5191fe9f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a7737838b5685202">Why match multiple positives in a MIMA request one-to-one with interests instead of independently choosing the closest?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amima">MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent selection can send all gradients to one interest. MIMA forms an interest–positive similarity cost matrix and finds a globally optimal one-to-one assignment, giving distinct interests supervision. Activation probabilities then calibrate channels. Specialization comes from set supervision, not just more vectors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Running shoes and a hiking pack can both choose one sports channel under independent matching. A one-to-one assignment makes two channels explain the positives separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12842">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.12842-mima/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a7737838b5685202">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mima" data-paper-title="MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-8833e9be64e7f356">When do exhaustive search and Hungarian matching optimize the same MIMA objective, and what cannot replace them?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amima">MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Both solve the same cost matrix&#x27;s optimal one-to-one assignment; exhaustive search can verify small cases. Greedy matching is generally not equivalent. Use aligned interest–positive similarities and separately calibrate channels with log activation probability. Plausible pairs do not establish optimality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A greedy first positive can take the only good slot for the second. Exhaustive enumeration can find the lower-cost allocation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12842">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.12842-mima/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8833e9be64e7f356">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mima" data-paper-title="MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-34e97c32a3372408">How does one-to-one MIMA matching avoid crowding one channel compared with independently taking the nearest interest?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amima">MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent argmax can give all positives to one interest and starve the others. Global assignment distributes slots to minimize total cost. Define unmatched handling when counts differ; forced matching can also give a noisy positive its own channel and does not ensure semantic independence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Two items slightly prefer interest one. One-to-one matching evaluates the total cost of assigning either to interest two, unlike greedy independent matching.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12842">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.12842-mima/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-34e97c32a3372408">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mima" data-paper-title="MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1132beb05c6cad64">Why treat positives in one MIMA request as a set rather than imposing an order?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amima">MIMA: Multi-Interest Recommendation via Multi-Positive Exclusive Assignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Coexisting interests need not be assigned by artificial order. Set matching is permutation-insensitive and encourages specialization; routing estimates actual activation. Historical encoding can still be causal; only positive supervision changes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A request can like shoes and a pack without defining which to learn first or letting the strongest sports channel explain both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12842">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.12842-mima/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1132beb05c6cad64">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:chronicle-rec" data-paper-title="ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-chronicle-rec-efcf1d9a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fe7e940e49d3f624">Why must a Chronicle Token have a time anchor and summarize only preceding events?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Achronicle-rec">ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Without the boundary, an earlier representation could include future events, violating temporal causality and making cache meaning unclear. ChronicleRec compresses different ranges, anchors queries on the timeline, reads earlier events only, and masks recent behavior in multiple ways to align short-term intent. Anchored candidate-independent summaries are reusable across candidates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A Wednesday summary must not include Friday&#x27;s camera purchase when scoring Thursday lens recommendations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.12375-chronicle-rec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fe7e940e49d3f624">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:chronicle-rec" data-paper-title="ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ae7ea3a33cae636b">Why normalize Chronicle Token pooling by valid mask count and read at the query position?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Achronicle-rec">ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Padding should not shrink short histories; masks and a safe denominator average real events only. Read after causal encoding at the query anchor so the state summarizes only earlier events. Other positions and padded events can alter semantics without causing shape errors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A four-slot window with two real actions divides by two. Put the query after both to summarize both; a query between them cannot see the later one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.12375-chronicle-rec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ae7ea3a33cae636b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:chronicle-rec" data-paper-title="ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-491ae24f291ae309">How does ChronicleRec alignment pretraining differ from ordinary next-item prediction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Achronicle-rec">ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Branches hide different lengths of recent actions so compressed older history must predict recent intent without nearby evidence. Ordinary next-item prediction may lean on adjacent actions. Do not return hidden targets to evaluation inputs, or the compression test loses its meaning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Hide the latest three parenting views and predict the new interest from older history instead of guessing the next item from the last parenting item.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.12375-chronicle-rec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-491ae24f291ae309">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:chronicle-rec" data-paper-title="ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ae60800a02e46d24">Why does ChronicleRec represent near, middle, and distant history instead of a few unordered interest tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Achronicle-rec">ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multi-scale pooling preserves temporal structure. Query anchors delimit the past being summarized so stable preferences and recent changes remain distinct. Candidate-independent Chronicle Tokens can be cached, but public compression can still discard target-specific details.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A long-term science-fiction preference and this week&#x27;s parenting interest mean more with time scales than as two unordered keywords.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.12375-chronicle-rec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ae60800a02e46d24">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:sas-attention" data-paper-title="SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-sas-attention-90d42e99" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d6b2dc7c35d29a0f">How does SAS train its selector despite nondifferentiable top-k indices?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asas-attention">SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent HY LLM Frontier / HKUST (Guangzhou) / HKUST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It preserves continuous gates for selected blocks and adds log gates inside attention softmax. LM loss differentiates through gate values, not indices. History gates normalize jointly and the current block stays at one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Changing two selected gates from 0.8/0.2 to 0.6/0.4 changes output and gradients without changing indices.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13141">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.13141-sas-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d6b2dc7c35d29a0f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:sas-attention" data-paper-title="SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5d9c14bab0803e99">Where does SAS add the log gate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asas-attention">SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent HY LLM Frontier / HKUST (Guangzhou) / HKUST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Add log gates for selected history to attention logits before shared softmax. Normalize history gates together and set current block to one. Post-output scaling changes the normalization relationship.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Current gate one adds zero; history blocks compete with their respective log gates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13141">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.13141-sas-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5d9c14bab0803e99">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:sas-attention" data-paper-title="SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-9fdfbe025d1dba3e">How does LM-loss selector training differ from distilling dense attention rankings?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asas-attention">SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent HY LLM Frontier / HKUST (Guangzhou) / HKUST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Token prediction provides task feedback rather than supervising imitation of dense attention. It needs continuous gates; hard top-k remains nondifferentiable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A block ranked highly by the dense model need not contribute equally to prediction loss.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13141">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.13141-sas-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9fdfbe025d1dba3e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:sas-attention" data-paper-title="SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8e073aa1cf873934">Why keep continuous SAS gates rather than only selected indices?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asas-attention">SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent HY LLM Frontier / HKUST (Guangzhou) / HKUST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The integer indices choose blocks but do not carry gradients. Gates in attention let prediction loss train selection scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Identical selected blocks with 0.8/0.2 versus 0.5/0.5 produce different outputs and gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13141">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.13141-sas-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8e073aa1cf873934">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hcrg" data-paper-title="Beyond Vector Similarity: Hierarchical Context-Aware Graph RAG vs Standard RAG in Enterprise Code Migration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-hcrg-d21831b9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-62471e72ac894fa6">Why can&#x27;t a cyclic dependency graph have a node-wise parents-first topological order?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahcrg">Beyond Vector Similarity: Hierarchical Context-Aware Graph RAG vs Standard RAG in Enterprise Code Migration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Nodes in a directed cycle depend on one another, so no linear order satisfies all edges. Identify strongly connected components and separate ordering across components from migration within them. AST context reveals this limit, but it does not invent a cycle-breaking method the paper never defines.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A calls B and B imports A. Analyze them as a cycle, not as though migrating A first satisfies all parent dependencies.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12464">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.12464-hcrg/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-62471e72ac894fa6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hcrg" data-paper-title="Beyond Vector Similarity: Hierarchical Context-Aware Graph RAG vs Standard RAG in Enterprise Code Migration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-febd84dd63974652">How should static graphs handle local-variable shadowing and unresolved symbols?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahcrg">Beyond Vector Similarity: Hierarchical Context-Aware Graph RAG vs Standard RAG in Enterprise Code Migration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Same names can denote different definitions, and local binding hides globals. Do not connect unresolved calls to arbitrary same-name repository nodes. Retain scope and unresolved status, then retrieve only known structure. Local support is bounded Python AST, not all dynamic calls or other paper languages.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: If a function assigns a local object to a global tool&#x27;s name, later calls use the local binding, not a global node with the same text.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 代码映射与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12464">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.12464-hcrg/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-febd84dd63974652">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hcrg" data-paper-title="Beyond Vector Similarity: Hierarchical Context-Aware Graph RAG vs Standard RAG in Enterprise Code Migration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-61a331bb82962207">How does three-hop structural context differ from vector retrieval over 800-character chunks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahcrg">Beyond Vector Similarity: Hierarchical Context-Aware Graph RAG vs Standard RAG in Enterprise Code Migration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Vector chunks return textually similar fragments. Structural retrieval follows inheritance, calls, and imports, potentially finding related code with different words. Both miss things. Some paper metrics on a single repository decline, so structure does not uniformly improve migrations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A utility&#x27;s name has little lexical overlap with a migration issue, but a call edge still brings it into context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12464">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.12464-hcrg/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-61a331bb82962207">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hcrg" data-paper-title="Beyond Vector Similarity: Hierarchical Context-Aware Graph RAG vs Standard RAG in Enterprise Code Migration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0f0b7b0eab559fdf">Why identify parent dependencies before migrating callers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahcrg">Beyond Vector Similarity: Hierarchical Context-Aware Graph RAG vs Standard RAG in Enterprise Code Migration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Parent classes, imports, and called interfaces shape assumptions in dependent code. Migrating resolvable parents first stabilizes context. HCRG extracts AST structure up to three hops. Static graphs cannot cover all dynamic calls, and unresolved symbols should not be matched to arbitrary same-name definitions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Migrating a superclass constructor signature first makes it easier to update subclasses consistently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12464">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.12464-hcrg/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0f0b7b0eab559fdf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:unirec" data-paper-title="UniRec: Cross-Stage Multi-Task Fusion with Preference Optimization for Cascaded Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0c25f39de037db51">Why preserve both directions for one pair in CPPA?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aunirec">UniRec: Cross-Stage Multi-Task Fusion with Preference Optimization for Cascaded Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Objectives can disagree, and a majority loses strength and minority signal. Both softplus penalties remain, CAPP selects confident directions, and grouped KL limits drift. Downstream supervision is training-only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Clicks favor A while purchases favor B; majority voting can hide the purchase signal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11052">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.11052-unirec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0c25f39de037db51">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:unirec" data-paper-title="UniRec: Cross-Stage Multi-Task Fusion with Preference Optimization for Cascaded Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7061b74a6ba3a598">How keep cross-stage gradient isolation and AGRR evidence separate from pruning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aunirec">UniRec: Cross-Stage Multi-Task Fusion with Preference Optimization for Cascaded Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Cross-stage alignment uses survivors and freezes the fine-ranker direction. AGRR builds grouped KL targets from unpruned inputs, not centered scores. Document variance and quantile ties.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Computing evidence after pruning changes the distribution AGRR should see.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11052">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.11052-unirec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7061b74a6ba3a598">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:unirec" data-paper-title="UniRec: Cross-Stage Multi-Task Fusion with Preference Optimization for Cascaded Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-dee5064fb3689990">How does CPPA differ from majority-voting among objectives?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aunirec">UniRec: Cross-Stage Multi-Task Fusion with Preference Optimization for Cascaded Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Opposing evidence contributes to two softplus terms rather than discarding the minority. CAPP chooses confident directed pairs and AGRR controls group drift separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Clicks can prefer A and watch time B; retain both directions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11052">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.11052-unirec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dee5064fb3689990">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:unirec" data-paper-title="UniRec: Cross-Stage Multi-Task Fusion with Preference Optimization for Cascaded Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-unirec-cd2efe22" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-505d1682319fe757">Why keep two separate pre-ranking and ranking towers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aunirec">UniRec: Cross-Stage Multi-Task Fusion with Preference Optimization for Cascaded Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Their features, candidate scales, and latency differ. Share some embeddings and align downstream preference through training, without exposing expensive online ranking input upstream.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Pre-ranking learns fine-ranker preference from supervision, not its full feature set.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11052">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.11052-unirec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-505d1682319fe757">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sirf" data-paper-title="SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-02322f33c7044fe8">Why train synthetic trigger/exemption rules and threshold one verdict?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asirf">SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Long-tail combinations are scarce in logs. Rule graphs, rewrites, and account reasoning teach combinations during continued pretraining; one verdict saves online work. Threshold trades precision and recall. Local interactions are not production capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Frequent trades can trigger concern, but verified merchant status may exempt them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.11752-sirf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-02322f33c7044fe8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sirf" data-paper-title="SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5f6775ad35692318">Does the local high-precision threshold reproduce full 8B continued pretraining?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asirf">SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It uses trigger/exemption proxies, not private accounts, EntiGraph/MAGA generation, or large training. Select thresholds on validation and keep held-out reporting separate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A small classifier reaching precision target does not reproduce a safety foundation model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.11752-sirf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5f6775ad35692318">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sirf" data-paper-title="SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-f64f6bf87f503425">How does learned rule internalization differ from a runtime rules engine?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asirf">SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Learned models can generalize language and context but need not obey every rule exactly. Explicit engines obey coded conditions with limited coverage. Accuracy is not formal proof.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A model may retain an old policy after the rule changes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.11752-sirf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f64f6bf87f503425">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sirf" data-paper-title="SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-sirf-2c896048" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4bba0f8aa5a2e65c">Why train on both triggers and exemptions in SIRF?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asirf">SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Safety decisions depend on exceptions as well as triggers. Synthetic rules and continued pretraining aim to cover rare combinations; thresholds manage precision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A keyword need not violate policy in an explicitly exempt explanatory context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.11752-sirf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4bba0f8aa5a2e65c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tasco" data-paper-title="Beyond Confidence: Stability-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for LLM Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3bf3e360a7863e6c">Why check stability in addition to confidence during TASCO adaptation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atasco">Beyond Confidence: Stability-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for LLM Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Chongqing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Confidence can reinforce wrong answers. Keep backbone fixed, tune a small prefix and penalize unstable predictions under neighborhood perturbations. Stability is unlabeled evidence, not a correctness oracle; no real local LM prefix training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If equivalent wording changes the answer, high original confidence alone is a poor signal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11393">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.11393-tasco/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3bf3e360a7863e6c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tasco" data-paper-title="Beyond Confidence: Stability-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for LLM Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-9e74343bb7ff5725">Does the local TASCO stability penalty train an actual LM prefix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atasco">Beyond Confidence: Stability-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for LLM Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Chongqing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It implements random neighborhood perturbation and a stability reference kernel without a frozen LM prefix path. Small-vector tests do not establish test-time gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Stable numeric features do not show a language model&#x27;s prefix was optimized on tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11393">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.11393-tasco/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9e74343bb7ff5725">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tasco" data-paper-title="Beyond Confidence: Stability-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for LLM Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7138500cadc224d7">How do TASCO prefix updates and best-of-N spend extra compute differently?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atasco">Beyond Confidence: Stability-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for LLM Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Chongqing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>TASCO optimizes conditioning before a frozen model predicts; best-of-N generates and selects more candidates. Compare optimizer forwards/backwards and generation, not just candidate count.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Several gradient steps and several independently generated answers are different workloads.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11393">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.11393-tasco/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7138500cadc224d7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tasco" data-paper-title="Beyond Confidence: Stability-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for LLM Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-tasco-a3638c7c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6ae37dc4a87906c6">Does TASCO adapt backbone weights or a lightweight prefix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atasco">Beyond Confidence: Stability-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for LLM Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Chongqing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Freeze the backbone and optimize an added prefix, changing conditioning without retraining the model or selecting only by sampling. It uses unlabeled current-task signals, never test gold.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Update prefix vectors and reread probabilities while leaving model layers and answer labels untouched.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11393">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.11393-tasco/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6ae37dc4a87906c6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:nsd" data-paper-title="Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b7073cf71d4eaf23">Why not suppress the entire erroneous answer in NSD?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Ansd">Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Virginia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Negative teacher gives a distribution to avoid, with dynamic gates selecting reasoning-critical tokens while preserving useful language/steps. Selection doesn&#x27;t prove errors and full LM training wasn&#x27;t reproduced.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A carry error needn&#x27;t suppress every connective and correct digit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11699">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.11699-nsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b7073cf71d4eaf23">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:nsd" data-paper-title="Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-fdf24dcd2d314d24">What supplies local NSD negative teachers and gates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Ansd">Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Virginia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Candidate policies test control flow, not full-parameter LLM. Freeze and align gates to penalized positions; test gold cannot preidentify errors under no-leakage claims.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Hand-labeled errors are a unit fixture, not autonomous error localization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11699">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.11699-nsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fdf24dcd2d314d24">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:nsd" data-paper-title="Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-886ee3b24ca799ed">How does negative self-distillation differ from lowering every wrong answer token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Ansd">Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Virginia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Wrong responses can contain valid facts, grammar and steps. Selective gating limits collateral damage, but isn&#x27;t a verified step label.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A wrong result doesn&#x27;t mean all numbers and connectives should be forgotten.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11699">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2609.11699-nsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-886ee3b24ca799ed">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:nsd" data-paper-title="Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/teacher-and-context">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/teacher-and-context/">LLM post-training / Teachers and correction: when extra context can help</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-nsd-9169c0f1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-156313e8fb4c0f9c">Why use self-generated mistakes as negative teaching material in NSD?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Ansd">Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Virginia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Failures identify directions to avoid. Negative teacher models error distribution and a dynamic gate concentrates suppression on key reasoning while protecting ordinary language.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A misused proof rule can supply an avoid signal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
