<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arandom-attention">Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Salesforce AI Research / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Prompt preservation keeps task conditions and initial evidence fixed. Per-head random retention avoids scoring and gives diverse coverage, but may miss important reasoning and must fit the protected prompt budget. GPU reconstruction is not full task or kernel evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Different heads can see different reasoning fragments while all still read the original question.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03430">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.03430-random-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-11ce14334bb11855">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:random-attention" data-paper-title="Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-2e7ddbb5a54699df">May the method drop prompt entries if B is smaller than prompt length?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arandom-attention">Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Salesforce AI Research / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Not under full prompt protection. B−|P| must be a valid generation budget. Raise the budget or report infeasibility rather than changing the method silently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A 100-entry prompt cannot fit untouched into 80 slots.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03430">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.03430-random-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2e7ddbb5a54699df">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:random-attention" data-paper-title="Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-bda7ea99e557586e">How does independent per-head sampling differ from a shared random set?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arandom-attention">Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Salesforce AI Research / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Head-specific sets vary evidence coverage; shared sampling applies one restriction everywhere. Average budgets can match while errors and coverage correlations differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One head can keep position five and another eight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03430">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.03430-random-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bda7ea99e557586e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:random-attention" data-paper-title="Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cd62a3fce54a9f29">Why omit KV importance scoring in Random Attention?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arandom-attention">Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Salesforce AI Research / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Scoring costs compute and can impose one shared ranking. Protect the prompt and sample generated positions uniformly per head as a simpler cache trade-off.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Keep part of each head&#x27;s history without scanning all tokens for importance first.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03430">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.03430-random-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cd62a3fce54a9f29">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lngram-v2" data-paper-title="Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-lngram-v2-f7907f6f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-194361272e173289">Why use counterfactual neighbor addresses and a zero sink with hard Lngram v2 lookups?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alngram-v2">Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications / Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Binary addresses are discrete and ordinary indexing gives no smooth address gradient. Neighbor comparisons train address choice. GQA reads retrieved tokens alongside a zero sink so irrelevant memory need not be injected.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A neighbor may be more useful than the addressed phrase; if neither helps, attend to zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03426">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.03426-lngram-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-194361272e173289">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lngram-v2" data-paper-title="Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d7d21dd14de1dcdd">Why include a zero sink instead of always using lookup results?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alngram-v2">Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications / Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It lets GQA reject irrelevant memory. Counterfactual adjacent addresses supply training signals; the integer index is not ordinarily differentiable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A query can attend to zero to keep an unhelpful lookup out of the residual.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03426">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.03426-lngram-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d7d21dd14de1dcdd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lngram-v2" data-paper-title="Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4e2fba325ae21ace">How do latent addresses differ from text n-gram hashes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alngram-v2">Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications / Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Backbone hidden projections carry context, while text hashes depend directly on discrete input fragments. They do not share an address space or interpretation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The same word in different contexts can yield different latent addresses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03426">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.03426-lngram-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4e2fba325ae21ace">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lngram-v2" data-paper-title="Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-138ae0d1173848d4">Why turn hidden states into discrete n-gram addresses?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alngram-v2">Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications / Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Recent-state combinations index a memory table in expected O(1); multiple results feed back into the backbone. Explicit addressing has a trainable projection and is not lookup of literal strings only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two binary hidden-state codes can form a 2-gram key.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03426">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.03426-lngram-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-138ae0d1173848d4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:silr" data-paper-title="SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2e48dd4d8eb6dd50">Why shouldn&#x27;t a safety gate reject every action that leaves any residual violation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asilr">SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Science Tokyo</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Recovery can require intermediate states that remain partly unsafe. Rejecting all of them can deadlock the system. SiLR shadow-executes and requires every constrained branch not to worsen, allowing gradual improvement. A total can hide branch regressions, and shadow outcomes must match real execution contracts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Revoke one of two problematic permissions first. The system remains imperfect but improves; requiring all violations to disappear in one step can block recovery.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04629">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.04629-silr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2e48dd4d8eb6dd50">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:silr" data-paper-title="SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f4644d5aa5ea7b39">Can SiLR substitute an unreliable simulator for real effects during shadow execution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asilr">SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Science Tokyo</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Not as a safety claim. Admission requires deterministic, adequately covering verification. Shadow first, compare states, then execute. Without a real simulator, local checks establish only structured criteria and process signals.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If shadowing omits deletion side effects, an unchanged vector can conceal actual risk.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04629">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.04629-silr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f4644d5aa5ea7b39">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:silr" data-paper-title="SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-28c3f5f612d987c1">How does product order differ from adding violation severities into one score?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asilr">SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Science Tokyo</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Componentwise non-worsening prevents improvement on one branch from offsetting deterioration on another. A scalar can hide that exchange. Preserve constraints; a weighted sum is not an equivalent safety gate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Storage savings do not justify expanded permissions even if a combined score decreases.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04629">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.04629-silr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-28c3f5f612d987c1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:silr" data-paper-title="SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-silr-f498d510" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0f68f6731f7ec1f4">Does SiLR shadow execution undo actions after real execution fails?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asilr">SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Science Tokyo</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It evaluates proposed state effects on a shadow path before a gate admits real execution. Separate proposal assessment from real effects; executing first cannot establish prevention, especially for irreversible effects.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Simulate which constraints a configuration edit touches before committing, rather than breaking the configuration and then attempting rollback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04629">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.04629-silr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0f68f6731f7ec1f4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:multi-harness-rl" data-paper-title="What Does Multi-Harness RL Learn? Credit Assignment and Portability in Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-multi-harness-rl-66c31df3" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2cb0d51874f501b1">What confound is isolated by freezing task–harness trajectories and changing only advantage grouping?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amulti-harness-rl">What Does Multi-Harness RL Learn? Credit Assignment and Portability in Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multi-harness training changes both data diversity and credit comparison groups. Comparing complete systems confounds them. Fixed trajectories let within-task comparison of cross-harness and within-harness normalization more directly test grouping. Report transfer differences and uncertainty on unseen minimal harnesses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reuse trajectories for one repair task under two interfaces and recompute grouped advantages without resampling. This reduces attribution of sampling changes to the credit rule.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04518">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.04518-multi-harness-rl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2cb0d51874f501b1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:multi-harness-rl" data-paper-title="What Does Multi-Harness RL Learn? Credit Assignment and Portability in Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f053cdb0bfd492e6">Why does a held-out Cross−Within interval spanning zero fail to establish transfer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amulti-harness-rl">What Does Multi-Harness RL Learn? Credit Assignment and Portability in Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A small positive point estimate is still compatible with no change; interpret the paper alongside its paired confidence interval. Old local gold-reading scores are invalid. Current checks cover grouping, gradients, and protocols, without Qwen RL, actual coding harnesses, or a sealed oracle. Counts are not SWE-bench capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A 0.25 percentage-point gain with negative values inside the interval does not establish reliable superiority over Within. Do not omit the interval and report only the positive estimate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04518">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.04518-multi-harness-rl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f053cdb0bfd492e6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:multi-harness-rl" data-paper-title="What Does Multi-Harness RL Learn? Credit Assignment and Portability in Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ed1a599911375548">How do Within and Cross change the relative meaning of the same reward?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amulti-harness-rl">What Does Multi-Harness RL Learn? Credit Assignment and Portability in Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Within normalizes inside each task–harness group, comparing sibling trajectories in one environment. Cross normalizes across harnesses for the same task, including between-environment reward differences in advantages. It can learn environment preferences; portability needs paired tests on an unseen minimal harness, not just training means.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A stronger-tool harness can earn generally positive Cross advantages because its rewards are higher. That does not imply better code repair on a minimal interface.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04518">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.04518-multi-harness-rl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ed1a599911375548">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:multi-harness-rl" data-paper-title="What Does Multi-Harness RL Learn? Credit Assignment and Portability in Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c9a85584b1ebed7b">Why separate base-model capability from execution-interface effects in multi-harness RL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amulti-harness-rl">What Does Multi-Harness RL Learn? Credit Assignment and Portability in Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different prompts, tools, and workflows change success on the same task; grouping changes the meaning of rewards. Multi-Harness RL examines their effects on learning and transfer. If the base, tasks, or samples also change, attribution is difficult. Control trajectories and evaluation definitions instead of calling all cross-harness gains capability growth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One harness fills arguments automatically while another requires the model to fill them. Success differences may reflect interface help rather than base reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04518">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2609.04518-multi-harness-rl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c9a85584b1ebed7b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:coral" data-paper-title="CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-coral-3b3ed34a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-89bd6b73ca40a757">Why does CORAL project configurations onto a budget-feasible set and retain only recent experiment memory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acoral">CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>LLM proposals can contain negative allocations or exceed quotas. Projection creates executable candidates before real feedback informs the next round. Short memory helps adapt to change and limits stale guidance but does not justify deleting audit records. Feasible proposals still need quality validation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If three retrieval allocations exceed a request cap, adjust them before testing. After traffic shifts, an old optimum should not automatically dominate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02730">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.02730-coral/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-89bd6b73ca40a757">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:coral" data-paper-title="CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-80652d133f4a6d24">Why not clip each CORAL allocation separately when projecting onto nonnegative values under a total budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acoral">CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Per-coordinate clipping fixes negative values but not the coupled sum bound B. Joint projection enforces both. Store the executed configuration with its observations, not the infeasible proposal. The five-round local run verifies constraints and loop executability only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Three individually legal allocations of 6 total 18, exceeding a cap of 10. Adjust together and record what actually ran.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02730">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.02730-coral/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-80652d133f4a6d24">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:coral" data-paper-title="CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b9b80dc33e148828">When is CORAL&#x27;s short memory preferable to retaining the all-time best configuration?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acoral">CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Recent feedback is more useful when the environment shifts; all-time maxima assume greater stability. CORAL updates from recent observations under projected constraints, potentially forgetting valuable long-run experience. A small proxy score cannot resolve the trade-off universally.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A holiday ad mix can be poor afterward. Recent evidence should matter, while durable safety constraints should not be forgotten.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02730">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.02730-coral/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b9b80dc33e148828">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:coral" data-paper-title="CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c6fbfac3347e3e68">Why does CORAL require structured objectives and budgets rather than free-form LLM optimization advice?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acoral">CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A system must verify, execute, and compare configurations. Budgets define legal allocations and objectives translate observations into feedback. A successful loop is not by itself production causal evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Asking for more retrieval compute is not executable until channels and amounts are specified and checked against the cap.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02730">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.02730-coral/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c6fbfac3347e3e68">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:tgr" data-paper-title="TGR: Advancing Industrial Recommendation from Generative-Paradigm Ranking toward Unified Generation and Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d75ea81538d30e34">Why put scalable ranking, hierarchical SID generation, and offline reason tokens in one framework?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atgr">TGR: Advancing Industrial Recommendation from Generative-Paradigm Ranking toward Unified Generation and Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Ranking discriminates finely, SID generation spans items and pages, and offline tokens carry prepared reasoning online. Inspect generation paths, list objectives, and reasoning interfaces separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Precompute interest explanations, generate a page from them, and rank without live long reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00986">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.00986-tgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d75ea81538d30e34">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:tgr" data-paper-title="TGR: Advancing Industrial Recommendation from Generative-Paradigm Ranking toward Unified Generation and Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f873bd8a2c7dea0f">Does local path confidence reproduce production CCFormer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atgr">TGR: Advancing Industrial Recommendation from Generative-Paradigm Ranking toward Unified Generation and Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The public core omits private SID catalog, checkpoints, and live generation. Align level probabilities and list scores explicitly; proxy fusion is not deployment evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A working multi-level code score is not a complete page generator or ranker.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00986">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.00986-tgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f873bd8a2c7dea0f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:tgr" data-paper-title="TGR: Advancing Industrial Recommendation from Generative-Paradigm Ranking toward Unified Generation and Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-29d2f0e011d8ee0d">What is the trade-off between offline reason tokens and live inference?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atgr">TGR: Advancing Industrial Recommendation from Generative-Paradigm Ranking toward Unified Generation and Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Offline reduces critical-path latency but can age and miss abrupt context changes. Live reasoning is flexible but expensive. Compare inputs and update cadence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Yesterday&#x27;s reasoning can miss today&#x27;s trending topic.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00986">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.00986-tgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-29d2f0e011d8ee0d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:tgr" data-paper-title="TGR: Advancing Industrial Recommendation from Generative-Paradigm Ranking toward Unified Generation and Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-tgr-d333ba35" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7bd5864e166f1cb2">Why combine ranking, generation, and offline reason in TGR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atgr">TGR: Advancing Industrial Recommendation from Generative-Paradigm Ranking toward Unified Generation and Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Industry needs scalable scoring and item/list generation at controlled latency. Offline reasoning supplies inputs without costly online rollouts; distinct modules are not one attention equation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Prepare reasoning offline, then generate and rank live candidates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00986">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.00986-tgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7bd5864e166f1cb2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rest" data-paper-title="From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-rest-5ed56a69" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ffc3ae495ed6b99c">Why separate heavy user encoding and light candidate interaction in ReST compute-once, decode-many?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arest">From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Long-history gated attention, order, and time intervals are shared user compute. Candidate cross-decoders read relevant evidence without rerunning history. Dual gates suppress noise, but only candidate-independent state is reusable and history/version changes invalidate it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Encode history once for 200 films, then let each query it; never share one film&#x27;s interaction result as general user state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01240">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.01240-rest/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ffc3ae495ed6b99c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rest" data-paper-title="From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-106636ac34f6a61f">What dependencies matter before reusing ReST encoder caches across requests?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arest">From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Same-request hU reuse requires unchanged history and version. New events, relative time encodings, or model updates can invalidate cross-request state. Candidate decoder outputs remain private to their candidates. Local structure does not prove production QPS or cache lifecycle.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: After a user buys a camera, update history instead of reusing the old summary forever because user ID matches.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01240">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.01240-rest/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-106636ac34f6a61f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rest" data-paper-title="From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b147c7ec89040e41">What evidence does ReST gating preserve compared with truncation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arest">From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Truncation discards events; gating can suppress noise across broader history while retaining distant evidence for candidate decoding. It can suppress important items too and still incurs input cost. A small local regression does not show gating beats recent-window baselines.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Keep a small weight on old photography and downweight accidental news; truncation could remove the useful photography event entirely.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01240">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.01240-rest/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b147c7ec89040e41">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rest" data-paper-title="From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-587482482f0ab50e">Why combine RoPE and relative time in ReST?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arest">From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Position and elapsed time differ: adjacent events can be a minute or a year apart. RoPE represents order, time encoding adds cadence, and dual gates filter noise. Not all periodicity is captured and large gaps are not always irrelevant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Camera views five minutes apart suggest one comparison; views six months apart may mark a new need.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01240">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.01240-rest/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-587482482f0ab50e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:cue2narrate-drl" data-paper-title="From Visual Cues to Spoken Narration: Rethinking Audio Description" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<span id="paper-multimodal-models-cue2narrate-drl-b44764fd" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-611aae51c5d5db99">Why backpropagate through a negative caption&#x27;s current likelihood if a frozen model generated it?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Acue2narrate-drl">From Visual Cues to Spoken Narration: Rethinking Audio Description</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TU Darmstadt &amp; hessian.AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Freezing its generator fixes the negative text, not the trainable model&#x27;s scores. DRL compares mean target-token log likelihoods for positive and negative texts with the same visual input. Gradients improve their relative preference; detaching the negative score changes the contrastive optimization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>For the same scene, one caption says a person walks and the other says they run. The strings are fixed, but the trainable model still changes their relative scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01725v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/2609.01725-cue2narrate-drl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-611aae51c5d5db99">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:cue2narrate-drl" data-paper-title="From Visual Cues to Spoken Narration: Rethinking Audio Description" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e8bcd9e2f80d297e">Can SFT and DRL use one shared length normalization?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Acue2narrate-drl">From Visual Cues to Spoken Narration: Rethinking Audio Description</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TU Darmstadt &amp; hessian.AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The pinned SFT sums valid target tokens per sample before the batch mean. DRL averages token log probabilities separately in each description. Both exclude prompt and padding; freezing the negative generator does not stop gradients through the current model&#x27;s negative-caption scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>For 10 positive tokens and 20 negative tokens, DRL compares their means. Raw sums would additionally penalize the longer description.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01725v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/2609.01725-cue2narrate-drl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e8bcd9e2f80d297e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:cue2narrate-drl" data-paper-title="From Visual Cues to Spoken Narration: Rethinking Audio Description" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0bcd2ec1cbd06a88">What does DRL add beyond SFT on positive descriptions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Acue2narrate-drl">From Visual Cues to Spoken Narration: Rethinking Audio Description</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TU Darmstadt &amp; hessian.AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>SFT raises correct target-token likelihood; DRL explicitly separates positive and negative mean log probabilities. This adds a relative signal whose meaning depends on how negatives are built. Trivial negatives do not automatically teach detailed visual grounding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Raising the likelihood of “She sits down” need not lower the model&#x27;s score for the wrong “She runs away.” The relative loss constrains the pair directly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01725v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/2609.01725-cue2narrate-drl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0bcd2ec1cbd06a88">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:cue2narrate-drl" data-paper-title="From Visual Cues to Spoken Narration: Rethinking Audio Description" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c735438cc2e66022">Why pair the negative caption with the same visual cue and prompt?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Acue2narrate-drl">From Visual Cues to Spoken Narration: Rethinking Audio Description</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TU Darmstadt &amp; hessian.AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Matching conditions isolates whether the descriptions suit the intended audio-description task. Changing image or prompt could instead change task difficulty. Offline negative captions are training material, not an extra deployment generation step.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Score “She sets down the cup” and an unrelated-action caption with the same film clip and instruction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01725v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/2609.01725-cue2narrate-drl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c735438cc2e66022">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:setmir" data-paper-title="SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-92167d9dee9cf98d">Why use one-to-one matching in training and presence/NMS in serving?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asetmir">SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Matching prevents training collapse onto one positive. Presence activates relevant slots per request; NMS removes redundant retrieval calls. These solve different problems.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Activate photography and camping, then suppress two nearly identical camera queries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30251">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.30251-setmir/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-92167d9dee9cf98d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:setmir" data-paper-title="SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-9c478711239026dd">Which SetMIR queries actually dispatch ANN?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asetmir">SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Only those passing presence and surviving query NMS. The public CPU path does not reproduce private histories, production Transformer, or ANN dispatch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Ten available slots need not make ten calls.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30251">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.30251-setmir/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9c478711239026dd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:setmir" data-paper-title="SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-37ab5a0653ba7420">How does one-to-one set matching differ from independent slot choices?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asetmir">SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Joint assignment limits slots from repeatedly explaining one easy positive. It needs reliable target sets; unique assignments do not prove complete interest discovery.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Assign slots to sports and photography rather than both greedily choosing sports.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30251">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.30251-setmir/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-37ab5a0653ba7420">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:setmir" data-paper-title="SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-setmir-231692c0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1dbb7554298c2ace">Is a SetMIR query a user-entered search string?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asetmir">SetMIR: Multi-Interest Retrieval as Set Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It is a generated interest vector or slot for ANN. Multiple slots capture possible interests; serving rules decide which activate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Opening recommendations can produce sports and photography vectors without a typed query.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30251">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.30251-setmir/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1dbb7554298c2ace">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:camie" data-paper-title="CAMIE: Co-Engagement-Aware Multimodal Item Embeddings for Snap Dynamic Product Ads Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-camie-634faffd" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1b92b9cd74adef7f">Why add co-engagement contrastive learning rather than training CAMIE item vectors only on image-text similarity?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acamie">CAMIE: Co-Engagement-Aware Multimodal Item Embeddings for Snap Dynamic Product Ads Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Content resemblance does not guarantee a consumption relationship. CAMIE uses item pairs jointly engaged with in a user journey for symmetric contrastive supervision, shaping multimodal embeddings for recommendation. The shared encoder supports variable modality availability. Co-engagement still reflects exposure and context, not universal complementarity or causal demand.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Similar furniture can serve incompatible uses, while visually different desks and chairs are often considered together. Behavior supervision adds that relation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30255">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.30255-camie/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1b92b9cd74adef7f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:camie" data-paper-title="CAMIE: Co-Engagement-Aware Multimodal Item Embeddings for Snap Dynamic Product Ads Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-74acf9ceaf1f9727">Why compute both directions of CAMIE&#x27;s symmetric in-batch InfoNCE?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acamie">CAMIE: Co-Engagement-Aware Multimodal Item Embeddings for Snap Dynamic Product Ads Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One direction uses a as query and its paired b as positive among the batch&#x27;s b values. Swap sides to supervise both encoders and average the losses. Pairs must share the intended journey relation, temperature controls sharpness, and duplicated positives should not blindly count as negatives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Learn camera-to-lens and lens-to-camera matching. A duplicate row for the same positive lens would otherwise give contradictory supervision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30255">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.30255-camie/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-74acf9ceaf1f9727">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:camie" data-paper-title="CAMIE: Co-Engagement-Aware Multimodal Item Embeddings for Snap Dynamic Product Ads Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-76fca7b0a2ff4204">How do CAMIE&#x27;s co-engagement positives differ from generic image-text contrastive positives?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acamie">CAMIE: Co-Engagement-Aware Multimodal Item Embeddings for Snap Dynamic Product Ads Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Image-text positives typically pair modalities of the same content. Co-engagement pairs different items that share user interactions in a journey, encoding potential complementarity or sequential needs. Exposure still affects which items co-occur, so it is not an unbiased complementarity label.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A tent and sleeping bag may convert together despite very different images; two popular items may merely co-occur because both receive heavy exposure.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30255">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.30255-camie/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-76fca7b0a2ff4204">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:camie" data-paper-title="CAMIE: Co-Engagement-Aware Multimodal Item Embeddings for Snap Dynamic Product Ads Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5287e4bcfb9cffed">Why should one CAMIE checkpoint support image-text and text-only products?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acamie">CAMIE: Co-Engagement-Aware Multimodal Item Embeddings for Snap Dynamic Product Ads Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Real catalog modality availability varies. A shared interface lets products without pictures enter the same retrieval space instead of requiring separate models. Joint training and behavior alignment support matching across inputs, but a missing image removes information, so accuracy need not be equal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A title-only launch and an item with images and attributes can both be indexed, but the former has no visual details to recover.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30255">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.30255-camie/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5287e4bcfb9cffed">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:skilldreamer" data-paper-title="Imagine Before Acting: Prospective Skill Identification for LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-skilldreamer-d1e698b9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-874ddf7bcc58f94f">After generating a pseudo skill, why does CSI recheck capability fit before execution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Askilldreamer">Imagine Before Acting: Prospective Skill Identification for LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Sichuan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The pseudo skill turns a goal into a procedural retrieval proxy. It may locate related documents, but it is not verified and may not fit the subgoal. CSI rechecks evidence, constraints, and the next bounded action, linking retrieval to correct use without assuming imagined steps are executable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A pseudo skill can find a web download procedure. Before executing, check whether the current page requires login instead of following a similar document title blindly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01642">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2609.01642-skilldreamer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-874ddf7bcc58f94f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:skilldreamer" data-paper-title="Imagine Before Acting: Prospective Skill Identification for LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-9583328c6cf5170b">Does CSI check every five reasoning turns or every five executed actions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Askilldreamer">Imagine Before Acting: Prospective Skill Identification for LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Sichuan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It counts actually executed actions. Before the next action, recheck the current subgoal, evidence, and constraints; MATCH or PARTIAL_MATCH loads the real procedure first.
