</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlvr-fusion" data-paper-title="Consolidating RLVR Capabilities Across Domains: A Deep Dive into Fusion Paradigms" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7a1eadf46dc7ae5e">Why are Merge, Mix RL and MOPD different fusion operations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlvr-fusion">Consolidating RLVR Capabilities Across Domains: A Deep Dive into Fusion Paradigms</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Fudan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Merge combines expert parameter increments, Mix RL trains on combined data, and MOPD uses expert guidance with data. Availability and budget determine feasible routes. Similar means or a probability-vector proxy do not establish lossless checkpoint fusion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Experts alone permit discussing parameter merging; data without experts cannot run the same distillation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.27409-rlvr-fusion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7a1eadf46dc7ae5e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlvr-fusion" data-paper-title="Consolidating RLVR Capabilities Across Domains: A Deep Dive into Fusion Paradigms" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3f2cc44b2ba85f0a">Why define Merge task vectors relative to a common base?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlvr-fusion">Consolidating RLVR Capabilities Across Domains: A Deep Dive into Fusion Paradigms</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Fudan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Expert minus base must share parameter coordinates and reference. Different bases/layouts don&#x27;t express comparable deltas. Local candidate merging isn&#x27;t checkpoint merging.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Experts with different vocabularies or tensor layouts cannot simply average deltas.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.27409-rlvr-fusion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3f2cc44b2ba85f0a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlvr-fusion" data-paper-title="Consolidating RLVR Capabilities Across Domains: A Deep Dive into Fusion Paradigms" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ceb497193b26b2dc">Why doesn&#x27;t similar average performance imply per-domain equivalence?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlvr-fusion">Consolidating RLVR Capabilities Across Domains: A Deep Dive into Fusion Paradigms</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Fudan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Averages can cancel larger task gaps. Compare target domains, available experts/data and compute, not only mean scores or similar formulas.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Better math and worse code can yield the same mean without meeting the same needs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.27409-rlvr-fusion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ceb497193b26b2dc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlvr-fusion" data-paper-title="Consolidating RLVR Capabilities Across Domains: A Deep Dive into Fusion Paradigms" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rlvr-fusion-9745b358" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1279a9ea40e51b64">What resources do Merge, Mix RL and MOPD reuse in RLVR Fusion?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlvr-fusion">Consolidating RLVR Capabilities Across Domains: A Deep Dive into Fusion Paradigms</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Fudan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Merge reuses expert weight deltas; Mix RL reuses training data; MOPD distills from experts using data. Resource requirements differ, so averages cannot choose a route alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Without original training data, available routes differ even if expert weights are present.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.27409-rlvr-fusion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1279a9ea40e51b64">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:normalized-dpo" data-paper-title="Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6f9a407550fa6eb6">Why can dividing by beta change gradients without moving Normalized DPO&#x27;s optimum?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Anormalized-dpo">Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Affiliation not listed in the paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>At fixed positive beta, subtracting a constant and multiplying by a positive scalar preserve optima. Ordinary DPO couples preference-curve scale with update size; dividing centered softplus by beta removes an extra beta in the margin gradient.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reducing beta can weaken ordinary updates; normalization separates curve scale from step-size effects.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.27032-normalized-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6f9a407550fa6eb6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:normalized-dpo" data-paper-title="Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c8ea679e776c4425">How can normalized DPO avoid zero-over-zero for tiny beta?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Anormalized-dpo">Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Affiliation not listed in the paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compute centered softplus minus log 2 stably or use its small-beta limit. The gradient is negative sigmoid and does not vanish from an extra beta factor. Test the limit rather than substituting zero in the quotient. Candidate checks are not full training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Confirm finite limiting loss and gradient instead of catching exceptions and returning zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.27032-normalized-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c8ea679e776c4425">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:normalized-dpo" data-paper-title="Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0e56aa9d911938bb">Is Normalized DPO equivalent to changing the learning rate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Anormalized-dpo">Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Affiliation not listed in the paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Centering and dividing by beta rescales loss gradients. Learning rate scales the optimizer&#x27;s update. They can be related under simple conditions, but momentum/adaptive statistics can change the trajectory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A second-moment optimizer need not maintain identical state under external step-size and loss scaling.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.27032-normalized-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0e56aa9d911938bb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:normalized-dpo" data-paper-title="Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-normalized-dpo-59718764" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d8f5f2448d0d1fc9">Is Normalized DPO&#x27;s margin a human score gap or a model-relative preference?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Anormalized-dpo">Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Affiliation not listed in the paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It is the model-side value in the loss. Data identify the winner; policy and reference probabilities determine the margin and beta sets its scale in the preference curve. Normalization does not rewrite labels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A human says A beats B without saying by three points; current probabilities still give a margin.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.27032-normalized-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d8f5f2448d0d1fc9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:twinkv" data-paper-title="TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-twinkv-b8f534bd" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3a498fa6937cd63c">Why swap redundant donors for orphans rather than raise TwinKV budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atwinkv">TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The base eviction can keep duplicates and lose unique evidence. Recover dropped keys without similar retained substitutes by removing redundant retained keys with distant twins. Protect sink/recent items. Key similarity is not semantic equivalence, and reconstruction is not generation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Replace one of two repeated explanations with a unique date at the same cache size.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27128">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.27128-twinkv/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3a498fa6937cd63c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:twinkv" data-paper-title="TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-42e6987ceebe0802">Why exclude local twins and sink/recent protected entries from donors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atwinkv">TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Find similar retained twins outside the local window and never sacrifice protected entries. Swap only min(orphans, donors) and preserve |R′|=|R|.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Nearby similar keys do not automatically qualify as distant redundancy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27128">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.27128-twinkv/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-42e6987ceebe0802">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:twinkv" data-paper-title="TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-eccc5ae1290fa1c0">How does TwinKV compose with StreamingLLM or H2O?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atwinkv">TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It repairs a wrapped policy&#x27;s result rather than replacing its score. Compare the same initial policy and KV budget with repair on or off.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>StreamingLLM and StreamingLLM+TwinKV retain equal counts, isolating swaps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27128">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.27128-twinkv/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eccc5ae1290fa1c0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:twinkv" data-paper-title="TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d1d65d81060d202f">Why repair retention under a fixed budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atwinkv">TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A base policy can keep redundant keys and drop unique ones. Donor–orphan swaps address gaps without adding entries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Trade one near duplicate for unique older evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27128">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.27128-twinkv/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d1d65d81060d202f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:pace-vlm" data-paper-title="PACE: A Unified Condense-and-Extract Paradigm for Fast VLM Inference" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-pace-vlm-f64143ef" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0da1b5df32b59d4e">Why separate image scaling and question-dependent token extraction in PACE?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Apace-vlm">PACE: A Unified Condense-and-Extract Paradigm for Fast VLM Inference</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Sun Yat-sen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Scaling controls input encoding cost; extraction controls what continues downstream. Late token dropping cannot reclaim prior encoding. A shallow preview estimates difficulty, and extraction mixes language and visual attention by confidence rather than using one fixed rule.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Shrink a blank image more than a dense menu, then use the question to select relevant regions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27206">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.27206-pace-vlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0da1b5df32b59d4e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:pace-vlm" data-paper-title="PACE: A Unified Condense-and-Extract Paradigm for Fast VLM Inference" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-79280489155e740b">Does the real-checkpoint run fully validate DDAE?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Apace-vlm">PACE: A Unified Condense-and-Extract Paradigm for Fast VLM Inference</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Sun Yat-sen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The small real-checkpoint smoke mainly exercises APC. DDAE is checked with equations and unit tests, without the original model fork or kernels. APC excludes diagonal self-similarity and picks the top-K deviations from the local mean. Correct compression direction does not establish lossless quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Five correct out of eight before and after compression is a small-sample observation, not verification of DDAE in generation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27206">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.27206-pace-vlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-79280489155e740b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:pace-vlm" data-paper-title="PACE: A Unified Condense-and-Extract Paradigm for Fast VLM Inference" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7b6eb0d63a176892">How does DDAE differ from an equal-weight attention average?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Apace-vlm">PACE: A Unified Condense-and-Extract Paradigm for Fast VLM Inference</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Sun Yat-sen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It converts the dispersions of two normalized attention maps into confidence weights using temperature softmax. Weights can favor different streams depending on evidence. Dispersion is a method signal, not a calibrated probability of correctness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Concentrated language attention and diffuse vision attention may favor language; another question can reverse the weights.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27206">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.27206-pace-vlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7b6eb0d63a176892">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:pace-vlm" data-paper-title="PACE: A Unified Condense-and-Extract Paradigm for Fast VLM Inference" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/visual-evidence-budget/">Multimodal models / Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-73728e1c45489aa8">Why can&#x27;t PACE infer equal vision budgets from equal image sizes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Apace-vlm">PACE: A Unified Condense-and-Extract Paradigm for Fast VLM Inference</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Sun Yat-sen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Equal-sized images can differ in global semantic density and local detail. APC estimates both off-diagonal feature similarities and top-K details that differ from background. Pixel count is not a substitute, and budget signals do not guarantee correctness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A blank wall and a densely printed page at the same resolution need not preserve the same amount of detail.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27206">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.27206-pace-vlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-73728e1c45489aa8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:criticl" data-paper-title="CritICL: Inference-Time Weak-to-Strong Generalization from Small Language Model Failure Modes" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-criticl-4a912854" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a53e3dc987414704">Why doesn&#x27;t CritICL need the strong model to fail first at deployment?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acriticl">CritICL: Inference-Time Weak-to-Strong Generalization from Small Language Model Failure Modes</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Offline weak-model failures become reusable critiques. Static mode uses common patterns and dynamic mode retrieves question-relevant ones before one strong-model generation. Transfer patterns, not weak answers; relevance and coverage matter.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Retrieve a unit-conversion reminder before answering, without reading test gold to craft it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27455">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2608.27455-criticl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a53e3dc987414704">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:criticl" data-paper-title="CritICL: Inference-Time Weak-to-Strong Generalization from Small Language Model Failure Modes" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-496c385698250dff">Why not select critiques with the current question&#x27;s correct answer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acriticl">CritICL: Inference-Time Weak-to-Strong Generalization from Small Language Model Failure Modes</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>That leaks evaluation targets into prompts. Dynamic retrieval uses only input similarity to the existing bank and then generates once. Offline failures and current hidden gold stay separate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Looking up the solution before picking the critique that fixes it is not deployable retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27455">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2608.27455-criticl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-496c385698250dff">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:criticl" data-paper-title="CritICL: Inference-Time Weak-to-Strong Generalization from Small Language Model Failure Modes" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-72ab8c1467b98e00">How do static and dynamic critique selection differ?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acriticl">CritICL: Inference-Time Weak-to-Strong Generalization from Small Language Model Failure Modes</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Static uses frequent global failures; dynamic retrieves relevant CritBank entries for the current input. Both act before generation, but only dynamic adds input-dependent retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A math question can retrieve calculation reminders different from those for other requests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27455">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2608.27455-criticl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-72ab8c1467b98e00">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:criticl" data-paper-title="CritICL: Inference-Time Weak-to-Strong Generalization from Small Language Model Failure Modes" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-429d311a384d5142">Why build CritBank from weak-model errors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acriticl">CritICL: Inference-Time Weak-to-Strong Generalization from Small Language Model Failure Modes</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Cluster recurring failures offline into reusable reminders for stronger models. This moves reflection cost upstream and avoids requiring a first failure on each deployed request.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Add a common missed-unit-conversion reminder before a new answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27455">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2608.27455-criticl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-429d311a384d5142">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:swe-prime" data-paper-title="SWE-Prime: Fewer Trajectories, Better Performance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-swe-prime-e014601a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-09148f0475ab00b9">Why retain complete context but apply SFT loss only to selected semantic segments?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aswe-prime">SWE-Prime: Fewer Trajectories, Better Performance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Sun Yat-sen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Unselected spans may be necessary causal context for later behavior even if redundant, dangerous, or unhelpful to imitate. Masking separates readable context from training targets. The model sees the real process while learning useful, learnable actions; not every token in a successful trajectory deserves supervision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keep a failed dangerous command to explain a repair, without rewarding the model for generating that command.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27449">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.27449-swe-prime/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-09148f0475ab00b9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:swe-prime" data-paper-title="SWE-Prime: Fewer Trajectories, Better Performance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7dac67bcfc67dd77">Do local filtering results show a code LLM was trained or SWE-bench ran?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aswe-prime">SWE-Prime: Fewer Trajectories, Better Performance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Sun Yat-sen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Local filtering strategies share an observation and tool interface without training a code model or running official SWE-bench. Verify that loss masks cover only selected spans, context stays complete, and data splits remain isolated. Small tool-routing metrics are not code-repair gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: More stable local routes after removing risky segments do not reproduce the paper&#x27;s outcome with one tenth of its code traces.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27449">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.27449-swe-prime/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7dac67bcfc67dd77">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:swe-prime" data-paper-title="SWE-Prime: Fewer Trajectories, Better Performance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-fe246fc75fa9c390">What different data-quality problems do whole-trajectory and within-trajectory segment selection solve?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aswe-prime">SWE-Prime: Fewer Trajectories, Better Performance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Sun Yat-sen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Trajectory selection chooses useful complete experiences by outcome, process, and representativeness. Segment selection chooses contributing, learnable, lower-risk behavior within them. Good traces can contain redundancy, and good fragments can come from failed overall runs. Sample selection and supervision are distinct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keep a passing repair&#x27;s complete execution as context, but exclude irrelevant dependency installation from imitation targets.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27449">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.27449-swe-prime/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fe246fc75fa9c390">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:swe-prime" data-paper-title="SWE-Prime: Fewer Trajectories, Better Performance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cabb17e601059f07">Why might a successful trajectory still be a poor full SFT target?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aswe-prime">SWE-Prime: Fewer Trajectories, Better Performance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Sun Yat-sen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Success can include redundant exploration, risky commands, or steps the current model cannot learn. SWE-Prime filters trajectories by process, outcome, and representativeness, then selects segments by contribution, learnability, and risk. Outcome success does not endorse every token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A bug fix ultimately passes after accidentally deleting and restoring a file. Do not teach deletion as a good action.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27449">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.27449-swe-prime/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cabb17e601059f07">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spt" data-paper-title="SPT: Skills as Pre-Training Data for Agentic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-spt-bfd17eb8" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-40ec6a0c367caa76">Why is inserting referenced files near first use more complete than pretraining on skill instructions alone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspt">SPT: Skills as Pre-Training Data for Agentic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Skill packages put argument rules or examples in companion files. Inlining at first reference exposes real dependencies at the right position in causal context rather than training on dangling references. Mixing with general text limits distribution shift. Reading skill documents is not validated execution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: &#x27;Use schema.json for arguments&#x27; does not teach the field constraints if the schema is absent; inserting it near the reference supplies them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26563">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.26563-spt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-40ec6a0c367caa76">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spt" data-paper-title="SPT: Skills as Pre-Training Data for Agentic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ca6f583af366bb98">Why retain general text and control its mixture with skill data in mid-training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspt">SPT: Skills as Pre-Training Data for Agentic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Training data changes both what a model learns and the text distribution it sees. An explicit mixture coefficient α controls the share of procedural packages. Replacing all training with skill documents does not leave other capabilities unchanged by assumption. Local assembly and mixture tests cannot establish general capability retention or execution skill.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A batch includes instructions and general prose. Raising the skill ratio changes the training emphasis, which requires training evaluation, not a file-count check.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26563">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.26563-spt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ca6f583af366bb98">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spt" data-paper-title="SPT: Skills as Pre-Training Data for Agentic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a101e15d0ef1c12a">How does skill mid-training differ from retrieving skill documents only at deployment?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspt">SPT: Skills as Pre-Training Data for Agentic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mid-training writes procedural patterns into weights, so the same document need not be retrieved each time. Runtime retrieval puts up-to-date skills explicitly in context but costs tokens. They can complement each other. Training on skill text does not prove tool execution; verify a real policy and environment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A model may remember to verify before submitting, while a changed API argument still needs current runtime documentation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26563">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.26563-spt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a101e15d0ef1c12a">Question link</a></p>
</details>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spt" data-paper-title="SPT: Skills as Pre-Training Data for Agentic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c27cd9a103e2836c">Why can multi-file skill packages serve as mid-training data for a causal LM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspt">SPT: Skills as Pre-Training Data for Agentic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>They contain reusable procedures and referenced materials. Predicting this text before post-training can build workflow priors. This is not a single execution trace or real tool use during training; downstream SFT or RL still must turn document patterns into behavior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Instructions with a configuration example and helper script teach a reusable method, not the accidental full tool log of one task.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
