<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:r2-opd" data-paper-title="Beyond Imitation: Filtering On-Policy Distillation by Reasoning Progress" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b71496cce2185ce2">How does rank filtering differ from summing rewards?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Ar2-opd">Beyond Imitation: Filtering On-Policy Distillation by Reasoning Progress</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Filtering requires agreement to retain teacher signal. Addition lets a large score offset a poor one. Agreement doesn&#x27;t prove either judge correct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A huge teacher score cannot buy back a span rejected by progress disagreement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19408">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.19408-r2-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b71496cce2185ce2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:r2-opd" data-paper-title="Beyond Imitation: Filtering On-Policy Distillation by Reasoning Progress" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-r2-opd-a6acbe83" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-dfc26c702e1baa99">Why estimate reasoning progress independently in R²-OPD?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Ar2-opd">Beyond Imitation: Filtering On-Policy Distillation by Reasoning Progress</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Teacher preference needn&#x27;t help solve the task. Compare independent progress and mask conflicting supervision rather than equate style with reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A fluent explanation may score high with teacher while moving farther from the solution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19408">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.19408-r2-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dfc26c702e1baa99">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spade" data-paper-title="SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-spade-5fdace60" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c7c3a5bda0319f3a">Why use hinted versus unhinted regret for the environment designer rather than simply maximizing agent failure?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspade">SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Failure alone can reward impossible or overly hard environments. A hint that substantially improves a difficult unhinted outcome identifies a more learnable frontier. Environments must still execute, and privileged information stays in training comparisons rather than leaking into unhinted evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A difficult maze solvable with direction hints can be useful. A maze with no exit fails both agents and should not score well just for being hard.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19197">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.19197-spade/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c7c3a5bda0319f3a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spade" data-paper-title="SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-fe52868b4be336c7">May a SPADE agent retain hints in the no-hint evaluation condition?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspade">SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Isolate condition inputs. Privileged hints belong only to their training or comparison branch and must not enter the unhinted policy. Executable environment checks still matter; the local mini-suite did not run original external environments or large-model training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If an unhinted callback still receives the designer&#x27;s saved plan, the return difference cannot be interpreted.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19197">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.19197-spade/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fe52868b4be336c7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spade" data-paper-title="SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a01da2b026001f3b">Do maximizing failure rate and maximizing hint/no-hint regret favor the same environments?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspade">SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Failure alone can favor unsolvable or meaningless environments. Regret also requires privileged help to improve return, distinguishing solvable but currently difficult tasks. It still needs real execution and feedback rather than a fixed difficulty label.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An environment that scores zero for both agents has a high failure rate but zero regret.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19197">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.19197-spade/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a01da2b026001f3b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spade" data-paper-title="SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8d3ed730866d322d">Why does SPADE use the same LLM as environment designer and inference agent?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspade">SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The designer creates executable synthetic environments, the agent tries them, and the difference between hinted and unhinted rewards identifies frontier tasks. The aim is learnable challenges rather than arbitrary unsolvable problems.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An environment that fails without hints but succeeds with them may be more informative than one that fails both conditions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19197">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.19197-spade/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8d3ed730866d322d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rtpo" data-paper-title="RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-rtpo-1c108353" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9c34e4b512e67b3c">Why do reverse-turn updates help keep decisions aligned with on-policy downstream continuations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Artpo">RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Adelaide University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Early action value depends on later policies. If downstream behavior has changed substantially, credit from old continuations can be inconsistent. A reverse tree handles turns near the outcome first, then propagates evidence backward so early decisions reflect the updated continuation. Update order does not remove importance or execution-alignment checks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After the last two steps learn recovery, assess opening decisions using that new recovery ability instead of values from the old failing continuation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18682">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.18682-rtpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9c34e4b512e67b3c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rtpo" data-paper-title="RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-dd588ecabba448b1">Why record both behavior policy and downstream continuation version for each RTPO turn?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Artpo">RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Adelaide University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Early advantages based on mismatched later policies can lose on-policy correspondence. Reversing indices alone is insufficient: check tree nodes, state, and continuation ownership. Local control flow is not complete external-environment RL.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After a node is reevaluated under a new continuation policy, its old continuation reward is not the current return for the same state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18682">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.18682-rtpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dd588ecabba448b1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rtpo" data-paper-title="RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d0b1be0b8eafd96b">Are reverse-turn updates the same as training on reversed token text?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Artpo">RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Adelaide University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Reverse order applies to decision updates and continuation dependencies. Causal language-model input still follows the legal trajectory. Reversing text changes the task and visibility and cannot substitute for reverse policy optimization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Updating turn three before turn two does not mean reading turn-three observations to predict a turn-one action.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18682">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.18682-rtpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d0b1be0b8eafd96b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rtpo" data-paper-title="RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-52f37824bda763dd">Why does RTPO organize multi-turn decisions into reverse updates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Artpo">RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Adelaide University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Early action value depends on downstream continuation. RTPO arranges rollouts in a sparse reverse tree and updates turns backward to keep decisions aligned with the downstream policy evaluating them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Handle the consequences of late actions first, then return to earlier decisions rather than treating the trajectory as unstructured text.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18682">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.18682-rtpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-52f37824bda763dd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ogr" data-paper-title="Once Generated, Ranked: End-to-End Generative Slate Recommendation with Unified Semantic-Collaborative IDs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-ogr-bedfe7b4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e953ac0fa93e88c7">Why fuse semantic and collaborative codes before conservative slate optimization in OGR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aogr">Once Generated, Ranked: End-to-End Generative Slate Recommendation with Unified Semantic-Collaborative IDs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Semantic codes share content structure and collaborative codes capture behavior relations; encoding organizes the generative space. Planning treats a slate as one action to model item combinations, and conservative feedback updates limit drift from supervision. Representation, joint action, and stable learning are separate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Four individually strong shoes can be redundant, while a slate can combine shoes, socks, and a pack without jumping to an unfamiliar combination for one reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17613">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.17613-ogr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e953ac0fa93e88c7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ogr" data-paper-title="Once Generated, Ranked: End-to-End Generative Slate Recommendation with Unified Semantic-Collaborative IDs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c51a2b6ad730034d">Why must OGR&#x27;s R(Y) and KL compare the whole slate rather than one item?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aogr">Once Generated, Ranked: End-to-End Generative Slate Recommendation with Unified Semantic-Collaborative IDs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Y is the slate, so reward, generation probability, and reference must apply to the same list or defined token decomposition with consistent IDs and deduplication. Mean item reward misses interactions and fixed score mixing is not policy updating. State the actual local path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Five individually relevant duplicates can have high mean item score but poor slate value.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17613">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.17613-ogr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c51a2b6ad730034d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ogr" data-paper-title="Once Generated, Ranked: End-to-End Generative Slate Recommendation with Unified Semantic-Collaborative IDs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d6bca16b182e0c0a">Why does conservative SPA keep an SFT anchor rather than maximize reward freely?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aogr">Once Generated, Ranked: End-to-End Generative Slate Recommendation with Unified Semantic-Collaborative IDs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sparse or misspecified rewards can favor extreme slates. KL limits drift from supervised behavior, trading improvement freedom for stability without fixing bad rewards. Local NDCG and Hit moved in different directions, not universal gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Novelty alone may favor irrelevant tail items; SFT preserves interest, but excessive constraint may block exploration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17613">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.17613-ogr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d6bca16b182e0c0a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ogr" data-paper-title="Once Generated, Ranked: End-to-End Generative Slate Recommendation with Unified Semantic-Collaborative IDs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-14454e397408092b">Why does OGR&#x27;s TUSID encode semantics and collaboration instead of only quantizing content?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aogr">Once Generated, Ranked: End-to-End Generative Slate Recommendation with Unified Semantic-Collaborative IDs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Content generalizes to new items; collaborative codes preserve consumption relations. GL2P plans a slate and SPA adapts from feedback, distinct from coding. Richer codes can conflict and do not guarantee better pages.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Visually different items bought together can connect via collaboration; new items can borrow semantic structure.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:netflix-mediafm" data-paper-title="Multimedia Asset Personalization via Multimodal Embeddings at Netflix" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-netflix-mediafm-31c991d9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8a14f7828b81c132">Why freeze shared multimodal features across Netflix MediaFM tasks rather than train a separate visual model for each?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anetflix-mediafm">Multimedia Asset Personalization via Multimodal Embeddings at Netflix</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Netflix</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A reusable feature layer amortizes media understanding. Downstream towers adapt users, queries, and assets, with query similarity complementing personalization in search. Sharing reduces duplicate encoding but cannot recover visual details absent from frozen features. Offline screening does not replace online validation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Reuse a poster vector for home artwork and search; emphasize query match for &#x27;seaside comedy&#x27; and long-term taste on home.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18322">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.18322-netflix-mediafm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8a14f7828b81c132">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:netflix-mediafm" data-paper-title="Multimedia Asset Personalization via Multimodal Embeddings at Netflix" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5b81e344e6b05c3a">Why calibrate all three vector scales when MediaFM combines two dot products?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anetflix-mediafm">Multimedia Asset Personalization via Multimodal Embeddings at Netflix</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Netflix</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>User, query, and asset vectors need comparable scales or explicit calibration, otherwise one norm dominates the nominal α. Select checkpoints and fusion weights without tuning on test and bind frozen features to versions. Local movie-content proxies are not the production multimodal pipeline.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A query norm ten times larger can dominate a nominal 50/50 mix; normalization makes the coefficients interpretable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18322">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.18322-netflix-mediafm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5b81e344e6b05c3a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:netflix-mediafm" data-paper-title="Multimedia Asset Personalization via Multimodal Embeddings at Netflix" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-065b8f3cc5f30c5a">How does query similarity add current search intent beyond user-only personalization?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anetflix-mediafm">Multimedia Asset Personalization via Multimodal Embeddings at Netflix</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Netflix</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>User similarity reflects long-term taste; query similarity adds the explicit current request. Balance them so neither erases the other. This does not establish a universal weight, and offline IPS and winner proxies do not replace online evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A user who likes action searches for a warm comedy. Query match should override some action preference to keep search artwork relevant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18322">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.18322-netflix-mediafm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-065b8f3cc5f30c5a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:netflix-mediafm" data-paper-title="Multimedia Asset Personalization via Multimodal Embeddings at Netflix" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e014134d24b2b7e0">Why does MediaFM provide shared media features rather than final recommendation probabilities?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anetflix-mediafm">Multimedia Asset Personalization via Multimodal Embeddings at Netflix</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Netflix</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multimodal features describe content, while downstream towers adapt them to users, queries, and task objectives. Freezing avoids duplicate computation but limits missing details. Verify feature reuse separately from business outcomes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: The same poster vector supports home artwork and search, but high similarity does not make it optimal in every context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18322">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.18322-netflix-mediafm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e014134d24b2b7e0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:planpo" data-paper-title="PlanPO: Group Planning-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Agentic LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-planpo-5fac2579" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2c01413b29f93499">Why compare turn counts and response lengths only among successful traces rather than rewarding every short trace?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aplanpo">PlanPO: Group Planning-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Agentic LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiamen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Short can mean efficient planning or premature abandonment. First separate successes by outcome, then compare turns and response length among comparable successes. Coarse-to-fine advantages supplement outcome, not correctness, and fewer tokens cannot excuse skipped evidence collection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two successful bug fixes can differ by three wasted searches. A shorter trace that declares completion without editing files should get no efficiency reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17289">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.17289-planpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2c01413b29f93499">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:planpo" data-paper-title="PlanPO: Group Planning-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Agentic LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ce24322d0dd67bb6">Why distinguish agent responses from environment observations when counting turns and response lengths?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aplanpo">PlanPO: Group Planning-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Agentic LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiamen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The two axes measure interaction turns and per-turn generation. Counting long tool returns as agent output changes credit. Record success filtering, counting boundaries, and each advantage coefficient, not just total mean tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A tool can return a long page without the agent generating the same number of tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17289">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.17289-planpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ce24322d0dd67bb6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:planpo" data-paper-title="PlanPO: Group Planning-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Agentic LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-724afe0ef4b5ce66">How does PlanPO efficiency among successes differ from rewarding the shortest answer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aplanpo">PlanPO: Group Planning-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Agentic LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiamen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A direct length reward can favor failure or early stopping. Comparing successful traces first requires completion, then optimizes turns and length. Length advantage is not global outcome advantage and must remain separate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An unexecuted one-line &#x27;done&#x27; should not beat a successful multi-turn execution just because it is short.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17289">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.17289-planpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-724afe0ef4b5ce66">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:planpo" data-paper-title="PlanPO: Group Planning-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Agentic LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-224fcadb29af723f">Why does PlanPO split planning efficiency into turn count and response length per turn?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aplanpo">PlanPO: Group Planning-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Agentic LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiamen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fewer environment interactions and shorter generated responses are distinct costs. PlanPO compares successes coarse-to-fine and combines efficiency with outcome advantage, retaining completion while improving the process.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two successful traces can differ in tool calls and explanation length; evaluate those dimensions separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17289">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.17289-planpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-224fcadb29af723f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sa-mrpo" data-paper-title="Learn What&#x27;s Left, Not What&#x27;s Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-70571048b7377895">Why adjust weights based on saturation instead of always treating objectives equally?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asa-mrpo">Learn What&#x27;s Left, Not What&#x27;s Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Florida</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mastered dimensions can waste budget needed elsewhere. Normalize per dimension, then reduce saturated goals by a specified statistic. High scores don&#x27;t mean permanent mastery, and raw scale isn&#x27;t mastery.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reduce formatting pressure if already solved, but check whether later reasoning training degrades it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16072">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.16072-sa-mrpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-70571048b7377895">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sa-mrpo" data-paper-title="Learn What&#x27;s Left, Not What&#x27;s Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1d3549ed36ff2513">Can SA-MRPO compute one saturation after aggregating rewards?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asa-mrpo">Learn What&#x27;s Left, Not What&#x27;s Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Florida</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. That removes per-dimension budget allocation. Track each mean, variance and saturation before aggregation. Candidate formulas don&#x27;t reproduce checkpoint training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One aggregate hides low correctness and high format performance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16072">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.16072-sa-mrpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1d3549ed36ff2513">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sa-mrpo" data-paper-title="Learn What&#x27;s Left, Not What&#x27;s Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-72131cb19fdb4037">How does saturation weighting differ from fixed reward weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asa-mrpo">Learn What&#x27;s Left, Not What&#x27;s Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Florida</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed weights ignore current mastery; saturation weighting adapts by batch. It doesn&#x27;t change ultimate importance or prevent forgetting.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After downweighting a mastered skill, keep monitoring rather than declare it permanently solved.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16072">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.16072-sa-mrpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-72131cb19fdb4037">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sa-mrpo" data-paper-title="Learn What&#x27;s Left, Not What&#x27;s Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-sa-mrpo-184fd311" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a0af90db8872ed3b">Why track reward saturation in SA-MRPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asa-mrpo">Learn What&#x27;s Left, Not What&#x27;s Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Florida</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Already mastered objectives can crowd out unlearned dimensions. Standardize each dimension and weight by one minus saturation; the saturation estimate must be meaningful.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If format nearly always passes, prioritize still-failing factual checks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16072">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.16072-sa-mrpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a0af90db8872ed3b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:trca" data-paper-title="TRCA: Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment for Long-horizon LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-trca-ae92667a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-92f4d424dd06d08a">Why score Evidence, Execution, and Invalidity separately instead of one process score?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atrca">TRCA: Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment for Long-horizon LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A transition can add evidence but fail to execute, or be well formed without advancing the task. Rubric components distinguish those cases and penalize invalid behavior. Breakthrough credit identifies key progress without a successful anchor, but still needs actual transitions, not fixed template scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A search can reveal an error cause, followed by a command syntax failure. A total score alone obscures whether retrieval or invocation needs fixing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16156">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.16156-trca/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-92f4d424dd06d08a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:trca" data-paper-title="TRCA: Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment for Long-horizon LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f234aa5e56240844">Why verify the sign and component logs when aggregating TRCA invalidity?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atrca">TRCA: Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment for Long-horizon LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Subtract r_invalid and add the other base and breakthrough terms as defined. Missing the negative sign rewards invalid behavior. Keep component scores linked to transitions, since a total can conceal mistakes. Fixed values are not real evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With other terms fixed, increasing invalidity must lower total reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16156">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.16156-trca/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f234aa5e56240844">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:trca" data-paper-title="TRCA: Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment for Long-horizon LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0b6075a31659322e">How does TRCA&#x27;s lack of a success anchor differ from feedback that needs a successful reference trace?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atrca">TRCA: Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment for Long-horizon LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reference-based approaches first need a comparable successful execution. TRCA derives base and breakthrough rewards from actual transition rubrics without first finding a success. This is a feedback prerequisite, not proof of a higher task-success rate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Even when both full traces fail, a transition can collect useful evidence and receive rubric feedback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16156">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.16156-trca/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0b6075a31659322e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:trca" data-paper-title="TRCA: Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment for Long-horizon LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-873192fd9718233f">Why does TRCA define a rubric for every state transition rather than scoring only the outcome?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atrca">TRCA: Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment for Long-horizon LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Terminal outcomes hide important actions. Transition rubrics separately check evidence, execution, and invalid behavior and add breakthrough rewards. They do not require a successful anchor and supply more detailed credit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A step can gather key evidence while failing execution, with separate scores rather than zeroing both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16156">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.16156-trca/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-873192fd9718233f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spec-driven-tests" data-paper-title="Grounding AI Agents in Contracts: An Empirical Evaluation of Spec-Driven Test Generation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d27f4aa512ac8b25">Why does writing preconditions and postconditions first expose coverage gaps missed by direct test generation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspec-driven-tests">Grounding AI Agents in Contracts: An Empirical Evaluation of Spec-Driven Test Generation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Specifications list input restrictions and guaranteed behavior per unit, then mark tested and untested items so tests target auditable coverage. Source interpretation can still be unfaithful. The paper&#x27;s automated comparison did not include human edits, so don&#x27;t treat optional developer steps as executed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A specification can flag empty input returning an empty list as an untested postcondition, whereas copying normal examples can miss it indefinitely.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17177v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.17177-spec-driven-tests/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d27f4aa512ac8b25">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spec-driven-tests" data-paper-title="Grounding AI Agents in Contracts: An Empirical Evaluation of Spec-Driven Test Generation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b7c7b70e668e862c">Does compilation failure or modifying source count as bug detection?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspec-driven-tests">Grounding AI Agents in Contracts: An Empirical Evaluation of Spec-Driven Test Generation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The same test must compile and pass on fixed code and compile but fail a real assertion on buggy code. Illegal file edits invalidate runs; use an external trusted diff, not self-reports.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An intentional call to a nonexistent API that breaks old compilation is not a valid regression test.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17177v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.17177-spec-driven-tests/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b7c7b70e668e862c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spec-driven-tests" data-paper-title="Grounding AI Agents in Contracts: An Empirical Evaluation of Spec-Driven Test Generation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-6cc9079f0e3f1ce6">How does fixed-source input differ from exposing historical bugs to test generation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspec-driven-tests">Grounding AI Agents in Contracts: An Empirical Evaluation of Spec-Driven Test Generation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The generator sees only repaired source and public requirements; the private evaluator uses buggy versions. Old patches or bug locations change difficulty and no longer test discovery under the same protocol.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Knowing which line broke supports targeted tests, not independent contract inference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17177v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.17177-spec-driven-tests/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6cc9079f0e3f1ce6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:spec-driven-tests" data-paper-title="Grounding AI Agents in Contracts: An Empirical Evaluation of Spec-Driven Test Generation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-spec-driven-tests-4c06eb29" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f1fb84391154bc6c">What do Pre, Post, and Sug mean in specification-driven testing, and can suggestions replace behavior contracts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aspec-driven-tests">Grounding AI Agents in Contracts: An Empirical Evaluation of Spec-Driven Test Generation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pre defines conditions before a call. Post specifies behavior given those conditions. Sug suggests verification. Suggestions are not contracts; define valid inputs and outcomes first, then mark tested and untested conditions to identify omissions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>For sorting, Pre may require comparable elements, Post requires order and element preservation, and Sug proposes duplicate and empty-list tests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17177v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.17177-spec-driven-tests/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f1fb84391154bc6c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hymem" data-paper-title="HyMem: Hierarchical Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents via Information Isolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-hymem-ebf0c9bb" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-79c1cf512c450ba6">Why can separating planning, execution, and isolated reasoning reduce context pollution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahymem">HyMem: Hierarchical Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents via Information Isolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The layers need different detail: planning needs goal progress, execution needs current actions, and transient reasoning need not persist. Structured summaries retain necessary state across refreshes without crowding long-term facts with guesses. Isolation does not guarantee correctness; summaries must preserve constraints and provenance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Pass verified interface changes and open issues from debugging to planning, not every tentative hypothesis as a lasting fact.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15703">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.15703-hymem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-79c1cf512c450ba6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hymem" data-paper-title="HyMem: Hierarchical Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents via Information Isolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e300338bfd858cc0">Do deterministic local PlanBench results show that GAIA or BrowseComp-plus ran?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahymem">HyMem: Hierarchical Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents via Information Isolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Local tests cover layered context, refresh summaries, and mechanism counts without browsers, external tools, or the paper&#x27;s large model. Cost units and saturated scores belong to the controlled protocol, not real long-horizon token costs or paper Pass@1.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Counting a summary as one fixture event does not show that a real web evidence summary preserves the same facts at the same cost.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15703">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.15703-hymem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e300338bfd858cc0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hymem" data-paper-title="HyMem: Hierarchical Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents via Information Isolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-6af66bb3ebb4bbd4">What do structured progress summaries versus raw execution logs retain during handoff?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahymem">HyMem: Hierarchical Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents via Information Isolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raw logs retain detail and many local attempts, leaving the next layer to identify what matters. Structured progress extracts completed work, current state, and open items, giving planning a stable starting point. Compression can omit constraints, so test whether the handoff supports continuation rather than counting text reduction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Summarize installation logs as dependencies installed, tests not run due to missing credentials. &#x27;Install succeeded&#x27; alone may be mistaken for completed verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15703">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.15703-hymem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6af66bb3ebb4bbd4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hymem" data-paper-title="HyMem: Hierarchical Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents via Information Isolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6f117905da9d1b3c">Why can a multi-stage task leak irrelevant details into global decisions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahymem">HyMem: Hierarchical Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents via Information Isolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Search, execution, and reasoning create many artifacts. Sending all of them to one context lets old logs or tentative assumptions distract planning. HyMem gives each stage the information it needs and uses progress records to continue, moving necessary evidence rather than sharing every token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Hundreds of compiler lines may help the repair worker; global planning may need only the cause and affected module.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15703">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.15703-hymem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6f117905da9d1b3c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:drem" data-paper-title="DrEM: Dual-Side Robust Ensemble Ranking from Noisy User Preference Predictions in Video Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-drem-6dedd99f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-bde83590cd02c905">Why does DrEM correct preference-flip risk instead of averaging prediction scores?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adrem">DrEM: Dual-Side Robust Ensemble Ranking from Noisy User Preference Predictions in Video Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shenzhen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Prediction noise can reverse pair preferences, and averaging can still learn the wrong order. DrEM selects perturbation-stable pairs, corrects the objective for flip risk, and applies consistency fusion to limit ranking drift. Correction assumes a noise estimate and becomes unstable near its boundary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A small CTR perturbation can reverse a close video pair; model that risk rather than trusting the observed order as a clean label.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12778">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12778-drem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bde83590cd02c905">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:drem" data-paper-title="DrEM: Dual-Side Robust Ensemble Ranking from Noisy User Preference Predictions in Video Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-8670300d1dfc49e8">Why separately check probability-to-logit conversion and `1−2ρ` in DrEM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adrem">DrEM: Dual-Side Robust Ensemble Ranking from Noisy User Preference Predictions in Video Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shenzhen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Probabilities of zero or one cause infinite logits, while flip rate ρ near one half makes the inversion denominator singular. Document handling rather than silently producing huge gradients, and verify filtering, correction, and consistency fusion separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A coin-flip preference contains no recoverable signal merely because it is divided by a tiny denominator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12778">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12778-drem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8670300d1dfc49e8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:drem" data-paper-title="DrEM: Dual-Side Robust Ensemble Ranking from Noisy User Preference Predictions in Video Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4cae3e0c16f4d980">What assumptions does DrEM risk inversion add beyond perturbation augmentation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adrem">DrEM: Dual-Side Robust Ensemble Ranking from Noisy User Preference Predictions in Video Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shenzhen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Augmentation exposes the model to noise. Inversion combines original and reversed-label losses according to estimated flip risk to recover the clean objective. It needs valid risk estimates and a nonsingular denominator; errors leave bias or amplify variance. Noise alone is not inversion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Correcting a true 40% flip rate as 20% remains biased. Random perturbations do not supply the inversion coefficient.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12778">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12778-drem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4cae3e0c16f4d980">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
