<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:drem" data-paper-title="DrEM: Dual-Side Robust Ensemble Ranking from Noisy User Preference Predictions in Video Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-44786acb8838e31e">Why study noise as pairwise preference flips in DrEM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adrem">DrEM: Dual-Side Robust Ensemble Ranking from Noisy User Preference Predictions in Video Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shenzhen University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rankings depend on relative order; small errors can swap close candidates. Logit perturbation, preference-preserving filtering, and risk correction target this instability, while consistency fusion limits drift. Accurate individual predictions do not guarantee stable pairs, and flip estimates can be wrong.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Scores only 0.01 apart can trade first place under small noise despite small individual errors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12778">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12778-drem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-44786acb8838e31e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:tcab" data-paper-title="Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-tcab-036a095f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-31a085596f880eba">Why match full context and action before sharing TCAB feedback?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atcab">Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Identical actions can yield different outcomes under different contexts. Tree maximal coupling matches complete pairs to share conditional rewards while preserving each policy&#x27;s marginal trajectory. Coupled policies are deliberately correlated, and savings do not prove global optimality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Picking the same product for different users does not justify sharing one click observation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12831">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12831-tcab/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-31a085596f880eba">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:tcab" data-paper-title="Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-35f6f43d12979124">Why not count identical action strings as saved feedback calls?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atcab">Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reuse depends on full context and state conditions. The same action in different environments can yield different feedback. Compare actual shared queries and tree-edge differences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two different users choosing A do not yield the same reusable observation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12831">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12831-tcab/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-35f6f43d12979124">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:tcab" data-paper-title="Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-6c5e5b73ef108829">Does correlated coupling alter each policy&#x27;s own trajectory distribution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atcab">Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Not necessarily. It changes joint dependence while preserving individual marginals. Equal final accuracy alone does not verify adaptive updates or marginal trajectory parity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two draws can coincide more frequently while each retains its original probabilities.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12831">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12831-tcab/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6c5e5b73ef108829">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:tcab" data-paper-title="Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0b3ed7d3bbc398fd">Why share real feedback across adaptive policies?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atcab">Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · New York University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate A/B/n runs may pay repeatedly for identical context/action pairs. Coupling permits valid reuse while preserving each policy&#x27;s marginal trajectory distribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If two policies choose the same action in the same state, one feedback can update both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12831">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12831-tcab/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0b3ed7d3bbc398fd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rubric-dropout" data-paper-title="Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-as-Reward RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea048f226344f026">Why share a rubric subset within a rollout group?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arubric-dropout">Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-as-Reward RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Scale AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Relative rewards need common criteria; different random criteria can misrank peers. Cross-group randomization reduces fixed shortcuts, but doesn&#x27;t guarantee valid remaining criteria or protect task performance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Omit brevity for both answers, not only one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11669">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.11669-rubric-dropout/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ea048f226344f026">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rubric-dropout" data-paper-title="Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-as-Reward RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b2ac7c4da469d607">When should Rubric Dropout sample and save the mask?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arubric-dropout">Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-as-Reward RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Scale AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sample one mask per rollout group, freeze for scoring and log seed. Never choose masks after seeing which response benefits. No local real rubric judge.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Hiding difficult criteria only after observing failure is cherry-picking, not dropout.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11669">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.11669-rubric-dropout/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b2ac7c4da469d607">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rubric-dropout" data-paper-title="Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-as-Reward RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c21118c94c319de5">How does group-shared dropout differ from independent masks per response?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arubric-dropout">Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-as-Reward RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Scale AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A shared subset keeps same-prompt responses comparable. Independent masks confound quality with scoring criteria. Randomize by group.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Comparing A on format and B on correctness doesn&#x27;t isolate answer quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11669">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.11669-rubric-dropout/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c21118c94c319de5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rubric-dropout" data-paper-title="Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-as-Reward RL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rubric-dropout-0c8d1da7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5a48a08bd29cde14">Why randomly hide rubric criteria?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arubric-dropout">Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-as-Reward RL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Scale AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed proxies can be repeatedly exploited. Random subsets make a single shortcut unreliable. Hidden criteria are not unimportant; the visible reward composition changes during training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A canned phrase cannot reliably earn total reward if its easy criterion is often absent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11669">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.11669-rubric-dropout/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5a48a08bd29cde14">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:pto" data-paper-title="Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ba4418ae346a8ba2">Why simulate later dialogue before labeling a current PTO response?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Apto">Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Reichman University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A pleasing immediate reply may harm long-term goals. Compare rolled-out user interactions and turn branch-level differences into current-response DPO preferences. Depth changes cost and horizon; simulator/oracle bias becomes training bias and is not real feedback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Guessing a need can read better in turn one, while simulating another turn may show clarification prevents a wrong direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12062">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.12062-pto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ba4418ae346a8ba2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:pto" data-paper-title="Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1a3b00a1932c6dec">Why preserve the mapping from current histories to future PTO branches?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Apto">Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Reichman University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One preference pair compares actions from the same state. Continue each action in its own branch and do not leak future outcomes into policy inputs. Deterministic local evaluators replace the expensive oracle only to test tree and credit flow.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If A prompts clarification and B confusion, attaching A&#x27;s success to B reverses the preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12062">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.12062-pto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1a3b00a1932c6dec">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:pto" data-paper-title="Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ade76e34fb07aaaa">What does adding more PTO branches expand compared with looking farther ahead?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Apto">Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Reichman University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Width compares more actions at one state; depth observes consequences farther into the future. Both cost simulations and judgments but aren&#x27;t substitutes. Shallow branches can miss delayed effects; one deep branch can miss better starts. This is a search distinction, not an empirical ranking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Five openings with one turn each increase width; one opening with many turns increases depth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12062">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.12062-pto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ade76e34fb07aaaa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:pto" data-paper-title="Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-pto-55a5beae" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ab711475e2acf5fb">What do PTO&#x27;s dialogue policy, virtual user and oracle do, and which is updated?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Apto">Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Reichman University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The policy proposes replies, the virtual user continues possible interactions, and the oracle evaluates expanded branches. Their comparisons label preferences for the current state and update only the dialogue policy. Simulated users and evaluators provide training signals, not real user behavior or joint updates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A consultation agent asks two possible questions, the simulator answers each, and the oracle compares progress. Train the agent&#x27;s current reply selection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12062">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.12062-pto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ab711475e2acf5fb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gcpo" data-paper-title="GCPO: Diagnosing and Constraining Subspace Geometry in Rollout RL for LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b228873198b3173b">Why project low-rank updates onto both singular complements rather than penalize overlap?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agcpo">GCPO: Diagnosing and Constraining Subspace Geometry in Rollout RL for LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Soft cost permits principal-space drift at sufficient reward. Hard bilateral projection excludes it, keeping both input and output directions outside frozen principal spaces. Vector diagnostics are not layered LoRA training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Every valid update must avoid protected directions, rather than merely pay a penalty for touching them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11674">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.11674-gcpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b228873198b3173b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gcpo" data-paper-title="GCPO: Diagnosing and Constraining Subspace Geometry in Rollout RL for LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5dff608003ae7cdb">Does local GCPO validate per-layer bilateral LoRA?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agcpo">GCPO: Diagnosing and Constraining Subspace Geometry in Rollout RL for LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A vector policy restricts the leading right space of empirical update covariance as a proxy. The paper fixes left and right matrix projections; one-sided vector tests do not verify them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A parameter vector lacks two independent matrix axes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11674">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.11674-gcpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5dff608003ae7cdb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gcpo" data-paper-title="GCPO: Diagnosing and Constraining Subspace Geometry in Rollout RL for LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-14dc24b93afc8e6b">How does hard orthogonality differ from a soft projection penalty?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agcpo">GCPO: Diagnosing and Constraining Subspace Geometry in Rollout RL for LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Hard constraints exclude violating updates. Soft penalties allow an optimizer to trade violations against task gains. A larger penalty doesn&#x27;t establish exact bilateral orthogonality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A soft update may briefly enter the principal space; hard projection removes that component every time.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11674">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.11674-gcpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-14dc24b93afc8e6b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gcpo" data-paper-title="GCPO: Diagnosing and Constraining Subspace Geometry in Rollout RL for LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-gcpo-c679efe1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d7473bf332d552ad">Why protect dominant pretrained singular spaces in GCPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agcpo">GCPO: Diagnosing and Constraining Subspace Geometry in Rollout RL for LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rollout update spikes in principal spaces may precede validation regressions. Restrict updates to bilateral orthogonal complements to avoid overwriting principal mappings. Correlation doesn&#x27;t forbid learning in all dominant directions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Add task behavior in remaining directions while preserving important input/output mappings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11674">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.11674-gcpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d7473bf332d552ad">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:c2-dpo" data-paper-title="Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-35469067fe68386f">Why compare full and degraded context margins rather than only raise chosen likelihood?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Ac2-dpo">Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Chosen likelihood may exploit language priors and ignore images. Context preference gain rewards the same pair changing preference with evidence while preserving the original ordering. It depends on appropriate degradation and does not itself establish correct visual understanding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If masking a chart leaves preference unchanged, language priors may dominate; correct evidence should provide extra support.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12158">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.12158-c2-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-35469067fe68386f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:c2-dpo" data-paper-title="Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-86d4bee16225c912">What must stay consistent across C²-DPO&#x27;s margins?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Ac2-dpo">Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use one prompt and one chosen/rejected pair under both contexts. Degraded context must not contain the answer. Local work does not complete fine-tuning the named multimodal model/data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Subtracting a full-image A/B comparison from degraded-image C/D does not isolate visual evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12158">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.12158-c2-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-86d4bee16225c912">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:c2-dpo" data-paper-title="Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-bb62ba4316cf25a3">Is positive context preference gain the same as the chosen response winning under full context?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Ac2-dpo">Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. CPG compares the two margins; winning needs a positive full-context margin. An improved but negative margin can still favor the wrong reply. Context gain and original preference ordering are separate constraints.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A change from −3 to −1 gives positive gain without a chosen win.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12158">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.12158-c2-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bb62ba4316cf25a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:c2-dpo" data-paper-title="Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-c2-dpo-2993ea41" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-24a30e0257152972">Why does C²-DPO require a response pair and two contexts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Ac2-dpo">Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Chosen/rejected compare responses to the same prompt; complete/degraded context varies evidence. They are independent axes. Hold the responses fixed to isolate context&#x27;s effect.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Compare red car and blue car with the original and degraded images, not with different questions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12158">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.12158-c2-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-24a30e0257152972">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gas" data-paper-title="Generation as Auxiliary Supervision: Enhancing Visual Understanding at Zero Inference Overhead via Decoupled Embedding Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-gas-1fb6a8b0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4f6e57e97260ca61">Why can GAS remove its entire auxiliary generation branch at deployment?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agas">Generation as Auxiliary Supervision: Enhancing Visual Understanding at Zero Inference Overhead via Decoupled Embedding Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>During training it predicts continuous visual embeddings and backpropagates into a lower vision path shared with understanding. Its upper generation parameters are separate and not used by inference. Removing the branch retains the trained shared parameters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Train on image understanding and target visual embeddings, then deploy only image question answering with the learned shared vision path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12209">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12209-gas/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4f6e57e97260ca61">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gas" data-paper-title="Generation as Auxiliary Supervision: Enhancing Visual Understanding at Zero Inference Overhead via Decoupled Embedding Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1371d6b9ed359eda">Why check inference dependencies before claiming GAS adds no deployment parameters?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agas">Generation as Auxiliary Supervision: Enhancing Visual Understanding at Zero Inference Overhead via Decoupled Embedding Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The generation upper layers, vision head, and EMA projector are removable only if understanding no longer reads them. Training still needs shifted prediction, EMA targets, and branch isolation. A local mirror-target diagnostic cannot validate the gains of large-scale generative data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Feeding an intermediate generation output back into understanding keeps that branch necessary at inference despite a claim of zero added parameters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12209">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12209-gas/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1371d6b9ed359eda">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gas" data-paper-title="Generation as Auxiliary Supervision: Enhancing Visual Understanding at Zero Inference Overhead via Decoupled Embedding Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea7ba395bdabb73a">How does GAS next-embedding prediction differ from reconstructing the current patch?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agas">Generation as Auxiliary Supervision: Enhancing Visual Understanding at Zero Inference Overhead via Decoupled Embedding Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>NEP predicts the next position from prior visual embeddings and allowed autoregressive context; an EMA projection supplies the target. Feeding the target at the same position changes what the model sees and can reduce the task to copying. Removability of the branch does not replace the shifted objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>To predict visual embedding i, provide earlier positions and allowed context, not embedding i itself.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12209">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12209-gas/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ea7ba395bdabb73a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gas" data-paper-title="Generation as Auxiliary Supervision: Enhancing Visual Understanding at Zero Inference Overhead via Decoupled Embedding Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a203eea136c296da">Does GAS next-embedding prediction output discrete image tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agas">Generation as Auxiliary Supervision: Enhancing Visual Understanding at Zero Inference Overhead via Decoupled Embedding Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It predicts continuous embeddings in the LM&#x27;s visual input space, with cosine alignment to an EMA-projected target. It does not classify a discrete image codebook. Generation is auxiliary to understanding and deployment need not generate images.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Predict the direction of a target patch embedding instead of choosing an index from thousands of image codes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12209">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.12209-gas/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a203eea136c296da">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:loongreflect" data-paper-title="LoongReflect: Boosting Long-Horizon Reflection in Search Agents via Global Perspective Distillation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-loongreflect-7debd709" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-47d09fe862087bb4">Why model reflection and backtracking as reversible memory-control actions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aloongreflect">LoongReflect: Boosting Long-Horizon Reflection in Search Agents via Global Perspective Distillation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Long searches must choose external actions, which traces to retain, and which fork to return to. Making reflection and backtracking policy actions lets the agent learn when to change memory. A privileged teacher supplies training signals and outcome reward covers long-run success, but evaluation must not give the student the teacher&#x27;s global view or future answers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: After a dead end, return to the previous branch and keep the reason for failure. Appending reflection text without changing trace state is not real backtracking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11967">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.11967-loongreflect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-47d09fe862087bb4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:loongreflect" data-paper-title="LoongReflect: Boosting Long-Horizon Reflection in Search Agents via Global Perspective Distillation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d989382ef608ad22">Does a low mini-suite average cost establish savings for a real long-context model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aloongreflect">LoongReflect: Boosting Long-Horizon Reflection in Search Agents via Global Perspective Distillation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The deterministic suite verifies reflection, backtracking, and state transitions without a real browser, external tools, or the paper&#x27;s large model. Cost follows the diagnostic definition. When accuracy is saturated, inspect branches and traces; proxy counts do not translate directly into real tokens or API fees.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A rule branch billed a fraction of a cost unit does not mean real model reflection uses the same fraction of tokens or time.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11967">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.11967-loongreflect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d989382ef608ad22">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:loongreflect" data-paper-title="LoongReflect: Boosting Long-Horizon Reflection in Search Agents via Global Perspective Distillation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b29d7bd63cdc6137">How do the fast privileged-teacher channel and slow outcome-GRPO channel supervise different signals?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aloongreflect">LoongReflect: Boosting Long-Horizon Reflection in Search Agents via Global Perspective Distillation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The fast channel distills fine-grained reflection decisions from the teacher&#x27;s view. The slow channel optimizes long-horizon policy using final trajectory outcomes. One provides local guidance, the other tests overall effectiveness. Privileged information belongs only with the training teacher or evaluator; the deployed student cannot read gold outcomes to choose backtracking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A teacher can identify missing evidence at one search step. Final reward checks whether the complete answer succeeds. Online, the student sees only current observations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11967">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.11967-loongreflect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b29d7bd63cdc6137">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:loongreflect" data-paper-title="LoongReflect: Boosting Long-Horizon Reflection in Search Agents via Global Perspective Distillation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-29d2ec8bb15b0afd">Why does a long-horizon search agent need reflection that recovers its route, not just an explanation at the end?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aloongreflect">LoongReflect: Boosting Long-Horizon Reflection in Search Agents via Global Perspective Distillation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multi-hop evidence gathering includes failed attempts. An early wrong turn can make later steps depend on bad evidence. LoongReflect changes current information and the continuation path so the agent can recover before the task ends. An accurate retrospective cannot improve the evidence gathering of an already completed run.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: If search keeps finding reprints of the same article, return to the earlier branch and change sources before submitting, not after admitting the evidence is narrow.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11967">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.11967-loongreflect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-29d2ec8bb15b0afd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sona" data-paper-title="Sona Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d656f31a07458ede">Why share user state between Sona generation and ranking, with teacher only in training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asona">Sona Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate models repeat history encoding and can learn inconsistent representations. One chronological compressed state supports joint generation and ranking, with training-only teacher supervision. It does not eliminate missed retrieval or compression loss; retain local negative results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Both paths respond to a shift from rock to classical without calling a large teacher online.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11015">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.11015-sona/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d656f31a07458ede">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sona" data-paper-title="Sona Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d8da9beed55e2ba5">Does Sona call its teacher at serving?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asona">Sona Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Teacher is training-only. Local work omits the full teacher, music tokenizer, and 15-plus-source production stack. Generation/ranking losses share state with distinct masks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Calling the large teacher online changes the cost contract.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sona" data-paper-title="Sona Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-f12020c85502e7d7">How does a unified model differ from deleting an intermediate ranker?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asona">Sona Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Joint generation, ranking, and distillation must replace functionality and handle long history. Compare coverage and robustness; fewer models alone do not prove improvement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Dropping pre-ranking without joint training can just remove functionality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sona" data-paper-title="Sona Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">

<span id="paper-recommendation-sona-74c5ab5b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-db84c085c9995808">Why use both SID generation and ranking in Sona?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asona">Sona Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Share user state across candidate generation and fine ranking instead of duplicating representations. A large teacher guides training only; one model serves.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Generate songs and score specific songs from the same user state.</p>
