<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:pmcoder" data-paper-title="Coupling Planning with Episodic Memory in LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-pmcoder-088b3672" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d5a49a3fee65a642">Why condition episodic retrieval on the current phase instead of querying the original issue every step?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Apmcoder">Coupling Planning with Episodic Memory in LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Vanderbilt University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Localization, editing, and verification need different evidence. Static retrieval can repeat topically related but phase-inappropriate traces. Hierarchical planning constrains retrieval by phase, detects stalls from behavior, and replans. Real execution verdicts decide whether repair succeeded, not phase changes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Localization needs files and verification needs regression tests. Repeatedly searching issue text can keep returning localization experiences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06811">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.06811-pmcoder/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d5a49a3fee65a642">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:pmcoder" data-paper-title="Coupling Planning with Episodic Memory in LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d42348ca21f71f7">Can perfect local phase/retrieval scores be compared with solving 25 more SWE-bench issues?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Apmcoder">Coupling Planning with Episodic Memory in LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Vanderbilt University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Deterministic PlanBench tests phase-conditioned retrieval, stalls, and replanning without repository containers or paper models. Proxy cost is not tool tokens. Report traces and branch evidence rather than call saturation issue-resolution capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Selecting a phase template and completing a three-step fixture does not establish locating, editing, and testing an unknown repository.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06811">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.06811-pmcoder/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d42348ca21f71f7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:pmcoder" data-paper-title="Coupling Planning with Episodic Memory in LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b8b4cfdcf0674ba0">What is the trade-off between trace-based stall detection and rewriting the whole plan after any failure?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Apmcoder">Coupling Planning with Episodic Memory in LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Vanderbilt University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Trace statistics recognize repeated nonprogress and allow targeted replanning. One failure can be useful evidence rather than a bad direction. Full rewrites repeat work, while never changing can stall indefinitely. Use actual verdicts rather than self-reported recovery.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: The same test error after two identical patches suggests another approach. A new first-time error can be normal progress.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06811">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.06811-pmcoder/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b8b4cfdcf0674ba0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:pmcoder" data-paper-title="Coupling Planning with Episodic Memory in LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-69e13b18b74254a0">What reusable experience does PMCoder retain across locating, fixing, and testing an issue?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Apmcoder">Coupling Planning with Episodic Memory in LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Vanderbilt University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A long fix yields clues, failed attempts, and test conclusions. Restarting from the issue repeats searches and mistakes. Phase-organized plans and reads give each step the right history. Memory supports execution but current code and tests still decide if the new issue is fixed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Remember the parser location and failing boundary input rather than search the whole repo again.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06811">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2608.06811-pmcoder/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-69e13b18b74254a0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:gryphon-v2" data-paper-title="Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade — Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-gryphon-v2-65508cc1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-68390dcde3890556">Why distill both current rollouts and actual exposure candidates in Gryphon-v2?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agryphon-v2">Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade — Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A changing generator proposes items rare in old logs; exposure-only training may not score its outputs well. Rollout-only training discards established coverage. One teacher calibrates both distributions, and a shared encoder links generation and ranking. Teacher bias can still transfer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Rollout supervision covers niche movies proposed by the new generator, while real exposures preserve knowledge of existing popular ones.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06213">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.06213-gryphon-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-68390dcde3890556">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:gryphon-v2" data-paper-title="Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade — Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-66abe065a27702a3">Why keep Gryphon-v2 rollout and impression distillation provenance separate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agryphon-v2">Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade — Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Counts, weights, and candidate identities from different distributions affect the loss. Compare teacher and student on matching items and cutoffs and track which source dominates. Both objectives updated locally, but quality regressed; updates are not gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Sixty thousand distilled rollout items are not 60,000 real impressions and must not be labeled user clicks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06213">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.06213-gryphon-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-66abe065a27702a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:gryphon-v2" data-paper-title="Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade — Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-98e08b58f6a6ac4b">Why does dual-source distillation better reflect generator serving candidates than logged impressions alone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agryphon-v2">Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade — Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Old impressions are policy-selected and can miss the current rollout distribution. Combined training sees actual exposure evidence plus the generator&#x27;s outputs. The teacher may be unreliable in new regions; the local comparison was negative despite broader coverage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Niche instrumental candidates missing from old logs get rollout supervision, but can inherit teacher bias.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06213">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.06213-gryphon-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-98e08b58f6a6ac4b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:gryphon-v2" data-paper-title="Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade — Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a1a741eb904c4131">Why do Gryphon-v2&#x27;s generation and ranking heads share a history encoder?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agryphon-v2">Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade — Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Re-encoding the same history wastes computation and can produce inconsistent user states. A shared encoder supports SID nomination and ranking, but the ranker still depends on the generated candidate set and cannot recover omissions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Both heads see a user&#x27;s recent switch to jazz, but missing jazz items cannot be reranked.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06213">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.06213-gryphon-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a1a741eb904c4131">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:u-opsd" data-paper-title="U-OPSD" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4ad69881270380a9">How avoid treating shortest consensus as truth without gold?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Au-opsd">U-OPSD</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Consensus selects a reference and repair targets as pseudo-supervision, not correctness verification. Shared errors may be reinforced. Report internal agreement separately from external holdout and keep gold out of student inputs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Several responses can use the same wrong formula; the shortest still isn&#x27;t a standard solution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06296">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06296-u-opsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4ad69881270380a9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:u-opsd" data-paper-title="U-OPSD" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-52f51dfab8f76d12">Can U-OPSD use gold before choosing an internal reference?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Au-opsd">U-OPSD</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Use predictions only for consensus, thresholds and length. Gold is for independent evaluation. Deterministic mini-suite isn&#x27;t full multi-turn self-distillation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Filtering correctness before voting smuggles answer information into training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06296">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06296-u-opsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-52f51dfab8f76d12">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:u-opsd" data-paper-title="U-OPSD" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-2947ac9c36e56042">Why distinguish shortest consensus answer from arbitrary shortest answer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Au-opsd">U-OPSD</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>First require majority agreement, then minimize length within eligible outputs. The shortest unrestricted may be an empty or outlier answer. Consensus isn&#x27;t gold.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A short erroneous refusal doesn&#x27;t become privileged guidance because it saves tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06296">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06296-u-opsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2947ac9c36e56042">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:u-opsd" data-paper-title="U-OPSD" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-u-opsd-4619f519" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-69cb74920e51aa07">Why is U-OPSD privileged view still externally unsupervised?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Au-opsd">U-OPSD</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It comes from internal sampling consensus, without external answers/reward or a larger teacher. One view sees an extra internally produced signal, not independently verified truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A short self-selected consensus solution can still be a shared error.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06296">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06296-u-opsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-69cb74920e51aa07">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rrc" data-paper-title="RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-efbd610af1123aeb">Why combine group and anchor ranking rather than ask for absolute scores?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arrc">RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Comparative judgments can be more stable than absolute scale. Group competition gives relative position; anchors give cross-group reference before centering. This still depends on candidates and judge, not absolute truth or full paper evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two group winners may have very different quality relative to a shared anchor.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06310">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06310-rrc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-efbd610af1123aeb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rrc" data-paper-title="RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-404cabbf88bd9a1e">Why check group size and rank direction before converting RRC ranks to rewards?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arrc">RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>K−1 requires more than one sample. Declare whether rank one is best. No local real judging or complete capability integration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A reversed formula can give the best rank the lowest reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06310">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06310-rrc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-404cabbf88bd9a1e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rrc" data-paper-title="RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a6fd8d121f808e69">What do group self-competition and anchor ranks each provide?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arrc">RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Group comparisons separate current candidates; anchors bridge groups where ranks alone hide absolute level. Specify weights; rank gaps aren&#x27;t equal quality distances.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An all-bad group still has a winner; an anchor can show it remains poor.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06310">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06310-rrc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a6fd8d121f808e69">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rrc" data-paper-title="RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rrc-3d32cfb6" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-aab7c26674050fe8">Why derive RRC generative reward from relative ranking?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arrc">RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Generative judges may compare reliably without calibrated standalone scores. Within-group ranks plus anchors yield centered rewards while exploiting comparative strength.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A judge may prefer one summary reliably but inconsistently use a ten-point scale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06310">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06310-rrc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aab7c26674050fe8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rp-opsd" data-paper-title="RP-OPSD" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e5b5363bc9a06ac0">Why compare matched views with and without English solutions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arp-opsd">RP-OPSD</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reference-induced distribution shifts can identify reasoning transitions rather than superficial translation. Concentrate privileged distillation there and keep reference anchoring. Match all other inputs and keep solutions teacher-only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Translated connectives and words determining operation order may shift differently after adding a solution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06347">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06347-rp-opsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e5b5363bc9a06ac0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rp-opsd" data-paper-title="RP-OPSD" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0f63d2dc1f5e666f">What must the two RP-OPSD teacher views share?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arp-opsd">RP-OPSD</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Same model, question and student prefix; remove only reference conditioning. Student rollout cannot see reference answers. Local deterministic proxies aren&#x27;t real multilingual teachers/corpora.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Changing both model and question prevents attributing probability changes to the English reference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06347">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06347-rp-opsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0f63d2dc1f5e666f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rp-opsd" data-paper-title="RP-OPSD" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-60ca89bd820aa23d">How does pivot detection differ from uniformly imitating all English tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arp-opsd">RP-OPSD</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Uniform imitation can copy style and translation artifacts. Conditional shifts highlight important positions while retaining reference anchoring. Shifts aren&#x27;t causal truth, so validate teacher quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Different English wording with unchanged mathematical state need not rewrite every student word.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06347">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06347-rp-opsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-60ca89bd820aa23d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rp-opsd" data-paper-title="RP-OPSD" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rp-opsd-6ed9619b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-02d09cb456980886">Why distill cross-lingually around reasoning pivots in RP-OPSD?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arp-opsd">RP-OPSD</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Surface wording differs across languages; state-changing tokens matter more. Compare matched teacher distributions with/without the English reference to locate large information-induced shifts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A connective and a key equation need not receive equal credit based on text differences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06347">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06347-rp-opsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-02d09cb456980886">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:opd2" data-paper-title="On-Policy Delta Distillation for Multilingual Math Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1c97a90289933840">Why copy the delta rather than every teacher preference?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aopd2">On-Policy Delta Distillation for Multilingual Math Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NAVER AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Comparing before/after logp isolates directions associated with post-training instead of inherited language/style/knowledge. It needs comparable checkpoints and isn&#x27;t proven pure capability. Local small distributions don&#x27;t verify language transfer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If RL improves conclusions but politeness is unchanged, the delta avoids treating the greeting as a new skill.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05802">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.05802-opd2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1c97a90289933840">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:opd2" data-paper-title="On-Policy Delta Distillation for Multilingual Math Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1397d152821b1244">May OPD² use arbitrary teacher families for its two probabilities?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aopd2">On-Policy Delta Distillation for Multilingual Math Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NAVER AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Not silently. Use paired base and post-trained checkpoint on the same prefix with aligned vocabulary/conditioning. Local candidates do not load multilingual math checkpoints.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An unrelated architecture as base confounds family calibration with the training delta.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05802">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.05802-opd2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1397d152821b1244">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:opd2" data-paper-title="On-Policy Delta Distillation for Multilingual Math Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-942a8457730a05d1">How does delta distillation differ from copying the post-trained distribution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aopd2">On-Policy Delta Distillation for Multilingual Math Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NAVER AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It subtracts the teacher base; direct matching includes old knowledge and preferences. Subtraction may discard useful information or retain training noise, so not universally better.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Learning the update is not copying the whole teacher knowledge base.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05802">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.05802-opd2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-942a8457730a05d1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:opd2" data-paper-title="On-Policy Delta Distillation for Multilingual Math Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-opd2-d840d7f7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-12b045ccfcff8b40">Why distill the teacher&#x27;s post-training change from base in OPD²?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aopd2">On-Policy Delta Distillation for Multilingual Math Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NAVER AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Teacher&#x27;s preexisting preferences may not come from target training. The delta emphasizes what changed instead of transferring all language/style bias; matching checkpoints is essential.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An unchanged long-sentence preference should not count as newly acquired skill.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05802">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.05802-opd2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-12b045ccfcff8b40">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dash" data-paper-title="DASH" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-67cd03485d3aa1a0">Why control DASH horizon by local disagreement rather than propagate everything?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adash">DASH</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Later teacher feedback may help or become unreliable after divergence. Detached gating varies effective horizon without extra teacher calls. Fixed long or short windows can mix irrelevant signals or miss important outcomes. Gate is not truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Carry future credit across consistent steps but weaken propagation at a severe divergence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06243">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06243-dash/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-67cd03485d3aa1a0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dash" data-paper-title="DASH" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-64ac46dc84be0cdf">How should DASH handle boundaries and gate gradients?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adash">DASH</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Recur backward with no next term at sequence end, detach gate and block padding or cross-response propagation. Candidate positions aren&#x27;t long-token traces.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not carry future credit from the next answer into the last token of this one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06243">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06243-dash/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-64ac46dc84be0cdf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dash" data-paper-title="DASH" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-1844471842da9817">How does DASH&#x27;s continuous gate differ from fixed discount?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adash">DASH</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed discount propagates equally by position; gate uses relative local disagreement to vary horizon. Proxy credit is not always correct and doesn&#x27;t add teacher rollouts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Consequences at equal distance can propagate differently under different local disagreement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06243">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06243-dash/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1844471842da9817">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dash" data-paper-title="DASH" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-dash-1d95c042" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-2ef1f243013623af">Why propagate later distillation differences to earlier positions in DASH?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adash">DASH</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Early choices have multi-step consequences. Local disagreement gates a backward recurrence with adaptive horizon, without extra teacher passes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An early fork causing repeated later errors should see some of their credit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06243">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2608.06243-dash/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2ef1f243013623af">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:macro" data-paper-title="MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-macro-6eaa3033" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9feb28422bcc1fc0">How does MACRO change input computation without changing weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amacro">MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A context-conditioned routing program can skip, repeat, or residual-add layers. Feedback updates route probabilities and search selects programs; the backbone is fixed. Use validation, not isolated test gold, for selection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two prompts can execute different paths through identical layers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.05872-macro/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9feb28422bcc1fc0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:macro" data-paper-title="MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-223e9229767279e9">Can MACRO greedily concatenate the highest-probability operation at each step?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amacro">MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Not generally. Top-k Viterbi preserves Markov dependencies. Locally greedy choices can miss a better full program; the classification mini-suite is not the paper&#x27;s scale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A likely repeat now can reduce the score of all later reachable paths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.05872-macro/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-223e9229767279e9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:macro" data-paper-title="MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a661f3ccf921f6ab">What does routing search change compared with fine-tuning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amacro">MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It changes how fixed layers execute, not internal parameters. Costs and generalization can differ, and a route is not a new trained backbone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Rearranging blocks differs from reshaping them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.05872-macro/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a661f3ccf921f6ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:macro" data-paper-title="MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-be5da7502289a7b9">Why treat layer execution as a program?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amacro">MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Context-conditioned Markov routes support skip, repeat, and residual-add rather than one fixed order. Feedback updates routes and candidate decoding chooses programs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One input can skip a layer and repeat another.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.05872-macro/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-be5da7502289a7b9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hilp" data-paper-title="Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-hilp-e751afd4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-988153cb726324b4">Why add a coarse temporal target to stepwise latent prediction in HiLP?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahilp">Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Texas at Austin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Small one-step errors can compound and lose distant structure. A coarse abstract latent supervises longer spans alongside next-token and local latent objectives. This does not eliminate rollout errors or replace long-horizon tests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Predict the next waypoint and the next stage to constrain gradual route drift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05806">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.05806-hilp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-988153cb726324b4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hilp" data-paper-title="Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-26cab03f82cf2939">How isolate the effect of HiLP&#x27;s coarse target?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahilp">Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Texas at Austin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Hold split, budget, and backbone fixed; ablate the block-level abstract objective and report fine and coarse errors. Synthetic diagnostics are not paper-scale LM results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Changing data and steps while adding λH confounds attribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hilp" data-paper-title="Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-6430efce8e8df83a">How does coarse latent loss differ from raising the next-step weight?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahilp">Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Texas at Austin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reweighting supervises the same horizon. A coarse target introduces a different span and structure, not simply larger λ1.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Doubling next-second loss does not ask for a prediction of the next minute.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hilp" data-paper-title="Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">

<h2 id="qa-c953a19c1dd72bb5">Why predict both next and abstract latents?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahilp">Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Texas at Austin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Local rollout may accumulate error; coarse targets constrain longer-term structure while preserving immediate detail.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:bakron" data-paper-title="BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-bakron-8758065a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-cb4b0da0ce3093eb">Why use bilateral Kronecker curvature instead of input activation alone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Abakron">BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Output-side curvature also changes the impact of weight error. A Kronecker approximation includes both sides in a quadratic objective, with structured parallel/divide-and-conquer rounding instead of a full Hessian. Independent rounding is not equivalent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal input errors can differ in loss sensitivity along different output directions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.06291-bakron/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cb4b0da0ce3093eb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:bakron" data-paper-title="BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5c531490304feada">Why check vectorization order and Kronecker factors together?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Abakron">BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Flattening convention determines which side each factor acts on. Swapped axes optimize a different error. Compare an explicit vectorized reference; random small weights are not checkpoint-scale evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Row- and column-major flattening require consistent factor conventions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.06291-bakron/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5c531490304feada">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:bakron" data-paper-title="BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-372536e06264d80f">What does BaKron add over input-side GPTQ-style rounding?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Abakron">BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Weight vectorized error with A⊗B to include both curvatures. Optimization must match that bilateral objective; row-wise rounding is not equivalent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Lower ordinary MSE can still incur greater bilateral weighted error.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.06291-bakron/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-372536e06264d80f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:bakron" data-paper-title="BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-123e76370ee763fb">Why isn&#x27;t BaKron ordinary elementwise rounding?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Abakron">BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It minimizes curvature-weighted joint error, not distance to each scalar grid point. Correlated rounding errors can amplify or cancel.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two small errors aligned in one output can be worse than a larger pair that cancels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2608.06291-bakron/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-123e76370ee763fb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>

<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2aacee6d37ba8428">Why doesn&#x27;t AMS activation separation establish behavioral safety?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aactivation-model-scanner">Detecting Safety Training Modification in Language Models via Activation Analysis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mid-layer contrast directions and same-architecture baseline drift provide structural evidence only. Layer numbering, variance, and baseline affect thresholds. Independent behavior evaluation is still required.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A model can distinguish safety concepts internally while still responding unsafely to a particular prompt.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:activation-model-scanner" data-paper-title="Detecting Safety Training Modification in Language Models via Activation Analysis" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">

<h2 id="qa-00d402cba51d2174">Why add one to the AMS block index in Hugging Face hidden_states?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aactivation-model-scanner">Detecting Safety Training Modification in Language Models via Activation Analysis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Block hooks are zero-based but hidden_states[0] is embeddings. Use block_id+1, select the last real token, and preserve population variance and strict threshold.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Block 9 reads hidden_states[10].</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:activation-model-scanner" data-paper-title="Detecting Safety Training Modification in Language Models via Activation Analysis" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-bc23a004bfa13d4a">What do AMS Tier 1 and Tier 2 measure?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aactivation-model-scanner">Detecting Safety Training Modification in Language Models via Activation Analysis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tier 1 measures separation of positive and negative projections. Tier 2 compares direction consistency and relative drift against matching layers/dimensions. Internal separation need not mean baseline alignment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Wide separation can coexist with a direction flip relative to baseline.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:activation-model-scanner" data-paper-title="Detecting Safety Training Modification in Language Models via Activation Analysis" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">

<h2 id="qa-2c950ffb6691c1f4">Why scan contrastive input activations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aactivation-model-scanner">Detecting Safety Training Modification in Language Models via Activation Analysis</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Identify safety-related separation in intermediate layers and compare direction/drift with a matched baseline. This does not generate or validate behavioral answers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Separable concepts do not guarantee all related requests are handled well.</p>
