<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28076">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.28076-grsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0cf8f23b8cf80af1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:grsd" data-paper-title="Group-Reflective Self-Distillation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d2cc0c2d48d654f2">How does GRSD&#x27;s success/failure group comparison differ from copying one successful trajectory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Agrsd">Group-Reflective Self-Distillation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Baidu Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A success can contain accidental or unnecessary steps. Group comparison uses failures to identify what to do or avoid. It is training guidance, not an oracle for independent testing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An irrelevant tool call in a successful trace is not automatically worth learning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28076">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.28076-grsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d2cc0c2d48d654f2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:grsd" data-paper-title="Group-Reflective Self-Distillation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e89fb2bb2adfb023">Why does GRSD reflect on verified success and failure trajectories for the same task?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Agrsd">Group-Reflective Self-Distillation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Baidu Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Terminal reward mixes useful behavior, repeated mistakes, and chance. Contrasting reflections within a task yields specific DO/AVOID guidance to modulate turn credit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Both trajectories retrieve information, but only one checks a key condition. The contrast helps isolate useful behavior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28076">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.28076-grsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e89fb2bb2adfb023">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:finance-harness-protocol" data-paper-title="FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9ffeae55e9d1c6ba">Why keep predictions verifiable after the cutoff with the post-submission evaluator?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Afinance-harness-protocol">FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud AI Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Research may use only evidence available by cutoff. Earlier access to future materials turns prediction into repetition. Thesis and rubric also remain with the grader; normalize per item before averaging. Leakage invalidates the run rather than justifying dropping or zeroing a row.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Later earnings can verify a forecast after submission, but must not be backfilled into the earlier evidence pack.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27853v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.27853-finance-harness-protocol/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9ffeae55e9d1c6ba">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:finance-harness-protocol" data-paper-title="FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-aebea6d3c661cc2f">Can a finance-protocol row with time leakage be set to zero and included in the mean?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Afinance-harness-protocol">FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud AI Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Invalidate the run rather than silently dropping or zeroing the row. publication_date must be no later than cutoff, and thesis, rubric, and future evidence stay away from the agent. This is a point-in-time evaluation protocol, not investment advice.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A tool finding an article published after the cutoff is not merely one wrong answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27853v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.27853-finance-harness-protocol/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aebea6d3c661cc2f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:finance-harness-protocol" data-paper-title="FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a30f6f4a0d087a4a">How does equal weighting by item differ from pooling all rubrics?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Afinance-harness-protocol">FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud AI Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Items have different counts. Pooling gives detailed items more weight; normalize per item first and then average. Do not replace the five-point rubric with an arbitrary continuous scale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An item with ten criteria should not automatically weigh five times one with two.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27853v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.27853-finance-harness-protocol/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a30f6f4a0d087a4a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:finance-harness-protocol" data-paper-title="FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-finance-harness-protocol-8c1ac9fa" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-bbb3ce54beabf3be">Is a FinanceGym rubric score of 3 a 3% success rate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Afinance-harness-protocol">FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Cloud AI Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A rubric uses five grades from 0 through 4, and 3 is one level. Normalize within each item by its four-point maximum before averaging items. Interpretation still depends on the rubric. Raw levels, normalized item scores, and overall Outcome are distinct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>For two rubrics scored 3 and 1, the item score is (3+1)/(4×2)=0.5, not 4% or a two-item hit rate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27853v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.27853-finance-harness-protocol/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bbb3ce54beabf3be">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:psg" data-paper-title="PSG: Pair-Space Generation for Efficient Generative Reranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-psg-c3e023ce" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-17163889d7416526">Why do PSG pair tokens reduce steps but need internal order?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apsg">PSG: Pair-Space Generation for Efficient Generative Reranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each token jointly models two positions and can be losslessly expanded, halving autoregressive steps for even lengths. Pair order affects display and future conditions, while cross-pair duplicates can invalidate the slate. Some complexity moves to the larger pairing/scoring space.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Six items take three ordered pairs. Coffee machine then beans differs from beans then machine; another pair containing the machine needs duplicate handling.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26427">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26427-psg/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-17163889d7416526">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:psg" data-paper-title="PSG: Pair-Space Generation for Efficient Generative Reranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e93e622c0c622dc8">Why deduplicate across PSG pairs instead of only within each pair?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apsg">PSG: Pair-Space Generation for Efficient Generative Reranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Local uniqueness does not prevent repeats across a slate. Check new pairs against the selected prefix and preserve internal order when expanding. Define odd lengths, leftovers, and empty legal sets instead of repeating items to fill slots.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Camera–lens and camera–bag are each unique internally but repeat the camera after expansion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26427">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26427-psg/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e93e622c0c622dc8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:psg" data-paper-title="PSG: Pair-Space Generation for Efficient Generative Reranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-36598c3f06a42d49">What dependency can PSG pair scoring capture beyond parallel individual item heads?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apsg">PSG: Pair-Space Generation for Efficient Generative Reranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Joint scoring evaluates two items and their order as one action, modeling complementarity. Parallel independent heads may not. The pair action space can be large, and the proxy regressed, so half-length alone is not lossless speedup.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Camera plus lens can be better than two redundant high-scoring cameras, but all possible pairs outnumber individual items.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26427">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26427-psg/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-36598c3f06a42d49">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:psg" data-paper-title="PSG: Pair-Space Generation for Efficient Generative Reranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-bd4316b465920770">Does lossless PSG expansion mean pair and item models have the same probabilities?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apsg">PSG: Pair-Space Generation for Efficient Generative Reranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The mapping recovers both items and their order for a given pair; the scorer and search distribution can still change. Fewer steps do not imply equal training error, coverage, or quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Packing A B C D as AB and CD recovers it exactly, but the new model can prefer other pairs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26427">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26427-psg/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bd4316b465920770">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:oneshot-index" data-paper-title="OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-oneshot-index-d86efe4f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-43a83253198c0a11">How does OneShot train discrete hierarchical addresses on ranking rather than embedding-distance clusters?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aoneshot-index">OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Instagram</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Forward passes take discrete paths; straight-through gradients approximate ranking-loss feedback to assignment parameters. Global balancing avoids crowded paths, and neural scoring ranks retrieved candidates. Joint learning aligns objectives, but approximate gradients and balanced load do not guarantee relevance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Similar text with different audiences can be assigned to different paths by behavior; balancing can keep popular items from overloading one bucket.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27475">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.27475-oneshot-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-43a83253198c0a11">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:oneshot-index" data-paper-title="OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-713862f67a90446c">Why check OneShot&#x27;s straight-through forward and backward behavior separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aoneshot-index">OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Instagram</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Forward must choose a real discrete one-hot route; backward approximates with softmax gradients. Fully soft assignment is not discrete serving, while hard argmax may block gradients. Align path, item map, and scorer versions to verify ranking trains addresses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Routing weights receive gradients, but one forward still chooses one prescribed path, not a mix of all buckets.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27475">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.27475-oneshot-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-713862f67a90446c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:oneshot-index" data-paper-title="OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ae072d6a59aa6979">Why do OneShot path balancing and popularity penalties affect different objects?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aoneshot-index">OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Instagram</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Path balancing manages bucket load and resources. Popularity penalties alter recommendation preference. Balanced buckets may spread popular items without reducing their exposure, so measure index use and business distribution separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Ten popular items can fill ten distinct buckets and still all be recommended.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27475">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.27475-oneshot-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ae072d6a59aa6979">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:oneshot-index" data-paper-title="OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-09ee1ff47d178754">Why make the index path part of OneShot rather than cluster after training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aoneshot-index">OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Instagram</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Post-training clustering follows existing geometry and can disagree with ranking. Joint training uses behavior loss to shape buckets, then a strong scorer distinguishes retrieved items. Discrete routing and balancing can still reduce coverage and may not help at every scale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Ranking can separate items with similar text but distinct buyers. A fixed bucket can hide the right item from even a good scorer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27475">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.27475-oneshot-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-09ee1ff47d178754">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:director" data-paper-title="DIRECTOR: Dynamic Index-based Recommendation with Transport-Optimized Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-director-8aa08907" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3f91ba74c893e498">Why does DIRECTOR combine Sinkhorn with global matching rather than independently choosing each position&#x27;s top item?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adirector">DIRECTOR: Dynamic Index-based Recommendation with Transport-Optimized Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent predictions can select the same item. Sinkhorn constructs a soft transport plan constrained by row and column marginals; global hard matching then creates a conflict-free list. Soft probabilities alone are not a displayable permutation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If all three positions favor A, matching assigns it where most useful and places B and C elsewhere.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26418">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26418-director/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3f91ba74c893e498">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:director" data-paper-title="DIRECTOR: Dynamic Index-based Recommendation with Transport-Optimized Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-adf26f4d49897225">How should DIRECTOR align score matrices and final permutations with candidate IDs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adirector">DIRECTOR: Dynamic Index-based Recommendation with Transport-Optimized Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rows are positions and columns are candidate identities. Maintain column identity through transport and matching, and retrieve by matched global indexes rather than per-row rank. Explicitly handle duplicate IDs or too few candidates. Local movie proxies do not establish production valid views.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If column two was movie B, indexing a reshuffled candidate table after matching can display the wrong movie.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26418">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26418-director/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-adf26f4d49897225">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:director" data-paper-title="DIRECTOR: Dynamic Index-based Recommendation with Transport-Optimized Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-33ef213afb9625c2">Why not decode DIRECTOR&#x27;s Sinkhorn matrix with independent row argmaxes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adirector">DIRECTOR: Dynamic Index-based Recommendation with Transport-Optimized Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Continuous soft constraints do not guarantee that independent maxima choose distinct columns. Discrete global matching trades per-position scores for total feasible assignment quality. Temperature and iteration affect approximation, not rowwise legality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If both rows favor A at 0.6 over B at 0.4, independent choices conflict; hard matching must give B to one row.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26418">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26418-director/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-33ef213afb9625c2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:director" data-paper-title="DIRECTOR: Dynamic Index-based Recommendation with Transport-Optimized Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-2b387bec5d3f4c84">Why does DIRECTOR&#x27;s dynamic index distribution cover all display positions jointly?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adirector">DIRECTOR: Dynamic Index-based Recommendation with Transport-Optimized Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Positions draw from competing candidate sets. Joint transport connects position supply and item allocation, and hard matching creates a feasible slate. Parallel generation reduces sequential dependencies, but still requires relevance and legality checks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Five positions can all favor the same movie; joint allocation restricts it to its allowed count and assigns other options elsewhere.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26418">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26418-director/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2b387bec5d3f4c84">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:clockrope" data-paper-title="ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-clockrope-0d0da402" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4dacd6aabb5cf7c7">Why can ClockRoPE give higher relevance to a one-week gap than to a two-day gap?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclockrope">ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · YouTube / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Behavior may recur periodically rather than decay monotonically. ClockRoPE samples rotary frequencies from the desired periodic kernel&#x27;s spectrum so query-key dot products strengthen again at matching times of day or week. Ordinary RoPE can share channels to retain recency. Periodicity is a bias, not a universal user habit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Last Monday morning commute news can be more relevant to this Monday than Saturday-night entertainment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26369">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26369-clockrope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4dacd6aabb5cf7c7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:clockrope" data-paper-title="ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-45fd047e4127727e">Why must ClockRoPE&#x27;s day and week periods match the timestamp unit?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclockrope">ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · YouTube / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The local kernel uses periods 24 and 168 when gaps are in hours. Raw seconds shift phase, and sampled frequencies and mixed channels must respect rotary dimension pairing. Test re-enhancement one period apart, not just tensor shapes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Convert seven days to 168 hours. Feeding the raw second count interprets the same interval as many incorrect periods.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26369">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26369-clockrope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-45fd047e4127727e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:clockrope" data-paper-title="ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5181ac128751cc15">How does ClockRoPE differ from adding a weekday feature?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclockrope">ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · YouTube / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A weekday feature is an absolute time label. ClockRoPE changes pairwise attention directly through relative query-key rotations and a periodic similarity kernel. They may overlap or complement one another; the mechanism alone does not guarantee better results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A Friday label says what day it is; rotation directly relates this Friday to last Friday in attention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26369">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26369-clockrope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5181ac128751cc15">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:clockrope" data-paper-title="ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a12f3605b45b2935">Why use a periodic kernel in ClockRoPE rather than assuming relevance always decays with distance?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclockrope">ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · YouTube / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Habits may repeat by hour or weekday. The periodic kernel restores similarity at specific offsets through its rotary frequencies. It is a prior, and proxies without real timestamps are not evidence of periodic behavior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A Friday film habit makes a seven-day gap informative; for an irregular viewer the same periodic bonus can add noise.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26369">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26369-clockrope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a12f3605b45b2935">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:asarl" data-paper-title="ASARL: Autonomous Social-Aware Relevance Learning for QQ Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-asarl-181d0e5f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2bf061e90f455235">Why not replace ASARL Critic and GenAgent with one LLM labeling pass?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aasarl">ASARL: Autonomous Social-Aware Relevance Learning for QQ Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent PCG</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A one-pass labeler can inherit bias and miss long-tail intent. ReasonAgent proposes, Critic finds repeated gaps, GenAgent targets them, and behavior feedback plus distillation adapts serving. Generated rationales are not automatically truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Diagnose campus-slang mistakes, then add matching counterexamples rather than more unrelated labels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26593">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26593-asarl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2bf061e90f455235">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:asarl" data-paper-title="ASARL: Autonomous Social-Aware Relevance Learning for QQ Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f737fc745ada373a">Does ASARL KL distill reasons or label distributions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aasarl">ASARL: Autonomous Social-Aware Relevance Learning for QQ Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent PCG</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The online student minimizes teacher/student label-distribution KL. Reasons support data and teacher training, not online explanations. Genre proxy classification improved without ranking transfer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Learn three relevance probabilities rather than generate long reasoning per request.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:asarl" data-paper-title="ASARL: Autonomous Social-Aware Relevance Learning for QQ Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-36bcca6a95183b32">How does PGO differ from synthetic three-level supervision?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aasarl">ASARL: Autonomous Social-Aware Relevance Learning for QQ Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent PCG</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>PGO uses interaction-validated reasoning/label preference pairs, not only generated and reviewed labels. Behavior can remain biased; lower classification loss is not retrieval evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Real users preferring camera-model groups can correct generic photography labels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26593">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.26593-asarl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-36bcca6a95183b32">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:asarl" data-paper-title="ASARL: Autonomous Social-Aware Relevance Learning for QQ Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5c546964529a7273">Why learn three social relevance levels before distilling an online student?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aasarl">ASARL: Autonomous Social-Aware Relevance Learning for QQ Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent PCG</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Colloquial, long-tail titles need contextual teacher supervision. Transfer fine-grained label distributions to a small model; validate against real search needs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>“Weekend group” can mean gaming or hiking; teacher reasons in context and student predicts strong, weak, or irrelevant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:serpo" data-paper-title="SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended Test-Time Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-40eccd1b65b34ba5">Why separate SERPO archive, rubric and actor roles?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aserpo">SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended Test-Time Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The archive stores comparisons, rubric defines current standards, and actor generates. Feedback can adapt or amplify bias. New archive or rubric doesn&#x27;t itself train or improve the model; use independent holdout.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A short-only archive, brevity rubric and short actor may agree while neglecting facts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26873">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.26873-serpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-40eccd1b65b34ba5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:serpo" data-paper-title="SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended Test-Time Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-eb6638f64a00a344">How should SERPO track its three evolving states?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aserpo">SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended Test-Time Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Record versions and ordering of generation, archive, rubric and actor updates. Don&#x27;t retrospectively score with later rubrics. Local candidates don&#x27;t implement full generation/judging.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Log the actual rubric used for each batch so training supervision is auditable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26873">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.26873-serpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eb6638f64a00a344">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:serpo" data-paper-title="SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended Test-Time Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-54db0361417a9679">How does SERPO differ from repeated RL under a fixed rubric?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aserpo">SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended Test-Time Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It updates query-specific rubrics and archives with the actor. Fixed criteria can lose discrimination, but coevolution risks drift and self-reinforcement. Self-scores aren&#x27;t proof.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>New criteria can distinguish harder negatives after the actor learns initial rules.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26873">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.26873-serpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-54db0361417a9679">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:serpo" data-paper-title="SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended Test-Time Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-serpo-1bbe9fff" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c2866c0ae1401306">Why keep a Good–Normal–Bad archive in SERPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aserpo">SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended Test-Time Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different qualities inform prompt-specific rubrics and policy learning. Actor and criteria evolve; storing only highest scores loses contrasts. Classification depends on judge quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Medium answers expose gaps and bad answers show patterns to avoid.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26873">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.26873-serpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c2866c0ae1401306">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:reco-grpo" data-paper-title="ReCo" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-24eff40b49e92f55">Why downweight common replies and adjust individual-token variance separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Areco-grpo">ReCo</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Seoul National University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Response weights correct expected repetition across the group; token variance measures local plasticity. Neither replaces the other. Coverage isn&#x27;t arbitrary randomness; candidate probabilities do not show long-text coverage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Downweighting repeated template responses can still leave nearly deterministic final tokens dominating.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26862">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.26862-reco/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-24eff40b49e92f55">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:reco-grpo" data-paper-title="ReCo" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b7324658a6699d93">Why preserve old versus current probability in ReCo&#x27;s Bernoulli variance ratio?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Areco-grpo">ReCo</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Seoul National University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compare current p(1−p) to old variance for changes in decision saturation. Protect near-zero denominators, not use current on both sides and get one. Candidate tests aren&#x27;t text pass@64.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Check numerical stability when old probability is near a boundary instead of accepting an enormous anomalous signal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26862">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.26862-reco/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b7324658a6699d93">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:reco-grpo" data-paper-title="ReCo" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-44a200aee7cb27b3">Is deduplication equivalent to ReCo expected-count weighting?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Areco-grpo">ReCo</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Seoul National University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Hard dedup drops repeated samples; expected-count weights vary continuously with policy likelihood. A separate variance ratio adjusts tokens. The objectives differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two responses may appear only once each while one has much higher underlying probability and different weight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26862">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.26862-reco/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-44a200aee7cb27b3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:reco-grpo" data-paper-title="ReCo" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-reco-grpo-97f782ad" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c34e2c8ac9baa559">Why does ReCo address both duplicate replies and saturated tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Areco-grpo">ReCo</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Seoul National University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Common responses dominate sample weight and already-certain tokens can be reinforced repeatedly. Expected response counts and token variance ratios target different redundancies to retain exploration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeated solutions and their nearly certain format tokens can both dominate gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26862">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.26862-reco/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c34e2c8ac9baa559">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:skillrise" data-paper-title="SkillRise" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-skillrise-fa529938" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9386b52986589e13">Why reward skill-document curation from later tasks rather than current task success?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Askillrise">SkillRise</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Current success mostly reflects solving, not whether the resulting skill helps later users or the same agent. Related tasks form a sequence, and discounted downstream returns supervise curation toward transferable experience. Apply the two phase advantages to their own generated tokens rather than broadcasting credit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A lucky correct answer can still yield a reusable testing procedure. Its curation value is visible only if it helps later tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.26784-skillrise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9386b52986589e13">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:skillrise" data-paper-title="SkillRise" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6488d5dae7432edc">Do local document-update and downstream-credit counts mean Qwen3 was trained with RL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Askillrise">SkillRise</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Controlled PlanBench tests state evolution, skill transfer, and phase-specific credit without Qwen3 training or the paper&#x27;s three environments. Writes show the action happened, not parameter learning. Perfect mini-suite scores are not comparable with paper Pass@k.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Deterministic rules can write 120 documents. Without real gradient updates, that is not the paper&#x27;s shared-policy training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.26784-skillrise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6488d5dae7432edc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:skillrise" data-paper-title="SkillRise" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e88f05c7ec0f5b77">How does a connected curriculum transfer experience differently from training episodes independently?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Askillrise">SkillRise</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A skill document curated from one task becomes input to the next, so transferable experience can be used and evaluated. Independent episodes normally do not expose this link. Related tasks can overfit a curriculum; distinguish downstream document benefit from current solving and do not infer generalization from transfer counts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A simple table cleanup produces checks for a constrained variant next. Random unrelated tasks may never use those checks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.26784-skillrise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e88f05c7ec0f5b77">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:skillrise" data-paper-title="SkillRise" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d86d7ab30cfa12bb">Why does one policy alternate solving the current task and curating a skill document?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Askillrise">SkillRise</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Solving produces experience; curation passes transferable material directly into the next task, making cross-task learning part of behavior. Related tasks progress from easy to hard, so documents must help later rather than simply explain present success. This is not independent episode training and not a mandate to keep all experiences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: After a simple file search, record location and verification methods for a harder modification task instead of copying the old answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.26784-skillrise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d86d7ab30cfa12bb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:cam-df" data-paper-title="CAM-DF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-cam-df-2b7f3d23" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0570cdc0a7c4faa1">Why derive stop labels from the payoff gap between the current prefix and best later prefix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acam-df">CAM-DF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Relevance ranking does not say how many exposed tools are sufficient. Early stop can miss capability and late stop costs resources. Virtual payoff subtracts cost from sufficiency; the difference sets stop or continue and its magnitude gives regret. This happens before execution, so virtual payoff is not tool success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two tools already suffice, while a related but expensive third reduces payoff. Stop labels should reflect that cost rather than rank alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27083">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.27083-cam-df/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0570cdc0a7c4faa1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:cam-df" data-paper-title="CAM-DF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c90b30ce9f21e6a3">Can local required-tools sufficiency be a general deployment scorer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acam-df">CAM-DF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Required-tools lists in the auditable mini-suite diagnose prefix choices rather than act as a learned semantic scorer. Do not reveal hidden requirements to an evaluated policy. Lower exposure is not live τ-bench token or success improvement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Knowing the third tool is required is useful for offline payoff, but a runtime router reading that list bypasses the learned sufficiency problem.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27083">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.27083-cam-df/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c90b30ce9f21e6a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:cam-df" data-paper-title="CAM-DF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-580c3367b255c392">How is regret weighting different from ordinary stop/continue labels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acam-df">CAM-DF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Error costs can differ. Gap sign supplies the class and magnitude represents lost payoff. Equal weights treat near ties like missed essential tools. A best later prefix is a comparison estimate that depends on sufficiency scoring, not hidden deployment truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Exposing one cheap extra tool has little cost. Stopping before an essential refund interface is a large error that deserves greater weight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27083">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.27083-cam-df/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-580c3367b255c392">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:cam-df" data-paper-title="CAM-DF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-20b5ca35f6a5f4ae">Why decide how many tools to expose after ranking them?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acam-df">CAM-DF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rank order does not identify a sufficient set. Too many tools add cost and distraction, while too few miss interfaces. CAM-DF compares virtual prefixes and heterogeneous costs before execution. It controls exposure, not dynamic stopping after actual calls.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: If the first two tools only query and the third modifies, a modification task may need the third regardless of the earlier scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27083">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.27083-cam-df/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-20b5ca35f6a5f4ae">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:twice" data-paper-title="TWICE: Two-Clock, Two-Window Learning for Long-Horizon Conversion Prediction in Online Advertising" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-90f01d7ee97d595c">Why learn final conversion and delay CDF separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atwice">TWICE: Two-Clock, Two-Window Learning for Long-Horizon Conversion Prediction in Online Advertising</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An unobserved conversion may be delayed. Event probability times delay CDF gives observable status. Two clocks/windows address maturity bias, subject to a suitable delay model. Public timestamps are not ad results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Five minutes without purchase is not equivalent to a week without purchase.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25404">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.25404-twice/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-90f01d7ee97d595c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
