<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24865">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.24865-dual-sid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0c88c2829edde23f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dual-sid" data-paper-title="Tokens are All You Need: Dual-purpose Semantic IDs for Achieving LLM-Level I/O Efficiency in Recommendation Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5608c346f04ecf0b">What is the resource trade-off between short SID plus SiDec and a cached dense embedding?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adual-sid">Tokens are All You Need: Dual-purpose Semantic IDs for Achieving LLM-Level I/O Efficiency in Recommendation Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind / YouTube</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Dense caches preserve vectors at storage and I/O cost. Short codes shift per-item storage into indices and shared decoding, adding compute and error. Lower I/O is not necessarily lower end-to-end latency, and a small-codebook retrieval regression remains meaningful.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A million vectors can become codes, but a decoding matrix on each request may be costly and a small codebook can hurt relevance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24865">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.24865-dual-sid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5608c346f04ecf0b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dual-sid" data-paper-title="Tokens are All You Need: Dual-purpose Semantic IDs for Achieving LLM-Level I/O Efficiency in Recommendation Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-46865ea59a025071">Why should a Dual-purpose SID code also reconstruct a content vector?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adual-sid">Tokens are All You Need: Dual-purpose Semantic IDs for Achieving LLM-Level I/O Efficiency in Recommendation Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind / YouTube</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It supports both generative nomination and ranking features. SiDec converts small indices into approximate content, reducing per-item storage and transmission while training the codes not to retain only collaborative identity. Measure quality loss.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Small codes save bandwidth but cannot reconstruct a waterproofing property they never encoded.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24865">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.24865-dual-sid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-46865ea59a025071">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:egr" data-paper-title="EGR: Embedding-Native Generative Retrieval with a Shared LLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-egr-a66d7f0c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-72f235af74f628cc">Why does EGR jointly train two tasks despite sharing the backbone for item indexing and user queries?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aegr">EGR: Embedding-Native Generative Retrieval with a Shared LLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Shared parameters alone do not align retrieval geometry. Item representation learning maintains indexable content; next-item prediction directs queries toward consumption relations. Training one side against a changing other can stale the index, and serving and evaluation must use matching versions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If new item vectors rotate while queries stay in old coordinates, nearest neighbors can break despite matching dimensions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23038">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.23038-egr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-72f235af74f628cc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:egr" data-paper-title="EGR: Embedding-Native Generative Retrieval with a Shared LLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-239efdbe5c28d9d1">Why verify item-index and query versions after EGR updates its shared backbone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aegr">EGR: Embedding-Native Generative Retrieval with a Shared LLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Updates can change dot-product meaning, so old index vectors may not match new queries. Record rebuild, training, and cutover boundaries and confirm both IRL and NIP run. A shared class name with one loss disabled is not joint training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An old item coordinate system and a new user coordinate system can have equal shapes but incompatible scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23038">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.23038-egr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-239efdbe5c28d9d1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:egr" data-paper-title="EGR: Embedding-Native Generative Retrieval with a Shared LLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-aebfbc8434aabce5">What deployment trade-off does EGR joint updating make versus freezing the item encoder?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aegr">EGR: Embedding-Native Generative Retrieval with a Shared LLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Freezing stabilizes the index but blocks user supervision from refining item geometry. Joint learning can adapt both sides, requiring item refresh and versioned serving. The local negative result should not be replaced by the design promise.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A new query direction for science fiction may not match an old index; freezing avoids drift but keeps old limitations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23038">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.23038-egr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aebfbc8434aabce5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:egr" data-paper-title="EGR: Embedding-Native Generative Retrieval with a Shared LLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-544a8e3547557490">Why jointly optimize item representation learning and next-item prediction in EGR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aegr">EGR: Embedding-Native Generative Retrieval with a Shared LLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Snap Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pure content optimization can omit recommendation distinctions. Next-item supervision retains consumption relationships while the item objective anchors semantics. Shared updates reduce separation but can conflict and do not guarantee alignment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Similar-genre movies can appeal to different audiences; joint learning can preserve that difference beyond text similarity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23038">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.23038-egr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-544a8e3547557490">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinequalizer" data-paper-title="PinEqualizer: Full Funnel Content Exploration and Debiasing System at Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-pinequalizer-1595745d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8ad2cb9fa87f3c82">Why check fresh-content survival at every stage in PinEqualizer instead of boosting it only in fine ranking?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinequalizer">PinEqualizer: Full Funnel Content Exploration and Debiasing System at Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Items filtered in corpus or retrieval never reach the ranker. Track stage inputs and survival to locate bottlenecks. Content features, interaction dropout, and calibration reduce dependence on old exposure; separate exploration and uncertainty rewards collect feedback. Relevance still constrains exploration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A new recipe filtered before retrieval cannot benefit from a ranking boost. Preserve entry and explore promising items selectively.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22518">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.22518-pinequalizer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8ad2cb9fa87f3c82">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinequalizer" data-paper-title="PinEqualizer: Full Funnel Content Exploration and Debiasing System at Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-429c749e92f0ed36">Why preserve validation&#x27;s UCB α=0 rather than tune α for a better fresh metric?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinequalizer">PinEqualizer: Full Funnel Content Exploration and Debiasing System at Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Validation rejected extra exploration under the current objective. Do not reselect on test. The debiased model itself can raise fresh exposure without UCB. Report freshness denominators and overall regression instead of changing objectives afterward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If the model already increases fresh impressions severalfold and UCB hurts relevance, do not force α above zero to claim bandit use.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22518">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.22518-pinequalizer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-429c749e92f0ed36">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinequalizer" data-paper-title="PinEqualizer: Full Funnel Content Exploration and Debiasing System at Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a636a4fd426b06ff">Why does PinEqualizer UCB consider uncertainty and relevance instead of merely lowering popular scores?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinequalizer">PinEqualizer: Full Funnel Content Exploration and Debiasing System at Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Popularity penalties do not identify worthwhile unknown items. UCB promotes low-exposure or uncertain items, with search relevance limiting unrelated exploration. Locally fresh exposure rose but overall NDCG fell, so report both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Explore a relevant new recipe, not unrelated news just because it is obscure.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22518">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.22518-pinequalizer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a636a4fd426b06ff">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinequalizer" data-paper-title="PinEqualizer: Full Funnel Content Exploration and Debiasing System at Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c43ee2f671ca7474">Why treat PinEqualizer exploration as both a supply and a model problem?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinequalizer">PinEqualizer: Full Funnel Content Exploration and Debiasing System at Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>New items can disappear in corpus, retrieval, or ranking. Content reduces dependence on old interactions, an exploration corpus allows entry, and uncertainty allocates feedback. Stage survival locates bottlenecks; a high fresh quota does not guarantee relevance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A favorable ranker cannot recommend an item that retrieval never includes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22518">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.22518-pinequalizer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c43ee2f671ca7474">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:barge" data-paper-title="Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-barge-1cfb2666" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1164e6c8c83dd97c">Why does BARGE both restore item boundaries and rerank accumulated semantic paths?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abarge">Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Ordinary sequence attention can treat the multiple SID codes of one item as separate events; ICA aggregates within-item context and gates it back into each code. HPR evaluates the accumulated generated path to limit propagation of early beam mistakes, while complementary quantization gives alternate decomposition views. These address boundaries, search errors, and diversity respectively.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Province, city, and street are one address, not three purchases. If the coarse province is wrong, refining the street cannot fix it, so check the path at every level.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21028">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21028-barge/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1164e6c8c83dd97c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:barge" data-paper-title="Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-263c5784a60fb5af">Why does BARGE&#x27;s HPR compare the accumulated path vector instead of only the latest code?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abarge">Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The cumulative sum includes every choice from coarse to fine and reveals whether the full semantic path fits the user. During inference combine generation log-probability with reranking; during training use contrastive comparisons over cumulative paths. DPD separately constrains projection orthogonality; it is not the same loss or proof of full independence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An entry-level code makes sense on its own, but the path has already entered home goods while the user wants a camera. Only the accumulated path exposes the mismatch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21028">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21028-barge/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-263c5784a60fb5af">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:barge" data-paper-title="Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-63bc94c75b23ca7b">How do BARGE&#x27;s two complementary decoding paths differ from widening a single beam?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abarge">Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A wider beam searches more paths within one encoding structure. Two orthogonal subspaces construct different representations and quantizations, so one early bias need not dominate both. HPR then scores cumulative paths. Extra paths add training and merge costs, and output count alone does not prove complementarity or independence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A wider beam may still explore a mistaken coarse code, while a second subspace can recover a missed book if it preserves different semantic cues.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21028">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21028-barge/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-63bc94c75b23ca7b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:barge" data-paper-title="Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-321f5c75e23f3457">Why do multiple SID tokens for one BARGE item require explicit item context?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abarge">Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>They are decompositions of the same item, but ordinary sequence attention may treat them as independent events. ICA aggregates within-item context and gates it back into each token, joining whole-item meaning to local detail. This addresses representation structure, not the separate task of learning preferences across items.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A book&#x27;s topic, subcategory, and collision code describe one book, not three successive reads.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21028">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21028-barge/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-321f5c75e23f3457">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:windowed-mtp" data-paper-title="Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-windowed-mtp-ad617a2b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-869f887ecd35e200">Why can shrinking only Windowed-MTP&#x27;s draft context save reads without changing the target distribution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Awindowed-mtp">Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Draft reads sinks and recent tokens; the full target still sees all history and corrects proposals. The window affects draft cost and acceptance, not the exact target definition. Cutting target context changes the guarantee; local latency does not transfer to production.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Target can reject a wrong draft caused by missing old evidence, provided its own history stays complete.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21535-windowed-mtp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-869f887ecd35e200">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:windowed-mtp" data-paper-title="Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-02f172d22260d687">Should overlaps between sinks and recent tokens duplicate KV?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Awindowed-mtp">Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Use the union without duplicates. Only draft indices change; target retains the full cache.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A position in both sets appears once in draft attention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21535-windowed-mtp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-02f172d22260d687">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:windowed-mtp" data-paper-title="Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e21f03e9bf00b0a4">Why doesn&#x27;t a large reduction in draft keys yield the same TPOT reduction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Awindowed-mtp">Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Draft forwards and target checks still cost time, and time per output depends on accepted length AL. Lower acceptance can offset savings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Cheaper verification that accepts fewer tokens may yield little throughput gain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21535-windowed-mtp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e21f03e9bf00b0a4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:windowed-mtp" data-paper-title="Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f4622ee554153341">Why window only the draft?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Awindowed-mtp">Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Draft KV reads can bottleneck long contexts. Retain sinks and recent draft history while the full target verifies, changing proposal cost and acceptance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Draft might read recent 64 and a few sinks while target reads all 16K.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21535-windowed-mtp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f4622ee554153341">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:naju" data-paper-title="Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-naju-616fb3d6" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2e4296cda59e007b">Why separate retention and writing rather than use complementary gates in Naju?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Anaju">Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent researchers</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A complementary write would shrink whenever retention is strong. Independent gates on native discrete dynamics can preserve old state and write new evidence together. Token-dependent directions, convolution, and feedthrough still matter.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Keep a name while adding age instead of erasing the name in proportion to the new write.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21000">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21000-naju/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2e4296cda59e007b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:naju" data-paper-title="Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e5b9b10c234e61db">How should preserve-first initialization set Naju&#x27;s two gates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Anaju">Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent researchers</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>forget_bias=5 and write_bias=−2 create strong initial retention and weak writes. Retain token-dependent B/C and direct feedthrough.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Sigmoid(5)≈0.993 and sigmoid(−2)≈0.119 are not equal gates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21000">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21000-naju/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e5b9b10c234e61db">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:naju" data-paper-title="Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e36079e843449dc1">How do Naju&#x27;s native discrete poles differ from Mamba discretizing continuous dynamics?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Anaju">Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent researchers</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Naju directly parameterizes discrete retention. Mamba derives a transition from continuous dynamics and input-dependent time steps. Both recur but formulas and gate coupling differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One learns the retained fraction per step directly; the other derives it from a time step and continuous matrix.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21000">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21000-naju/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e36079e843449dc1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:naju" data-paper-title="Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5585d4a9b7fbb306">Why independently control old-state retention and new writes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Anaju">Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent researchers</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A shared complementary gate creates a tradeoff. Separate retain/write gates in the discrete transition let both adjust independently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reading an important new fact need not erase an old fact.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21000">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21000-naju/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5585d4a9b7fbb306">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mobius-rope" data-paper-title="Anti-Periodic Positional Encoding: Möbius Boundary Conditions Make In-Context Retrieval Reliable" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-mobius-rope-d829e106" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9cea57bf909d2052">How does Möbius position encoding differ from standard RoPE across a training window?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amobius-rope">Anti-Periodic Positional Encoding: Möbius Boundary Conditions Make In-Context Retrieval Reliable</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Antiperiodic frequencies on some heads yield −I at one window and I at two. Other heads retain standard RoPE for language modeling. This changes positional geometry, not accessible history or guaranteed retrieval at all lengths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>At N positions the selected heads reverse phase; at 2N they realign. Actual retrieval still depends on Q/K and training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21405">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21405-mobius-rope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9cea57bf909d2052">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mobius-rope" data-paper-title="Anti-Periodic Positional Encoding: Möbius Boundary Conditions Make In-Context Retrieval Reliable" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c8f3ab0c1ff95aa5">Should Möbius RoPE change N dynamically with inference length?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amobius-rope">Anti-Periodic Positional Encoding: Möbius Boundary Conditions Make In-Context Retrieval Reliable</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. N is fixed training context; local N=64 replaces one of four heads. Dynamic N changes frequencies for identical positions and breaks the boundary definition. Retain negative local results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Length-32 and length-80 inputs both use the same training N.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21405">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21405-mobius-rope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c8f3ab0c1ff95aa5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mobius-rope" data-paper-title="Anti-Periodic Positional Encoding: Möbius Boundary Conditions Make In-Context Retrieval Reliable" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7909d719708669df">What explicit frequency boundary does Möbius add?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amobius-rope">Anti-Periodic Positional Encoding: Möbius Boundary Conditions Make In-Context Retrieval Reliable</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Set some two-dimensional frequencies to π(2i+1)/N, producing −I across N and I across 2N. Other heads keep standard RoPE. This is geometry, not measured improvement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reverse phase after one window and recover after two, not arbitrary scaling across every head.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21405">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21405-mobius-rope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7909d719708669df">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mobius-rope" data-paper-title="Anti-Periodic Positional Encoding: Möbius Boundary Conditions Make In-Context Retrieval Reliable" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a35ee6b0b63900fc">What retrieval instability is Möbius RoPE intended to address?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amobius-rope">Anti-Periodic Positional Encoding: Möbius Boundary Conditions Make In-Context Retrieval Reliable</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Independent researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Standard RoPE long-range needle retrieval can vary strongly by training seed. Antiperiodic frequencies on some heads aim to stabilize cross-window phase while leaving others unchanged.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Identical needles in long text can produce very different retrieval results across seeds.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21405">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21405-mobius-rope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a35ee6b0b63900fc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gzip-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-gzip-sparse-attention-4236c23c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ff5a539f7aa258a3">Why give hard-to-gzip blocks long-range edges, and are they necessarily important?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agzip-sparse-attention">Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pennsylvania State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Blocks above the sample&#x27;s average compression-ratio threshold are treated as literal-rich and connected at range while preserving local windows and causality. Compressibility is a training-free proxy, not semantic gold; random noise can also be incompressible and too many literal blocks make edges costly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An unusual ID may need cross-section access while a repeated template compresses easily, but incompressible gibberish need not help.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21752-gzip-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ff5a539f7aa258a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gzip-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-33a4f2c162cacc0b">Why intersect literal, local, and self edges with the causal mask?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agzip-sparse-attention">Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pennsylvania State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Their union expresses relevance, not chronology. Intersect it with causality and assign the appropriate masks to the three head types. Masking dense local scores does not accelerate a sparse kernel.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Selecting two literal blocks cannot let the early one read future tokens in the other.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21752-gzip-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-33a4f2c162cacc0b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gzip-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-95f4b53dbe2b61f2">How does a gzip mask vary compared with a fixed BigBird or Longformer pattern?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agzip-sparse-attention">Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pennsylvania State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed masks use predetermined positions; gzip uses per-example block compressibility for literal edges and retains local windows. It avoids learned mask weights but pays for compression and construction, so edge counts do not establish speed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Moving a unique passage can move gzip edges without changing a positional pattern.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21752-gzip-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-95f4b53dbe2b61f2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gzip-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b01cb35887c2065a">Why compress raw byte blocks first?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agzip-sparse-attention">Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pennsylvania State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compression ratio is a training-free proxy for unique byte density and guides long-range edges, not a semantic importance label.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeated templates compress differently from unique IDs, but hard-to-compress gibberish can be useless.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21752-gzip-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b01cb35887c2065a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:adadsf" data-paper-title="Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-adadsf-0ee93157" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-641401c9edeae52a">Why give more compute to AdaDSF layers with lower input/output similarity?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadadsf">Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei ACS Lab / Southern University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Lower cosine suggests a stronger representation transformation. Dense calibration maps layer differences to a globally corrected budget. Layer routers choose tokens and others bypass residually; allocation and alignment training serve different roles.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With fixed total budget, run the more transformative layer on more tokens instead of uniformly skipping half in each.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21291-adadsf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-641401c9edeae52a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:adadsf" data-paper-title="Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-25065d84348e3527">Should tokens outside layer top-k be removed?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadadsf">Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei ACS Lab / Southern University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Bypass the block with the residual and merge in original order. Correct layer ratios to the global budget. Dropping/reordering positions changes later attention and teacher alignment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Token five can skip one layer but stays at position five for the next.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21291-adadsf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-25065d84348e3527">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:adadsf" data-paper-title="Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7a31595da2cce6b4">What controls should AdaDSF share with Uniform Mixture-of-Depths?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadadsf">Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei ACS Lab / Southern University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Match global budget, teacher initialization, alignment steps, and optimizer. Vary layerwise allocation. The local negative result shows adaptation is not necessarily better.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Comparing 80% and 50% retention confounds strategy with compute.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21291-adadsf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7a31595da2cce6b4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:adadsf" data-paper-title="Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cffc38b1cb7d9602">Why not give each AdaDSF layer the same token budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadadsf">Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei ACS Lab / Southern University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Layers transform inputs by different amounts. Dense-teacher similarities allocate more to stronger transformations; routers and sparse paths then align with the teacher.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A nearly identity layer may need fewer active tokens than one that reorganizes features.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.21291-adadsf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cffc38b1cb7d9602">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tcr" data-paper-title="TCR" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-28193c59a175f590">Why subtract a moving outcome baseline rather than add both rewards directly?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atcr">TCR</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文未列机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Process ratings often track correctness, so direct sums can count success twice. The moving residual attempts to isolate extra reasoning benefit. It depends on checklist and baseline quality, and local proxies don&#x27;t establish full reasoning performance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If correct answers routinely earn high process scores, only an improvement beyond the usual outcome level gives new evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19824">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.19824-tcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-28193c59a175f590">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tcr" data-paper-title="TCR" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-742d03a7a9c6d3b5">Does local TCR call a model to generate per-example checklists?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atcr">TCR</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文未列机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Candidate policies test residual computation, not real checklist generation or free-text training. Update EMA in training order, not from test performance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A hand-provided checklist does not validate automatic checklist quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19824">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.19824-tcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-742d03a7a9c6d3b5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tcr" data-paper-title="TCR" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-871611a87be6887c">How does TCR residual differ from adding process and outcome rewards?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atcr">TCR</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文未列机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Addition accumulates both signals. Subtracting a dynamic outcome baseline reduces duplicate credit. It does not prove exact decorrelation or remove judge bias.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A higher outcome baseline reduces extra credit for an unchanged process score.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19824">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.19824-tcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-871611a87be6887c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:tcr" data-paper-title="TCR" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-tcr-a5ef9cee" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ba053d62fb8e7cba">Why subtract outcome EMA from TCR process scores?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Atcr">TCR</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文未列机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Process and outcome can double-reward success. The residual captures improvement not already explained by outcome before combining them. EMA is training state, not item truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A correct answer should not automatically earn the same success signal again through process scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19824">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2607.19824-tcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ba053d62fb8e7cba">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dynamic-rubric" data-paper-title="Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies via DynamicRubric" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-59f9cc11b48a7651">Why balance hard-negative discrimination and anchoring?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adynamic-rubric">Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies via DynamicRubric</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · WeChat / Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed rubrics can stop separating improved replies; dynamic dimensions help. Discrimination alone can learn stylistic shortcuts, so an anchor stabilizes the reference. Coevolution is not objective improvement without independent tests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>When formatting saturates, new criteria should not simply favor verbosity unchecked.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20083">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.20083-dynamic-rubric/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-59f9cc11b48a7651">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dynamic-rubric" data-paper-title="Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies via DynamicRubric" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7573cde7b2242058">Why tie DynamicRubric weights to prompt and candidate version?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adynamic-rubric">Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies via DynamicRubric</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · WeChat / Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Both determine scoring and new candidates may imply new criteria. Log rubric and anchor versions; don&#x27;t compare rewards under undeclared weight changes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Score changes across two rounds can reflect changed criteria, not actor gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20083">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.20083-dynamic-rubric/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7573cde7b2242058">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dynamic-rubric" data-paper-title="Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies via DynamicRubric" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-78a5fcd1bb4f3dc8">How do discrimination and anchoring pull DynamicRubric in different directions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adynamic-rubric">Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies via DynamicRubric</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · WeChat / Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Discrimination increases sensitivity to current hard cases; anchors retain prior standards and deter co-adaptation. Either alone can reward irrelevant differences or preserve stale criteria.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Length is easy to distinguish, but an anchor should constrain it if unrelated to quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20083">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.20083-dynamic-rubric/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-78a5fcd1bb4f3dc8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dynamic-rubric" data-paper-title="Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies via DynamicRubric" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-dynamic-rubric-5fe56c96" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0ec541e2997598ca">Why build DynamicRubric criteria from the current candidate set?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adynamic-rubric">Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies via DynamicRubric</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · WeChat / Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Old rules can saturate after policy gains. New hard negatives need discriminating dimensions and weights, while anchors limit judge drift. Not permission to change rules after outcomes arbitrarily.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Once every answer meets formatting, look for evidence that still separates quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20083">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.20083-dynamic-rubric/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0ec541e2997598ca">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gaugequant" data-paper-title="GaugeQuant: Online Learning of Quantization-Optimal Bases from LLM Symmetries" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
