</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memcon" data-paper-title="Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-memcon-717a2e37" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8957db0ab44f22e6">Why must the memory controller count UCB visits per discrete state rather than use global action frequencies?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemcon">Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未明确标注（正文 HTML 未显示一作机构映射）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An operation useful early may not help later or under memory pressure. State-local values and counts let the controller learn those trade-offs separately. It explores unvisited actions first, then updates from terminal success and efficiency. No extra LLM call applies to selection; retrieval and execution still have costs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Deep retrieval may help at the start and delay completion near the end. Count attempts separately instead of sharing one global success rate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13591">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.13591-memcon/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8957db0ab44f22e6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memcon" data-paper-title="Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-67d5abfc2cadf284">Can MemCon&#x27;s Q update use sample-mean UCB or TD bootstrapping?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemcon">Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未明确标注（正文 HTML 未显示一作机构映射）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The local implementation follows v3 state-local counts, discounts terminal success and efficiency by distance, and updates repeated state-action pairs in reverse order. It does not bootstrap future Q. Unvisited actions go first with initial Q tie-breaking. Differences from mutable upstream main counts are documented.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: An action seen twice in one episode receives two discounted updates in reverse order, not one reward averaged by visits.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13591">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.13591-memcon/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-67d5abfc2cadf284">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memcon" data-paper-title="Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d2c33c0e1bbf4b0c">What is the trade-off between tabular UCB and asking an LLM to choose a memory policy every round?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemcon">Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未明确标注（正文 HTML 未显示一作机构映射）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tabular control needs no extra model call and has interpretable states and actions, but limited discrete features cannot express arbitrary semantic contexts. LLM control is flexible but costs calls. State-local UCB does not guarantee convergence as the environment and memory change.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A repetition flag can trigger deeper retrieval immediately. Semantically different tasks with the same discrete state may still look identical to the table.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13591">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.13591-memcon/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d2c33c0e1bbf4b0c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memcon" data-paper-title="Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c3c0d162719c7ac">Why does MemCon make whether to use memory a control action?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemcon">Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未明确标注（正文 HTML 未显示一作机构映射）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retrieval, plan injection, query changes, and maintenance cost work. Some simple tasks are cheaper without memory. MemCon selects based on discrete progress, repetition, and memory size, then learns from terminal success and efficiency. Memory need not run on every turn.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: With an obvious next tool, skip retrieval. After repeated failure and with a relevant successful plan, inject it or search deeper.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13591">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2607.13591-memcon/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c3c0d162719c7ac">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:slimper" data-paper-title="SlimPer: Make Personalization Model Slim and Smart" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c8469615c85e200f">If SlimPer already selects evidence with attention, why explicitly dot-product it with knowledge templates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aslimper">SlimPer: Make Personalization Model Slim and Smart</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Platforms, Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Select builds queries from the current bank and aggregates a few user evidence vectors. Match compares those vectors with templates from the same bank, yielding a query-by-template relevance matrix. Refine updates knowledge from these explicit relations rather than treating the aggregate as final interest. Retrieval and aspect-specific relevance are separate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>For running shoes, Select finds running distances and sizes. Match evaluates comfort and intended use separately. Finding evidence does not tell which candidate aspect it supports.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12281">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12281-slimper/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c8469615c85e200f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:slimper" data-paper-title="SlimPer: Make Personalization Model Slim and Smart" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4a13e5753d9c783b">How does SlimPer keep its knowledge base fixed in size while reading the full history at every layer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aslimper">SlimPer: Make Personalization Model Slim and Smart</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Platforms, Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Only a small set of candidate-specific slots is updated. Original user tokens are revisited as read-only evidence. Select retrieves relevant evidence, Match compares it with templates, and Refine updates slots. The full hidden history does not propagate between layers. Candidates share user encodings, but each evolves its own knowledge base rather than using one final interest vector.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Shoe and camera candidates can read the same purchase records but organize size and photography signals in separate banks. Slots updated for shoes must not be reused unchanged for cameras.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12281">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12281-slimper/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4a13e5753d9c783b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:slimper" data-paper-title="SlimPer: Make Personalization Model Slim and Smart" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-8b4dfeda1146dd5b">Once SlimPer fixes the knowledge-base size, can later layers stop reading long histories?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aslimper">SlimPer: Make Personalization Model Slim and Smart</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Platforms, Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Each layer queries shared original tokens. It saves updates to N history states at each layer but still accesses KN query–history pairs. Short MovieLens runs, AdamW, and analytical element counts do not reproduce production QPS or Shampoo results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A small bank must still revisit the evidence; it is not a one-shot compression that discards the history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12281">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12281-slimper/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8b4dfeda1146dd5b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:slimper" data-paper-title="SlimPer: Make Personalization Model Slim and Smart" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c31fdda2ede9afd6">Does not updating all history at each SlimPer layer eliminate relationships between adjacent behaviors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aslimper">SlimPer: Make Personalization Model Slim and Smart</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Platforms, Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Section 2.5 adds local context when tokenizing events, for example via convolution or windowed attention. Later layers repeatedly read those tokens and update a fixed bank. This avoids deep all-pairs history interaction, not every historical relation. Fixed slots cap intermediate state; storing and reading inputs still grows with history length.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Search, compare, and add-to-cart events can get local context before candidate-specific slots read them, without rewriting the full history at every layer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12281">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12281-slimper/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c31fdda2ede9afd6">Question link</a></p>

</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:slimper" data-paper-title="SlimPer: Make Personalization Model Slim and Smart" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-slimper-ce7fc963" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-85f55baa2ea8d44b">Why is SlimPer not just a sequence encoder when compared with HSTU or LONGER?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aslimper">SlimPer: Make Personalization Model Slim and Smart</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Platforms, Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>SlimPer models user–item relevance. Its knowledge base also receives item and cross features, and each Select–Match–Refine layer forms a personalized ranking state. A matched comparison needs candidate interactions and the task head, not only a user-sequence vector.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two candidates can produce different knowledge bases from the same history. Do not compare them solely to a candidate-independent encoder output.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12281">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12281-slimper/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-85f55baa2ea8d44b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sam" data-paper-title="Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-90747e26d9c7c6ae">Why suppress related history after buying and restore it near replenishment?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asam">Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A purchase can complete an intent. Find its related history and estimate personal rhythm; time gates and log masks suppress then restore it. Completion is not dislike. Local ratings proxy purchases, not actual replenishment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reduce detergent repeats immediately, then restore after likely use rather than suppress forever.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12714">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12714-sam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-90747e26d9c7c6ae">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sam" data-paper-title="Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-2bd429203c7ebdc1">Where is SAM&#x27;s mask applied, and what are the local limits?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asam">Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Add a positive log mask to attention logits with numeric safeguards, not a multiplier on final scores. No real replenishment or censored purchase logs; only mechanisms and failure boundaries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Guard near-zero masks without claiming accurate repurchase cycles.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12714">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12714-sam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2bd429203c7ebdc1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sam" data-paper-title="Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c312c786eab5bae1">How does SAM differ from a fixed post-purchase cooldown?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asam">Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It personalizes suppression by history and long-term purchase rhythm. Errors can still hurt, and nonreplenishable products may not fit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Coffee and televisions should not share a one-week rule.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12714">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12714-sam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c312c786eab5bae1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sam" data-paper-title="Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-sam-b9df9dfc" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f667ebf89a92beef">Does SAM blacklist same-category items after a purchase?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asam">Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It softly suppresses attention to related history and restores it over time, not permanent candidate filtering. Other evidence can still support recommendations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Buying shampoo reduces old browsing influence without banning hair products.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12714">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12714-sam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f667ebf89a92beef">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:proximity-features" data-paper-title="Proximity Features: Privacy-Compliant Cold-Start Personalization at Airbnb" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-proximity-features-c055e9e4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2b212bc7d176d0cc">Why split dense regions and merge sparse regions in Airbnb proximity keys?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aproximity-features">Proximity Features: Privacy-Compliant Cold-Start Personalization at Airbnb</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Airbnb</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A fixed grid can be too coarse downtown and contain too few users elsewhere. Hash subdivision and coarser merging maintain group support. Daily aggregates provide anonymous cold-start priors, not persistent personal identity. Geography proxies cohort preferences, not individual interests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Split a block with thousands of users, but enlarge an equally sized suburban cell with ten people.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12246">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12246-proximity-features/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2b212bc7d176d0cc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:proximity-features" data-paper-title="Proximity Features: Privacy-Compliant Cold-Start Personalization at Airbnb" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-61996e1d79f98663">Why version proximity coordinate quantization, hashes, and daily aggregation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aproximity-features">Proximity Features: Privacy-Compliant Cold-Start Personalization at Airbnb</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Airbnb</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Group behavior is accumulated by stable keys. Changing precision or hashing can move a region to a new bucket and mismatch serving history. Handle small groups and missing coordinates explicitly, without secretly using precise personal locations. Small MovieLens buckets are not production groups of around a thousand or privacy evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Changing decimal precision today and looking up yesterday&#x27;s key can read the wrong aggregate; successful base64 encoding proves little.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12246">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12246-proximity-features/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-61996e1d79f98663">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:proximity-features" data-paper-title="Proximity Features: Privacy-Compliant Cold-Start Personalization at Airbnb" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d24a218d06f62fb0">What does Airbnb proximity aggregation add beyond a global cold-start aggregate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aproximity-features">Proximity Features: Privacy-Compliant Cold-Start Personalization at Airbnb</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Airbnb</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Global aggregates give all anonymous requests one prior. Proximity aggregates condition on nearby groups with adequate support. They capture local demand but reduce samples per bucket and may amplify regional bias. ZIP proxies test local signals, not recovered personal tastes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A group may favor weekend trips while the global population favors large cities; one traveler in that group can still want an international trip.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12246">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12246-proximity-features/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d24a218d06f62fb0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:proximity-features" data-paper-title="Proximity Features: Privacy-Compliant Cold-Start Personalization at Airbnb" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-41229477669023db">Why are Proximity Features group keys rather than anonymous personal IDs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aproximity-features">Proximity Features: Privacy-Compliant Cold-Start Personalization at Airbnb</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Airbnb</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Keys aggregate geographic groups meeting count thresholds, with denser regions split and sparser ones merged. Serving consumes group behavior without persistent individual tracking. Cohort priors miss fine individual preferences, and proxy ZIP counts are not production privacy thresholds.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Nearby users&#x27; short-stay preferences can seed an anonymous request without identifying one user&#x27;s bookings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12246">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12246-proximity-features/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-41229477669023db">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:nontp" data-paper-title="Not Only NTP: Extending Training Signal Coverage for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-nontp-bd610948" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0d443595c80ba49d">Which two kinds of locality do TCL and TDL address in NONTP next-token prediction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anontp">Not Only NTP: Extending Training Signal Coverage for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meituan</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>TCL predicts a later EMA-teacher state, extending immediate next-step supervision. TDL predicts the target through a shared item head from earlier cross-domain states, helping sparse domains. Both are training-only; inference stays on the original backbone and cannot read future states.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Before a lamp purchase, TCL teaches longer trajectories and TDL uses preceding home-content behavior. Serving sees only events already observed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12277">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12277-nontp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0d443595c80ba49d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:nontp" data-paper-title="Not Only NTP: Extending Training Signal Coverage for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e76a922081830518">Why must TDL use pre-target cross-domain history and the same item head?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anontp">Not Only NTP: Extending Training Signal Coverage for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meituan</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Time order prevents leakage, domain mismatch supplies cross-business transfer, and averaging into the shared NTP head trains the target item space directly. Skip empty groups rather than inventing labels; an independent head is not the same transfer interface.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Predict a shopping target from earlier other-domain states, not videos afterward. No cross-domain history means no TDL evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12277">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12277-nontp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e76a922081830518">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:nontp" data-paper-title="Not Only NTP: Extending Training Signal Coverage for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea47c7bf8e79cb75">How is TCL&#x27;s EMA teacher more stable than a direct online future-state target?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anontp">Not Only NTP: Extending Training Signal Coverage for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meituan</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>EMA smooths updates and gives a stopped-gradient target rather than two sides chasing each other. Future state remains training-only; use other users as negatives rather than mislabeling nearby same-user interests. Stability does not ensure correctness and can preserve old biases.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A slow teacher changes less than a recent online update, but a consistently popularity-biased teacher is still biased.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12277">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12277-nontp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ea47c7bf8e79cb75">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:nontp" data-paper-title="Not Only NTP: Extending Training Signal Coverage for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-56b178d9e31f5503">Why add NONTP auxiliary modules only during training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anontp">Not Only NTP: Extending Training Signal Coverage for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meituan</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>TCL and TDL teach long-range and cross-domain signals to the backbone without future teachers or extra branches at serving time. Richer supervision is not uniformly better, especially with weak domain labels and short histories. Future targets are not available online.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Train for a trajectory several steps ahead but serve with the current history and original item head.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12277">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12277-nontp/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-56b178d9e31f5503">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mesh" data-paper-title="MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-mesh-881b1237" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-23bf7dbdc9d448ab">Why scale user, item, and context sub-towers separately in MESH before global interaction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amesh">MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Flattening early lets strong common-item gradients obscure fresh and tail signals. Residual cross interactions within each sub-tower retain specialized capacity; a context gate then adjusts user–item affinity per request. A cacheable item tower does not remove candidate-dependent scoring costs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Model a tail item&#x27;s content before it competes with popular exposure counts, then judge the item in the request context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12392">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12392-mesh/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-23bf7dbdc9d448ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mesh" data-paper-title="MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-296affeb40c412ba">Why does RGBC gate elementwise user–item affinity with context and add a context residual?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amesh">MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The product models corresponding dimensions of user and item vectors. A sigmoid context gate selects affinities useful now, while the residual retains context itself. Align dimensions and identity across towers. Averaging context loses sample conditioning, and layer-normalization and residual placement matter.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Commuting and weekend contexts can emphasize different affinity dimensions for the same pair, while context independently represents time. A final constant bias cannot do this.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12392">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12392-mesh/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-296affeb40c412ba">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mesh" data-paper-title="MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-323fdf049a2e98cf">When can MESH&#x27;s parallel towers be faster than a flat serial model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amesh">MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent towers permit concurrency and async item caching, but speed depends on runtime, hardware, batch size, and synchronization. A parallelizable graph is not necessarily executed in parallel by small-batch Python. The local slowdown is valid evidence. Compare quality and compute separately instead of inferring throughput from tower count.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Three towers run sequentially in one CPU loop with no GPU concurrency and more scheduling overhead; they do not become three times faster by design alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12392">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12392-mesh/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-323fdf049a2e98cf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mesh" data-paper-title="MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c782c1ba17874b8">Why scale inside the user, item, and context sub-towers first in MESH?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amesh">MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Flat interaction can let frequent evergreen signals dominate gradients. Separate cross interactions retain structure before a context gate adjusts affinity. The aim is more balanced capacity use, not guaranteed fresh/tail gains; inspect cohort and aggregate metrics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Encode stable preferences, item freshness, and request context separately so popular-item statistics do not drown out context from the start.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12392">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12392-mesh/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c782c1ba17874b8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:danet" data-paper-title="Cheaper is Better: A Discount-Aware Network for Conversion Rate Prediction in E-commerce Recommendation System" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-danet-112ada17" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-10d7141209c02687">Why does DANet separate high- and low-frequency discount history rather than using only today&#x27;s discount?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adanet">Cheaper is Better: A Discount-Aware Network for Conversion Rate Prediction in E-commerce Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group / Tmall</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Current price cannot describe long-term sensitivity and short-term promotion reactions. DPN separates stable patterns from fast variations and modulates preferences with similar purchases and promotion context; another network models general interest. Purchase-only discount labels are auxiliary and do not identify causal effects.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two users see 20% off, but one shops only during annual events and the other reacts to regular small offers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12578">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12578-danet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-10d7141209c02687">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:danet" data-paper-title="Cheaper is Better: A Discount-Aware Network for Conversion Rate Prediction in E-commerce Recommendation System" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-55f9897e4488e735">Why does DANet regress observed discounts only on purchases?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adanet">Cheaper is Better: A Discount-Aware Network for Conversion Rate Prediction in E-commerce Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group / Tmall</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The target is a transaction discount conditioned on purchase, which unpurchased items lack. Mask with purchase positives rather than inventing labels. After FFT filtering, low-frequency reconstruction plus high-frequency residual should recover the sequence. Local popularity/rating intensity is not real coupon-price regression.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An unpurchased shoe has no transaction discount; do not assign it zero. Use actual purchase discounts for this head and separate click or ranking supervision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12578">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12578-danet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-55f9897e4488e735">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:danet" data-paper-title="Cheaper is Better: A Discount-Aware Network for Conversion Rate Prediction in E-commerce Recommendation System" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-9a3d1093600eb1bc">What structure does DANet&#x27;s FFT frequency decomposition preserve beyond a recent discount average?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adanet">Cheaper is Better: A Discount-Aware Network for Conversion Rate Prediction in E-commerce Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group / Tmall</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A mean compresses trends and fluctuations into one number. Frequency separation reveals promotion rhythm, but depends on temporal sampling and quality, and high frequencies can be noise. Public data without prices provide proxy diagnostics only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Steady 10% off with a rare 50% sale can average similarly to weekly swings between 20% off and full price, but behavior can differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12578">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12578-danet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9a3d1093600eb1bc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:danet" data-paper-title="Cheaper is Better: A Discount-Aware Network for Conversion Rate Prediction in E-commerce Recommendation System" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5f4d3b95fcfb94c4">Why model general interest and discount preference separately in DANet?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adanet">Cheaper is Better: A Discount-Aware Network for Conversion Rate Prediction in E-commerce Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group / Tmall</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Category interest is not the same as willingness to wait for discounts. IPN models general interest, DPN learns discount rhythms, and user and promotion context modulate them. The signals can interact but are not interchangeable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two sneaker fans may buy at full price or wait for a season-end sale despite similar browsing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12578">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.12578-danet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5f4d3b95fcfb94c4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-retrieval" data-paper-title="Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-causal-retrieval-c13802af" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-188923aec4e8da1a">Why decide whether to trigger causal retrieval by uplift instead of underlying shopping probability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-retrieval">Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>High-propensity users might buy without retrieval, so allocate compute by the outcome changed by triggering. Use randomized logs to learn treated and control outcomes, doubly robust correction to estimate increment, and replay to select a threshold. Adequate experimental support and overlap are still necessary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A likely buyer may gain little, while a less likely buyer can be persuaded by relevant candidates. Under a budget, compare intervention increments rather than base propensity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.14161-causal-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-188923aec4e8da1a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-retrieval" data-paper-title="Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-edf0a7c6fee81043">Why check propensity values near zero or one in causal retrieval?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-retrieval">Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The DR residuals divide by e(x) or 1−e(x); extremes amplify noise, and missing overlap can prevent estimation. Choose trigger thresholds on independent replay or validation rather than test. Document any clipping because it changes estimator bias and variance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A subgroup triggered only 1% of the time can give one outcome enormous weight; a high score caused by that denominator is not high-confidence uplift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.14161-causal-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-edf0a7c6fee81043">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-retrieval" data-paper-title="Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8b7a2a15a35fac28">What does DR uplift add beyond two outcome models for treatment and control?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-retrieval">Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The model difference estimates the outcome gap; a propensity-weighted residual uses observed assignment information to correct fitting error. Double robustness depends on its assumptions and suitable model specification, not immunity to arbitrary bias. Local synthetic randomized treatments do not establish production uplift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The residual may correct underestimated treated purchases, but cannot fix zero support when this group has never received treatment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.14161-causal-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8b7a2a15a35fac28">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-retrieval" data-paper-title="Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-dd18e3e23c61a9ea">What are the treatment and outcome in causal retrieval?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-retrieval">Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Treatment is whether the shopping candidate generator runs; outcomes are later business responses across events. Estimate the trigger/no-trigger difference for comparable users, not ordinary shopping-model accuracy. Both decisions must be sufficiently represented in the data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The question is whether running shopping retrieval changes purchase or consumption for the same context, not whether that user likes to shop anyway.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.14161-causal-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dd18e3e23c61a9ea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:prompt-generation" data-paper-title="Prompt Generation Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8d412e12f27fcb01">Why configure Prompt Generation&#x27;s preprocessor, projector, and merger with templates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aprompt-generation">Prompt Generation Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Taobao Search</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate training and serving implementations drift. One protocol composes cleaning, projection, and fusion/compression with common interpretation. Merger changes token cost and information loss, not merely text assembly. Mean compression does not justify discarding all order.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Configure cleaning, projection, and pooling for one title token in both paths; truncating to ten words only on one side creates skew.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:prompt-generation" data-paper-title="Prompt Generation Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">

<h2 id="qa-64a9ffca7a083428">Why check PG_train(x,c)=PG_serve(x,c) by replaying raw serving features?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aprompt-generation">Prompt Generation Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Taobao Search</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Matching JSON does not ensure tokenizer, dependencies, truncation, or missingness match. Replay inputs and compare final tensors with versioned interpreters/configurations. Validation selected Title but test regressed; shorter compression does not establish effectiveness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If serving strips model numbers but training retains them, replay reveals skew despite the same configuration name.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:prompt-generation" data-paper-title="Prompt Generation Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-bc543930148110c9">What are the defaults and costs of parameterless mean merger versus learned compression?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aprompt-generation">Prompt Generation Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Taobao Search</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mean pooling is simple, cheap, and consistent without new weights. It loses order and details. Learned compression is flexible but adds cost and overfitting. Compression ratio is not relevance evidence, and mean need not fit every feature.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Pool redundant item attributes, but averaging a history with negation and ordering can lose critical meaning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11326">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2607.11326-prompt-generation/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bc543930148110c9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:prompt-generation" data-paper-title="Prompt Generation Technical Report" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cc9e170b1b09019e">Why separate feature type from processing components in Prompt Generation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aprompt-generation">Prompt Generation Technical Report</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Taobao Search</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Text, embedding, combo, and sequence say what the input is; preprocessing, projection, and merger say how to transform it. Orthogonal configuration composes without changing model code, but bad configuration can lose data or introduce skew.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A title and a behavior sequence can reuse component families with different settings; text does not imply one fixed pipeline.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
