<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21969">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.21969-llm-ad-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-14f5757cdd50ff78">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:llm-ad-retrieval" data-paper-title="LLM Retrieval for Stable and Predictable Ad Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ec68ff836f180cae">Why must an A/A′ shadow-ad perturbation preserve ad meaning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Allm-ad-retrieval">LLM Retrieval for Stable and Predictable Ad Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It tests stability to irrelevant changes. Meaningful edits can reasonably change distribution. Alter formatting or equivalent wording to probe reliance on IDs or superficial sparse features. Stability is distinct from relevance: identical wrong retrieval is stable too.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Punctuation and equivalent year formats should largely preserve audience; replacing children&#x27;s shoes with hiking boots genuinely changes the product.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21969">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.21969-llm-ad-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ec68ff836f180cae">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pearl-percentile" data-paper-title="PEARL: Unbiased Percentile Estimation via Contrastive Learning for Industrial-Scale Livestream Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-pearl-percentile-dbf6d244" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4447b64d4565cd98">Why estimate PEARL percentiles via repeated comparisons rather than regress raw behaviors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apearl-percentile">PEARL: Unbiased Percentile Estimation via Contrastive Learning for Industrial-Scale Livestream Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raw values differ in scale and bias. Comparing a behavior against references estimates its relative position, with more independent comparisons reducing variance. Value weighting and long-term co-training connect objectives. Percentiles depend on the reference and are not causally debiased value.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Thirty seconds means different things for a 15-second clip and a ten-minute video; compare within suitable references.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.21752-pearl-percentile/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4447b64d4565cd98">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pearl-percentile" data-paper-title="PEARL: Unbiased Percentile Estimation via Contrastive Learning for Industrial-Scale Livestream Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b544a9feebc5aa13">Why check dependence among PEARL comparisons before using p(1−p)/N?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apearl-percentile">PEARL: Unbiased Percentile Estimation via Contrastive Learning for Industrial-Scale Livestream Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The expression assumes appropriate Bernoulli comparisons and sampling. Repeated or correlated references do not add N independent observations. Record weights, bootstrap, and co-training provenance; sampling variance is not training variance. Do not use test references to choose targets.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Comparing the same video 100 times does not reduce uncertainty tenfold as 100 independent references might.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.21752-pearl-percentile/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b544a9feebc5aa13">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pearl-percentile" data-paper-title="PEARL: Unbiased Percentile Estimation via Contrastive Learning for Industrial-Scale Livestream Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e8375492d01fdaa2">How do repeated pairwise comparisons trade scale and variance against raw-label regression?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apearl-percentile">PEARL: Unbiased Percentile Estimation via Contrastive Learning for Industrial-Scale Livestream Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Regression preserves units but is sensitive to extremes. Comparisons organize relative position across scales but lose absolute gaps and introduce sampling error. Under independence, larger N reduces variance; bootstrap does not remove systematic bias. Neither objective is universally superior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: 100 and 101 seconds can differ in percentile despite a small raw gap, while a huge anomaly no longer dominates linearly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.21752-pearl-percentile/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e8375492d01fdaa2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pearl-percentile" data-paper-title="PEARL: Unbiased Percentile Estimation via Contrastive Learning for Industrial-Scale Livestream Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-60a85dba32ab471e">Why identify PEARL&#x27;s reference distribution when reporting a percentile?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apearl-percentile">PEARL: Unbiased Percentile Estimation via Contrastive Learning for Industrial-Scale Livestream Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A percentile is the fraction of reference outcomes exceeded, so users, context, and windows change its meaning. More comparisons reduce sampling noise, and value weights connect goals. Relative rank does not remove logging bias or prove causal incrementality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Thirty seconds can be high for short clips and low for long tutorials; a wrong reference reverses interpretation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.21752-pearl-percentile/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-60a85dba32ab471e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:fluid" data-paper-title="FLUID: From Ephemeral IDs to Multimodal Semantic Codes for Industrial-Scale Livestreaming Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-fluid-d95a4248" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c0acb1d4423aebec">Why does FLUID keep slice and room LUCIDs and phase out item IDs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afluid">FLUID: From Ephemeral IDs to Multimodal Semantic Codes for Industrial-Scale Livestreaming Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Short-lived rooms accumulate little stable ID feedback. Slice codes describe current content and room codes aggregate stable history. Late fusion keeps the time scales distinct; add slices, remove IDs, then add rooms to ease training transitions. Content codes can still collide or go stale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A sportswear room may currently sell shoes; room and slice codes describe different evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21832">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.21832-fluid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c0acb1d4423aebec">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:fluid" data-paper-title="FLUID: From Ephemeral IDs to Multimodal Semantic Codes for Industrial-Scale Livestreaming Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ddf0ab5507e099e9">Why index each LUCID embedding by the full prefix rather than an isolated codeword?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afluid">FLUID: From Ephemeral IDs to Multimodal Semantic Codes for Industrial-Scale Livestreaming Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A later code depends on earlier residual choices; cumulative prefix indexes retain path identity. Isolated codewords merge different branches. Final candidate tokens must contain only room and slice codes to implement item-ID removal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Fine code 3 after beauty and after travel needs separate embedding entries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21832">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.21832-fluid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ddf0ab5507e099e9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:fluid" data-paper-title="FLUID: From Ephemeral IDs to Multimodal Semantic Codes for Industrial-Scale Livestreaming Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-66592890548a71b4">What shared information does FLUID use after removing transient item IDs instead of randomly initializing new room IDs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afluid">FLUID: From Ephemeral IDs to Multimodal Semantic Codes for Industrial-Scale Livestreaming Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Random IDs learn only after interactions. Semantic prefixes reuse cross-domain content patterns immediately, useful for short-lived rooms, but lose distinct identity memory. Removing IDs lowered overall local quality; report that alongside improved freshness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A ten-minute stream has little time to train an ID. Content can place it immediately but may not distinguish hosting styles.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21832">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.21832-fluid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-66592890548a71b4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:fluid" data-paper-title="FLUID: From Ephemeral IDs to Multimodal Semantic Codes for Industrial-Scale Livestreaming Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a48a51ad5530b68f">Why treat live slices and room-history summaries as distinct tokens in FLUID?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afluid">FLUID: From Ephemeral IDs to Multimodal Semantic Codes for Industrial-Scale Livestreaming Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The slice LUCID reflects fast-changing current content while the room LUCID aggregates stable historical semantics. Late fusion prevents historical majority from erasing fresh themes. A room vote can miss minority changes and cannot replace the slice.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A beauty creator currently discussing travel storage has different room and slice signals.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21832">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.21832-fluid/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a48a51ad5530b68f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-grafting" data-paper-title="Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-memory-grafting-16992e0e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-bda5b2f934f9e644">Why pre-encode frequent phrases and fall back to hashed Engram?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-grafting">Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University / Microsoft Research Asia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An offline model encodes common n-grams into frozen memory; the recipient tries longest-suffix exact lookup. Trainable hash memory covers misses. Projection and contextual gating decide how to use the result, separating offline knowledge cost from online access.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A common trigram hits the bank while a rare combination falls back to hashing; either can be gated away.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20948">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.20948-memory-grafting/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bda5b2f934f9e644">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-grafting" data-paper-title="Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-934c6a4993813078">Which phrase state is stored in the offline bank?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-grafting">Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University / Microsoft Research Asia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Freeze the final token&#x27;s hidden state at the specified intermediate grafting layer. The recipient uses separate projection, context gate, and short convolution. End-to-end bank retraining changes the method.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Store token four&#x27;s state for a four-word phrase rather than arbitrarily averaging all four.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20948">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.20948-memory-grafting/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-934c6a4993813078">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-grafting" data-paper-title="Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-32a57367afab0c29">How does grafted memory differ from Engram trained from scratch?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-grafting">Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University / Microsoft Research Asia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A pretrained model encodes and freezes the exact bank; longest-suffix lookup precedes trainable hash fallback. Table size alone is not the difference, and local results do not beat equal-parameter Engram.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An absent exact phrase uses the explicit hash fallback, not a fabricated value.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20948">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.20948-memory-grafting/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-32a57367afab0c29">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-grafting" data-paper-title="Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ff481455d1eea76b">What are the roles of grafting model and recipient?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-grafting">Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University / Microsoft Research Asia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The grafting model supplies offline intermediate phrase states; the recipient reads this frozen memory online without rerunning the teacher for each phrase.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Encode phrases once and look up values later.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20948">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.20948-memory-grafting/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ff481455d1eea76b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mdcns" data-paper-title="Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-mdcns-8e8ced60" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-451af1c0d313f3a2">Why consider Self–Peer disagreement in MDCNS rather than always choosing Self&#x27;s highest-scoring negative?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amdcns">Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文作者团队（原文未标注公司）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A high Self score may be bias or an unlabeled positive; repeatedly choosing it reduces diversity. A heterogeneous Peer adds another view, disagreement finds informative candidates, and Teacher distills relationships across the full pool to Self. Disagreement does not establish a negative label; manage false negatives and training stability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If Self over-scores popular items and Peer disagrees, the discrepancy reveals uncertainty, not proof that every disputed item is irrelevant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.19651-mdcns/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-451af1c0d313f3a2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mdcns" data-paper-title="Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-55b0814cd9fac24b">Why compute MDCNS Teacher KL over the whole pool instead of the chosen negative alone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amdcns">Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文作者团队（原文未标注公司）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One negative supplies a local pair; the full Teacher distribution conveys relative difficulty across candidates. Align Self/Peer columns by identity and preserve temperature and τ² scaling. Build unobserved candidates at the training cutoff rather than using test answers to filter them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Even if one pair is sampled from 30 candidates, KL can convey which of the other 29 are close. A single scalar normalized to one contains no distributional knowledge.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.19651-mdcns/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-55b0814cd9fac24b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mdcns" data-paper-title="Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-1cc07ab0f592c36a">Why sample randomly from top M in MDCNS instead of DNS&#x27;s fixed highest-score choice?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amdcns">Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文作者团队（原文未标注公司）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Always taking the hardest candidate can repeatedly chase one outlier or false negative. Sampling within top M broadens hard-region coverage. Disagreement reranking and multiple losses reduce dependence on one model but still depend on pool quality. The small Markov backbone supports the sampling result only, not large sequence-model reproduction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If one popular film always tops the negatives, sampling among five hard items avoids centering every update on that suspected false negative.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.19651-mdcns/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1cc07ab0f592c36a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mdcns" data-paper-title="Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c4b021a66342a05">Why does MDCNS use Self, Peer, and Teacher for negatives?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amdcns">Divergence Meets Consensus: A Multi-Source Negative Sampling Framework for Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文作者团队（原文未标注公司）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One model&#x27;s high score can reflect bias or a true unlabeled positive. Peer provides a heterogeneous judgment, Teacher aggregates both, and disagreement identifies hard informative items. False negatives remain possible; distillation over the pool conveys relations a single selected negative misses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Self and Peer can disagree about a camera&#x27;s relevance. A missing interaction does not show the user dislikes it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.19651-mdcns/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c4b021a66342a05">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:growthgr" data-paper-title="Towards Sustainable Growth: A Multi-Value-Aware Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-growthgr-aa9df061" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fcd351b4112088fb">Why does GrowthGR use ItemLTV incremental value and multi-objective post-training instead of only increasing new-item exposure?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agrowthgr">Towards Sustainable Growth: A Multi-Value-Aware Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group / Taobao &amp; Tmall</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Exposure is a means, not an outcome. ItemLTV estimates changes in future orders or value relative to what would happen anyway; multi-objective training balances click, purchase, and coverage. Clip rare high-value weights to limit instability. Counterfactual assumptions and rewards need validation; more new items do not prove growth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A first exposure can open a sustained use case or cause one accidental click; equal traffic treats these differently valuable opportunities alike.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.17994-growthgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fcd351b4112088fb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:growthgr" data-paper-title="Towards Sustainable Growth: A Multi-Value-Aware Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0acfd97ef595f1da">Why clip GrowthGR rarity weights based on `−log πold` and fix the reference policy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agrowthgr">Towards Sustainable Growth: A Multi-Value-Aware Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group / Taobao &amp; Tmall</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tiny old probabilities create extreme weights, high variance, and single-sample dominance. πold must match the sample&#x27;s generating policy and context, not current probabilities. Policy ratios and reward weights have different roles; separate ItemLTV proxies from real orders.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Clipping can stop one noisy low-probability example from dominating a batch without making its value estimate reliable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.17994-growthgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0acfd97ef595f1da">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:growthgr" data-paper-title="Towards Sustainable Growth: A Multi-Value-Aware Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b6962cf96eaddecd">How do GrowthGR rare high-value weights differ from a uniform novelty reward?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agrowthgr">Towards Sustainable Growth: A Multi-Value-Aware Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group / Taobao &amp; Tmall</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A novelty reward uses newness alone. Rarity weights use previous-policy probability and multi-objective value to emphasize potentially useful low-opportunity items. Low probability is not quality; clipping limits amplified noise. Neither alone proves growth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two new items with little exposure should not get identical boosts if estimated long-term relevance differs, though a bad estimate can be amplified.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.17994-growthgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b6962cf96eaddecd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:growthgr" data-paper-title="Towards Sustainable Growth: A Multi-Value-Aware Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-caed8bc40762fb5b">Why use ItemLTV instead of immediate new-item purchases in GrowthGR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agrowthgr">Towards Sustainable Growth: A Multi-Value-Aware Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group / Taobao &amp; Tmall</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Low initial exposure leads to few immediate purchases and can hide effects of first clicks on later orders. ItemLTV separates baseline and increment; MoPO aligns generation with multiple behavioral goals. Predicted incremental value is not inherently causal without credible assumptions and feedback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A click today might lead to a later series purchase despite no same-day conversion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.17994-growthgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-caed8bc40762fb5b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dadf" data-paper-title="DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-dadf-696311de" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3c6b5e2b06c5bf58">Why does DADF freeze the mature first-stage model and learn a multiplicative factor?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adadf">DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retraining can damage established capabilities or interfaces. Distribution-conditioned proportional residuals adapt to inputs and base predictions while preserving the scalar output. Tiny predictions can destabilize ratios, so check denominator protection and conditional distribution calibration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If two groups each start at 10 seconds but one is overestimated and one underestimated, learn distinct factors instead of adding five seconds everywhere.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17863">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.17863-dadf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3c6b5e2b06c5bf58">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dadf" data-paper-title="DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea006a6d3351f5f2">Why check small denominators in DADF&#x27;s `y/max(y0,ε)` even with frozen y0?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adadf">DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Freezing stabilizes supervision but tiny predictions can produce huge noisy ratios. Record epsilon and use the same baseline version for correction inputs, ratio targets, and output multiplication. Do not update the first-stage model while claiming second-stage-only training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An observed 10 seconds divided by a 0.01-second baseline creates a huge factor that is not necessarily reliable preference evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17863">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.17863-dadf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ea006a6d3351f5f2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dadf" data-paper-title="DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-03765f3ee2f1d912">How do DADF&#x27;s multiplicative and additive residuals affect scale differently?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adadf">DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multiplication expresses proportional error and therefore larger absolute adjustments for large predictions; addition expresses fixed-unit error. Choose based on error structure. The local ranking was unchanged, so calibration changes are not automatic recommendation gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A 10% underestimate at 10 and 100 seconds suits multiplication; a consistent five-second error suits addition. A global multiplier preserves ranking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17863">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.17863-dadf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-03765f3ee2f1d912">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dadf" data-paper-title="DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4ed21b3ed0463b49">Why treat DADF&#x27;s mature predictor as a baseline and learn a relative correction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adadf">DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The predictor already captures stable relationships. A separate factor focuses on conditional systematic errors with the same scalar interface and less risk than full retraining. Near-zero or badly misspecified predictions are harder to correct, and factors cannot recreate missing information.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Correct a 10% long-video underestimate without discarding every learned user-content relationship.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17863">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.17863-dadf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4ed21b3ed0463b49">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gprl" data-paper-title="GPRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d36e96fff938a5a3">Why normalize GPRL advantages by dimension before context aggregation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agprl">GPRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raw sums let large scales or variance dominate and hide tradeoffs among helpfulness, format and brevity. Standardize, weight by context and monitor drift. Normalization isn&#x27;t value prioritization; exact accuracy isn&#x27;t a multi-dimensional evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Separate a 100-point metric&#x27;s units from how much users want it weighted.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18721">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2605.18721-gprl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d36e96fff938a5a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gprl" data-paper-title="GPRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f517255fce38ba7b">Does local GPRL exact-answer regression refute the paper&#x27;s open-ended results?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agprl">GPRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Retain the negative accuracy result, but real human multi-dimensional preferences and open generation judging are absent. Track per-dimension mean, variance and effective weights.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Brevity can improve while exact match worsens, so answer score alone isn&#x27;t complete.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18721">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2605.18721-gprl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f517255fce38ba7b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gprl" data-paper-title="GPRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4acbb9a1f4e30016">How does GPRL differ from summing rewards then applying GRPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agprl">GPRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Summation mixes scales and conflicts before normalization. Separate standardization preserves each dimension&#x27;s relative information before aggregation; the operations do not commute. Test context weights and drift separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One high-variance dimension can dominate normalized totals while others barely matter.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18721">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2605.18721-gprl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4acbb9a1f4e30016">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gprl" data-paper-title="GPRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-gprl-3009fd16" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-fcd8ef0ba525dcfd">Why compute GPRL group advantages per preference dimension?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agprl">GPRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Dimensions have different units and variance. Normalize separately, then aggregate by task context. Normalization avoids accidental numerical dominance, not a claim of equal importance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A 100-point format scale would swamp binary correctness under raw summation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18721">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2605.18721-gprl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fcd8ef0ba525dcfd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:prompts" data-paper-title="PROMPTS: Performance Optimization via Multi-Agent Planning for LLM Training and Serving" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-prompts-61564db7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a638de4eb75357c6">Why ground sharding proposals in profiling rather than retrieving a common best configuration?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aprompts">PROMPTS: Performance Optimization via Multi-Agent Planning for LLM Training and Serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Maryland / Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Optimal parallelism depends on measured compute, communication, and memory constraints. The knowledge base offers options; Analyzer locates bottlenecks, Proposal generates explainable candidates, and Coordinator organizes verification. A config or formula check does not run training or measure speedup.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A configuration is fast on a model card, but local profiling shows all-reduce dominates. Compare options that address communication.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://research.google/pubs/prompts-performance-optimization-via-multi-agent-planning-for-llm-training-and-serving/">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/mlsys2026-prompts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a638de4eb75357c6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:prompts" data-paper-title="PROMPTS: Performance Optimization via Multi-Agent Planning for LLM Training and Serving" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a73f467c2768d482">Do local profiler ranking and bounded proposals include TPU/GSPMD measurements?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aprompts">PROMPTS: Performance Optimization via Multi-Agent Planning for LLM Training and Serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Maryland / Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Local reference tests cover evidence ranking and proposal constraints without Google TPU profiling, GSPMD, or a production workload matrix. Top-three hits and peak gains are author measurements, not consequences of local candidate ordering.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Synthetic profiling can recommend less communication. Until compiling and running that configuration, there is no observed training speed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式或操作, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://research.google/pubs/prompts-performance-optimization-via-multi-agent-planning-for-llm-training-and-serving/">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/mlsys2026-prompts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a73f467c2768d482">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:prompts" data-paper-title="PROMPTS: Performance Optimization via Multi-Agent Planning for LLM Training and Serving" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5bb83b305c81a947">How does separating Coordinator, Analyzer, and Proposal differ from configuration-table search?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aprompts">PROMPTS: Performance Optimization via Multi-Agent Planning for LLM Training and Serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Maryland / Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate roles coordinate work, explain bottlenecks, and propose targeted settings from evidence. Table search mainly enumerates predefined options. Multiple agents have their own cost; real training or serving results determine benefit, not explanation length or votes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Analyzer identifies communication as dominant, then Proposal changes sharding accordingly instead of testing every dimension randomly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://research.google/pubs/prompts-performance-optimization-via-multi-agent-planning-for-llm-training-and-serving/">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/mlsys2026-prompts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5bb83b305c81a947">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:prompts" data-paper-title="PROMPTS: Performance Optimization via Multi-Agent Planning for LLM Training and Serving" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6c5e1155db8327b8">Why does PROMPTS treat model-parallel partitioning as iterative measured optimization?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aprompts">PROMPTS: Performance Optimization via Multi-Agent Planning for LLM Training and Serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Maryland / Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Training bottlenecks vary by hardware and configuration among compute, memory, and communication. Agents use profiler evidence to propose partitioning and observe effects rather than apply stock settings. A recommendation is not a speedup until measured for runtime, resources, and feasibility on target hardware.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: More sharding may save memory but slow cross-device communication. Profiling distinguishes the bottleneck.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://research.google/pubs/prompts-performance-optimization-via-multi-agent-planning-for-llm-training-and-serving/">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/mlsys2026-prompts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6c5e1155db8327b8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:policy-facet" data-paper-title="Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-policy-facet-10555aa9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1a873ae567d00c7d">Why maintain a policy-controlled taxonomy before small-model retrieval and single-token scoring in Policy Facet?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apolicy-facet">Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A curated set bounds themes, preventing arbitrary out-of-policy generation. Embeddings retrieve cheaply within it and a compact generator scores a token such as &#x27;Okay&#x27; conditioned on user and query. Caching and batching lower latency. High model probability does not complete policy enforcement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Choose a family travel facet from maintained destination and activity categories rather than inventing one live.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16479">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.16479-policy-facet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1a873ae567d00c7d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:policy-facet" data-paper-title="Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-eaf1989efcddb804">Why verify tokenizer and full conditioning prefix for Policy Facet&#x27;s &#x27;Okay&#x27; score?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apolicy-facet">Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The word may tokenize differently across models. Read the designated output under the right user, query, and facet prefix. A hardcoded vocabulary ID can score another word after model changes; caches must not include another facet. Local proxy latency is not production evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If &#x27;Okay&#x27; becomes two tokens, the old single ID may be wrong even though it returns a finite number.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16479">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.16479-policy-facet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eaf1989efcddb804">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:policy-facet" data-paper-title="Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4f7b6dbe5963d4ef">Why is an &#x27;Okay&#x27; token probability cheaper than generating full judgments?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apolicy-facet">Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A bounded output gives a pointwise score without long decoding for every candidate; prefix caching and batching add reuse. It loses detailed reasoning and needs calibration. Scoring cannot recover facets missed in retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Read one probability for ten facets instead of generating ten long reviews, but an unretrieved option never gets scored.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16479">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.16479-policy-facet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4f7b6dbe5963d4ef">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:policy-facet" data-paper-title="Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1d64a12b7237f3f1">Are Policy Facet&#x27;s facets the same candidates as final products or documents?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apolicy-facet">Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Facets are refinement options that alter later search or browsing; items satisfy the resulting request. A facet must meet taxonomy and usefulness requirements. A high-scoring item title does not automatically make a useful refinement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: &#x27;Family activities&#x27; narrows travel search; a specific museum ticket is a result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16479">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.16479-policy-facet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1d64a12b7237f3f1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gemini-for-google" data-paper-title="Customizing an LLM for Enterprise Software Engineering" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-gemini-for-google-0c2d88a0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-88875c261b2a4f2b">Why include general replay in enterprise code adaptation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agemini-for-google">Customizing an LLM for Enterprise Software Engineering</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Internal examples teach private code, tools, and workflows but can displace general ability. Replay adds a retention constraint; deduplication, filtering, and contamination controls protect the comparison. Validate both sides.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Learning internal build commands need not preserve general reasoning if training drops all general examples.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16517">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2605.16517-gemini-for-google/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-88875c261b2a4f2b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gemini-for-google" data-paper-title="Customizing an LLM for Enterprise Software Engineering" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-64bacf05df89aa95">What do the two extreme replay weights verify?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agemini-for-google">Customizing an LLM for Enterprise Software Engineering</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>λ=0 leaves enterprise loss and λ=1 leaves general replay. This checks branch wiring and coefficient direction. Local tests use no Google private data, Gemini weights, or A/B.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Enterprise loss dominating at λ=1 suggests reversed weighting or routing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16517">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2605.16517-gemini-for-google/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-64bacf05df89aa95">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gemini-for-google" data-paper-title="Customizing an LLM for Enterprise Software Engineering" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-dbddc43401d20e73">What extra constraints distinguish enterprise midtraining?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agemini-for-google">Customizing an LLM for Enterprise Software Engineering</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It includes internal code, interaction, and tools while controlling duplicates and evaluation leakage and preserving general ability. General training loss does not replace internal workflow evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Memorizing old fixes can lower loss without helping new internal problems.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16517">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2605.16517-gemini-for-google/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dbddc43401d20e73">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gemini-for-google" data-paper-title="Customizing an LLM for Enterprise Software Engineering" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0ae31377ea1cdc2c">Why not continue training on all internal code unchanged?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agemini-for-google">Customizing an LLM for Enterprise Software Engineering</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
