<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankup" data-paper-title="RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-rankup-a9399758" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0478859fae50a11a">Why use permutation grouping and global tokens against RankUp rank collapse instead of merely adding embeddings or depth?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankup">RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Added parameters can reuse the same subspace. Different groupings and tables alter interaction paths, global tokens connect groups, and external features and task decoupling add signals. These aim to turn capacity into richer directions, not guarantee effective rank.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: New groupings let fields interact that never shared a group under a fixed partition.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.17878-rankup/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0478859fae50a11a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankup" data-paper-title="RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-075dc39c4c00dc0e">Why track RankUp permutation matrices and field identities together?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankup">RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>XP rearranges inputs; corresponding embedding and group weights must follow the same map. Align global-token residual widths, and do not choose permutations using test labels. A local proxy does not verify production scaling laws.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Swapping price and age while keeping the original lookup can interpret age 18 as a price.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.17878-rankup/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-075dc39c4c00dc0e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankup" data-paper-title="RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-f98e38ec565ff9d5">How does permutation grouping change interaction opportunities versus fully shared RankUp input?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankup">RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>New partitions let previously separated fields meet, independent embeddings add views, and global tokens connect groups. Shared inputs can favor strong fields, while groups can miss or duplicate crosses. Combined local changes do not attribute gains to one component.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Another permutation can put age with category; unaligned parameter shuffling can instead destroy meaning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.17878-rankup/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f98e38ec565ff9d5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankup" data-paper-title="RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-94f1626a3266cd89">Why isn&#x27;t higher RankUp representation rank proof of useful interests?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankup">RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rank measures independent directions, not task information. Noise can raise rank and obscure useful structure. Inspect spectra with task and subgroup metrics rather than claiming quality when tokens become less alike.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Random orthogonal user noise can yield full rank without adding any predictive preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.17878-rankup/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-94f1626a3266cd89">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:marc" data-paper-title="Modular Representation Compression: Adapting LLMs for Efficient and Effective Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-marc-216b86ce" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e7980095d4e002eb">Why separate representation compression from recommendation adaptation in MARC, and why might an intermediate LLM layer be chosen?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amarc">Modular Representation Compression: Adapting LLMs for Efficient and Effective Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The last layer favors the language objective, whereas an intermediate layer can retain more compressible general features. What compression preserves is not necessarily what recommendation needs. Separate modules and information constraints distinguish dimensional cost from task relevance. Intermediate-layer superiority must be measured per model and dataset.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: The final layer excels at next-word prediction, but a middle layer may retain product use. Reconstruction alone can preserve costly language details irrelevant to purchase preferences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18146">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.18146-marc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e7980095d4e002eb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:marc" data-paper-title="Modular Representation Compression: Adapting LLMs for Efficient and Effective Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-db89084985cb4dc0">How should MARC avoid mixing validation and test during layer and nuisance-projection selection?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amarc">Modular Representation Compression: Adapting LLMs for Efficient and Effective Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Estimate directions from training data and choose layer, dimension, and removed directions on validation, then freeze for test. Match projections to the selected hidden-state space. A fixed-score proxy without full information-objective training must be described within that boundary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Choosing the highest test NDCG layer turns test into tuning. Pick it first, then check transfer on independent data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18146">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.18146-marc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-db89084985cb4dc0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:marc" data-paper-title="Modular Representation Compression: Adapting LLMs for Efficient and Effective Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c62caff06e1cb6d1">What are the benefits and risks of separate MARC compression and adaptation versus one linear reducer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amarc">Modular Representation Compression: Adapting LLMs for Efficient and Effective Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One projection conflates information loss with task learning. Separate modules make each effect measurable, but add choices and objective interactions. Removing a supposed nuisance can delete useful signals. The public proxy was negative, so information constraints alone do not establish generalization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Removing content-specific style may help matching unless style itself drives user preference. Ablate both stages.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18146">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.18146-marc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c62caff06e1cb6d1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:marc" data-paper-title="Modular Representation Compression: Adapting LLMs for Efficient and Effective Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-23b84a11d274b3f0">Why might MARC choose an intermediate layer instead of assuming the LLM&#x27;s final layer is best?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amarc">Modular Representation Compression: Adapting LLMs for Efficient and Effective Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Final layers specialize in pretraining outputs. MRA observations motivate separating compression and adaptation to remove proxy-task interference while retaining recommendation information. Select layers on validation; middle layers are not universally superior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A middle layer may distinguish two user groups better in a compact representation even if the final layer is best at predicting words.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18146">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.18146-marc/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-23b84a11d274b3f0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fuse-verifiers" data-paper-title="FUSE: Ensembling Verifiers with Zero Labeled Data" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">

<span id="paper-foundation-models-fuse-verifiers-1ae3c639" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1971a030f622491f">Why doesn&#x27;t label-free FUSE get more reliable simply by adding correlated verifiers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afuse-verifiers">FUSE: Ensembling Verifiers with Zero Labeled Data</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Moment estimation needs identifiability assumptions such as a better-than-random majority and conditionally independent triplets. Transforms mitigate correlation, but shared errors can remain. Posteriors are not gold, which stays evaluation-only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Three verifiers copying one wrong rule are not three independent correctness signals.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18547v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2604.18547-fuse-verifiers/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1971a030f622491f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fuse-verifiers" data-paper-title="FUSE: Ensembling Verifiers with Zero Labeled Data" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-025e98a438bb7ffe">Can gold choose score transforms or ensemble parameters?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afuse-verifiers">FUSE: Ensembling Verifiers with Zero Labeled Data</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Not in the documented label-free fit. Use score matrices only and reserve labels for independent evaluation. Choosing transforms by gold on the same questions breaks both boundaries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Trying transforms and selecting the best by answers is not unsupervised selection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18547v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2604.18547-fuse-verifiers/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-025e98a438bb7ffe">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fuse-verifiers" data-paper-title="FUSE: Ensembling Verifiers with Zero Labeled Data" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-28aa8f0196230b9c">Do moment-based posteriors provide the same guarantees as gold labels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afuse-verifiers">FUSE: Ensembling Verifiers with Zero Labeled Data</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. They depend on identifiability; high correlation or constant scores can break estimation. High estimated probability is not truth or safety.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Shared wrong rules can produce agreement on the wrong answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18547v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2604.18547-fuse-verifiers/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-28aa8f0196230b9c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fuse-verifiers" data-paper-title="FUSE: Ensembling Verifiers with Zero Labeled Data" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0e8d40806e950df8">Why not average verifier scores in FUSE?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afuse-verifiers">FUSE: Ensembling Verifiers with Zero Labeled Data</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Correlated errors get counted repeatedly. Estimate query-conditioned quality from scores, transform to mitigate dependencies, then build posteriors for ensemble optimization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Three near-identical verifiers need not add three times the evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:steppo" data-paper-title="StepPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-steppo-4ceaabe2" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-77600865a38c44dc">Why does StepPO aggregate token ratios within a step before clipping the step ratio?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asteppo">StepPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The environment executes a whole action, so independent token clipping differs from action-level probability change. Average within-step log ratios and exponentiate, then compute value and GAE at step boundaries, aligning credit with environment transitions. Exclude tool observations from action tokens and preserve consistent length normalization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A shell command has many tokens but executes once when complete. Evaluate the step&#x27;s overall change rather than assigning its state reward independently to each subword.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18401">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2604.18401-steppo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-77600865a38c44dc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:steppo" data-paper-title="StepPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-4af94536ae2c6cbc">How does StepPO keep observation tokens out of action-ratio aggregation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asteppo">StepPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mark step and response-token boundaries and aggregate only policy ratios of tokens in the action. Observations are conditions, not generated actions. Deterministic local tool plans verify a step state machine but not real LLM token rollouts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A thousand-character tool response must not become a thousand policy tokens in the action&#x27;s ratio mean.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18401">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2604.18401-steppo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4af94536ae2c6cbc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:steppo" data-paper-title="StepPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-bb09405ae546c81a">Is clipping token ratios before averaging equivalent to aggregating and clipping a step ratio?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asteppo">StepPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Clipping is nonlinear, so order changes which actions are constrained. Average log ratios and exponentiate to obtain a geometric step ratio, not the arithmetic mean of raw ratios.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>For one large and one small ratio in an action, geometric aggregation can produce a different update from individual clipping.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18401">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2604.18401-steppo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bb09405ae546c81a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:steppo" data-paper-title="StepPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ee8199c6224d4965">Why does StepPO use observation–action as the natural decision unit?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asteppo">StepPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tool actions span tokens while environment feedback follows the complete action. StepPO computes value and GAE at step boundaries and aggregates action-token ratios into a step ratio before clipping.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A tool call has a name and arguments, but the environment returns feedback only after the complete invocation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18401">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2604.18401-steppo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ee8199c6224d4965">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:group-dpo" data-paper-title="GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-31c1d45cb19d9504">Why not recompute GroupDPO coefficients inside each response microbatch?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agroup-dpo">GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Freeze derivatives from the entire group at the same parameter point and replay response gradients to recover the first-order result. Local recomputation changes sets and normalization. Recompute after every update. Loss values and Hessians are not equivalent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Each response carries fixed full-group credit rather than re-ranking within a small compute batch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15602v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2604.15602-group-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-31c1d45cb19d9504">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:group-dpo" data-paper-title="GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c09b70ec0aa149ab">Can GroupDPO coefficients be reused after the optimizer step?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agroup-dpo">GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Derivatives change with parameters. Recompute. Do not divide microbatch backpropagation by local groups or microbatch count; positive NLL also uses the full-batch group normalization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reusing old coefficients saves a pass but becomes a stale approximation, not exact current gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15602v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2604.15602-group-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c09b70ec0aa149ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:group-dpo" data-paper-title="GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ee0899295d4a06f6">Are GroupDPO Margin, MPO, Softmax and All-Pairs equivalent objectives?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agroup-dpo">GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. They compare sets differently. What is shared is precomputing derivatives of the chosen full-group objective and replaying separately. Changing the objective differs from changing compute batches while retaining its first derivative.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>All pairwise comparisons may assign different coefficients than pooling positives first; the same memory method serves both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15602v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2604.15602-group-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ee0899295d4a06f6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:group-dpo" data-paper-title="GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-group-dpo-93d61191" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b8740cc2992f39de">Does GroupDPO concatenate all responses into one long response?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agroup-dpo">GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. One prompt has nonempty positive and negative sets; responses retain separate probabilities and IDs. The joint objective uses set relationships without requiring simultaneous activation storage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two positive and two negative answers are encoded independently while the objective compares both sets.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15602v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2604.15602-group-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b8740cc2992f39de">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:naijas2st" data-paper-title="NaijaS2ST: A Multi-Accent Benchmark for Speech-to-Speech Translation in Low-Resource Nigerian Languages" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<span id="paper-multimodal-models-naijas2st-20646330" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-dbd5bc66fec4aff6">Why not use exact match against reference text for speech-to-speech translation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Anaijas2st">NaijaS2ST: A Multi-Accent Benchmark for Speech-to-Speech Translation in Low-Resource Nigerian Languages</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Mila - Quebec AI Institute</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Audio output needs real ASR before scoring with prescribed semantic translation metrics. Both transcription and translation errors matter. Exact text matching rejects valid paraphrases and bypasses audio. Few-shot examples come from development data, not test references.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two spoken versions of “Please come tomorrow” can both be correct with different wording; preserve both the semantic and audio pipeline.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16287v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/2604.16287-naijas2st/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dbd5bc66fec4aff6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:naijas2st" data-paper-title="NaijaS2ST: A Multi-Accent Benchmark for Speech-to-Speech Translation in Low-Resource Nigerian Languages" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-4223dcd722be9bd5">What limits apply to NaijaS2ST five-shot examples and proxy language tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Anaijas2st">NaijaS2ST: A Multi-Accent Benchmark for Speech-to-Speech Translation in Low-Resource Nigerian Languages</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Mila - Quebec AI Institute</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Take five examples from DEV, never formal test. Some Seamless adaptations map Hausa to Arabic and Naijá to French tokens as conventions, not native model support. Local work has not downloaded audio or run complete training and evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Assigning an Arabic control token for Hausa fine-tuning does not mean the audio is translated to Arabic or that untrained Hausa support exists.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16287v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/2604.16287-naijas2st/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4223dcd722be9bd5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:naijas2st" data-paper-title="NaijaS2ST: A Multi-Accent Benchmark for Speech-to-Speech Translation in Low-Resource Nigerian Languages" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-3ae01580dff4059e">Do SSA-COMET and ChrF++ measure the same kind of agreement?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Anaijas2st">NaijaS2ST: A Multi-Accent Benchmark for Speech-to-Speech Translation in Low-Resource Nigerian Languages</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Mila - Quebec AI Institute</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>SSA-COMET uses a multilingual semantic model; ChrF++ mainly uses character and word n-gram overlap. The scores are complementary and not interchangeable accuracy percentages. Speech output still needs the prescribed ASR path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two valid paraphrases can preserve meaning with different character overlap; the larger number is not automatically a larger fraction correct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16287v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../multimodal-models/2604.16287-naijas2st/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3ae01580dff4059e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:naijas2st" data-paper-title="NaijaS2ST: A Multi-Accent Benchmark for Speech-to-Speech Translation in Low-Resource Nigerian Languages" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-3e74dca2ad6800c6">What does accent diversity require in NaijaS2ST evaluation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Anaijas2st">NaijaS2ST: A Multi-Accent Benchmark for Speech-to-Speech Translation in Low-Resource Nigerian Languages</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Mila - Quebec AI Institute</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pronunciation variation affects understanding and speech evaluation. Cover multiple speakers and accents, report translation directions separately, and distinguish speech-to-text from speech-to-speech. One direction or a few speakers cannot characterize all Nigerian languages or accents.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>English→Hausa is not Hausa→English, and understanding one accent does not prove reliable synthesis of another.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:lwgr" data-paper-title="LWGR: Lagrangian-Constrained Personalized World Knowledge for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-lwgr-831cc9dc" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e153cabf62c29685">Why does LWGR learn personalized soft instructions while limiting degradation against a frozen reference?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alwgr">LWGR: Lagrangian-Constrained Personalized World Knowledge for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International / CAS</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A fixed prompt cannot adapt across users. Subspace codebooks produce trainable soft tokens to personalize knowledge extraction. LLM knowledge can conflict with behavioral evidence, so the frozen reference anchors a confidence degradation constraint; nearline computation controls serving cost. Learned prompts do not make extracted knowledge true or more reliable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Two travelers care about price and photography respectively. Soft prompts can retrieve different knowledge, while the constraint should discourage new evidence from overriding reliable existing scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18771">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.18771-lwgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e153cabf62c29685">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:lwgr" data-paper-title="LWGR: Lagrangian-Constrained Personalized World Knowledge for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c6d7ced9871671c">How should LWGR&#x27;s straight-through code selection and dual update be checked separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alwgr">LWGR: Lagrangian-Constrained Personalized World Knowledge for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International / CAS</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use hard codes forward and soft-distribution gradients backward; verify soft-instruction parameters change. Update λ using C−ε and project to nonnegative values. A rising multiplier signals violation, not satisfaction. Frozen reference, BOS fusion, and nearline cache are separate interfaces.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If C remains above tolerance while λ rises, report failure to satisfy the constraint. A hard index cutting gradients also prevents learning even though it selects codes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18771">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.18771-lwgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c6d7ced9871671c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:lwgr" data-paper-title="LWGR: Lagrangian-Constrained Personalized World Knowledge for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a7040336605d65fd">What does LWGR&#x27;s reference confidence constraint protect compared with ordinary KL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alwgr">LWGR: Lagrangian-Constrained Personalized World Knowledge for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International / CAS</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It penalizes the amount by which a positive target&#x27;s mean token log-probability falls below the reference tolerance. KL instead measures whole-distribution drift. Updating the multiplier is not sufficient: locally λ changed without an improvement in degradation, so protection was not demonstrated.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Moving probability to another reasonable candidate may raise KL without much target damage; a large target drop directly activates the one-sided constraint.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18771">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.18771-lwgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a7040336605d65fd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:lwgr" data-paper-title="LWGR: Lagrangian-Constrained Personalized World Knowledge for Generative Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b637c222009ec19f">How can LWGR&#x27;s soft instruction express user differences beyond handwritten wording?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alwgr">LWGR: Lagrangian-Constrained Personalized World Knowledge for Generative Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba International / CAS</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Split user context into subspaces and select codewords from independent codebooks. The resulting differentiable prompt tokens and history generate user knowledge; recommendation supervision can change them. Capacity and training coverage limit personalization, and the tokens need not correspond to readable instructions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A photography novice and a professional may select different soft tokens even though the handwritten prompt says &#x27;analyze interests&#x27; for both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18771">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2605.18771-lwgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b637c222009ec19f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrec" data-paper-title="GenRec: A Preference-Oriented Generative Framework for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-genrec-e5f875fa" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e1b9b517b34000d1">Why does GenRec target a next-page sequence and keep NLL alongside GRPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrec">GenRec: A Preference-Oriented Generative Framework for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · JD.com</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Item targets alone do not teach order and complementarity within pages. Sequence targets model composition, group-relative reward shapes full-page utility, and NLL anchors to logged behavior against reward drift. Rewards that omit relevance or feasibility can still mislead.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A page objective can replace one of three redundant items; an NLL anchor can restrain a novelty-only reward from recommending irrelevant content.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.14878-genrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e1b9b517b34000d1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrec" data-paper-title="GenRec: A Preference-Oriented Generative Framework for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-071c67569a5ee13d">Why compare GenRec page advantages only within the same context?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrec">GenRec: A Preference-Oriented Generative Framework for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · JD.com</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Same-context pages share history and candidate difficulty, so mean subtraction measures relative quality. Mixing users confounds request difficulty. Update prefix and duplicate masks together, apply NLL to legal targets, and do not use Token Merger to expose future test pages.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Compare pages within each photography or cold-start user rather than marking every harder request negative.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.14878-genrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-071c67569a5ee13d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrec" data-paper-title="GenRec: A Preference-Oriented Generative Framework for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c79d1223eeb4334a">What drift does GenRec&#x27;s NLL limit compared with optimizing GRPO-SR reward alone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrec">GenRec: A Preference-Oriented Generative Framework for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · JD.com</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Group-relative rewards compare page utility while NLL preserves logged behavior, limiting drift toward sparse or biased rewards. Their balance trades imitation for exploration. Local relative gains depend on proxy labels and baseline and do not establish real satisfaction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Diversity reward alone can produce irrelevant novelty; NLL retains basic interests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.14878-genrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c79d1223eeb4334a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrec" data-paper-title="GenRec: A Preference-Oriented Generative Framework for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-2f8db993ea0b2837">Why organize consecutive positives as a next-page target in GenRec?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrec">GenRec: A Preference-Oriented Generative Framework for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · JD.com</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Within-page consumption has order and complementarity that point prediction misses. Generate with prefix dependence and score the entire page with grouped rewards. Pages assembled from consecutive public actions are proxies, not observed impression pages.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Tent, sleeping bag, and pad can form a useful page; three consecutive movie views do not prove simultaneous display.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.14878-genrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2f8db993ea0b2837">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:unirec-coa" data-paper-title="UniRec: Bridging the Expressive Gap between Generative and Discriminative Recommendation via Chain-of-Attribute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-5ec2902153dfbf8c">Why generate attributes before SID and constrain quantization capacity?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aunirec-coa">UniRec: Bridging the Expressive Gap between Generative and Discriminative Recommendation via Chain-of-Attribute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation / large-scale e-commerce platform</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Category, seller, and brand condition generation explicitly. Capacity prevents popular codes monopolizing the space; task context handles differing needs. Early attribute errors propagate, so interpretable steps do not guarantee correct items.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Choosing dress shoes instead of sneakers early can derail the path despite precise later decoding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12234">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.12234-unirec-coa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5ec2902153dfbf8c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:unirec-coa" data-paper-title="UniRec: Bridging the Expressive Gap between Generative and Discriminative Recommendation via Chain-of-Attribute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-9e5f5e882d487833">Can future target behavior reveal attributes used as inputs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aunirec-coa">UniRec: Bridging the Expressive Gap between Generative and Discriminative Recommendation via Chain-of-Attribute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation / large-scale e-commerce platform</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Attributes come from allowed item metadata. Target attributes can supervise generation, not be given as known answers. Public MovieLens lacks private multi-scenario serving.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Supplying the true next item&#x27;s brand leaks a clue.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12234">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.12234-unirec-coa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9e5f5e882d487833">Question link</a></p>
</details>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:unirec-coa" data-paper-title="UniRec: Bridging the Expressive Gap between Generative and Discriminative Recommendation via Chain-of-Attribute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-1ca55275b4b52784">How does capacity-limited quantization differ from maximizing popular-code likelihood?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aunirec-coa">UniRec: Bridging the Expressive Gap between Generative and Discriminative Recommendation via Chain-of-Attribute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation / large-scale e-commerce platform</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Capacity limits reduce hotspots and disperse usage, while likelihood alone follows frequency. Evaluate relevance and balance together.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Avoid crowding a bucket without randomly distributing items just to equalize counts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12234">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.12234-unirec-coa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1ca55275b4b52784">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:unirec-coa" data-paper-title="UniRec: Bridging the Expressive Gap between Generative and Discriminative Recommendation via Chain-of-Attribute" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-unirec-coa-7ee11184" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0d1560da99d7ac98">Why generate an attribute chain before SIDs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aunirec-coa">UniRec: Bridging the Expressive Gap between Generative and Discriminative Recommendation via Chain-of-Attribute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Authors did not disclose affiliation / large-scale e-commerce platform</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Explicit category, seller, and brand context can bridge generative and discriminative representations. The chain guides content and does not establish independent language reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Generate category and brand before the detailed semantic path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hill-index" data-paper-title="Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-hill-index-46d50ccf" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0781092bdcfe4d94">Why does HILL train index nodes with users and interaction towers instead of only clustering item vectors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahill-index">Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Facebook and Instagram Ads</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pure item geometry may not match an interaction model&#x27;s choices. Train node proxies in user–item scoring and let deeper residuals recover information missed above. Beam search can still omit paths; isolated test answers cannot guide any test-time updates or selection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Similar products may serve different users, so interaction-informed nodes can organize them better than content proximity alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12965">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.12965-hill-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0781092bdcfe4d94">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hill-index" data-paper-title="Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cbced8f5719b2196">Why validate HILL soft assignments and hierarchical beam separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahill-index">Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Facebook and Instagram Ads</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Continuous training assignments create pseudo-items and gradients; serving explores a limited discrete tree. Check normalization, residual updates, parent-child mapping, and actual budgets independently, including small-catalog variance. Good reconstruction does not establish beam coverage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A target can receive small mass from several soft nodes and be absent from every retained hard branch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12965">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.12965-hill-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cbced8f5719b2196">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hill-index" data-paper-title="Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5406f6bb678f4cbe">Why can HILL residual layers complement each other instead of repeating raw-vector clustering?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahill-index">Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Facebook and Instagram Ads</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each layer quantizes the prior layer&#x27;s unexplained residual, while repeated clustering can relearn dominant directions. Complementarity is not guaranteed and beam budgets can miss items. Local compression worked but quality regressed; fewer candidates are not automatically better.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After a coarse electronics node, residuals can express use and price rather than repeatedly learning the broad theme.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12965">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.12965-hill-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5406f6bb678f4cbe">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hill-index" data-paper-title="Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b6cf5a4612015d03">Why involve user and interaction signals in HILL index-node training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahill-index">Efficient Retrieval Scaling with Hierarchical Indexing for Large Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta / Facebook and Instagram Ads</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>ANN organizes item neighbors geometrically, which may disagree with complex relevance. Scoring pseudo-items with users transfers retrieval relations to the tree before narrowing candidates. Training, tree versions, and serving need to stay aligned.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two content neighbors with different audiences can be organized by recommendation value, not just item distance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12965">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2604.12965-hill-index/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b6cf5a4612015d03">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:lightning-opd" data-paper-title="Lightning OPD" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d662b69ce7015b40">Why isn&#x27;t cached teacher scoring equivalent to continuously online distillation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Alightning-opd">Lightning OPD</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MIT HAN Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Initial student samples are scored under one teacher config. Later updates shift visitation without refreshing labels. Coverage and teacher consistency govern the cost tradeoff; local evidence is data flow only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Cached early error prefixes help initially but later new approaches need an explicit refresh protocol.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13010">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2604.13010-lightning-opd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d662b69ce7015b40">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:lightning-opd" data-paper-title="Lightning OPD" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
