<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-31e5f1063f754e80">How does HCUB incremental reward plus UCB differ from greedy absolute CTR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahcub">Hierarchical Contextual Uplift Bandits for Catalog Personalization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dream11</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Increment measures change relative to a reference, and the exploration bonus addresses uncertainty. CTR greedy favors already responsive groups. Increment needs suitable causal data; confidence bonuses are not identification, and movie proxies do not establish interventions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An active group might click anyway, while a less active group may respond more to the action.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14333">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.14333-hcub/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-31e5f1063f754e80">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hcub" data-paper-title="Hierarchical Contextual Uplift Bandits for Catalog Personalization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d31f882b2fed638">Why choose context-tree granularity dynamically in HCUB?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahcub">Hierarchical Contextual Uplift Bandits for Catalog Personalization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dream11</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fine nodes are relevant but sparse; parents are better sampled but coarse. Reward inheritance handles cold starts and yields to local data. Tree design and mixing affect bias, so more partitions do not ensure accuracy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Borrow a parent estimate after two events, then rely more on the child after 100 observations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:lifeagentbench" data-paper-title="LifeAgentBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Long-Horizon, Cross-Dimensional Lifestyle Health Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d23f60fee3459ab1">Why doesn&#x27;t an SQL scorer computing definitive answers implement LifeAgent tool reasoning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alifeagentbench">LifeAgentBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Long-Horizon, Cross-Dimensional Lifestyle Health Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The scorer uses rules and records to verify final answers; it does not decompose tasks, retrieve evidence, maintain statistics, or revise plans. Keep scorer and tool baseline distinct and do not let actors read reference calculations. Field checks are not long-term health-record reasoning; this describes evaluation, not health advice.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A verifier can compute mean weekly sleep, but the agent must choose the window, query records, and check missing values without calling the reference-answer function.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13880v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2601.13880-lifeagentbench/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d23f60fee3459ab1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:lifeagentbench" data-paper-title="LifeAgentBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Long-Horizon, Cross-Dimensional Lifestyle Health Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d7e908d939e49c24">How do read-only SQL and Context Prompting isolate gold answers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alifeagentbench">LifeAgentBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Long-Horizon, Cross-Dimensional Lifestyle Health Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>For SQL, the model generates an allowed query before receiving results. Context Prompting selects public evidence by user first. Gold stays with the scorer. Numeric grading follows piecewise tolerances, and multi-item answers must match item counts, not merely substrings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A correct term accompanied by extra incorrect items is not a fully correct answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13880v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2601.13880-lifeagentbench/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d7e908d939e49c24">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:lifeagentbench" data-paper-title="LifeAgentBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Long-Horizon, Cross-Dimensional Lifestyle Health Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">

<h2 id="qa-5961b103e689800b">How do executable SQL, complete evidence, and final correctness differ?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alifeagentbench">LifeAgentBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Long-Horizon, Cross-Dimensional Lifestyle Health Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Executability concerns syntax and runtime. EX measures evidence completeness on its defined denominator, and Acc|EX checks answers given complete evidence. Mixing denominators conceals retrieval or reasoning problems.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A query can execute but omit a required user and fail to collect all evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13880v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2601.13880-lifeagentbench/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5961b103e689800b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:lifeagentbench" data-paper-title="LifeAgentBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Long-Horizon, Cross-Dimensional Lifestyle Health Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d90e5f74c4f4986f">Why do LifeAgentBench&#x27;s long-term life records require more than classifying one event?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alifeagentbench">LifeAgentBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Long-Horizon, Cross-Dimensional Lifestyle Health Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Questions span times, dimensions, or users across diet, sleep, activity, and mood records. Gather relevant evidence before calculating or comparing. Filtering and aggregation scope are part of the answer; a single record rarely suffices.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>To compare activity and sleep for one user over a week, use both kinds of records for the same dates. One day&#x27;s step count is incomplete.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hyformer" data-paper-title="HyFormer: Revisiting the Roles of Sequence Modeling and Feature Interaction in CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-hyformer-d0fa9291" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-64a45769bae35220">Why does HyFormer apply Query Boosting after every history read and pass the queries back to the next layer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahyformer">HyFormer: Revisiting the Roles of Sequence Modeling and Feature Interaction in CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin Search</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>If history is compressed once before field interactions, those interactions cannot change what evidence is read next. HyFormer alternates sequence reads and non-sequence token mixing, letting new evidence enter field interactions and boosted queries return to history. The compact queries and field representations co-evolve; this does not require rewriting the raw history for every candidate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: The first layer finds an outdoor interest. After mixing in rainy weather and item material, the next query can focus on waterproof gear. A one-shot summary followed by an MLP cannot easily ask that new question of the history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12681">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.12681-hyformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-64a45769bae35220">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hyformer" data-paper-title="HyFormer: Revisiting the Roles of Sequence Modeling and Feature Interaction in CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-26d294f33aa7d17b">Why must HyFormer feed the boosted query back into the next cross-attention layer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahyformer">HyFormer: Revisiting the Roles of Sequence Modeling and Feature Interaction in CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin Search</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reusing the original Q would make each layer repeat the same question and eliminate co-evolution. Sequence K/V, decoded queries, and non-sequence tokens also need aligned layouts; per-token transforms operate on the mixed layout. The local two-query reduction is a specific implementation, not an exact match for production parameters and cache paths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: The second query should carry the first layer&#x27;s budget and use-case information. If code accidentally reuses Q0, a deeper model can still reduce loss without implementing the paper&#x27;s iterative information loop.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12681">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.12681-hyformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-26d294f33aa7d17b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hyformer" data-paper-title="HyFormer: Revisiting the Roles of Sequence Modeling and Feature Interaction in CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a3b7a374c10d8c91">When do interactions occur in HyFormer&#x27;s query co-evolution versus LONGER followed by RankMixer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahyformer">HyFormer: Revisiting the Roles of Sequence Modeling and Feature Interaction in CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin Search</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The serial path summarizes the sequence before field mixing, so the initial history read cannot react to later field results. HyFormer sends boosted queries back for another read, conditioning it over several layers. Earlier interaction adds expressiveness but may also strengthen popularity bias: the source reports a large local increase in head share, not unequivocally better personalization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: One round finds camping signals, field mixing adds a budget constraint, and the next round seeks lightweight gear. A completed one-shot summary generally cannot reread raw history under the new constraint.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12681">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.12681-hyformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a3b7a374c10d8c91">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hyformer" data-paper-title="HyFormer: Revisiting the Roles of Sequence Modeling and Feature Interaction in CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-2138dbf99ca17a2d">Why initialize HyFormer&#x27;s Global Queries from non-sequence fields and the sequence mean?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahyformer">HyFormer: Revisiting the Roles of Sequence Modeling and Feature Interaction in CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin Search</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The query needs the current global context and a history overview so it can read the long sequence purposefully instead of starting from an unconditional slot. Each decoding step is followed by boosting to combine fields with history. The initial summary can lose details; later reads can help but cannot guarantee complete recovery.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A travel setting and a photography-heavy history can steer the initial query toward lightweight camera needs. A constant query sees the current setting only in a later layer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12681">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.12681-hyformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2138dbf99ca17a2d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:calibration-aware-rl" data-paper-title="Balancing Classification and Calibration Performance in Decision-Making LLMs via Calibration Aware Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4c73529324e3dd75">Why constrain decision probability if accuracy improves while ECE worsens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acalibration-aware-rl">Balancing Classification and Calibration Performance in Decision-Making LLMs via Calibration Aware Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Southern California</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Correctness only needs the top class right; calibration requires confidence to match actual hit frequency. RLVR can make correct choices overconfident. Measure separately, choose T on validation and reserve test. Post-hoc calibration is not full RL reproduction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two models with identical labels can assign near-certainty or moderate confidence and differ in probability quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13284">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2601.13284-calibration-aware-rl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4c73529324e3dd75">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:calibration-aware-rl" data-paper-title="Balancing Classification and Calibration Performance in Decision-Making LLMs via Calibration Aware Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-586428ee262c0ee4">May calibration T be selected on test NLL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acalibration-aware-rl">Balancing Classification and Calibration Performance in Decision-Making LLMs via Calibration Aware Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Southern California</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Fit validation NLL, freeze, then report test accuracy and calibration. Choosing on test biases final evaluation. Local coverage is calibration and split isolation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Trying all temperatures on test and reporting the best overstates generalization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:calibration-aware-rl" data-paper-title="Balancing Classification and Calibration Performance in Decision-Making LLMs via Calibration Aware Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4e7311780075723f">How does local temperature calibration differ from full RLVR training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acalibration-aware-rl">Balancing Classification and Calibration Performance in Decision-Making LLMs via Calibration Aware Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Southern California</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Temperature rescales existing logits; full training changes the decision model. Shared calibration goals do not make postprocessing a full reproduction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A frozen model with tuned T uses no resampled trajectories or policy gradient.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:calibration-aware-rl" data-paper-title="Balancing Classification and Calibration Performance in Decision-Making LLMs via Calibration Aware Reinforcement Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b4f067719b7ff0b1">Does calibration-aware RL score the entire explanation through its decision token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acalibration-aware-rl">Balancing Classification and Calibration Performance in Decision-Making LLMs via Calibration Aware Reinforcement Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Southern California</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It studies final-decision probability and calibration, not factual fidelity of all reasoning. Correct choices and credible probabilities require separate measurement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>High probability for A doesn&#x27;t make every preceding explanation step correct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:coreflect" data-paper-title="CoReflect: A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9336a21730fbc0d6">Why can&#x27;t editing rubric strings or averaging supplied scores reproduce CoReflect&#x27;s reflective co-evolution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acoreflect">CoReflect: A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The core needs semantic planning of scenarios, dialogue simulation, evaluation, and an analyzer that uses reasons to identify deficits and update both tasks and criteria. Mechanical state transitions are scaffolding without semantic judgment or real interaction. Source formulas explain the loop, not local execution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An analyzer should identify missed empathy criteria and create relevant scenarios. Manually changing a weight from one to two does not provide that reflection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12208v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2601.12208-coreflect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9336a21730fbc0d6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:coreflect" data-paper-title="CoReflect: A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-16d199a59b834d14">Did the local project implement CoReflect&#x27;s 953 scenarios and full semantic modules?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acoreflect">CoReflect: A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. This is literature coverage without a heuristic adapter. JSON state transitions or averaging supplied values do not replace LLM checks and dialogue generation; formulas explain the source method.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>More loop iterations do not show the evaluator learned a new judgment dimension.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12208v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2601.12208-coreflect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-16d199a59b834d14">Question link</a></p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:coreflect" data-paper-title="CoReflect: A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-27514a4a3c2740e3">How does CoReflect persona–scenario consistency checking differ from valid JSON?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acoreflect">CoReflect: A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Syntax only makes fields readable, not semantically compatible. The paper retains pairs passing actual LLM consistency checks. This filter is part of task quality; a state machine or manual score does not replace semantic checking and reflection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A persona unable to use the internet paired with a completed online booking can be valid JSON and still require semantic review.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12208v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2601.12208-coreflect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-27514a4a3c2740e3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:coreflect" data-paper-title="CoReflect: A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-coreflect-7d1f277e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-73a0fa96c34acc53">What do CoReflect&#x27;s planner, simulator, evaluator, and analyzer produce?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acoreflect">CoReflect: A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The planner organizes tasks, the simulator generates interactions, the evaluator applies current criteria, and the analyzer distills reflection that changes later tasks and criteria. These are semantic model roles, not four JSON fields. Local work did not substitute handwritten rules for them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An ambiguous criterion appears during dialogue. The analyzer identifies it, then later rounds revise the rubric and plan scenarios that test the issue.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12208v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2601.12208-coreflect/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-73a0fa96c34acc53">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:engram" data-paper-title="Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">

<span id="paper-foundation-models-engram-7eeee5b9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-89a8dbb57f4df6dc">Why is Engram conditional memory rather than another set of MoE experts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aengram">Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MoE conditionally executes networks; Engram hashes normalized n-grams to deterministic table lookups and gates them into state. Stored patterns complement compositional compute, but memory size, collisions, bandwidth, and fusion cost remain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A common phrase can fetch a vector, but context still determines its meaning here.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.07372-engram/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-89a8dbb57f4df6dc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:engram" data-paper-title="Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a110c6b00b2052be">Should Engram replace h_t with retrieved m_t?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aengram">Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. h′=h+sigmoid(W[h;m])⊙m preserves the residual and gates by context. Record bucket count, n-gram orders, and added-parameter training budget; preserve small-budget negative results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A poorly trained memory should not overwrite the original hidden state unconditionally.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.07372-engram/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a110c6b00b2052be">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:engram" data-paper-title="Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-40494fc31520acc4">How do Engram and MoE increase different resources?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aengram">Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MoE routes compute experts. Engram reads embeddings by n-gram address. O(1) lookup still requires storing, training, and moving table values.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Neural expert execution differs from fetching a phrase vector.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.07372-engram/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-40494fc31520acc4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:engram" data-paper-title="Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0920b734f8751eb0">Why add lookup memory for frequent local patterns?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aengram">Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reconstructing common patterns repeatedly consumes compute. A learned n-gram table provides gated cached representations so attention and FFNs can focus on combinations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Look up a common phrase locally and compute novel combinations in the backbone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.07372-engram/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0920b734f8751eb0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:airbnb-ebr" data-paper-title="Applying Embedding-Based Retrieval to Airbnb Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-airbnb-ebr-a90e62e0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b96313817395d985">Why build hard negatives from search, browsing, and booking journeys?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aairbnb-ebr">Applying Embedding-Based Retrieval to Airbnb Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Airbnb</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Random listings often differ obviously by geography or conditions. Browsed but unbooked listings are closer decision alternatives, though not necessarily disliked; explain sampling and retain serving filters/versioning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Within a Paris trip, similar local listings are harder than Tokyo, but sold-out homes are not necessarily irrelevant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06873">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.06873-airbnb-ebr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b96313817395d985">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:airbnb-ebr" data-paper-title="Applying Embedding-Based Retrieval to Airbnb Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b7ceaa141a992d9f">How match hard negatives and eligible candidates with targets?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aairbnb-ebr">Applying Embedding-Based Retrieval to Airbnb Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Airbnb</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use a positive from the same request and reasonable unselected journey listings in the contrastive denominator. Keep serving versions consistent. Local movie proxies lack inventory/geography.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two viewed but unbooked nearby homes are harder than an unavailable home in another city.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06873">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.06873-airbnb-ebr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b7ceaa141a992d9f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:airbnb-ebr" data-paper-title="Applying Embedding-Based Retrieval to Airbnb Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-03cce997a8ff19b3">How does traffic replay differ from static negatives?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aairbnb-ebr">Applying Embedding-Based Retrieval to Airbnb Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Airbnb</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Replay reconstructs real requests, journey candidates, and filters; static negatives may be too easy. Replay better matches first-stage competition but not live feedback or changing inventory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Distinguish New York listings available on matching dates, not just New York versus nationwide random homes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06873">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.06873-airbnb-ebr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-03cce997a8ff19b3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:airbnb-ebr" data-paper-title="Applying Embedding-Based Retrieval to Airbnb Search" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f7de56d9be73fcab">Why combine query/listing towers with geography and inventory filters?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aairbnb-ebr">Applying Embedding-Based Retrieval to Airbnb Search</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Airbnb</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Dot-product retrieval finds relevant homes, but availability and destination remain request-specific constraints. An index accelerates matching without making eligibility inferable from similarity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A highly relevant apartment can be in the wrong city or unavailable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06873">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.06873-airbnb-ebr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f7de56d9be73fcab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:promise" data-paper-title="PROMISE: Process Reward Models Unlock Test-Time Scaling Laws in Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-promise-c348f413" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-bd05a70bed64223d">Why reward intermediate SID paths in PROMISE rather than score only complete items?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apromise">PROMISE: Process Reward Models Unlock Test-Time Scaling Laws in Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Early wrong semantic branches waste later computation. A lightweight process reward supplies dense training feedback and prunes drifting beams at inference. Wider beams can explore better paths but depend on reward quality and cost, not automatic improvement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Reject a home-decoration prefix early for a hiking request instead of waiting to generate a cushion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04674">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.04674-promise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bd05a70bed64223d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:promise" data-paper-title="PROMISE: Process Reward Models Unlock Test-Time Scaling Laws in Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-93c178126616bf5a">Why define comparable scales across prefix lengths in PROMISE reward accumulation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apromise">PROMISE: Process Reward Models Unlock Test-Time Scaling Laws in Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Long paths naturally sum more terms, potentially creating length bias. Compare beam candidates at consistent depths or with defined length handling, calibrate log-probability and λR, and retain legality, deduplication, and termination separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Three positive rewards are not inherently better than one if the paths have different depths. High PRM cannot legitimize an illegal item.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04674">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.04674-promise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-93c178126616bf5a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:promise" data-paper-title="PROMISE: Process Reward Models Unlock Test-Time Scaling Laws in Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-f4c75f7ff9dd3eba">What extra judgment does PRM-guided beam widening add beyond likelihood?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apromise">PROMISE: Process Reward Models Unlock Test-Time Scaling Laws in Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Likelihood prioritizes current model probability; PRM adds process value, allowing lower-likelihood but task-relevant paths. Scoring costs compute and can be biased. Test-time scaling is a budget–quality curve, not a guarantee.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: PRM can keep a less popular but correct branch; a popularity-biased PRM may still explore the wrong region.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04674">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.04674-promise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f4c75f7ff9dd3eba">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:promise" data-paper-title="PROMISE: Process Reward Models Unlock Test-Time Scaling Laws in Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e151a7faaadabf83">What does a SID prefix represent in PROMISE, and why does pruning remove many items?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apromise">PROMISE: Process Reward Models Unlock Test-Time Scaling Laws in Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It is a hierarchical address prefix shared by a reachable subset of items. Descendants only refine that branch. Pruning can remove many unexplored items at once, so a bad process score can cause broad misses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Pruning photography excludes all cameras, lenses, and accessories below it, including a perfectly relevant lens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04674">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.04674-promise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e151a7faaadabf83">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:harmonrank" data-paper-title="Rethinking Multi-objective Ranking Ensemble in Recommender System: From Score Fusion to Rank Consistency" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-harmonrank-1abfcd00" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-460ed145b6ab2671">Why align task ranks before fusing raw predicted probabilities in HarmonRank?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aharmonrank">Rethinking Multi-objective Ranking Ensemble in Recommender System: From Score Fusion to Rank Consistency</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different base rates and scales make raw fusion sensitive to calibration and sparsity. Differentiable rank-sum learns within-task order; inter-task attention models dependencies such as purchases and comments before unified ranking. Rank alignment discards magnitude and is not a general probability calibrator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Purchase probabilities are much smaller than click probabilities; ranking candidates within each task reduces raw-scale dominance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02955">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.02955-harmonrank/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-460ed145b6ab2671">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:harmonrank" data-paper-title="Rethinking Multi-objective Ranking Ensemble in Recommender System: From Score Fusion to Rank Consistency" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-205f2c06bfda2ec2">Why require both classes and identify invalid tasks in a soft-AUC batch?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aharmonrank">Rethinking Multi-objective Ranking Ensemble in Recommender System: From Score Fusion to Rank Consistency</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>AUC needs comparable positive-negative pairs; one-class slices must be masked or reported not estimable, not scored as perfect. Align candidate IDs across tasks. Temperature and sampling affect the differentiable approximation and its gradients, not actual full-data AUC.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An all-zero purchase batch has no pairs and must not send a perfect score into task fusion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02955">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.02955-harmonrank/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-205f2c06bfda2ec2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:harmonrank" data-paper-title="Rethinking Multi-objective Ranking Ensemble in Recommender System: From Score Fusion to Rank Consistency" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-2689dff0a475a4a9">How does inter-objective self-attention handle conflicts differently from fixed fusion?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aharmonrank">Rethinking Multi-objective Ranking Ensemble in Recommender System: From Score Fusion to Rank Consistency</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed coefficients impose a global trade-off. Attention learns dependencies and conditional combinations, increasing flexibility but risking domination by frequent objectives. Check by task and example; the local negative result does not establish quality benefits.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A highly clicked but rarely purchased item can be treated differently from one high on both, instead of applying the same 7:3 ratio.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02955">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.02955-harmonrank/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2689dff0a475a4a9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:harmonrank" data-paper-title="Rethinking Multi-objective Ranking Ensemble in Recommender System: From Score Fusion to Rank Consistency" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c91d11da9694e889">Why move from classification scores to rank relationships in HarmonRank?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aharmonrank">Rethinking Multi-objective Ranking Ensemble in Recommender System: From Score Fusion to Rank Consistency</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different target base rates and scales can dominate arithmetic fusion. Differentiable rank-sum/AUC first emphasizes each task&#x27;s internal order, then learns task dependencies. Ranking loses absolute value magnitude rather than preserving every business unit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A purchase score can be numerically tiny but still rank items meaningfully, without saying how much more value one brings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02955">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.02955-harmonrank/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c91d11da9694e889">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:podcast-mtl" data-paper-title="Cold-Starting Podcast Ads and Promotions with Multi-Task Learning on Spotify" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-podcast-mtl-fc67da12" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-bf5d9b50db60650a">How does Podcast MTL use organic promotion for cold ads, and why balance gradients?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apodcast-mtl">Cold-Starting Podcast Ads and Promotions with Multi-Task Learning on Spotify</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Spotify</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>User, content, and context representations share abundant organic signals while separate heads preserve objectives. Sample and gradient imbalance can drown the sparse advertising task, so adjust contributions. Transfer can fail when tasks differ; sharing does not guarantee gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A new podcast has organic plays but no ad clicks. Learn audience clues in the shared encoder while preventing organic gradients from overwhelming ad supervision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.02306-podcast-mtl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bf5d9b50db60650a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:podcast-mtl" data-paper-title="Cold-Starting Podcast Ads and Promotions with Multi-Task Learning on Spotify" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6cb40b601772ffa9">Why not fill missing Podcast MTL labels with zeros?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apodcast-mtl">Cold-Starting Podcast Ads and Promotions with Multi-Task Learning on Spotify</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Spotify</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An organic example may never expose the ad, so its ad response is unobserved, not negative. Mask that loss; observed objectives can still train shared features. Record task identity, data construction, and α. Movies proxy for podcasts only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Listening after organic exposure does not imply the user ignored an unseen ad.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.02306-podcast-mtl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6cb40b601772ffa9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:podcast-mtl" data-paper-title="Cold-Starting Podcast Ads and Promotions with Multi-Task Learning on Spotify" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c78cd2c217eacbf6">How does gradient balancing treat a small podcast task differently from mixing by counts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apodcast-mtl">Cold-Starting Podcast Ads and Promotions with Multi-Task Learning on Spotify</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Spotify</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Counts let the large task dominate shared weights. Balancing actual contributions preserves the sparse ad direction, but too much can amplify noise. Evaluate per task; duplicating records cannot guarantee cold-start gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: One million organic and one thousand ad examples can bury ad gradients. Moderate balancing does not mean infinitely upweighting a single ad label.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.02306-podcast-mtl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c78cd2c217eacbf6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:podcast-mtl" data-paper-title="Cold-Starting Podcast Ads and Promotions with Multi-Task Learning on Spotify" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ce83c5c320e4d33e">Does cold start in Podcast MTL mean no content or no target feedback?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apodcast-mtl">Cold-Starting Podcast Ads and Promotions with Multi-Task Learning on Spotify</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Spotify</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The gap is ad click/play labels for new podcasts, not necessarily missing titles or topics. Shared content and context help without representing observed ad outcomes. Transfer supplies a training signal, not a real click log.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A show&#x27;s host and description can suggest likely audiences before exposure, but cannot verify their ad clicks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2601.02306-podcast-mtl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ce83c5c320e4d33e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:higr" data-paper-title="HiGR: Industrial-Scale Hierarchical Generative Slate Recommendation Framework in Tencent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-higr-d87ebf0f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f29b5cfbf4107740">Why does HiGR need whole-page preference alignment after choosing semantic clusters then items?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahigr">HiGR: Industrial-Scale Hierarchical Generative Slate Recommendation Framework in Tencent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Hierarchical codes make identification easier but individual relevance does not ensure useful order or complementarity. The Hierarchical Slate Decoder generates coarse-to-fine choices; ORPO reshapes combinations from preferred and rejected pages. Evaluated preferences do not guarantee long-tail or utility gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Sports clusters can yield only near-duplicate shoes; page preferences can add socks or training content.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24787">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2512.24787-higr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f29b5cfbf4107740">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:higr" data-paper-title="HiGR: Industrial-Scale Hierarchical Generative Slate Recommendation Framework in Tencent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-29d8f706697c4551">Why define HiGR sequence probabilities and numerical boundaries before calculating log odds?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahigr">HiGR: Industrial-Scale Hierarchical Generative Slate Recommendation Framework in Tencent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Page probability is a product of conditional token probabilities and can underflow; use stable log-space arithmetic for both the joint and its complement. Arbitrary scores are not probabilities. Match hierarchical mappings and repetition constraints to page identity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Taking logs after a long-page probability rounded to zero fails; silently replacing the sequence probability with a length average changes the objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24787">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2512.24787-higr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-29d8f706697c4551">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:higr" data-paper-title="HiGR: Industrial-Scale Hierarchical Generative Slate Recommendation Framework in Tencent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d13d7f938c1fcfbc">How does HiGR ORPO preference evidence differ from page-level SFT?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahigr">HiGR: Industrial-Scale Hierarchical Generative Slate Recommendation Framework in Tencent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>SFT imitates positive pages. ORPO compares preferred and rejected page odds to teach relative composition. Preference and quantization biases remain, and local NDCG declined; report it with head-share changes instead of declaring overall improvement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An equally relevant but more complementary page can beat a repetitive one; a winner-only target provides no explicit relative signal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24787">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2512.24787-higr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d13d7f938c1fcfbc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:higr" data-paper-title="HiGR: Industrial-Scale Hierarchical Generative Slate Recommendation Framework in Tencent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-75d3a4b1b9164993">Why choose semantic clusters before items in HiGR&#x27;s page generation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahigr">HiGR: Industrial-Scale Hierarchical Generative Slate Recommendation Framework in Tencent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Hierarchy divides a large space into coarse interests and precise identities, enabling composition across groups. Wrong coarse codes restrict later candidates, and apparent diversity does not prove relevance. Evaluate both quantization and whole-page utility.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Choose tutorial, tool, and example groups before specific items, while recognizing a wrong entertainment branch can remain diverse but irrelevant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24787">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2512.24787-higr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-75d3a4b1b9164993">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mhc" data-paper-title="mHC: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-mhc-cde7f1ea" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d5c14b4fa80176f3">Why constrain mHC residual mixing to a doubly stochastic matrix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amhc">mHC: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek-AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
