<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:crsd" data-paper-title="From Reasoning LLMs to BERT: A Two-Stage Distillation Framework for Search Relevance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-16dedeae125cf8d6">How does CRSD&#x27;s contrastive self-distillation differ from fitting external teacher logits?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acrsd">From Reasoning LLMs to BERT: A Two-Stage Distillation Framework for Search Relevance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meituan</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One lightweight student produces distributions under both views, and a contrastive loss also constrains representations. Shared parameters can reduce scale mismatch but do not eliminate erroneous rationales. Check actual gradient and stop-gradient paths rather than assuming self-distillation is unbiased.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The same model reads ordinary product information and an augmented rationale; a separate fixed teacher would not share its parameters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11056">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2510.11056-crsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-16dedeae125cf8d6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:crsd" data-paper-title="From Reasoning LLMs to BERT: A Two-Stage Distillation Framework for Search Relevance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/retrieval-matching">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/retrieval-matching/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Candidate generation and search matching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-94dea0d87b1d446e">Why is reasoning a training augmentation in CRSD rather than a permanent serving requirement?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acrsd">From Reasoning LLMs to BERT: A Two-Stage Distillation Framework for Search Relevance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meituan</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rationales can enrich supervision but cost real-time generation. A student learns from plain and rationale-augmented views, transferring augmented-view distributions to the plain path. This does not guarantee retention of complete reasoning or faithful explanations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Train with a commuting-lightweight rationale, but serve on current features without first generating a long explanation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11056">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2510.11056-crsd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-94dea0d87b1d446e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:plum" data-paper-title="PLUM: Adapting Pre-trained Language Models for Industrial-scale Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-plum-515f2ca7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0d1840f495739871">Why use hierarchical video SIDs and continue language pretraining in PLUM instead of enlarging an ID table?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aplum">PLUM: Adapting Pre-trained Language Models for Industrial-scale Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind / YouTube</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Huge ID tables memorize items and share little with new ones. Composable SIDs and CPT connect behavior, text, ASR, and metadata to LM capacity before next-SID training. Beam search generates candidates online, but code quality still determines retrieval usefulness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A new baking video can borrow a coarse baking code and distinguish itself at a fine level instead of learning an isolated ID from scarce clicks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2510.07784-plum/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0d1840f495739871">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:plum" data-paper-title="PLUM: Adapting Pre-trained Language Models for Industrial-scale Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e504366a2a68836e">Why reconstruct the first r codeword layers in PLUM progressive masking instead of shuffling levels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aplum">PLUM: Adapting Pre-trained Language Models for Industrial-scale Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind / YouTube</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Residual levels accumulate coarse-to-fine meaning. Random prefix depths require each prefix to work; shuffling destroys that order. Mask SFT prompt loss, supervise only target SIDs, and use catalog trie legality. Training on prompt text changes the objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Sometimes reconstruct with coarse codes and sometimes add detail; using level three as the first code is not progressive reconstruction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2510.07784-plum/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e504366a2a68836e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:plum" data-paper-title="PLUM: Adapting Pre-trained Language Models for Industrial-scale Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-1fb69e0e018a5cfa">Why cross random versus LM initialization with CPT on versus off in PLUM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aplum">PLUM: Adapting Pre-trained Language Models for Industrial-scale Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind / YouTube</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Four cells separate initialization, extra continued training, and their interaction. Locally CPT lowered loss without improving Recall and LM-initialized arms had zero hits. Convergence is not successful retrieval or general scaling evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Run random/no CPT, random/CPT, LM/no CPT, and LM/CPT to distinguish pretrained knowledge from extra training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2510.07784-plum/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1fb69e0e018a5cfa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:plum" data-paper-title="PLUM: Adapting Pre-trained Language Models for Industrial-scale Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-099601afbacbb260">Why mix behavior and SID–metadata examples during PLUM CPT instead of only tuning next-item codes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aplum">PLUM: Adapting Pre-trained Language Models for Industrial-scale Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind / YouTube</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Behavior teaches consumption transitions; text and ASR connect addresses to language semantics. CPT adapts pretrained knowledge to recommendation, then SFT focuses on retrieval. Mixture ratio matters, and lower loss need not improve search.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Learn both that a code means a camping tutorial and what users consume afterward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2510.07784-plum/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-099601afbacbb260">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:watch-and-learn" data-paper-title="Watch and Learn: Learning to Use Computers from Online Videos" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-watch-and-learn-e9cf239b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d5dc634ef7c4b6c">Why learn inverse dynamics from tutorials instead of treating before/after pixel differences as mouse actions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Awatch-and-learn">Watch and Learn: Learning to Use Computers from Online Videos</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Screen changes may come from scrolling, keystrokes, or program responses, so pixels do not identify actions uniquely. The inverse model predicts action type, coordinates, and text from screen pairs, then assembles trajectories. These are estimated labels, not rule guesses or proof an IDM was trained locally.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A screen can move down from a wheel or a key. Use visual context and supervision instead of labeling every downward shift as a click.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04673v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2510.04673-watch-and-learn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d5dc634ef7c4b6c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:watch-and-learn" data-paper-title="Watch and Learn: Learning to Use Computers from Online Videos" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-30274243761e3d5f">Why can&#x27;t one simple rule head replace action, coordinate, and text prediction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Awatch-and-learn">Watch and Learn: Learning to Use Computers from Online Videos</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The paper uses action classification, coordinates discretized into 0–1000 classes, and a GPT-2 small autoregressive text head with SigLIP-2 and a four-layer Transformer. Do not invent loss weights. Local work is literature and cost review, not IDM training, corpus download, or desktop evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A cursor-difference click rule cannot recover typed text from two frames or replace joint IDM training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04673v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2510.04673-watch-and-learn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-30274243761e3d5f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:watch-and-learn" data-paper-title="Watch and Learn: Learning to Use Computers from Online Videos" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-26c0fe3cc14e615b">What changes when retrieving video examples versus training on annotated trajectories?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Awatch-and-learn">Watch and Learn: Learning to Use Computers from Online Videos</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retrieval puts a relevant demonstration in context without updating the executor. SFT writes trajectory patterns into weights. Both rely on IDM label quality, so video count is not correct action count. Similar titles do not establish actual desktop learning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Use one tutorial as a prompt example or offline training input. Inference cost and how errors propagate differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04673v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2510.04673-watch-and-learn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-26c0fe3cc14e615b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:watch-and-learn" data-paper-title="Watch and Learn: Learning to Use Computers from Online Videos" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-78e1133fbfd419f4">Why use online tutorial videos rather than rely only on expensive action annotations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Awatch-and-learn">Watch and Learn: Learning to Use Computers from Online Videos</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Ohio State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tutorials contain genuine software behavior without machine-readable click coordinates, keys, and actions. Converting visible demonstrations broadens training sources. Frames are not action ground truth: occlusion, edits, and missing typed text can harm conversion and execution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A file moves across windows, but training data needs to distinguish dragging from a copy command rather than invent a click.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04673v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2510.04673-watch-and-learn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-78e1133fbfd419f4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:legomem" data-paper-title="LEGOMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-legomem-3e37af3a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-21c86cef36853d28">Why separate orchestration and execution memory for recombination on new tasks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alegomem">LEGOMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Decomposition and delegation capture high-level dependencies, while action templates ground calls. One full trace binds them to particular people and environments. Layers can reuse structure while swapping execution units. Admit verified units only and recheck interfaces and prerequisites when combining them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Collect, verify, and summarize stays the same while data comes from a database in one task and a file in another.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04851">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2510.04851-legomem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-21c86cef36853d28">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:legomem" data-paper-title="LEGOMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-8e26df792894a3d7">Does local reused_plans verify real multi-agent Office delegation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alegomem">LEGOMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The local run extracts action/domain units from structured verifiable plans and reuses high-level and fine-grained steps. It does not execute Office apps, LLM delegation, or complete recovery. Reuse counts are neither OfficeBench success nor real tool cost.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A rule reuses a subplan 100 times without showing a model can delegate between real document and email apps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式与算法, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04851">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2510.04851-legomem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8e26df792894a3d7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:legomem" data-paper-title="LEGOMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-2732f77db1bafc8e">What generalization trade-off separates procedural recombination from whole-trace retrieval?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alegomem">LEGOMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Whole traces preserve complete context but may be tied to one task. Procedural units recombine for new needs but can lose cross-unit prerequisites. Legal dependencies and validation are needed; individual success does not imply arbitrary compositions work.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Reading a spreadsheet and sending email may both work alone. Verify recipients and data permissions before combining.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04851">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2510.04851-legomem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2732f77db1bafc8e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:legomem" data-paper-title="LEGOMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c4c27071fd8d1be5">Why does LegoMem focus on recurring workflows with multiple roles and steps?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alegomem">LEGOMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Office workflows share portions but change goals and roles. Reorganizable procedures let new tasks reuse the right steps rather than copy one complete run. Units must retain dependencies and context; pieces that look composable can still lack inputs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Weekly reports and project briefs both need collection and source verification, but different approvers. Reuse collection and replan handoff.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04851">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2510.04851-legomem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c4c27071fd8d1be5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:combinatorial-watermark" data-paper-title="Detecting Post-generation Edits to Watermarked LLM Outputs via Combinatorial Watermarking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-combinatorial-watermark-183aedb0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-66b97bbf9772dff1">Why can testing all cyclic phases still miss full-period deletion?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acombinatorial-watermark">Detecting Post-generation Edits to Watermarked LLM Outputs via Combinatorial Watermarking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Minnesota</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Phase search handles global offsets, but deleting a whole period can preserve the repeating pattern and phase. Independently calibrate global/local thresholds; a hard-pattern diagnostic is not perfect soft-watermark localization. No full local model edit matrix.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Removing one full red/blue cycle leaves the remaining pattern unchanged.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01637v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2510.01637-combinatorial-watermark/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-66b97bbf9772dff1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:combinatorial-watermark" data-paper-title="Detecting Post-generation Edits to Watermarked LLM Outputs via Combinatorial Watermarking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cb75a73b696eddd8">Can local E(t) zero-pad edges?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acombinatorial-watermark">Detecting Post-generation Edits to Watermarked LLM Outputs via Combinatorial Watermarking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Minnesota</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It is defined only for complete interior t=w−1 through T−w, without zero padding or changing denominators. Check all phases and preserve full-period deletion as a blind negative control.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Edge positions with incomplete windows should not be falsely flagged because zeros were added.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01637v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2510.01637-combinatorial-watermark/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cb75a73b696eddd8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:combinatorial-watermark" data-paper-title="Detecting Post-generation Edits to Watermarked LLM Outputs via Combinatorial Watermarking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-9acb87bf75defb5d">Can global D and local E(t) thresholds replace each other?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acombinatorial-watermark">Detecting Post-generation Edits to Watermarked LLM Outputs via Combinatorial Watermarking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Minnesota</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>D detects a watermark across the whole passage; E(t) uses window coverage to flag possible edits. They differ in scope and threshold direction. Calibrate false positives independently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Global passage can pass while a short span scores low; that does not precisely identify every edit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01637v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2510.01637-combinatorial-watermark/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9acb87bf75defb5d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:combinatorial-watermark" data-paper-title="Detecting Post-generation Edits to Watermarked LLM Outputs via Combinatorial Watermarking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/evaluation-and-evidence/">Foundation models / Capability evidence: sampling, readout, and reliability</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c09d9ae85d58f347">Why bias vocabulary partitions by a periodic pattern?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acombinatorial-watermark">Detecting Post-generation Edits to Watermarked LLM Outputs via Combinatorial Watermarking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Minnesota</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tag-specific logit biases induce a statistical periodic structure. The detector compares windows across all cyclic shifts for watermark and edit evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>AB partition alternation is detectable without knowing where the observed text starts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01637v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../foundation-models/2510.01637-combinatorial-watermark/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c09d9ae85d58f347">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:probabilistic-autorater" data-paper-title="Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f08ba902f4cd5432">Why can&#x27;t Autorater backpropagate through parsed probability text?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprobabilistic-autorater">Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The policy generates text, parses it to a fixed reward and uses policy gradients. Discrete text-to-float parsing has no ordinary differentiable path. Brier/log rewards encourage calibration, with separate invalid penalties. Derivatives of numeric scores alone are not GRPO.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An unformatted &#x27;very confident&#x27; response fails parsing; don&#x27;t silently substitute a plausible number.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00263v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2510.00263-probabilistic-autorater/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f08ba902f4cd5432">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:probabilistic-autorater" data-paper-title="Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-37c219be1787c9bd">Why can&#x27;t invalid numbers enter the formula before multiplying by a zero mask?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprobabilistic-autorater">Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate invalid outputs first. NaN can propagate through nonlinearities and multiplication by zero; out-of-range values are not probabilities. Use the parse-failure reward. The local strict parser is a contract, not the authors&#x27; parser or full RL.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Route NaN directly to invalid reward rather than computing log(NaN) first.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00263v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2510.00263-probabilistic-autorater/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-37c219be1787c9bd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:probabilistic-autorater" data-paper-title="Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-87f7465105cb6097">How do Brier and log rewards penalize confident errors differently?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprobabilistic-autorater">Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Both are proper probability scores, but squared and logarithmic tails differ; log loss is especially sensitive to extremely confident mistakes. Parse failures also have a separate reward, beyond legal probability gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A near-certain win prediction followed by defeat is penalized by both, with different magnitudes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00263v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2510.00263-probabilistic-autorater/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-87f7465105cb6097">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:probabilistic-autorater" data-paper-title="Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-probabilistic-autorater-421e42ad" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-86cdf4efbe8d3fa3">Why should a probabilistic autorater output a preference probability, not just a winner?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprobabilistic-autorater">Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Real preferences can disagree. Brier/log rewards fit observed preference frequencies rather than force binary certainty. Reliable target distributions matter; arbitrary numbers are not calibrated.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Near-even annotator votes warrant an intermediate probability rather than an absolute winner.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00263v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2510.00263-probabilistic-autorater/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-86cdf4efbe8d3fa3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:benchmark-self-bias" data-paper-title="When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-bae0503700524a2d">Why rank each segment and exclude self from the peer mean?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Abenchmark-self-bias">When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Segment scales may differ, so rank before averaging to preserve the protocol. Remove self from the peer comparison. Score direction, axes and tie handling affect the sign; peer consensus is not external truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A low-is-better metric and high-is-better metric need consistent rank direction. Never put the self score back into peers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26600v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2509.26600-benchmark-self-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bae0503700524a2d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:benchmark-self-bias" data-paper-title="When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0b238a5ebb648838">Why do axis order and leave-self-out matter for self-bias?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Abenchmark-self-bias">When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rank within segments, average over segments, then subtract the peer mean excluding self from the diagonal. Specify whether scores are higher- or lower-is-better; negative bias indicates favorable self-rank.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>MetricX-QE is lower-is-better. Descending ranks would reverse the bias direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26600v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2509.26600-benchmark-self-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0b238a5ebb648838">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:benchmark-self-bias" data-paper-title="When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b2350803a5a27539">How does the protocol distinguish self-evaluation advantage from a stronger model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Abenchmark-self-bias">When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compare one target&#x27;s ranks under its own role and peers to isolate evaluator preference from target quality. Peers can share biases, so this is relative audit evidence, not a definitive capability verdict.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Consistently leading under all judges differs from leading only under one&#x27;s own judge.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26600v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2509.26600-benchmark-self-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b2350803a5a27539">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:benchmark-self-bias" data-paper-title="When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-benchmark-self-bias-143e8f64" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7ea7ef39b1edfe7d">Which axis is target, which is benchmark role, and which cell measures self-evaluation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Abenchmark-self-bias">When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The target is evaluated; the benchmark role performs evaluation. Self-evaluation is the diagonal where they match. Compare own and other roles for one fixed target, not different targets.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A answering with B judging is off-diagonal; A answering and judging is diagonal. Keep A as the target in both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26600v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2509.26600-benchmark-self-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7ea7ef39b1edfe7d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:intsr" data-paper-title="IntSR: An Integrated Generative Framework for Search and Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-intsr-9d48eca1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fb387442d699fb31">How does IntSR handle both explicit search terms and recommendation intent without a query?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aintsr">IntSR: An Integrated Generative Framework for Search and Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Amap</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An explicit query expresses the current request; implicit session history supplies unspoken needs. Both inform latent intent, and results are generated in a unified item or POI vocabulary. Time context helps determine whether needs still apply and bridges search and recommendation. Sharing a vocabulary does not excuse ignoring query constraints or treating old interests as explicit current requests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: When a user searches for nearby coffee, a history of quiet venues can supplement the query. With no search, the session can suggest a need, but yesterday&#x27;s location should not be assumed to apply today.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21179">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2509.21179-intsr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fb387442d699fb31">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:intsr" data-paper-title="IntSR: An Integrated Generative Framework for Search and Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3b3becae3d60389c">How should IntSR distinguish an absent query from a real empty-string search?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aintsr">IntSR: An Integrated Generative Framework for Search and Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Amap</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use the missingness marker or branch specified by the model contract. Time conditioning may only use the request timestamp, and the target POI must not enter latent-intent estimation. Both entry points share item identity, not necessarily every label. The source&#x27;s movie proxy cannot test real locations or opening hours.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Never starting a search and deliberately submitting a blank query can have different log meanings. Do not collapse them to one unexplained string and leave the model to guess.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21179">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2509.21179-intsr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3b3becae3d60389c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:intsr" data-paper-title="IntSR: An Integrated Generative Framework for Search and Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-42ca84522a89bc1e">What does IntSR&#x27;s latent-intent mixture make explicit compared with concatenating q and h for scoring?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aintsr">IntSR: An Integrated Generative Framework for Search and Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Amap</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It first estimates an intent distribution and then generates items conditioned on intent and time, keeping multiple plausible needs explicit. Direct concatenation may express this implicitly without learning the same structure. A latent variable need not have a stable human meaning, and a more decomposable output does not prove recovery of true intent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: &#x27;Weekend activities&#x27; could mean hiking or an exhibition. Keeping probabilities for both before choosing a venue is natural, but those probabilities remain model estimates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21179">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2509.21179-intsr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-42ca84522a89bc1e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:intsr" data-paper-title="IntSR: An Integrated Generative Framework for Search and Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e9621be987a8d381">Why combine explicit queries and implicit session intent in the same item space in IntSR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aintsr">IntSR: An Integrated Generative Framework for Search and Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Amap</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Search terms can omit background, while session activity offers context without directly stating the current request. Joint intent inference uses both, and a shared vocabulary avoids fragmented item identities across the two entry points. Time represents drift. An absent query should follow a defined missing-input path, not be replaced with something the user supposedly said.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A query of &#x27;nearby&#x27; combined with a recent vegetarian search can suggest dining. A recommendation-only visit should use its session without inventing a user query.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21179">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2509.21179-intsr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e9621be987a8d381">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:onepiece" data-paper-title="OnePiece: Bringing Context Engineering and Reasoning to Industrial Cascade Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-onepiece-1b14efa1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-10aa9ef73312afbd">How do OnePiece&#x27;s latent blocks and progressive task weights differ from simply summing all losses?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aonepiece">OnePiece: Bringing Context Engineering and Reasoning to Industrial Cascade Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shopee</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Residual blocks repeatedly update contextual state before heads read it. Scheduled weights change which objectives dominate training stages so shared representations adapt to retrieval, click, and value. Both path and order matter; a local proxy does not prove verifiable linguistic reasoning in latent states.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Learn relevance before raising purchase-value weight to avoid an early sparse objective dominating basic ranking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18091">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2509.18091-onepiece/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-10aa9ef73312afbd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:onepiece" data-paper-title="OnePiece: Bringing Context Engineering and Reasoning to Industrial Cascade Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d554085990e57412">How verify OnePiece&#x27;s H(k+1) residual update and αt(k) schedule separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aonepiece">OnePiece: Bringing Context Engineering and Reasoning to Industrial Cascade Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shopee</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One updates contextual state per block, the other weights losses per training stage. Distinguish the two meanings of k and verify both state propagation and applied loss weights. A fixed scorer proxy cannot establish full cascade training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: More blocks do not imply progressive weights, and changing losses does not establish multi-step latent updates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18091">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2509.18091-onepiece/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d554085990e57412">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:onepiece" data-paper-title="OnePiece: Bringing Context Engineering and Reasoning to Industrial Cascade Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d12bd2773766ed64">How does progressive weighting change learning order relative to fixed equal task weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aonepiece">OnePiece: Bringing Context Engineering and Reasoning to Industrial Cascade Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shopee</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed weights exert the same pressure throughout. A schedule lets basic relevance and harder value objectives converge in stages. This can reduce conflicts or cause forgetting, so inspect stage metrics. Proxy results do not make all curricula superior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Emphasize relevance early and transaction value later; forgetting relevance could yield expensive but unrelated items.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18091">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2509.18091-onepiece/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d12bd2773766ed64">Question link</a></p>
</details>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:onepiece" data-paper-title="OnePiece: Bringing Context Engineering and Reasoning to Industrial Cascade Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6cb4f874464f620f">Why does OnePiece jointly cover retrieval, clicks, and value?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aonepiece">OnePiece: Bringing Context Engineering and Reasoning to Industrial Cascade Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shopee</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Cascade stages have distinct labels and independent training can lose transferable clues. Shared context and latent updates model multiple needs, while progressive weights schedule learning. Objectives can conflict; a &#x27;reasoning&#x27; name does not verify language reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Relatedness, click likelihood, and expected value complement one another, but high clicks need not imply purchases.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18091">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2509.18091-onepiece/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6cb4f874464f620f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:drl-put" data-paper-title="Deep Reinforcement Learning for Ranking Utility Tuning in the Ad Recommender System at Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">

<span id="paper-recommendation-drl-put-ba6d0f54" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a39e4cbdc0eedaf9">Does DRL-PUT learn which items to recommend or how to combine utility scores?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adrl-put">Deep Reinforcement Learning for Ranking Utility Tuning in the Ad Recommender System at Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Actions specify weights for relevance, CTR, CVR, and related scores. A request-conditioned policy combines existing predictors, while offline updates correct action distribution differences using logging probabilities. Rarely logged weights lack evidence for claims of live optimality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Keep ad representations fixed but emphasize relevance for exploration and conversion for purchase intent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:drl-put" data-paper-title="Deep Reinforcement Learning for Ranking Utility Tuning in the Ad Recommender System at Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-96e89b6778bf510d">Why must action identities match logged propensities in DRL-PUT&#x27;s `π/μ`?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adrl-put">Deep Reinforcement Learning for Ranking Utility Tuning in the Ad Recommender System at Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Keep executed weights, behavior probability, context, and reward tied to one event. With μ=0, no support exists; a tiny replacement does not enable unbiased extrapolation. Baseline b cannot read test outcomes, and final lists alone cannot reconstruct the update.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Logging the propensity of 4:6 for an executed 7:3 mix gives the wrong gradient multiplier despite a genuine reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05292">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2509.05292-drl-put/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-96e89b6778bf510d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:drl-put" data-paper-title="Deep Reinforcement Learning for Ranking Utility Tuning in the Ad Recommender System at Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d5788a31ee9ff996">How does DRL-PUT off-policy updating differ from fitting high-reward logged examples directly?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adrl-put">Deep Reinforcement Learning for Ranking Utility Tuning in the Ad Recommender System at Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Logs are generated by μ and target choices follow π; the probability ratio addresses differing action frequencies. Without it, frequently tried actions dominate. Valid support and logging are required, extreme ratios increase variance, and public proxies are not randomized ad logs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the old system nearly always emphasized CTR, most high rewards may follow that choice without showing alternatives are worse.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:drl-put" data-paper-title="Deep Reinforcement Learning for Ranking Utility Tuning in the Ad Recommender System at Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4769e145ec181242">Why make utility weights the action instead of generating items in DRL-PUT?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adrl-put">Deep Reinforcement Learning for Ranking Utility Tuning in the Ad Recommender System at Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Existing CTR, CVR, relevance, and revenue models score candidates. The policy chooses a controlled mix, and feedback evaluates the induced list, not isolated causal item effects.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A 7:2:1 versus 4:3:3 mix changes order while leaving item embeddings and the click model unchanged.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
