<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memtool" data-paper-title="MemTool" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-memtool-13c64e5c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-356e892465a4deff">Why protect workflow-required tools before considering recency or historic success?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemtool">MemTool</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · PricewaterhouseCoopers Commercial Technology and Innovation Office</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retention scores reflect past usage and may undervalue an uncalled but required future tool. Protect dependencies first, then evict lower-scoring unprotected entries. If required tools exceed capacity, silent truncation does not preserve a valid workflow.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Upload is required at the end of archiving even if not recently used. Do not remove it solely for low recency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21428">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2507.21428-memtool/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-356e892465a4deff">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memtool" data-paper-title="MemTool" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c38703d1cf219e1f">How should recency and historical success scores evict unprotected tools?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemtool">MemTool</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · PricewaterhouseCoopers Commercial Technology and Innovation Office</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Restrict candidates to those outside the protected workflow set. Keep scores λ times recency plus (1−λ) times success; evict the lowest. The weight trades off recency and history without redefining protection. Local deterministic descriptions and eviction counts do not establish live tool completion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: One evictable tool was just used but often fails; another is older but reliable. λ controls the choice, and required tools do not enter this ranking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式与算法, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21428">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2507.21428-memtool/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c38703d1cf219e1f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memtool" data-paper-title="MemTool" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-13511d15aa68dae4">How do autonomous, workflow, and hybrid tool-description policies make decisions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemtool">MemTool</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · PricewaterhouseCoopers Commercial Technology and Innovation Office</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Autonomous lets the agent decide retention; workflow uses current process requirements; hybrid protects those requirements and dynamically manages remaining tools. Freedom and structural constraints differ. Removal rate is insufficient if eviction prevents completion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: An agent may discard rare payments before one is needed. Workflow information protects payment while hybrid manages other entries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21428">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2507.21428-memtool/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-13511d15aa68dae4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memtool" data-paper-title="MemTool" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-30295a2477bae0ec">Why do tool descriptions need bounded dynamic memory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemtool">MemTool</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · PricewaterhouseCoopers Commercial Technology and Innovation Office</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MCP schemas and instructions consume context, while static truncation can remove tools in use. MemTool protects current workflow requirements and manages other descriptions dynamically. Preserve executable interfaces rather than maximizing removals.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: An order lookup followed by refund still needs the refund tool even if it was not called recently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21428">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2507.21428-memtool/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-30295a2477bae0ec">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gspo" data-paper-title="GSPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b968145af51dfe73">Why average token log ratios before exponentiation and clipping?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agspo">GSPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Qwen Team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One outcome belongs to one answer. One geometric weight gives all tokens the same relative advantage and clipping decision despite local noise. It changes credit aggregation and doesn&#x27;t eliminate all length/MoE mismatches.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A correct answer with one anomalous ratio gets different credit under token clipping and shared weighting.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2507.18071-gspo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b968145af51dfe73">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gspo" data-paper-title="GSPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e9419f1e0394ebb6">Should GSPO clip per token or per response?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agspo">GSPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Qwen Team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Clip one ratio per response, shared across tokens. Mask padding from length. Candidate experiments do not reproduce real token rollouts, MoE routes or clusters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Clipping each token and averaging usually differs from averaging then clipping.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2507.18071-gspo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e9419f1e0394ebb6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gspo" data-paper-title="GSPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d23ce2ac81343580">Is GSPO&#x27;s geometric-mean ratio the actual sequence probability ratio?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agspo">GSPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Qwen Team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. GSPO exponentiates the mean log ratio; the exact sequence ratio exponentiates the sum, multiplying token ratios. Averaging changes length scaling and the objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeated small shifts accumulate in a product but the geometric mean measures typical shift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2507.18071-gspo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d23ce2ac81343580">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gspo" data-paper-title="GSPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-gspo-8ccc0734" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5b426bfd8e95bfd5">Why use one importance ratio for a full response in GSPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agspo">GSPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Qwen Team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Terminal reward is sequence-level, and token outliers can cause fragmented clipping. Average token log ratios to form one response weight and avoid local outlier dominance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One rare token&#x27;s large shift need not determine distinct clips throughout a long reply.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2507.18071-gspo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5b426bfd8e95bfd5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcr" data-paper-title="Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e491a49ab4ec08e3">Why need proper scoring in addition to correctness rewards?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlcr">Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Massachusetts Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Binary reward cannot distinguish justified caution from false certainty. Proper scoring couples probabilities with outcomes to incentivize honesty. Report accuracy and calibration separately; local Brier gradients aren&#x27;t full RL.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A quiz bot claiming certainty on unfamiliar items can be penalized for that confidence even when ordinary rewards ignore it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16806">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2507.16806-rlcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e491a49ab4ec08e3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcr" data-paper-title="Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7e79bc66d4f44aa7">Which classes receive local RLCR Brier gradients?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlcr">Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Massachusetts Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compute squared differences between the complete softmax distribution and one-hot target and backpropagate over all candidates, not just the displayed choice. Hybrid includes CE; no paper-checkpoint RL.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Unselected classes consume probability mass and contribute to scoring.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16806">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2507.16806-rlcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7e79bc66d4f44aa7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcr" data-paper-title="Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-bf73ac1980f7fa4e">How does RLCR differ from displaying confidence after training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlcr">Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Massachusetts Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A displayed field needn&#x27;t affect optimization; RLCR incorporates a scoring rule. Local Brier/hybrid objectives are mechanism evidence, not full rollouts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A 90% badge doesn&#x27;t mean bad calibration was penalized in training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16806">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2507.16806-rlcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bf73ac1980f7fa4e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlcr" data-paper-title="Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rlcr-9a05e032" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0ac0af70774f8783">Why predict both an answer and confidence in RLCR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlcr">Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Massachusetts Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Correctness-only reward does not incentivize honest probabilities. A proper score evaluates probability and outcome, rewarding truthful probabilities in expectation under its assumptions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A model that often errs should report moderate confidence instead of certainty.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16806">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2507.16806-rlcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0ac0af70774f8783">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankmixer" data-paper-title="RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-67c000ac06ff074b">Why require H=T and divisible hidden dimension?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankmixer">RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Splitting T tokens of width D into H slices gives H outputs of width TD/H. H=T restores T×D for residual addition; D must divide by H.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four 64-wide tokens split into four 16-wide slices; three heads cannot split 64 evenly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15551-rankmixer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-67c000ac06ff074b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankmixer" data-paper-title="RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-rankmixer-298d1226" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a18a983529fe37d7">How do independent FFNs learn interactions after fixed TokenMix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankmixer">RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Split every input by head and concatenate matching-index slices into new tokens, so specialized nonlinear FFNs receive cross-field signals. H=T and divisible width are layout conditions. Field mixing does not forbid sequence attention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>User, product, and context slices can jointly enter an FFN without similarity weights.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15551-rankmixer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a18a983529fe37d7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankmixer" data-paper-title="RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ad1e554a4b682966">Do RankMixer per-token FFNs attach to original fields or mixed positions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankmixer">RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each FFN sees a mixed token containing same-index slices from all fields. Its parameters specialize in that subspace, not one original field. Preserve field/head/output layout.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The first mixed FFN processes parts of all four fields, not only the first one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15551-rankmixer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ad1e554a4b682966">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankmixer" data-paper-title="RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-473b102f64b8ecd6">What do ReLU routing and DTSI solve beyond fixed top-k?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankmixer">RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sparse ReLU permits variable activated experts. Separate training and inference routers apply sparsity only on inference so experts can learn without starvation. Local sparse code does not validate full dual routing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Complex tokens can use more experts while rarely deployed experts still train.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15551-rankmixer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-473b102f64b8ecd6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankmixer" data-paper-title="RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-603d4772b072a0eb">Why not credit TokenMix alone for the dense versus shared-FFN gain?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankmixer">RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Both arms use TokenMix; dedicated versus shared FFNs and different parameter counts change together. The sparse arm also trails dense. Report budgets and popularity bias; local results do not establish paper MFU or A/B.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Both cars already use the same transmission, so a larger engine&#x27;s gain does not isolate it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15551-rankmixer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-603d4772b072a0eb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankmixer" data-paper-title="RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-558c5d17470ec022">Which attention does RankMixer replace?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankmixer">RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It replaces attention for heterogeneous field interactions, not necessarily independent behavior sequence encoding. TokenMix and specialized FFNs process fields after feature extraction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>History attention can extract photography interest before mixing it with price and item fields.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15551-rankmixer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-558c5d17470ec022">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:argus" data-paper-title="Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-argus-3c7d662d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-34e00691c873ae6a">How does feedback-then-item differ from direct next-item prediction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aargus">Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>ARGUS factors joint action into feedback type then conditional item, sharing a trunk while preserving feedback distinctions. Inference cannot read future feedback. Local module ablation is negative.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Expected long watch and quick skip can favor different items for the same history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15994-argus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-34e00691c873ae6a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:argus" data-paper-title="Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a3a287cea14c8c52">Why distinguish DIN and next-item-only baselines?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aargus">Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>DIN compares whole models; matched next-item-only isolates feedback factorization. Both local comparisons lack gains, and neither should hide the other&#x27;s negative evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Overall proximity to DIN can coexist with degradation after adding the feedback path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15994-argus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a3a287cea14c8c52">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:argus" data-paper-title="Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e31c2f745c08191d">How does conditional factorization differ from a parallel auxiliary head?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aargus">Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A parallel head adds loss without necessarily changing item prediction. ARGUS explicitly conditions items on feedback, so feedback errors can propagate. Measure both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Separate “will like” and item outputs are multitask, not a feedback-conditioned generator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15994-argus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e31c2f745c08191d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:argus" data-paper-title="Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-06db608db356f93c">How read ARGUS&#x27;s feedback–item joint distribution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aargus">Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Predict feedback from history, then condition item probability on it and multiply. True feedback is training supervision, not an inference input unless specified externally under protocol.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Likes can favor relatable clips while long watches favor tutorials.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15994-argus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-06db608db356f93c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:click-a-buy-b" data-paper-title="Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-click-a-buy-b-aac757e9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fb5e3facbeeba7ab">Why not attribute a purchase of B entirely to clicked item A as a conversion of A itself?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclick-a-buy-b">Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The clicked and purchased objects can differ; same-item last-click attribution misses cross-item paths. Separate Click-A-Buy-A and Click-A-Buy-B tasks and use taxonomy to describe relations between A and B. This improves observed attribution and prediction, not causal identification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A user views an entry-level camera and buys an upgrade. Same-item counting marks the first camera as worthless despite its role in the decision path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15113">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15113-click-a-buy-b/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fb5e3facbeeba7ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:click-a-buy-b" data-paper-title="Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-2cc0afb634ea21f7">How should a CABB viewing-sequence proxy be reported without inventing purchase labels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclick-a-buy-b">Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>State that sequential views proxy Click-A/Buy-B, compare matched data, candidates, and baselines, and limit conclusions to the proxy. Taxonomy weights connect corresponding items and must not use test targets to decide candidate categories. Public ratings are not transaction amounts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Report simulated cross-item paths from successive views, not that users really clicked A and bought B. A target category known only afterward is not an inference input.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15113">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15113-click-a-buy-b/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2cc0afb634ea21f7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:click-a-buy-b" data-paper-title="Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-006455c4de387e4b">Why does CABB need behavior types and item hierarchy beyond ordinary next-item prediction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclick-a-buy-b">Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Adjacency alone need not distinguish browsing, clicking, and purchase or describe the A–B relationship. CABB explicitly supervises cross-item purchase paths and uses taxonomy to organize transferable relations. Sequential viewing preserves adjacency only and does not validate real purchase attribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Watching movie B after A can test cross-item connections, but there is no ad-click and transaction loop.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15113">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15113-click-a-buy-b/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-006455c4de387e4b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:click-a-buy-b" data-paper-title="Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-fba99f94af149fd0">Why does Click-A-Buy-B distinguish clicked and purchased items?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclick-a-buy-b">Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An item can reveal a need and another item satisfy it through price or specs. Separate CABA and CABB supervision retains direct conversions and cross-item guidance; taxonomy offers relation cues. Observed co-occurrence does not prove that A causes purchase of B.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Clicking one camera brand and buying another is not a conversion of A, but A can still participate in the decision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15113">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.15113-click-a-buy-b/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fba99f94af149fd0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinfm" data-paper-title="PinFM: Foundation Model for User Activity Sequences at a Billion-scale Visual Discovery Platform" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-pinfm-c653f7d8" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4eaf16c90d354ace">How does PinFM DCAT retain early candidate fusion without re-encoding user context per item?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinfm">PinFM: Foundation Model for User Activity Sequences at a Billion-scale Visual Discovery Platform</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Early fusion lets candidates interact with history internally. DCAT self-attends once over deduplicated context, caches layer K/V, and lets candidate queries read it. Shared state must be candidate-independent. Serving savings and pretraining gains are distinct; retain local negative outcomes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Encode 500 events once for 100 candidates rather than copying all history 100 times, while candidates still read it inside layers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12704">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.12704-pinfm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4eaf16c90d354ace">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinfm" data-paper-title="PinFM: Foundation Model for User Activity Sequences at a Billion-scale Visual Discovery Platform" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-fdbf98eb2bd2f065">Why confirm actual context K/V reuse during DCAT full-catalog inference?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinfm">PinFM: Foundation Model for User Activity Sequences at a Billion-scale Visual Discovery Platform</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compute context self-attention once and let candidate layers perform only legal candidate-dependent work. Equal scores do not imply equal execution cost, so check call counts and dependencies. Bind caches to history and version and exclude candidate-conditioned states.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Recomputing history for 1,000 candidates can give the same NDCG while yielding no amortization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12704">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.12704-pinfm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fdbf98eb2bd2f065">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinfm" data-paper-title="PinFM: Foundation Model for User Activity Sequences at a Billion-scale Visual Discovery Platform" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c67c18389f789088">Why does scratch versus pretrained DCAT answer a different question from DCAT versus ordinary Transformer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinfm">PinFM: Foundation Model for User Activity Sequences at a Billion-scale Visual Discovery Platform</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Keeping DCAT fixed isolates pretraining, while changing architecture tests cache decomposition or fusion. The selected local pretrained model regressed on test; mathematical DCAT fidelity does not establish pretraining value. Measure serving efficiency separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Training two models with the same architecture differently says nothing about a third architecture that was never tested.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12704">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.12704-pinfm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c67c18389f789088">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinfm" data-paper-title="PinFM: Foundation Model for User Activity Sequences at a Billion-scale Visual Discovery Platform" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-73e242cb9a591ae2">Why combine next-, multi-, and future-token objectives in PinFM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinfm">PinFM: Foundation Model for User Activity Sequences at a Billion-scale Visual Discovery Platform</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The immediate item, future window, and future from a specified position supply distinct time scales, helping learn more than recency before transfer. Future labels are training-only. Cross-scenario pretraining can negatively transfer despite being a foundation model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Next click teaches immediate intent, a window teaches coexisting interests, and later targets add long-term direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12704">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2507.12704-pinfm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-73e242cb9a591ae2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spiral" data-paper-title="SPIRAL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7816033509093ce3">Why require automatically decidable game rules in zero-sum SPIRAL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspiral">SPIRAL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Apple</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Adversarial progress creates curriculum, but independent rules must decide wins. Zero-sum incentives do not guarantee broad reasoning coverage. Local state/objective checks don&#x27;t reproduce self-play training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The proposer can&#x27;t change rules midgame to make every solution lose.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.24119">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2506.24119-spiral/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7816033509093ce3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spiral" data-paper-title="SPIRAL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-aa88b77e42aae8aa">Why preserve zero-sum rewards across SPIRAL roles?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspiral">SPIRAL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Apple</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One outcome gives opposite credit under aligned states/rules. Rewarding both for the same victory changes the game. Local kernel isn&#x27;t large multi-round training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A proposer win cannot also be a solver win.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.24119">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2506.24119-spiral/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aa88b77e42aae8aa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spiral" data-paper-title="SPIRAL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a8712f25147d80f3">What are limits of self-play vs fixed hard-problem banks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspiral">SPIRAL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Apple</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Self-play adapts but can get trapped in game-specific tricks. Fixed banks have defined coverage but no evolving opponent. Game gains don&#x27;t imply general reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Winning a word game needn&#x27;t improve math, retrieval or tools.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.24119">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2506.24119-spiral/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a8712f25147d80f3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spiral" data-paper-title="SPIRAL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-spiral-8df7f07c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c95c0c1a16fcba51">Why let one SPIRAL model propose and solve games?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspiral">SPIRAL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Apple</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An adversarial, decidable zero-sum game creates a curriculum as opponents evolve. Roles need distinct rewards and explicit rules; proposer cannot declare outcomes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One role creates a position, another tries to solve it, and a program judges.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.24119">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2506.24119-spiral/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c95c0c1a16fcba51">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cispo" data-paper-title="CISPO / MiniMax-M1" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ce326a3ad19568a3">Why does CISPO retain gradients for some tokens PPO would clip flat?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acispo">CISPO / MiniMax-M1</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MiniMax</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Clipped weights scale log-probability gradients while retaining advantage direction. PPO&#x27;s minimum is flat in certain quadrants. Test gradients, not only values or clipped advantages.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A rare negative-advantage token can still receive bounded suppression even if PPO is flat.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13585">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2506.13585-cispo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ce326a3ad19568a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cispo" data-paper-title="CISPO / MiniMax-M1" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0a45c23f226dd11a">What if CISPO differentiates directly through the clipped ratio?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acispo">CISPO / MiniMax-M1</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MiniMax</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Extra weight derivatives change the policy-gradient objective. Keep rollout, weight construction and logp path separate. Local checks do not reproduce MiniMax training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Current action logp should supply gradient without duplicating it through the weight branch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13585">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2506.13585-cispo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0a45c23f226dd11a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cispo" data-paper-title="CISPO / MiniMax-M1" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-45e7baa94a6c0de4">Why aren&#x27;t CISPO and PPO the same because both clip?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acispo">CISPO / MiniMax-M1</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MiniMax</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>PPO takes the minimum of clipped and unclipped surrogates. CISPO multiplies logp and advantage by clipped weight. Backward and out-of-range behavior differ despite matching bounds.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One boundary can stop gradients; the other preserves updates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13585">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2506.13585-cispo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-45e7baa94a6c0de4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:cispo" data-paper-title="CISPO / MiniMax-M1" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-cispo-73dd09ad" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ba75db1b56d9b580">Why clip importance weights in CISPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Acispo">CISPO / MiniMax-M1</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MiniMax</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Bound magnitude while preserving advantage direction and learning, unlike PPO min-surrogate flat regions. Separate frozen weights from differentiable logp.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A capped positive weight can still reinforce through logp.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13585">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2506.13585-cispo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ba75db1b56d9b580">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mgoe" data-paper-title="Macro Graph of Experts for Billion-Scale Multi-Task Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-mgoe-e3468d6f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7af4301a11225bf7">What does MGOE&#x27;s explicit task graph add to MMoE&#x27;s sample-level gate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amgoe">Macro Graph of Experts for Billion-Scale Multi-Task Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sample-level mixtures do not explicitly encode stable task relationships. Graph bottom and experts propagate between related objectives before task towers, separating global structure from local routing. Wrong edges can propagate negative transfer. Compare related and unrelated tasks rather than assuming the graph is correct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Clicks, cart additions, and purchases may share paths, while reports need other signals; the gate need not relearn every task relationship per sample.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10520">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2506.10520-mgoe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7af4301a11225bf7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mgoe" data-paper-title="Macro Graph of Experts for Billion-Scale Multi-Task Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-9f0b168dfe442d78">Why align MGOE&#x27;s normalized adjacency and task indices with expert tensors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amgoe">Macro Graph of Experts for Billion-Scale Multi-Task Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rows and columns of A identify nodes and task towers must read the correct propagated rows of H. Normalization, self-loops, and depth determine mixing. Use labels only in training; do not rebuild the graph from test feedback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A purchase node paired with watch-time features still multiplies correctly but shares the wrong information.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10520">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2506.10520-mgoe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9f0b168dfe442d78">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mgoe" data-paper-title="Macro Graph of Experts for Billion-Scale Multi-Task Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d46d50e1c7231b58">What additional sharing bias does MGOE introduce relative to independent MMoE task gates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amgoe">Macro Graph of Experts for Billion-Scale Multi-Task Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MMoE shares experts implicitly by example. MGOE adds graph-constrained task propagation, which can help sparse objectives or transmit wrong relations. Overall gains and changed head share do not establish all-task improvement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A sparse purchase task can borrow click knowledge; a mistakenly connected returns task may inherit the wrong direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10520">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2506.10520-mgoe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d46d50e1c7231b58">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mgoe" data-paper-title="Macro Graph of Experts for Billion-Scale Multi-Task Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f4ad32d70416c198">Why build a Macro Task Merging Graph before expert propagation in MGOE?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Amgoe">Macro Graph of Experts for Billion-Scale Multi-Task Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The graph represents stable sharing relations that a per-sample gate does not explicitly encode. Macro Graph Bottom/Experts propagate information before task-specific towers. Relations can change across scenarios, and edges do not establish causality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Click, watch time, and purchase can share information without implying clicks cause purchases.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10520">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2506.10520-mgoe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f4ad32d70416c198">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:radar" data-paper-title="RADAR: Recall Augmentation through Deferred Asynchronous Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-radar-206d8edd" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f22b0db4a797c31d">Why use asynchronous post-request ranking to supplement retrieval for the next RADAR request?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aradar">RADAR: Recall Augmentation through Deferred Asynchronous Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A strong ranker cannot usually scan the entire catalog within request latency. RADAR does the expensive scan afterward, caches good candidates, and merges them with live retrieval next time. Old history makes caches stale, so live retrieval still captures new intent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Precompute likely movies after one visit and add them on the next, while live retrieval uses newly observed clicks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07261">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2506.07261-radar/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f22b0db4a797c31d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:radar" data-paper-title="RADAR: Recall Augmentation through Deferred Asynchronous Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-10c293e7dee1f7e0">Why deduplicate and recheck eligibility when merging RADAR live and cached top-k?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aradar">RADAR: Recall Augmentation through Deferred Asynchronous Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Old items may be unavailable, consumed, or ineligible. Merge by item ID and preserve provenance for incremental evaluation. Record cache generation time and history cutoff; the next target cannot enter the async job ahead of time.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Drop a listing that filled since yesterday and count a movie retrieved by both channels only once.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07261">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2506.07261-radar/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-10c293e7dee1f7e0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:radar" data-paper-title="RADAR: Recall Augmentation through Deferred Asynchronous Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/research-serving-loop">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/research-serving-loop/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Automated research and efficient serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
