<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:ragen" data-paper-title="RAGEN" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-3a4fb5b58a42b90f">How does StarPO-S trajectory filtering differ from clipping ratios only inside PPO loss?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aragen">RAGEN</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northwestern</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Filtering controls which trajectories enter the objective. Ratio clipping limits drift for admitted samples, while the critic and gradient controls are separate. One clipping operation does not replace the complete stabilization chain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeated low-information trajectories can still dominate training samples even if their ratios are clipped.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20073">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.20073-ragen/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3a4fb5b58a42b90f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:ragen" data-paper-title="RAGEN" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ef11042a5e1ad9ea">Why does RAGEN monitor Echo Trap separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aragen">RAGEN</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northwestern</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multi-turn stochastic training can enter self-reinforcing repetition, with collapsed reward variance and gradient spikes. StarPO-S uses trajectory filtering, a critic baseline, and gradient/clipping stabilization rather than interpreting low variance as learning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A policy can consistently follow a failed path without any improvement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20073">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.20073-ragen/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ef11042a5e1ad9ea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ttrl" data-paper-title="TTRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c6d9c41a8ac4de24">Why label TTRL as adaptation rather than fixed-model evaluation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Attrl">TTRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · PRIME-RL author team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Test inputs trigger sampling and immediate parameter updates, so the evaluated model changes. Report sampling/adaptation budgets and keep gold in independent scoring. Pseudo-label consensus can reinforce errors; unlabeled isn&#x27;t no learning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Sampling and updating before answering differs from one call to the original model even without gold.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16084">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.16084-ttrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c6d9c41a8ac4de24">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ttrl" data-paper-title="TTRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-764787173229e3b9">May TTRL answer normalization see test gold?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Attrl">TTRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · PRIME-RL author team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Equivalence and votes must use permitted output rules; gold is scored afterward. Local loops aren&#x27;t paper-scale real rollouts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not filter by the correct number before claiming an autonomous vote.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16084">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.16084-ttrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-764787173229e3b9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ttrl" data-paper-title="TTRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-de29d2e53a75bceb">How does TTRL differ from majority-vote inference?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Attrl">TTRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · PRIME-RL author team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Voting just aggregates outputs; TTRL updates parameters using pseudo-rewards and affects later behavior. Account for training compute and persistent state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After the same samples, voting returns; TTRL additionally optimizes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16084">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.16084-ttrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-de29d2e53a75bceb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ttrl" data-paper-title="TTRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-ttrl-f1272098" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e13260c6de1f2d65">Where does TTRL get rewards on unlabeled test tasks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Attrl">TTRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · PRIME-RL author team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sample several answers, use majority consensus as a pseudo-label, reward agreement and update online. No gold, but consensus can be wrong; evaluate separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeatedly guessing the same wrong number creates agreement, not truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16084">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.16084-ttrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e13260c6de1f2d65">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:luffy" data-paper-title="LUFFY" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3e37406dcb0a268f">Why track behavior μ in mixed demonstration/rollout batches?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aluffy">LUFFY</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Shared batch doesn&#x27;t make sources on-policy. Importance ratios and regularization address source shift while keeping exploration. Students must still reach uncovered states; do not leak demos into evaluated inputs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Record expert success separately from failed student rollouts, not as a student sample.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14945">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.14945-luffy/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3e37406dcb0a268f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:luffy" data-paper-title="LUFFY" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-8d4452a51f7d0b3b">What roles do μ and ref have in LUFFY?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aluffy">LUFFY</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>μ describes mixture sampling; ref anchors KL. Track online vs demonstration provenance. Local candidates aren&#x27;t paper text/distributed training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Expert data and initial-student reference need not have the same probabilities.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14945">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.14945-luffy/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8d4452a51f7d0b3b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:luffy" data-paper-title="LUFFY" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e45f299abee943ba">How does LUFFY differ from inserting demonstrations into an ordinary GRPO group?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aluffy">LUFFY</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>External demonstrations have another sampling source and need correction/regularization. Treating them as student samples gives wrong denominator. Source-aware updates are more than adding good text.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An inserted expert solution is not a lucky current-policy sample.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14945">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.14945-luffy/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e45f299abee943ba">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:luffy" data-paper-title="LUFFY" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-luffy-8fd3aff1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c299f856a9e50d38">Why combine offline demonstrations and online exploration in LUFFY?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aluffy">LUFFY</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Demonstrations reveal paths students rarely sample; online rollouts preserve current exploration. Handle shared support and source probabilities rather than pure imitation or narrow exploration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Experts show a proof while the student still generates attempts and receives feedback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14945">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.14945-luffy/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c299f856a9e50d38">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:toolrl" data-paper-title="ToolRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-toolrl-7e3d5cc8" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-39b3cc929256b458">Why dynamically scale rewards by tool when their reward difficulties differ?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atoolrl">ToolRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>High raw rewards from easy tools can dominate updates, burying improvements on harder tools. Center and scale by tool distribution to compare relative performance while retaining selection, argument, execution, and answer signals. Normalization does not fix wrong rewards or equalize actual difficulty.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Calculator successes are common and database queries often fail. Normalize separately so easy calculator rewards do not monopolize learning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13958">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.13958-toolrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-39b3cc929256b458">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:toolrl" data-paper-title="ToolRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ecda3bd045c50ef5">Do local reward and state updates prove full multi-tool RL training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atoolrl">ToolRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Local tests cover paper objectives, transitions, and budgets without the original large model, multi-GPU RL, or full real-tool benchmark. Correct reward arithmetic still needs policy sampling, real external execution, and parameter updates. Registration and perfect mini-suites cannot fill those gaps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Computing advantage from four reward dimensions tests an objective, not learned argument generation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13958">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.13958-toolrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ecda3bd045c50ef5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:toolrl" data-paper-title="ToolRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-119474e77ea679ab">Why are tool-selection, execution, and answer rewards not substitutes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atoolrl">ToolRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Selection checks task fit, execution checks whether a call runs, and answer reward checks final goal. Correct tools can fail from bad arguments, and successful calls can return irrelevant data. Separate signals expose different errors; any one high score does not establish end-to-end ability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A database query runs with the wrong month. Selection and execution pass without deserving answer reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13958">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.13958-toolrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-119474e77ea679ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:toolrl" data-paper-title="ToolRL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7dbdad52ce7f9b4a">Why doesn&#x27;t checking only ToolRL&#x27;s final answer establish a good tool policy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atoolrl">ToolRL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The result conflates choosing tools, generating arguments, executing, and using outputs. Granular feedback constrains each behavior. Calibrate rewards without letting format or execution hide wrong answers. Local reward computation is not large-model RL.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A weather tool can be correct but use the wrong city. A single answer score cannot identify argument versus selection failure.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13958">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.13958-toolrl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7dbdad52ce7f9b4a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:retool" data-paper-title="ReTool" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-retool-db452677" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f341f5ec4e371354">Why not learn to avoid tools entirely when calls carry penalties?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aretool">ReTool</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The objective also rewards correct answers. Fewer calls matter only if quality does not suffer. Alternating reasoning and actual feedback teaches when to outsource, recover, and stop. Optimizing call count alone may replace needed computation with fluent guesses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Mental arithmetic can avoid calls, but complex statistics need code. One reliable result can be worth more than saving a call and answering incorrectly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11536">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.11536-retool/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f341f5ec4e371354">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:retool" data-paper-title="ReTool" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-888b668a9e5c1718">Can the model fill in a tool observation to complete a reasoning/action trajectory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aretool">ReTool</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Actual tool or environment execution must supply feedback. The model generates its reasoning and actions only. Fabricated outputs remove learning evidence for calls and corrections. Local controlled state/budget tests do not train the paper model or run real math benchmarks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Writing &#x27;Python output: 42&#x27; without running code is neither tool success nor grounds for execution reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11536">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.11536-retool/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-888b668a9e5c1718">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:retool" data-paper-title="ReTool" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-68920b8b5af8933d">How does outcome reward minus call cost compare with one fixed call per task?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aretool">ReTool</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed counts ignore difficulty and evidence, wasting calls on simple tasks and starving complex ones. Costed rewards adapt counts to value but can suppress needed tools if penalties are excessive. Report correctness and total call costs, not reductions alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Mental arithmetic can use zero calls, while multi-stage calculation may need two checks. One call does not fit both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11536">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.11536-retool/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-68920b8b5af8933d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:retool" data-paper-title="ReTool" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-da7a79464de2183e">Why does ReTool learn calling, correction, and stopping together?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aretool">ReTool</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tools can help but fail and cost resources. A policy must decide when to call, how to respond to errors, and when evidence suffices. Tool syntax alone does not control a full trajectory. Early stopping and repeated unnecessary calls can both hurt.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Run code to check a calculation, fix arguments after an error, then stop once results agree rather than loop or submit unchecked.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11536">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.11536-retool/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-da7a79464de2183e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinrec" data-paper-title="PinRec: Outcome-Conditioned, Multi-Token Generative Retrieval for Industry-Scale Recommendation Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-pinrec-66bf0193" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2ea183949a2f6b44">Why condition PinRec on desired outcomes and predict multiple item vectors for a future window?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinrec">PinRec: Outcome-Conditioned, Multi-Token Generative Retrieval for Industry-Scale Recommendation Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One next-item target overrepresents common behavior and imposes a unique order. Desired outcomes guide heads, and multiple ANN-compatible vectors cover coexisting interests. Align predictions with window positives; do not treat duplicate popular vectors as distinct interests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Set a save goal rather than casual browsing, and cover both gardening and baking from an unordered window.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10507">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2504.10507-pinrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2ea183949a2f6b44">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinrec" data-paper-title="PinRec: Outcome-Conditioned, Multi-Token Generative Retrieval for Industry-Scale Recommendation Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d2ba63933a870c32">Why normalize PinRec ANN outputs per head and deduplicate items?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinrec">PinRec: Outcome-Conditioned, Multi-Token Generative Retrieval for Industry-Scale Recommendation Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each vector must share index geometry and scale. Per-head normalization controls norms, and duplicate retrieved items need defined merging or deduplication. Match window target identities; repeating the same vector does not establish multi-interest learning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Three heads returning one popular camera cover one item; count unique hits and inspect whether heads differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10507">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2504.10507-pinrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d2ba63933a870c32">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinrec" data-paper-title="PinRec: Outcome-Conditioned, Multi-Token Generative Retrieval for Industry-Scale Recommendation Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-9ee1c6eb0e5343e2">Why are PinRec unordered-window retrieval and strict next-token hits different?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinrec">PinRec: Outcome-Conditioned, Multi-Token Generative Retrieval for Industry-Scale Recommendation Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multiple window positives allow alternative orders and coexisting interests. Strict next-item metrics accept only the immediately adjacent target. Align labels and pools for comparison; both local measures were negative and a looser metric should not hide that.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Retrieving a camera and tent fits the day window, but a tent does not count as the next item if the camera came first.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10507">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2504.10507-pinrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9ee1c6eb0e5343e2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:pinrec" data-paper-title="PinRec: Outcome-Conditioned, Multi-Token Generative Retrieval for Industry-Scale Recommendation Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-98e4eb3523117a34">Why is PinRec desired outcome different from the next observed feedback label?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Apinrec">PinRec: Outcome-Conditioned, Multi-Token Generative Retrieval for Industry-Scale Recommendation Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Desired outcome is a valid request condition. Future observed action is training supervision only; selecting conditions from test outcomes leaks information. Multi-vector windows represent several possible interests, not a guaranteed behavioral sequence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Request save-worthy candidates, but do not first check that the held-out item was saved and choose the condition accordingly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10507">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2504.10507-pinrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-98e4eb3523117a34">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:vapo" data-paper-title="VAPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0e539b78de945446">Why repair critic quality and adapt GAE to length instead of dropping the critic?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Avapo">VAPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sparse rewards and varying horizons amplify value error. VAPO pretrains the critic and adapts advantage estimation and actor to length. It doesn&#x27;t remove value learning, and local proxy lengths aren&#x27;t long-CoT evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Short and long solutions receive reward at different delays, so one estimator can have different bias/variance across them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05118">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.05118-vapo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0e539b78de945446">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:vapo" data-paper-title="VAPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0f259ddc6b3c4d6b">Why isn&#x27;t the local VAPO critic a reproduced pretrained value model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Avapo">VAPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Candidate actions and proxy lengths simulate value–length coupling, not real long prefixes. Retain response-dependent GAE λ rather than claiming a fixed λ is equivalent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A table of candidate values isn&#x27;t a neural critic reading thousands of reasoning tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05118">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.05118-vapo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0f259ddc6b3c4d6b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:vapo" data-paper-title="VAPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d806ff9fba95bf37">What does VAPO trade for critic-free GRPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Avapo">VAPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>GRPO uses same-prompt relative rewards without a critic. VAPO trains a critic for prefix values. Their costs and error sources differ; fewer models isn&#x27;t higher capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An all-wrong group has no relative signal while a critic can still estimate, possibly incorrectly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05118">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.05118-vapo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d806ff9fba95bf37">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:vapo" data-paper-title="VAPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-vapo-b94393ac" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8e6b5956ce7b7a3c">Why emphasize a critic for long reasoning in VAPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Avapo">VAPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sparse terminal rewards leave prefixes without direct feedback; a critic supplies a baseline. Bias can grow with length, motivating pretrained value and length adaptation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Estimate later returns before an intermediate reasoning step gets terminal reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05118">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2504.05118-vapo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8e6b5956ce7b7a3c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:smolvlm" data-paper-title="SmolVLM: Redefining small and efficient multimodal models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-smolvlm-5de2167d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-14e67387d09772aa">Where does pixel shuffle put neighborhood information when it reduces visual token count?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asmolvlm">SmolVLM: Redefining small and efficient multimodal models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hugging Face</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It concatenates nearby spatial tokens along channels and projects them through an MLP to the LM. It trades attention length for wider local representations rather than dropping patches. Fine text and spatial relations still require task-specific verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four adjacent patches merge into one wider vector, quartering token count but coarsening the LM&#x27;s spatial granularity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05299">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2504.05299-smolvlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-14e67387d09772aa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:smolvlm" data-paper-title="SmolVLM: Redefining small and efficient multimodal models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-99a7266698fe9edc">Does the local r=2 check include SmolVLM&#x27;s high-resolution and long-video recipe?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asmolvlm">SmolVLM: Redefining small and efficient multimodal models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hugging Face</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It uses 32×32 clothing images and 2×2 space-to-depth without high-resolution tiling, video sampling, long context, learned position tokens, or a SmolLM decoder. Results only check the rearrangement and projection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reducing 16 patches to four verifies tensor shapes, not cross-frame localization or 8,000-token context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05299">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2504.05299-smolvlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-99a7266698fe9edc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:smolvlm" data-paper-title="SmolVLM: Redefining small and efficient multimodal models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-9ffdba7ecafa65b8">What does space-to-depth preserve compared with averaging four patches?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asmolvlm">SmolVLM: Redefining small and efficient multimodal models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hugging Face</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Averaging erases independent patch positions; space-to-depth concatenates them in fixed spatial order so later projection can distinguish them. It trades shorter sequences for wider input tokens. Fine recognition still depends on projector capacity and training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Swapping black upper-left and white lower-right blocks can preserve their average but change their ordered concatenation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05299">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2504.05299-smolvlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9ffdba7ecafa65b8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:smolvlm" data-paper-title="SmolVLM: Redefining small and efficient multimodal models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6da8d28c15e0fd0d">Does SmolVLM just remove language-model layers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asmolvlm">SmolVLM: Redefining small and efficient multimodal models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hugging Face</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It reallocates vision and language compute with visual token compression, tiling, positional tokens, long context, and data mixtures. Parameter count and vision input cost are separate; one rearrangement operator is not the full recipe.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A smaller LM still pays vision encoding and context costs if given many high-resolution visual tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05299">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2504.05299-smolvlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6da8d28c15e0fd0d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:deepresearcher" data-paper-title="DeepResearcher" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-deepresearcher-9b53178e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-aff7e18e331cc491">Why isn&#x27;t citation count enough when adding citation rewards to answer rewards?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adeepresearcher">DeepResearcher</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · HKU</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Citations connect claims to real evidence, while counts can reward repeated or irrelevant links. Search, browsing, and answering form one trajectory. Joint objectives should enforce support and correctness while penalizing wasted queries. Check claim–source links; one browse call does not establish evidence use.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Ten irrelevant links should not beat two sources that directly support the conclusion, or the policy will learn link stuffing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03160">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.03160-deepresearcher/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aff7e18e331cc491">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:deepresearcher" data-paper-title="DeepResearcher" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-fc41b0278af88bb1">How should DeepResearcher align citation rewards with actual retrieved evidence?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adeepresearcher">DeepResearcher</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · HKU</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Citations must point to genuinely available material supporting corresponding statements, not just count as links. N_query counts actual search calls. The mini-suite has no real web or full LLM RL, so fixture citations are not external evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A title never retrieved and irrelevant to the claim should not receive credit for looking like a citation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03160">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.03160-deepresearcher/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fc41b0278af88bb1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:deepresearcher" data-paper-title="DeepResearcher" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4a779c50af1afc7e">Why aren&#x27;t citation quality rewards and query-count penalties the same efficiency objective?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adeepresearcher">DeepResearcher</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · HKU</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Citation reward measures evidential support; query penalty controls cost. Fewer searches do not ensure reliable evidence, and more citations do not ensure useful searches. The three weights govern trade-offs; short traces alone do not establish research quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Answering quickly after one bad query is cheap but unsupported.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03160">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.03160-deepresearcher/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4a779c50af1afc7e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:deepresearcher" data-paper-title="DeepResearcher" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-88cf40121cb186e1">Why does DeepResearcher treat search, browsing, evidence, and answers as one trajectory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Adeepresearcher">DeepResearcher</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · HKU</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Answers depend on how evidence is found and used, and final text alone obscures credit. Answer and citation rewards plus query cost balance quality and expense over the full search.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One useful browse can make the answer verifiable, beyond making its final sentence fluent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03160">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2504.03160-deepresearcher/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-88cf40121cb186e1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dr-grpo" data-paper-title="Dr. GRPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-72916d57d18ee4c3">Why remove both group SD and within-response averaging?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adr-grpo">Dr. GRPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · SAIL 研究团队</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>SD reweights difficulty groups by their local variation; token averaging changes long-versus-short contribution. Keep centered rewards and fixed aggregation, not remove all normalization or promise universal gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A tiny group SD can amplify a comparable reward gap; response length adds another weight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20783">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2503.20783-dr-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-72916d57d18ee4c3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dr-grpo" data-paper-title="Dr. GRPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5ba362a618993555">Can proxy lengths establish removal of long-CoT length bias?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adr-grpo">Dr. GRPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · SAIL 研究团队</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A candidate policy has no generated length distribution. Proxy lengths expose normalization differences, not real token losses or long responses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Changing a simulated length doesn&#x27;t produce early stopping behavior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20783">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2503.20783-dr-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5ba362a618993555">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dr-grpo" data-paper-title="Dr. GRPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b75da045562bf37a">Does Dr. GRPO still center group rewards like GRPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adr-grpo">Dr. GRPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · SAIL 研究团队</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Yes. Subtract same-prompt mean, but omit the specified length and SD normalization. Dropping SD does not remove the baseline, and adding a global SD would change the target.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Judge each reply relative to group mean without dividing by group variation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20783">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2503.20783-dr-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b75da045562bf37a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dr-grpo" data-paper-title="Dr. GRPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-dr-grpo-c17c40d0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-aad7fc2a0748abfc">Why audit both response-length averaging and group standard deviation in Dr. GRPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adr-grpo">Dr. GRPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · SAIL 研究团队</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>They change weights by length and problem difficulty, not just numerical stability. Remove both while retaining group mean centering so reward differences preserve their scale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal reward gaps get different magnitudes after normalization when group variances differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20783">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2503.20783-dr-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aad7fc2a0748abfc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dapo" data-paper-title="DAPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ebd8d3555febbac3">Why drop all-correct groups in Dynamic Sampling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adapo">DAPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Centering equal all-correct/all-wrong rewards yields no relative direction, not worthless replies. Resample differentiable groups; Clip-Higher, token aggregation and length shaping handle other effects. Never select questions on test.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A mixed-success group provides group-relative learning absent from an equal-reward group.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14476">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2503.14476-dapo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ebd8d3555febbac3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dapo" data-paper-title="DAPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f25cd80adbf410cf">How does DAPO token-level normalization differ from per-response averages?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adapo">DAPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sum over valid response tokens, then normalize together. Per-response means weight lengths differently. Also preserve dynamic filtering and overlength penalty. Proxy lengths don&#x27;t reproduce real masks or 32B training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Averaging a short and long reply separately is not averaging every token together.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14476">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2503.14476-dapo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f25cd80adbf410cf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dapo" data-paper-title="DAPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e1eb83514170cabf">Which side does DAPO Clip-Higher relax?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adapo">DAPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raise the upper bound to retain room for beneficial probability increases; lower bound remains separate. Dynamic sampling, token loss and overlength shaping are also defining pieces.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Easier increase of a useful action needn&#x27;t loosen downward changes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14476">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2503.14476-dapo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e1eb83514170cabf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dapo" data-paper-title="DAPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-dapo-b7495c1f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-22a113575bc73943">Why dynamically skip all-correct and all-wrong DAPO groups?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adapo">DAPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance Seed</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Binary rewards without variance give no relative advantage and waste batch slots. Sample groups with distinctions; this doesn&#x27;t solve exploration on every difficult problem.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four failures give no ordering, so resample rather than repeatedly train on zeros.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14476">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2503.14476-dapo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-22a113575bc73943">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:search-r1" data-paper-title="Search-R1" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-search-r1-fce4d489" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c61b1b171492b766">Why mask retrieved tokens even though they occur in the input sequence?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asearch-r1">Search-R1</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Search returns are environment output, not sampled policy actions. Policy loss there would teach the model to generate external evidence. Only its queries, reasoning, and answers are policy tokens; retrieval conditions later decisions. Iterative adaptation is not equivalent to a single static RAG retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A search result that says &#x27;published Tuesday&#x27; is not agent behavior. Train how to query and answer from evidence, not how to generate that environment text.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09516">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2503.09516-search-r1/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c61b1b171492b766">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:search-r1" data-paper-title="Search-R1" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7ba876b05ccaf382">How does Search-R1&#x27;s loss mask avoid masking the query action?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asearch-r1">Search-R1</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate model-generated reasoning and search instructions from environment information. The former remain policy tokens and the latter get mask zero. Use provenance boundaries, not a text match for &#x27;search.&#x27;</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The query inside `&lt;search&gt;` is an action; the following `&lt;information&gt;` text is an observation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09516">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2503.09516-search-r1/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7ba876b05ccaf382">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:search-r1" data-paper-title="Search-R1" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-38e311ec6e4bf35a">How does visible search context differ from training on retrieved text as policy-generated tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asearch-r1">Search-R1</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Documents can condition later actions, but their tokens come from the environment, not the policy. Mask their loss. Treating them as student outputs corrupts action probabilities for policy optimization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A thousand-character webpage does not count as a thousand-character agent action with policy gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09516">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2503.09516-search-r1/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-38e311ec6e4bf35a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:search-r1" data-paper-title="Search-R1" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/agent-policy-learning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/agent-policy-learning/">Agents / Interactive policy learning: converting trajectory feedback into updates</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-79676ef5125d404d">Why does Search-R1 repeatedly decide whether to search rather than using one-shot RAG?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asearch-r1">Search-R1</a></p>
