<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Attention directly retrieves positions, while the SSM compresses history into state. The same layer can use both without forcing either to carry every dependency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Explicit access can recover a name while recurrence carries grammar context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:twin-v2" data-paper-title="TWIN V2: Scaling Ultra-Long User Behavior Sequence Modeling for Enhanced CTR Prediction at Kuaishou" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-646dc7ef8fc54339">Why build sized virtual items before candidate-related retrieval?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atwin-v2">TWIN V2: Scaling Ultra-Long User Behavior Sequence Modeling for Enhanced CTR Prediction at Kuaishou</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Offline clustering compresses repeated events. GSU retrieves relevant clusters and ESU performs size-aware interactions without naively duplicating large groups. Rare details may disappear.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Represent years of similar shoe browsing with a count rather than recomputing attention on thousands of events.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:twin-v2" data-paper-title="TWIN V2: Scaling Ultra-Long User Behavior Sequence Modeling for Enhanced CTR Prediction at Kuaishou" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d3fdc1036f68dd31">Does public full-catalog ranking verify million-event serving?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atwin-v2">TWIN V2: Scaling Ultra-Long User Behavior Sequence Modeling for Enhanced CTR Prediction at Kuaishou</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It tests candidate search and hierarchical compression without private lifelong logs or serving. Align memberships, sizes, and time masks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Small MovieLens retrieval is not production latency evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:twin-v2" data-paper-title="TWIN V2: Scaling Ultra-Long User Behavior Sequence Modeling for Enhanced CTR Prediction at Kuaishou" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-041577c428d8fcae">How does cluster retrieval differ from SIM raw-behavior search?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atwin-v2">TWIN V2: Scaling Ultra-Long User Behavior Sequence Modeling for Enhanced CTR Prediction at Kuaishou</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Cluster search filters prototypes before finer interaction; raw retrieval selects original behaviors. Compression changes coverage, accuracy, and cost, with possible rare-detail loss.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A large cluster may hide a niche event that raw search can still find.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16357">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2407.16357-twin-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-041577c428d8fcae">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:twin-v2" data-paper-title="TWIN V2: Scaling Ultra-Long User Behavior Sequence Modeling for Enhanced CTR Prediction at Kuaishou" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-twin-v2-72f26bc8" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-9b5a1473f6d5e8e0">Why compress lifelong history into sized virtual items?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atwin-v2">TWIN V2: Scaling Ultra-Long User Behavior Sequence Modeling for Enhanced CTR Prediction at Kuaishou</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Per-event matching over millions is expensive. Offline hierarchy summarizes groups and tracks size, then online retrieval and ranking read relevant clusters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Many repeated events should differ from one isolated event.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:openhands" data-paper-title="OpenHands" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-openhands-e21fcd2c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7201d318abb3e27c">Why does a unified event stream make editor, terminal, and browser workflows auditable?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aopenhands">OpenHands</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · All-Hands-AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Actions and sandbox returns enter one timeline. Policies continue from observed results and reviewers can trace changes and validation. Shared events do not erase tool-specific semantics or establish code safety and correctness. Isolation, permissions, and tests have distinct roles.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Editor events change a file, terminal events run tests, and browser events check a page. The stream shows whether tests preceded or followed edits.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16741">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2407.16741-openhands/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7201d318abb3e27c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:openhands" data-paper-title="OpenHands" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-56484f867d35a859">Does a local browser interface mean real web interaction is connected?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aopenhands">OpenHands</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · All-Hands-AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Local work emits editor events and runs fixed regressions in an isolated temp directory. Browser action semantics are retained without a live environment or full controller. Claim only observed events and outcomes, not real navigation from a type definition.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Recording browser_open does not open a page, fetch its DOM, or click an element. Those require real browser evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16741">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2407.16741-openhands/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-56484f867d35a859">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:openhands" data-paper-title="OpenHands" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-9579dd55c1112b36">Why are platform runtime and agent controller distinct contributions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aopenhands">OpenHands</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · All-Hands-AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The runtime supplies actions, observations, and isolation. A controller chooses plans and tool usage; different policies can share one platform. Running editor and terminal verifies execution paths, not full model reasoning or official SWE-bench resolution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A script and LLM may use the same sandbox without equal issue understanding or repair ability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16741">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2407.16741-openhands/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9579dd55c1112b36">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:openhands" data-paper-title="OpenHands" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-718d5bd7d13021cc">Why is OpenHands a software-agent work platform for editing, execution, and browsing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aopenhands">OpenHands</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · All-Hands-AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Real software tasks require inspecting files, commands, pages, and continuing long workflows, not only generating code. OpenHands connects operations to feedback in a consistent environment. Platform support and a controller&#x27;s ability are separate evidence; tools alone do not make policies reliable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: After editing a frontend, start the service, inspect the page, and return to code when it fails. Code generation alone misses that loop.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16741">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2407.16741-openhands/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-718d5bd7d13021cc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cdm" data-paper-title="Contextual Distillation Model for Diversified Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-cdm-24f0cce6" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1ab2a07320495384">Why must CDM&#x27;s student see same-request candidates when distilling an MMR teacher?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acdm">Contextual Distillation Model for Diversified Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MMR selection depends on other candidates and redundancy, so isolated item features cannot recover it. CDM learns selection propensity relative to context and combines it with the original recommendation score, transferring costly iterative redundancy reduction to a serving-time scorer. Student approximation need not reproduce the list exactly, and a small local run does not establish production diversity gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A travel clip may be redundant among ten similar clips but distinctive in a cooking list.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09021">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2406.09021-cdm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1ab2a07320495384">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cdm" data-paper-title="Contextual Distillation Model for Diversified Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-491caed66cdd9445">Why update similarity penalties after selecting each item in the CDM teacher?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acdm">Contextual Distillation Model for Diversified Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MMR penalizes maximum similarity to the current selected prefix. Every addition changes remaining marginal scores; one fixed ranking is not the same contextual decision. Student targets must correspond to the relevant prefix rather than conflating stages in a static item label.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After selecting a camping tutorial, reduce the score of its near-duplicate. An empty-prefix score could put both next to each other.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09021">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2406.09021-cdm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-491caed66cdd9445">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cdm" data-paper-title="Contextual Distillation Model for Diversified Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8bc42bf8da4f58b1">What does CDM distillation save compared with online MMR, and what error can it introduce?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acdm">Contextual Distillation Model for Diversified Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MMR recomputes redundancy against the selected set at each step. The student approximates those decisions quickly, reducing iterative serving cost. It can drift on new candidate distributions or longer lists, so test precision and diversity as well as latency. Proxy gains do not prove exact imitation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One student score can replace repeated comparisons, but the student may underestimate redundancy in a near-duplicate set absent from training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09021">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2406.09021-cdm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8bc42bf8da4f58b1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cdm" data-paper-title="Contextual Distillation Model for Diversified Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/slates-business-value">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/slates-business-value/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Slates and business control: reranking, bidding, and long-term value</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-93a791dccea8c9a7">Why does CDM view diversity as marginal value given the selected prefix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acdm">Contextual Distillation Model for Diversified Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Value depends on what the list already contains: the first science-fiction item can add variety while the fourth similar one is redundant. MMR combines relevance with redundancy penalties; CDM learns the contextual gain for low-latency serving. Diversity is not a permanent per-item bonus.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A third movie by a director may add little if two are already selected, yet be valuable when no work by that director appears.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09021">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2406.09021-cdm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-93a791dccea8c9a7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cwm" data-paper-title="Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-cwm-65e93cb4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-08cd76fbd0f6979a">Why might counterfactual watch-time scoring better capture preferences than raw watched seconds?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acwm">Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology / Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raw seconds combine attraction with the viewing opportunity allowed by duration. CWM estimates potential watch benefit under a common duration intervention. This depends on counterfactual assumptions, is not just dividing by duration, and local proxies do not establish that actual duration or exposure confounding was removed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Completing a 20-second clip and abandoning a long clip after 30 seconds may imply a different preference under equal viewing opportunity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07932">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2406.07932-cwm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-08cd76fbd0f6979a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cwm" data-paper-title="Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1a473e83d1d8b5a0">How should training and prediction duration differ for CWM&#x27;s `do(D=d0)`?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acwm">Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology / Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fit the duration mechanism using observed D; for prediction comparisons fix d0 and output the defined potential quantity and bias term. Using each item&#x27;s original duration is not a common intervention. Local movie proxies do not measure real short-video potential watch benefit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Set the same d0 for a 30-second clip and a five-minute clip; setting 30 and 300 reintroduces the original difference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07932">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2406.07932-cwm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1a473e83d1d8b5a0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cwm" data-paper-title="Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5537f98a3b8a194f">How do CWM and completion-rate ranking differ in their assumptions about duration?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acwm">Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology / Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Completion rate is an observed ratio and can favor short content; it has no explicit counterfactual. CWM estimates a potential outcome under common duration to separate preferences and duration effects. Bias differs, and misspecification can prevent the causal objective from helping.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A three-second ad is easy to complete, unlike a long tutorial. CWM instead asks which would offer more value at equal duration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07932">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2406.07932-cwm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5537f98a3b8a194f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cwm" data-paper-title="Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-26b7e8adddd68f37">How does CWM&#x27;s potential watch benefit under common duration differ from observed watched seconds?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acwm">Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology / Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Observed seconds mix preference, duration constraints, and content-type relationships. A common duration intervention compares potential outcomes at equal opportunity, reducing inherent long-video advantage. It is unobserved and requires modeling and identification assumptions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Completing a 15-second clip versus watching two minutes of a longer clip cannot determine preference from seconds alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07932">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2406.07932-cwm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-26b7e8adddd68f37">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:simpo" data-paper-title="SimPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-864ca18fd75dda04">Without a reference, how does SimPO avoid favoring short responses by sequence probability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asimpo">SimPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Total log probability accumulates per token and changes reward scale with length. Average per token and require the preferred response to beat the rejected one by a margin, without an extra reference forward. This removes one length effect, not all quality bias.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A short wrong answer can beat a longer correct one on summed log probability; averaging removes the direct sum-length penalty.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14734">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2405.14734-simpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-864ca18fd75dda04">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:simpo" data-paper-title="SimPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cb729e6cab9ed41b">Which tokens enter SimPO&#x27;s log-probability sum and length?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asimpo">SimPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use the same valid-response mask for both; no padding or prompt tokens. The loss updates only the policy. A token objective does not reproduce the paper&#x27;s judge/model matrix.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Counting padding in the denominator distorts the short answer&#x27;s average reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14734">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2405.14734-simpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cb729e6cab9ed41b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:simpo" data-paper-title="SimPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-85c5fbdd0f8ee884">Is SimPO&#x27;s training margin equivalent to reducing inference temperature?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asimpo">SimPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Margin sets desired average-reward separation and changes parameter gradients. Temperature rescales next-token logits at inference. They can coexist but shorter output at one temperature does not validate the margin.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Training compares complete response average log probabilities; inference temperature doesn&#x27;t read that preference pair.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14734">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2405.14734-simpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-85c5fbdd0f8ee884">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:simpo" data-paper-title="SimPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-simpo-d55ff0e4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-19268f541c6ed5d9">Does reference-free SimPO mean there is no training feedback?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Asimpo">SimPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Chosen/rejected pairs still supply preferences. It removes a resident reference model, using length-averaged policy log-probability as implicit reward with a fixed margin.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>You still need a better answer label; no frozen reference scores need be computed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14734">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2405.14734-simpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-19268f541c6ed5d9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:learn" data-paper-title="Knowledge Adaptation from Large Language Model to Recommendation for Practical Industrial Application" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-learn-c99c03ce" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2eed10f4831732c0">Why does LEARN freeze LLM content encoding but train a causal PCH to learn preferences?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alearn">Knowledge Adaptation from Large Language Model to Recommendation for Practical Industrial Application</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A frozen content encoder retains open-world semantics at lower update cost, but semantic closeness is not co-consumption. PCH learns order and next-item prediction from historical content vectors, then projects them into recommendation space. Respect history cutoffs; freezing the LLM does not mean nothing is trained or that semantic similarity proves transfer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Two films mention adventure, but the user&#x27;s viewing sequence can reveal a more specific storytelling preference that frozen text semantics alone do not express.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03988">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2405.03988-learn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2eed10f4831732c0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:learn" data-paper-title="Knowledge Adaptation from Large Language Model to Recommendation for Practical Industrial Application" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3fecff7cba4aa75c">Is a frozen content cache enough to prevent future leakage in PCH next-item prediction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alearn">Knowledge Adaptation from Large Language Model to Recommendation for Practical Industrial Application</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Enforce a causal mask and cutoff in PCH: the next item belongs only on the target side and must not enter pooling. Align encoder and projection versions. Frozen parameters prevent gradient updates, not input leakage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Putting the test movie&#x27;s frozen vector into history before predicting it still leaks the answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03988">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2405.03988-learn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3fecff7cba4aa75c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:learn" data-paper-title="Knowledge Adaptation from Large Language Model to Recommendation for Practical Industrial Application" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d5d6d58a64e951ab">Why isn&#x27;t LEARN&#x27;s large gain over frozen semantic mean necessarily a cold-start gain?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alearn">Knowledge Adaptation from Large Language Model to Recommendation for Practical Industrial Application</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The mean lacks trainable preference modeling, so PCH can improve ranking by learning sequences. The source also shows strong head concentration, so gains may come from popularity rather than new-item understanding. Cold-start subgroups and matched controls are needed; overall NDCG does not prove gains for all groups.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Recommending popular movies can substantially beat a semantic average without helping a new film reach its audience.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03988">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2405.03988-learn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d5d6d58a64e951ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:learn" data-paper-title="Knowledge Adaptation from Large Language Model to Recommendation for Practical Industrial Application" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e3fa0af7e5835487">Why freeze the content LLM while letting LEARN&#x27;s PCH learn?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alearn">Knowledge Adaptation from Large Language Model to Recommendation for Practical Industrial Application</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The LLM provides stable content semantics; recommendation objectives still need to adapt behavioral relationships. PCH reads the content sequence, models causal preference dependencies, and projects into serving space. Freezing saves cost but limits content adjustment. Pretrained semantics are not collaborative preferences and need not improve all cold-start cases.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Films of the same genre may have different audiences. PCH can learn the difference from viewing order, whereas averaging frozen vectors does not train preference structure.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03988">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2405.03988-learn/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e3fa0af7e5835487">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:swe-agent" data-paper-title="SWE-agent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-swe-agent-79904a33" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-dafefde79785114c">Why can a specialized ACI work better than an unrestricted shell?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aswe-agent">SWE-agent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Broad actions and verbose output increase selection and localization load. An ACI makes search, viewing, precise edits, and tests easier to act on and interpret. This improves the repository interaction contract, not hidden patch access. Real tests still verify completion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Showing nearby lines and an exact replacement makes editing easier than printing a whole file, but regression tests must validate the patch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2405.15793-swe-agent/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dafefde79785114c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:swe-agent" data-paper-title="SWE-agent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-52983128b5e50c57">What do the initial failure and fixed unittest prove in local swebench-local?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aswe-agent">SWE-agent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A real initial failure shows a problem exists. The exit code after editing verifies the covered regression. Local tools only read files, write solution.py, and run fixed tests. This is executable micro-benchmark evidence, not official SWE-bench Lite or broader coverage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Fixing arithmetic until one suite passes verifies the edit-and-run path, not official GitHub issue resolved rate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2405.15793-swe-agent/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-52983128b5e50c57">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:swe-agent" data-paper-title="SWE-agent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-99e902304d6ed5e3">Why compare ACI with raw shell using the same model and tasks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aswe-agent">SWE-agent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Otherwise stronger models or easier tasks confound interface effects. ACI changes action and observation boundaries, so control other conditions and assess actual patches and tests. One good edit or valid command syntax cannot establish broad repair ability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Give the same model the same bug with a narrow editor versus a raw shell to isolate differences in localization and editing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2405.15793-swe-agent/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-99e902304d6ed5e3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:swe-agent" data-paper-title="SWE-agent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-260212a2f996528e">Why does a GitHub issue agent need a convenient repository viewing and editing interface?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aswe-agent">SWE-agent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The model must locate unknown code, read needed context, make small edits, and verify. Raw terminal output can be long or fragile. SWE-agent&#x27;s interface better fits that workflow without replacing issue understanding or tests. A successful command does not mean resolution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Open matching files and relevant lines rather than printing the repository, then run the target tests after edits.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2405.15793-swe-agent/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-260212a2f996528e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bahe" data-paper-title="Breaking the Length Barrier: LLM-Enhanced CTR Prediction in Long Textual User Behaviors" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-bahe-7645b8ec" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0e6d87b8ce07426e">Why does BAHE still train higher-layer aggregation when shallow encodings of atomic behavior are cached?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abahe">Breaking the Length Barrier: LLM-Enhanced CTR Prediction in Long Textual User Behaviors</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Ant Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Shallow layers encode reusable text semantics for individual actions; higher layers need the current history and candidate and cannot be frozen into a universal answer. This moves repeated text computation off training and request paths while retaining interactions. Stale or excessively compressed cache entries can harm quality despite better efficiency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Cache a movie title once, but aggregate it differently when watched alongside science fiction or family movies and when scoring different candidates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19347">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.19347-bahe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0e6d87b8ce07426e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bahe" data-paper-title="Breaking the Length Barrier: LLM-Enhanced CTR Prediction in Long Textual User Behaviors" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c1dad8a6e15629cc">How does the local two-layer BERT-tiny BAHE split caching and training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abahe">Breaking the Length Barrier: LLM-Enhanced CTR Prediction in Long Textual User Behaviors</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Ant Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The first layer generates and caches atomic MovieLens title vectors. The copied upper layer processes CLS, 12 history entries, and the candidate. The control runs frozen lower and trainable upper layers per sample with matched data and budget. Bind the cache to the shallow version; a two-layer timing ratio does not predict production-scale gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the upper layer expects a different shallow encoder version from the cache producer, vector semantics can mismatch. Record the vector and upper-layer versions together.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19347">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.19347-bahe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c1dad8a6e15629cc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bahe" data-paper-title="Breaking the Length Barrier: LLM-Enhanced CTR Prediction in Long Textual User Behaviors" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-cdffe7e92c04133d">Where does BAHE save computation compared with rerunning the full text model per sample, and what can it lose?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abahe">Breaking the Length Barrier: LLM-Enhanced CTR Prediction in Long Textual User Behaviors</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Ant Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Repeated shallow encoding is avoided, and upper layers process actions rather than every word token. Compression removes detail and changes capacity, so measure time and quality together. Local time fell but AUC also fell, supporting the efficiency mechanism rather than a quality-preserving substitution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Ten titles may contain over a hundred words; ten cached behavior vectors are quicker to process, but losing a critical phrase can damage ranking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19347">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.19347-bahe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cdffe7e92c04133d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bahe" data-paper-title="Breaking the Length Barrier: LLM-Enhanced CTR Prediction in Long Textual User Behaviors" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-3738cc4f91a5ce4c">Why is BAHE&#x27;s atomic behavior cache different from caching the final user representation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abahe">Breaking the Length Barrier: LLM-Enhanced CTR Prediction in Long Textual User Behaviors</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Ant Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An atomic cache holds shallow single-item content encodings reusable across histories. The final user representation also depends on order, the current candidate, and higher-layer interactions. Asynchronous shallow updates remove repeated text work; the upper layer still learns personalized combinations. Finer caching increases reuse but requires version consistency and care over compression losses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two users can read the same cached title vector in different history orders without sharing final interest scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19347">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.19347-bahe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3738cc4f91a5ce4c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:data-mixing-laws" data-paper-title="Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-data-mixing-laws-e8c71fa2" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8a72a4e046d49e6c">How do Data Mixing Laws search untrained mixtures, and what limits them?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adata-mixing-laws">Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge / Shanghai AI Laboratory</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Small matched runs observe domain losses, a fitted relation predicts mixture/scale performance, and a weighted objective searches it. This avoids exhaustive large runs but depends on pilot coverage and assumptions. Keep final test isolated.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Use pilots at 20%, 50%, and 80% code to select a few intermediate candidates; predictions are not measured large-model results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16952">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.16952-data-mixing-laws/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8a72a4e046d49e6c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:data-mixing-laws" data-paper-title="Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5c41aafffdf87cb9">How keep test outcomes out of mixture selection?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adata-mixing-laws">Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge / Shanghai AI Laboratory</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fit and choose domain weights/candidates under prespecified train/validation rules. Test once at the end. Mixtures are nonnegative and sum to one. A unigram proxy is not RedPajama scaling.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not retune w_i after seeing test domain losses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16952">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.16952-data-mixing-laws/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5c41aafffdf87cb9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:data-mixing-laws" data-paper-title="Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b7de02f902644429">How does fitted mixture search differ from measuring every mix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adata-mixing-laws">Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge / Shanghai AI Laboratory</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fitted predictions save compute but can have approximation and extrapolation error. Direct runs give measured outcomes at higher cost. Independently validate a predicted optimum.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A predicted best 70/30 mix has not necessarily trained at target scale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16952">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.16952-data-mixing-laws/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b7de02f902644429">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:data-mixing-laws" data-paper-title="Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-345a9b000888cf40">Why train small pilots across mixtures?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adata-mixing-laws">Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge / Shanghai AI Laboratory</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pilots observe each domain and support fitting mixture and scale effects. This reduces exhaustive runs but depends on coverage and modeling assumptions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Ten pilot mixes can shortlist others, not turn untrained points into measurements.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16952">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.16952-data-mixing-laws/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-345a9b000888cf40">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:lsvcr" data-paper-title="A Large Language Model Enhanced Sequential Recommender for Joint Video and Comment Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-lsvcr-e1dd0222" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-189ea1f5c254e5d0">Why give LSVCR personalized LLM preferences during training if no generative LLM runs at serving time?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alsvcr">A Large Language Model Enhanced Sequential Recommender for Joint Video and Comment Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Video and comment semantics differ and may exceed what ID sequences capture. Cross-fusion and alignment transfer teacher knowledge into a deployable dual-sequence model. Tasks can interfere: local video and comment metrics move in different directions, so neither alone establishes overall success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A teacher can explain sarcasm in a comment during training; the serving student must judge from available sequences without secretly consulting it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13574">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.13574-lsvcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-189ea1f5c254e5d0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:lsvcr" data-paper-title="A Large Language Model Enhanced Sequential Recommender for Joint Video and Comment Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ccd0b0d9cfb4fb94">Why sample an ordered subset for LSVCR position encoding instead of shuffling positions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alsvcr">A Large Language Model Enhanced Sequential Recommender for Joint Video and Comment Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A short alignment sequence should cover the span of the full position table without changing chronology. An ordered subset samples uneven gaps; shuffling changes temporal relations. Cross-sequence fusion must also exclude target video and comment events not yet observed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Assign positions 3, 20, and 80 from a 1–100 table. Assigning 80, 3, and 20 instead changes which event appears newest.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13574">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.13574-lsvcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ccd0b0d9cfb4fb94">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:lsvcr" data-paper-title="A Large Language Model Enhanced Sequential Recommender for Joint Video and Comment Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-678f95df550c57b9">What relationships do LSVCR&#x27;s SSC and VCC constrain?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alsvcr">A Large Language Model Enhanced Sequential Recommender for Joint Video and Comment Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>SSC aligns the sequential recommender&#x27;s user preferences with the LLM; VCC links video or item preferences with comment preferences. They operate across models and across objects, respectively, and can conflict. The local comment metric improved while the item metric declined; report both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Learning the teacher&#x27;s photography preference is different from deciding whether a user likes photography products and photography comments equally.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13574">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.13574-lsvcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-678f95df550c57b9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:lsvcr" data-paper-title="A Large Language Model Enhanced Sequential Recommender for Joint Video and Comment Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-dbc93eb9f52f98ed">Why encode video and comment consumption separately in LSVCR instead of treating comments as video metadata?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Alsvcr">A Large Language Model Enhanced Sequential Recommender for Joint Video and Comment Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Comments have their own reading behavior and semantics. Dual sequences preserve the distinction before cross-fusion, and the training-time LLM adds personalized knowledge. Co-consumption can correlate or conflict, so better comment ranking does not prove better video ranking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Someone may dislike a video but enjoy its discussion. Adding comment text only to a video description can lose this independent preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13574">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.13574-lsvcr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dbc93eb9f52f98ed">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orpo" data-paper-title="ORPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-713377bce48ffbf5">What do SFT and the odds-ratio term each constrain in ORPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorpo">ORPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · KAIST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>SFT raises chosen likelihood; the odds term widens separation from rejection. Both update one policy without reference in the objective. Odds are boundary-sensitive. Reporting reference KL as a diagnostic does not add it to training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Raising only chosen likelihood can also raise similar bad answers; odds explicitly separate them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2403.07691-orpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-713377bce48ffbf5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orpo" data-paper-title="ORPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-533c71e635c7676c">Why handle probabilities near zero or one in ORPO&#x27;s log-odds margin?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorpo">ORPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · KAIST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Log odds are log(p)−log(1−p), then contrasted across replies. Boundaries cause log zero or huge ratios. The local kernel adds 1e−12 to both terms and uses logaddexp, not probability subtraction. Candidate probabilities are not token-level response probabilities.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>0.9→0.99 is +0.09 probability but odds go 9→99.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
