<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2403.07691-orpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-533c71e635c7676c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orpo" data-paper-title="ORPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8b37223053c895c4">How does ORPO&#x27;s single stage differ from SFT followed by separate preference optimization?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorpo">ORPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · KAIST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One policy update combines chosen NLL and preference odds without a resident frozen reference for another stage. Two-stage training first produces an SFT policy then changes objective/reference. One stage is not universally better.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One preference batch supplies NLL and odds gradients instead of finishing chosen-only SFT first.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2403.07691-orpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8b37223053c895c4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orpo" data-paper-title="ORPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-orpo-e4a32db7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-898ddc81df5c3d9b">What is the difference between ORPO odds and probability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorpo">ORPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · KAIST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Probability p is an event&#x27;s share of all outcomes. Odds p/(1−p) compare occurrence to nonoccurrence and can exceed one. ORPO compares preferred and rejected odds, not percentages.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>p=1/2 gives odds 1; p=3/4 gives odds 3, not 300% probability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2403.07691-orpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-898ddc81df5c3d9b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:notellm" data-paper-title="NoteLLM: A Retrievable Large Language Model for Note Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-notellm-9364e133" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fb498d5617532d9c">Why train NoteLLM&#x27;s compression state on co-read contrastive learning and content generation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anotellm">NoteLLM: A Retrievable Large Language Model for Note Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Co-read pairs capture collaborative relations but contrastive similarity alone can lose fine semantics. Generating tags and categories from the same bottleneck forces it to preserve recoverable content. The two objectives shape a retrieval vector that does not merely memorize co-occurrence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Tent and cookware notes can be close for campers yet retain enough detail to generate distinct tags.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01744">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.01744-notellm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fb498d5617532d9c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:notellm" data-paper-title="NoteLLM: A Retrievable Large Language Model for Note Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-818da7eef23dbbae">How verify NoteLLM&#x27;s contrastive vector and CSFT initial state use the same compression position?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anotellm">NoteLLM: A Retrievable Large Language Model for Note Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Read the same special-token hidden state for both, not a last position for one and mean for the other. Align batch pairs and causal generation masks and exclude padding. Frozen versus joint training tests representations, not a full DIN ranking comparison.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Title-mean contrastive features and an independent CLS for generation can both train without constraining the same bottleneck.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01744">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.01744-notellm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-818da7eef23dbbae">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:notellm" data-paper-title="NoteLLM: A Retrievable Large Language Model for Note Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-2fe13bdf9a3534e6">What relation does GCL co-reading add beyond text-similarity positives?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anotellm">NoteLLM: A Retrievable Large Language Model for Note Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Text similarity is content-driven; co-reading links consumption across superficially different notes but can reflect exposure and popularity. CSFT constrains content retention. Complementarity is not absence of bias, and simplified labels do not reproduce real hashtag generation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Tent reviews and camp recipes may be co-read despite different text, whereas two near-identical tent reviews are textual matches.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01744">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.01744-notellm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2fe13bdf9a3534e6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:notellm" data-paper-title="NoteLLM: A Retrievable Large Language Model for Note Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-2cf64a8c96cdbab5">Why is NoteLLM&#x27;s compression token both a retrieval and generation interface?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Anotellm">NoteLLM: A Retrievable Large Language Model for Note Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Contrastive retrieval and label generation use the same compressed state, requiring collaborative and semantic evidence. If generation bypasses it to read raw text, the constraint changes. Compression does not preserve every note detail.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A token must bring co-read notes together and still generate &#x27;camping gear,&#x27; not just encode shared popularity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01744">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2403.01744-notellm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2cf64a8c96cdbab5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hstu" data-paper-title="Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-hstu-2703dd1e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d1b7f594100aaa20">Why remove softmax but normalize after aggregation and apply a U gate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahstu">Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Softmax fixes weight mass and can suppress behavior-frequency intensity. Pointwise SiLU aggregation preserves variation; post-normalization stabilizes and the token-conditioned U gate modulates output. Causal window interactions are not linear complexity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One versus ten related events can differ before the gate controls how much information passes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2402.17152-hstu/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d1b7f594100aaa20">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hstu" data-paper-title="Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a6dfb7484be36691">What does M-FALCON share, and why not cache every ranking score?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahstu">Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Section 3.4/Appendix H isolate candidate microbatches and share per-layer candidate-independent history KV. Each candidate still projects and interacts separately. Versions and history constrain reuse; local HSTU omits this serving optimization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A thousand items can share history while cameras and shoes retain different scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2402.17152-hstu/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a6dfb7484be36691">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hstu" data-paper-title="Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e74368e779e676f8">How does all-position HSTU training preserve causality?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahstu">Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each valid state reads its prefix and predicts the next item; mask padding and invalid targets. One encoding supplies multiple losses. Candidate action interleaving is a separate contract.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A predicts B and A/B predicts C without A seeing B or C.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2402.17152-hstu/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e74368e779e676f8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hstu" data-paper-title="Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d826e4c63d0f978">Do HSTU history tokens interact, unlike a static history vector?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahstu">Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Yes. Each position updates by reading visible earlier tokens, producing contextual history that a target later reads. Causality restricts direction, not history interaction; outside-window events remain absent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A lens event can incorporate earlier camera context before a tripod candidate reads it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2402.17152-hstu/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d826e4c63d0f978">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hstu" data-paper-title="Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-3b88d0c3b149bbc6">Why not interpret local matched-budget SASRec losses as industrial superiority?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahstu">Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Matched width, layers, loss, and steps isolate a local core. MovieLens lacks heterogeneous events, timing, long histories, and scale. Preserve local negatives without dismissing paper production evidence or importing it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A short-film-sequence loss neither predicts 100,000-event failure nor becomes a local win from online results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2402.17152-hstu/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3b88d0c3b149bbc6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hstu" data-paper-title="Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-defbb4068319dd08">Why do ranking and retrieval predict different objects in HSTU?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahstu">Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retrieval predicts a relevant next item. Ranking conditions on the candidate to predict actions, interleaving item/action tokens. Full-catalog next-item metrics do not validate every action task.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Guess a film versus predict clicks or long watch for an already given film.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2402.17152-hstu/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-defbb4068319dd08">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rloo" data-paper-title="RLOO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8f08c5af1cc0c720">Why exclude the current response from RLOO&#x27;s same-prompt baseline?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arloo">RLOO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Cohere For AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Peers provide an independent reference, not the current action&#x27;s random reward. Treating a response as one action avoids a value network but still requires enough samples, consistent rewards and any specified reference/evaluator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>For reply one of four, average the other three so the baseline doesn&#x27;t move with its own reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14740">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.14740-rloo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8f08c5af1cc0c720">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rloo" data-paper-title="RLOO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-593dd7b298e4697f">Can RLOO use the same formula at K=1?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arloo">RLOO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Cohere For AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. K−1 is zero and there are no peers. Require sufficient group size and KL-shaped returns as appropriate. Local K=4 candidates aren&#x27;t 7B generation and real RM.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Zero-filling an empty baseline changes the estimator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14740">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.14740-rloo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-593dd7b298e4697f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rloo" data-paper-title="RLOO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7349629a82265af6">How does leave-one-out differ from a mean including the current sample?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arloo">RLOO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Cohere For AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>LOO excludes the sample&#x27;s own reward from its baseline. Including it changes dependency and scaling. Both are critic-free, but group size matters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With two replies, the first&#x27;s LOO baseline is the second, not both averaged.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14740">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.14740-rloo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7349629a82265af6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rloo" data-paper-title="RLOO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rloo-064c4d91" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4b9c6d8a40ab7e4f">Why does RLOO treat a full response as one action?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arloo">RLOO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Cohere For AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Terminal RLHF rewards suit response-level REINFORCE and avoid prefix values. Other same-prompt samples form a variance-reducing baseline; multiple samples are still needed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A summary&#x27;s terminal score weights its complete logp relative to peers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14740">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.14740-rloo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4b9c6d8a40ab7e4f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:grpo" data-paper-title="DeepSeekMath / GRPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-62e639b015b8e33e">How does GRPO obtain advantages without critic, and what are old and reference for?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agrpo">DeepSeekMath / GRPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek-AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Center and scale group rewards for relative signal. Old gives sampling probabilities for ratio/clipping; reference anchors KL. Equal rewards provide no contrast. Candidate updates don&#x27;t reproduce full math training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A reference change alters regularization, not the historical rollout source.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.03300-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-62e639b015b8e33e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:grpo" data-paper-title="DeepSeekMath / GRPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ad9a955723733b8a">What should GRPO do with equal group rewards?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agrpo">DeepSeekMath / GRPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek-AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Centered advantages are zero and SD needs protection; never invent differences using evaluator gold. Local six-action candidates aren&#x27;t DeepSeekMath generation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Don&#x27;t rank four incorrect attempts by gold proximity unless the reward protocol actually says so.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.03300-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ad9a955723733b8a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:grpo" data-paper-title="DeepSeekMath / GRPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5af499f3d629e3b1">Why are GRPO old and reference policies different roles?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agrpo">DeepSeekMath / GRPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek-AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Old supplies rollout and proximal ratios, reference anchors long-term KL. Old can refresh each batch independently of the reference; mixing couples update limits and regularization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Fresh sampling updates old policy, not necessarily initial reference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.03300-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5af499f3d629e3b1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:grpo" data-paper-title="DeepSeekMath / GRPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/policy-optimization">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/policy-optimization/">LLM post-training / Policy optimization: which policy samples and which policy learns?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-grpo-679757d4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a1014e27ef04ab41">Why can GRPO omit a policy-sized value model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Agrpo">DeepSeekMath / GRPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek-AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Same-prompt group mean and SD estimate relative advantages instead of a learned prefix value. Save critic resources but require repeated rollouts and differing feedback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Better attempts receive positive advantage relative to peers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.03300-grpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a1014e27ef04ab41">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:kto" data-paper-title="KTO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2aa2521a67232958">How does KTO update from single desirable feedback without same-prompt pairs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Akto">KTO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Contextual AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use response policy/reference log ratio against expected KL as a dynamic baseline and define separate desirable/undesirable utilities. Independent examples can be reweighted without fictitious comparisons. Reference and imbalance still matter; a label is not absolute reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Upvote and downvote on separate inquiries enter separate branches, not a fabricated preference pair.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.01306-kto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2aa2521a67232958">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:kto" data-paper-title="KTO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-51338639a8b4c3b6">What is KTO&#x27;s reference point, and what does the local policy establish?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Akto">KTO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Contextual AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It is expected policy-to-reference KL, not one answer&#x27;s log ratio. Separate aggregate baseline and sample signal. The local six-candidate linear policy checks this relation, not free generation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Compare a high log ratio to the moving baseline; don&#x27;t treat the example as the entire KL expectation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.01306-kto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-51338639a8b4c3b6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:kto" data-paper-title="KTO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b7b11de358098425">Does KTO differ from DPO only by unpairing the data?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Akto">KTO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Contextual AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. KTO defines gains/losses around a KL reference point; DPO compares same-prompt response margins. Standalone feedback cannot be arbitrarily paired, and class weights alter tradeoffs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One user&#x27;s upvote and another&#x27;s downvote on different queries do not order their answers to one prompt.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.01306-kto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b7b11de358098425">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:kto" data-paper-title="KTO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-kto-edf0a49a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea3586d73fba657b">Are KTO desirable and undesirable weights feedback probabilities?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Akto">KTO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Contextual AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Labels describe single accepted/rejected outputs; λ weights control class utility contributions. Class frequency and explicit weight are separate, neither a predicted satisfaction probability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Rebalance many upvotes and few downvotes without inventing matched same-question pairs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2402.01306-kto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ea3586d73fba657b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:medusa" data-paper-title="Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-medusa-8eb57905" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-91bfb6f20f55ba61">Why verify a candidate tree rather than concatenate each Medusa head&#x27;s top token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amedusa">Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Together AI / Princeton University / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Heads predict different offsets from the same state and may not form a valid autoregressive chain. A tree exposes combinations for backbone validation. Independent losses do not prove correctness or sampling guarantees, and local work has no GPU tree kernel.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Separately chosen nouns and verbs need not form a coherent phrase.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2401.10774-medusa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-91bfb6f20f55ba61">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:medusa" data-paper-title="Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-321b91366afe4f45">How align Medusa&#x27;s k-th head targets?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amedusa">Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Together AI / Princeton University / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Predict x_{t+k} from h_t, matching slices and valid endpoints. One common next-token target would train duplicate offsets.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Head two at h_10 predicts x_12, not x_11.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2401.10774-medusa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-321b91366afe4f45">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:medusa" data-paper-title="Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ecbaa441479f51df">Why don&#x27;t fewer backbone calls imply the same percentage latency reduction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amedusa">Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Together AI / Princeton University / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Extra heads, tree construction and validation, batch shape, kernels, and acceptance all matter. Mechanism call counts are not measured GPU speed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Halving calls may double the work per verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2401.10774-medusa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ecbaa441479f51df">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:medusa" data-paper-title="Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/generation-paths">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/generation-paths/">Foundation models / Generation paths: draft verification, parallel denoising, and few-step refinement</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-700adaef304fe397">Why add multiple future-token heads to one hidden state?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amedusa">Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Together AI / Princeton University / University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different offsets provide multiple proposals at once. Tree verification can reduce sequential calls without removing backbone verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Propose t+1 and t+2 from h_t before checking accepted combinations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2401.10774-medusa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-700adaef304fe397">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:self-rewarding" data-paper-title="Self-Rewarding LM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-154b2587d78b6046">Where do Self-Rewarding LM preferences come from, and why can errors compound?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aself-rewarding">Self-Rewarding LM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each round ranks its own generated candidates and trains the next round with DPO on those judgments. They are not independent human labels; persistent judge biases can become stronger. Keep external held-out evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A judge rewarding verbosity may repeatedly choose long arithmetic errors; an external check can break the loop.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2401.10020-self-rewarding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-154b2587d78b6046">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:self-rewarding" data-paper-title="Self-Rewarding LM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7824f1f8ceec3d9a">What provenance must Self-Rewarding iterations retain?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aself-rewarding">Self-Rewarding LM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Record generating policy round, judge round and pair-selection rule. Don&#x27;t backfill old data with post-update scores. Use isolated evaluation. Local tests cover state and objective, not paper judge quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After training a new model, don&#x27;t rescore old candidates and present those scores as original supervision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2401.10020-self-rewarding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7824f1f8ceec3d9a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:self-rewarding" data-paper-title="Self-Rewarding LM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-64e85cc5effd028f">How does Self-Rewarding differ from a fixed external reward model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aself-rewarding">Self-Rewarding LM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A fixed judge doesn&#x27;t coevolve; self-reward hopes both generation and judgment improve but can amplify shared errors. Compare at equal budget with independent evaluation, not rising self-scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A model can learn to please its own scoring rule without becoming more useful to users.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2401.10020-self-rewarding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-64e85cc5effd028f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:self-rewarding" data-paper-title="Self-Rewarding LM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-self-rewarding-38dd38b1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b295099775e750b6">Does a Self-Rewarding judge tie reveal the preferred answer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aself-rewarding">Self-Rewarding LM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A tie gives no strict preference; display order cannot create one. Candidate count and distinguishable judging are separate. Even unequal scores are the current judge&#x27;s judgment, not new human truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If two candidates tie, don&#x27;t label the first shown the winner.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2401.10020-self-rewarding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b295099775e750b6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spin" data-paper-title="SPIN" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c0b13386310cfbca">How does SPIN&#x27;s previous-policy negative differ from self-judged preferences?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspin">SPIN</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Los Angeles</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Human demonstrations are positives; prior-policy samples are negatives. Train relative to the prior policy, then refresh it. No self-judge scoring is needed. Human supervision remains and negatives aren&#x27;t necessarily false.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Use fixed expert examples and regenerate opponents next round instead of replaying all old negatives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01335">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2401.01335-spin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c0b13386310cfbca">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spin" data-paper-title="SPIN" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-68b65f63205056ef">Why freeze SPIN&#x27;s opponent during a round and refresh it afterward?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspin">SPIN</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Los Angeles</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The previous policy supplies both samples and the reference. Changing it mid-round changes the objective. Refresh after the round to align generation, scoring and updates. No full-scale local text experiment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Using old reference for half the batches and a new one for the rest does not define one consistent round.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01335">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2401.01335-spin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-68b65f63205056ef">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spin" data-paper-title="SPIN" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-de51d109d380cea3">How does SPIN&#x27;s refreshed negatives differ from repeated SFT on fixed examples?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspin">SPIN</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Los Angeles</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>SFT raises fixed demonstration likelihood. SPIN resamples a comparison distribution from the previous policy on the same prompts and distinguishes demonstrations from it. Both negatives and relative reference change, not just training rounds.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After fixing earlier mistakes, the next opponent may make different ones. Fixed SFT won&#x27;t refresh those negatives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01335">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2401.01335-spin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-de51d109d380cea3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spin" data-paper-title="SPIN" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-spin-6b40abc1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-2d79d9ecff10c497">Where do SPIN positives come from without new human preference data?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspin">SPIN</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Los Angeles</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Existing human SFT demonstrations stay positive. The previous policy generates negatives on the same prompts. Self-play changes negatives and reference; it still uses demonstrations and generated replies are not necessarily factually wrong.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A standard answer already exists; generate a comparison without asking a human to rank it again.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01335">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2401.01335-spin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2d79d9ecff10c497">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:math-shepherd" data-paper-title="Math-Shepherd" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-162d99ef25d3753e">Why isn&#x27;t a continuation-based step label a direct correctness judgment?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amath-shepherd">Math-Shepherd</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It estimates success under a particular policy and sampling budget. Correct prefixes can get low estimates and wrong ones can be repaired. Separate reachability from correctness; use gold only for annotation or independent scoring.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Low success after a correct second step may reflect frequent final arithmetic mistakes, not a wrong second step.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08935">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2312.08935-math-shepherd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-162d99ef25d3753e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:math-shepherd" data-paper-title="Math-Shepherd" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-92344e3f0c9b1409">Can Math-Shepherd continuations see gold when constructing labels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amath-shepherd">Math-Shepherd</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Gold is only for terminal checking; actually sample from the specified prefix rather than constructing a path from known answers. No full local LLM data/PRM training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The grader can know the result without including it in the continuation prompt.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08935">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2312.08935-math-shepherd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-92344e3f0c9b1409">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:math-shepherd" data-paper-title="Math-Shepherd" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a1b3f74d41607794">How does continuation success differ from correctness of a step?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amath-shepherd">Math-Shepherd</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Later policy can repair an error or fail after correct reasoning. Estimated reachability combines prefix and continuation policy, not a logical proof.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A wrong step followed by frequent corrections should not be imitated simply because continuations succeed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08935">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2312.08935-math-shepherd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a1b3f74d41607794">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:math-shepherd" data-paper-title="Math-Shepherd" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-math-shepherd-cc3174ec" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4aa9a43e201b22c1">How does Math-Shepherd get step supervision without human step labels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Amath-shepherd">Math-Shepherd</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Continue repeatedly from a prefix and estimate reachable success from final answer checks, then train a process verifier. This is not direct human judgment of each line.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A prefix with mostly correct continuations receives a higher success estimate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08935">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2312.08935-math-shepherd/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4aa9a43e201b22c1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mamba" data-paper-title="Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-mamba-0b65990c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-53597ba087ad9762">What does Mamba&#x27;s selectivity change inside the SSM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amamba">Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University / Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Token-dependent step sizes and read/write vectors control retention, write direction, and readout within recurrence. This is not output scaling of a fixed SSM. Linear sequence cost still does not guarantee exact arbitrary-token retrieval from finite state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Preserve state on filler but write differently for a key number; retrieval still depends on what remains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2312.00752-mamba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-53597ba087ad9762">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mamba" data-paper-title="Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-275f57141b520ee1">Does a Python or PyTorch selective scan reproduce Mamba kernel throughput?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amamba">Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University / Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A loop can check input-dependent parameters and recurrence, but not a fused parallel CUDA scan. The local run also omits 2.8B pretraining. Validate correctness, language quality, and throughput separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Seven steps agreeing with a reference check mechanics, not tokens per second.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2312.00752-mamba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-275f57141b520ee1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mamba" data-paper-title="Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7b1c8ad148c1bce8">How does Mamba memory differ from reweighting historical KV?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amamba">Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University / Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mamba accumulates history in state and uses input-dependent readout. Attention assigns weights directly to retained positions. Linear complexity does not imply lossless per-token history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A summary can retain a fact without separately addressable slots for every old word.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2312.00752-mamba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7b1c8ad148c1bce8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mamba" data-paper-title="Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7a505778b7bd7571">Why does Mamba selectivity depend on the current token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amamba">Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University / Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Step size and read/write vectors depend on input, so retention, updates, and readout vary by content while still using recurrent state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A separator and answer token can trigger different updates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2312.00752-mamba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7a505778b7bd7571">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:gaia" data-paper-title="GAIA" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/evaluation-and-reliability/">Agents / Evaluation and reliability: how do we know it worked?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7f1f7590b48a18a3">Why can exact short answers still test multi-tool reasoning rather than memorization?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Agaia">GAIA</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Short output is the scoring interface; finding it can require browsing, multimodal understanding, calculation, and cross-source checks. Normalized matching makes endpoints clear, not evidence quality or failure location. Distinguish accuracy from executed traces and never put reference answers into agent prompts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One final year may require identifying a person from a picture, researching an event, and verifying dates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12983">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2311.12983-gaia/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7f1f7590b48a18a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
