Cache only from training-visible behavior so preferences do not absorb test answers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A ranker can output scores while never reading the knowledge on disk, but that is not KAR. Summarizing user preferences after seeing test behavior instead leaks the target into evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10933">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2306.10933-kar/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fccb1acc024f0dc4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:kar" data-paper-title="Towards Open-World Recommendation with Knowledge Augmentation from Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-804816a74c553ef3">How do cost and error propagation differ between KAR&#x27;s offline knowledge enhancement and online LLM recommendation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Akar">Towards Open-World Recommendation with Knowledge Augmentation from Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Offline generation reuses a cache, so serving runs only the adapter and original recommender without autoregressive latency. Mistakes are also reused, making versions and refreshes important. Online generation is more flexible but incurs a cost on every request. The twenty-user reduction in the source shows only a small trend, not general industrial gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: One cached film fact can serve many users, but an incorrect year propagates until refreshed. Asking on each request can update it at the cost of extra latency and inconsistency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10933">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2306.10933-kar/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-804816a74c553ef3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:kar" data-paper-title="Towards Open-World Recommendation with Knowledge Augmentation from Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/content-semantic-ids">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/content-semantic-ids/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Semantic representations, user knowledge, and cold start</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1b495bedf4e8e1f2">Why separate user preference knowledge and item facts in KAR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Akar">Towards Open-World Recommendation with Knowledge Augmentation from Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A preference explains why a user might like something, while a fact describes what it is; evidence and update frequencies differ. Factorization prompting generates them separately, and the hybrid-expert adapter injects them into the ID recommender rather than conflating facts and guesses in one text. Generated knowledge can still hallucinate and is not observed ground truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Enjoying light plots is an inferred preference; a film&#x27;s release year is factual. Writing the preference as an item attribute can contaminate matching and explanations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10933">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2306.10933-kar/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1b495bedf4e8e1f2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:minillm" data-paper-title="MiniLLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-446e1e3109c8e57a">How does reverse KL affect small students&#x27; treatment of teacher tails?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aminillm">MiniLLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Student expectation focuses capacity on visited teacher-supported modes; forward KL covers teacher mass. Direction changes gradients and expectation. Preserve teacher-mixed stabilization; candidate checks aren&#x27;t long-text distillation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A limited student may concentrate on a few reliable phrasings rather than cover every rare teacher expression.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08543">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2306.08543-minillm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-446e1e3109c8e57a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:minillm" data-paper-title="MiniLLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d3b8dc61e2654a7c">Whose distribution defines MiniLLM reverse-KL expectation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aminillm">MiniLLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Student, with explicit teacher-mixed sampling and corrections in practice. Arbitrary fixed teacher text is not a substitute. Local candidates lack real tokenizer, long generation and GPT judging.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Scoring teacher solutions with a KL-looking formula doesn&#x27;t provide student on-policy coverage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08543">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2306.08543-minillm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d3b8dc61e2654a7c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:minillm" data-paper-title="MiniLLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-668adaf234eb9d00">What coverage tradeoff separates MiniLLM from forward KL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aminillm">MiniLLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Forward emphasizes teacher-mass coverage; reverse follows student-sampled modes. Teacher-mixed sampling and variance reduction also matter; direction alone isn&#x27;t the full method.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Few reliable modes versus many weak modes requires task evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08543">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2306.08543-minillm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-668adaf234eb9d00">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:minillm" data-paper-title="MiniLLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/student-trajectory-distillation">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/student-trajectory-distillation/">LLM post-training / Trajectory distillation: students, proposals, and prefix distributions</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-minillm-8f5f3ddd" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0d5b1df040633afb">Why favor reverse KL in MiniLLM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aminillm">MiniLLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Small students may not cover all teacher modes. Reverse KL concentrates on student-supported reliable teacher regions, possibly missing modes. Sharpness isn&#x27;t always desirable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Learn several reliable phrasings rather than spread over all teacher continuations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08543">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2306.08543-minillm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0d5b1df040633afb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:awq" data-paper-title="AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-awq-9367c7ce" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d1ecb6d714c57abd">Why use equivalent scaling in AWQ rather than separately storing a few higher-precision weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aawq">AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MIT / NVIDIA / Harvard / SJTU</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Calibration activations identify output-sensitive input channels. Reciprocal input/weight scaling preserves the float function while making those weights easier to represent in one low-bit format. Large weights alone do not determine sensitivity, and KV growth is unrelated.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal weight errors have different output effects on channels with small versus large activations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2306.00978-awq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d1ecb6d714c57abd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:awq" data-paper-title="AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1ef8b97ca8a3077d">Must input be inversely scaled when weights are scaled by S?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aawq">AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MIT / NVIDIA / Harvard / SJTU</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Yes: XW=(XS⁻¹)(SW). Without reciprocal scaling the floating function already changes. Search scales by quantized reconstruction error; local MSE does not establish TinyChat throughput.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Multiply one weight channel by two and divide its input by two.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2306.00978-awq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1ef8b97ca8a3077d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:awq" data-paper-title="AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-aedd4f3cf22864ab">What does AWQ add over round-to-nearest W4?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aawq">AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MIT / NVIDIA / Harvard / SJTU</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Search activation-aware equivalent channel scales before W4 rounding. RTN uses the given scale and nearest grid. Both can retain a uniform low-bit format.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Rescale an important channel before rounding rather than round original weights directly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2306.00978-awq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aedd4f3cf22864ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:awq" data-paper-title="AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d1a4162d95cfb1d5">Why use activations instead of weight magnitude alone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aawq">AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · MIT / NVIDIA / Harvard / SJTU</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Output error depends on input activation. Calibration identifies salient channels and equivalent scaling protects them before uniform low-bit weight-only quantization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The same weight error is more consequential when multiplied by large activations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2306.00978-awq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d1a4162d95cfb1d5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:process-supervision" data-paper-title="Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c928a3ae66cbf1b">Why actively label uncertain steps instead of only checking final answers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprocess-supervision">Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Final outcomes don&#x27;t locate early mistakes. Step labels provide detailed reward-model supervision; uncertainty targets current ambiguous decisions but isn&#x27;t a universal error proxy. Control candidate/evaluation budgets; no full local annotation dataset.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Review an uncertain key algebraic move rather than repeatedly labeling obvious format.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.20050-process-supervision/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c928a3ae66cbf1b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:process-supervision" data-paper-title="Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-fc42fa618967fd6a">How separate PRM labels and predictions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprocess-supervision">Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Step truth is fixed supervision, probabilities differentiable, and entropy used only in allowed acquisition. Test step labels cannot select training samples. Candidate budget tests mechanism only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Training on observed test-label errors leaks evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.20050-process-supervision/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fc42fa618967fd6a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:process-supervision" data-paper-title="Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-14599bd243e344eb">What tradeoff separates active uncertain-step labeling from random labeling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprocess-supervision">Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Active selection spends budget on hard judgments; random selection better reflects the original distribution. Uncertainty isn&#x27;t importance and selection bias/label quality remain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An ambiguous formatting step can be less valuable to review than a key mathematical transition.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.20050-process-supervision/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-14599bd243e344eb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:process-supervision" data-paper-title="Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/reward-and-credit">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/reward-and-credit/">LLM post-training / Reward and credit: which steps deserve a good final score?</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-process-supervision-e0dd1357" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-db9edb2d592cf144">Why do process supervision methods label steps rather than only outcomes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprocess-supervision">Let&#x27;s Verify Step by Step</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Failure doesn&#x27;t identify the broken step. Local labels provide finer learning and selection, requiring annotations or reliable process judges. Do not broadcast terminal correctness as step truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If step three fails, steps one and two needn&#x27;t be marked wrong.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.20050-process-supervision/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-db9edb2d592cf144">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dpo" data-paper-title="DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f795703a61b6c34c">Why use DPO policy changes relative to reference instead of raw answer probabilities?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adpo">DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raw scores inherit pretraining preferences. Relative ratios measure redistribution against the baseline, jointly comparing preferred/rejected in the classification margin implied by KL regularization. No explicit reward model, but same-prompt preferences and fixed reference remain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If a phrase starts with high likelihood, distinguish inherited preference from a further supervised increase.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.18290-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f795703a61b6c34c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dpo" data-paper-title="DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d9471cd43ba2d2a4">Why freeze DPO&#x27;s reference and align response masks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adpo">DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The reference anchors changes; updating it changes the objective. Score identical response tokens in both paths, with neither prompt nor padding mismatches.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Adding prompt likelihood only to reference introduces irrelevant input length into the margin.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.18290-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d9471cd43ba2d2a4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dpo" data-paper-title="DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-fb674fbd601d1a3d">How does DPO&#x27;s data flow differ from reward-model PPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adpo">DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Classic DPO consumes fixed preference pairs without sampling and reward-model scoring at every step. PPO usually includes those stages. A fixed dataset may omit states future policies visit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A preference bank without a wrong-prefix category doesn&#x27;t automatically gain it from offline updates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.18290-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fb674fbd601d1a3d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dpo" data-paper-title="DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-dpo-0073c0b6" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5b1bca6549e89038">Why doesn&#x27;t DPO need a separately fitted reward model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Adpo">DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The KL-regularized policy expresses implicit reward as a policy/reference log ratio. Direct paired classification uses chosen and rejected labels. Reward information still comes from preference supervision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With labels on two answers, compute the paired loss without first training a scorer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.18290-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5b1bca6549e89038">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rewoo" data-paper-title="ReWOO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-rewoo-abc51544" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b9de714c020722cd">How can a planner express tool dependencies without rereading intermediate observations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arewoo">ReWOO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The planner writes dependencies as variable references. The Worker substitutes obtained evidence into later tool arguments, and the Solver combines results at the end. This reduces repeated planning calls without deleting data flow. A static plan is less adaptive if an unexpected observation determines a later route that was never encoded.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Store a person&#x27;s birthplace as E1, then look up its population using E1. The city is bound later without regenerating the whole plan.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18323">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.18323-rewoo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b9de714c020722cd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rewoo" data-paper-title="ReWOO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-124386a640c92e78">When can a Worker run tools in parallel, and when must it wait for an evidence variable?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arewoo">ReWOO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Calls without unmet dependencies can run in parallel. A call referencing an earlier E variable must wait for that result. The Solver reads both the plan and actual evidence at the end, not imagined planner results. Local tests verify control flow and counts without real search APIs or a multi-size LLM comparison.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Weather requests for two known cities can run together. Weather for the newly found city must wait for lookup rather than guess its argument.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18323">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.18323-rewoo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-124386a640c92e78">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rewoo" data-paper-title="ReWOO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b757f2600787d3fc">What do ReWOO and ReAct trade off when handling unexpected intermediate results?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arewoo">ReWOO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>ReAct reasons after each observation and can revise its route, but repeated model calls cost more. ReWOO plans before execution and avoids repeatedly reading evidence, but relies more on a workable initial dependency plan. Unexpected errors require separate recovery; a static plan is not inherently a feedback loop.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: When the first query returns several namesakes, ReAct can add disambiguation immediately. ReWOO needs an outer recovery if its original plan has no such branch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18323">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.18323-rewoo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b757f2600787d3fc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:rewoo" data-paper-title="ReWOO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f60bde583743c4b5">Why can a multi-step tool task spend heavily on rereading existing content?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Arewoo">ReWOO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>If every return makes the planner reread the task, old plan, and all evidence, input grows even when the next action only substitutes a known result. ReWOO separates planning, tool execution, and final synthesis to reduce repetition. It fits workflows whose dependencies can be expressed in advance, while surprises still need recovery.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Finding an author and then their birthplace is a known two-step pattern. Each returned string does not require regenerating the plan and rereading all earlier evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18323">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.18323-rewoo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f60bde583743c4b5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:voyager" data-paper-title="Voyager" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-voyager-f3989bf0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-aa9ceda6b2719950">Why admit only programs verified by the environment to Voyager&#x27;s skill library?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Avoyager">Voyager</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Plausible code can fail because materials are missing, APIs are wrong, or goals are unmet. Environment feedback exposes these failures. Index confirmed successes for reuse. The automatic curriculum picks new goals and the library retains verified behavior; code generation alone cannot substitute.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A program for crafting an iron pickaxe is not a successful skill if inventory lacks iron. Only actual completion supports future reuse.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.16291-voyager/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aa9ceda6b2719950">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:voyager" data-paper-title="Voyager" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cf860a830a3dce6b">Is the local structured-plan skill library equivalent to Mineflayer JavaScript programs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Avoyager">Voyager</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Curriculum, skills, verification, and cross-episode reuse are retained with structured tool plans. The run omits Minecraft, GPT-4, and embedding retrieval. Controlled retry counts do not represent real program debugging or paper item and distance gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Reusing a plan template does not show handling Mineflayer&#x27;s asynchronous movement errors or achieving its technology-tree gains in a new world.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.16291-voyager/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cf860a830a3dce6b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:voyager" data-paper-title="Voyager" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e1d7d24beac16b9f">How does automatic curriculum differ from a fixed checklist for accumulating skills?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Avoyager">Voyager</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The curriculum chooses novel goals from current state and skills. A fixed list is controlled but cannot adapt to capability. Self-selected goals can favor easy novelty, so validate outcomes and progress rather than treat task count or exploration distance as general capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: After acquiring stone tools, mining explores more than repeated wood gathering, but completion still depends on inventory and milestones.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.16291-voyager/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e1d7d24beac16b9f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:voyager" data-paper-title="Voyager" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-fc830cd6a7e32dd0">Why does Voyager use code as an action instead of only a natural-language plan?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Avoyager">Voyager</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Code invokes environment APIs over extended behavior and can be iteratively repaired from errors and observations. Successful programs enter the library for reuse. Natural-language plans still need executable mapping. Runnable code can also be wrong and needs environmental validation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Compile collecting wood into movement, search, and harvesting loops, then inspect inventory. Saying &#x27;chop a tree&#x27; does not perform those actions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.16291-voyager/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fc830cd6a7e32dd0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:toolbench" data-paper-title="ToolBench" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-toolbench-89c52f4b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-effa1825464a63ea">Why constrain format and check real execution in addition to retrieving usage examples?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atoolbench">ToolBench</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Examples show when and how to call tools but cannot guarantee schema or argument meaning. Format constraints ensure parseability; execution tests whether the goal is achieved. Experience, contracts, and observed results are distinct. JSON-like text is not actual tool capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A complete weather-call schema can still name the wrong city. Valid JSON does not answer the requested forecast.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16504">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.16504-toolbench/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-effa1825464a63ea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:toolbench" data-paper-title="ToolBench" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-9b063717d0acaa6b">Does local planbench-mini tool success equal the paper&#x27;s eight tasks or live API success?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atoolbench">ToolBench</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Local work tests demonstration, constraint, or state protocols without paper-scale models, training, or the full real tool matrix. Tool results and scoring require independent execution. Perfect controlled results are not public benchmark scores, and similarly named ToolBench datasets must not be conflated.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A preset plan can parse and execute without proving the model can call an unseen service from documentation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16504">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.16504-toolbench/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9b063717d0acaa6b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:toolbench" data-paper-title="ToolBench" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-1f0d05b126401e20">How does retrieving in-context demonstrations differ from always using one fixed example set?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atoolbench">ToolBench</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retrieval chooses examples for the current task, avoiding irrelevant context and broader coverage gaps of fixed examples. It can still choose badly or encourage copied arguments. Reuse procedures, not answers. Compare fixed models and tasks and include example-reading cost.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: SQL examples help database queries more than weather samples, but their table names cannot be reused unverified.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16504">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.16504-toolbench/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1f0d05b126401e20">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:toolbench" data-paper-title="ToolBench" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-2a0f6c07e30bff56">Why teach a model multiple tools rather than handwrite calls for each ToolBench task?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atoolbench">ToolBench</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Real catalogs have varied interfaces and parameters. A model must understand intent, find relevant demonstrations, and generate executable calls. ToolBench studies data and constraints for transferable tool use. Format is one step; verify API behavior, outputs, and final answers rather than synthetic success alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Weather and map tools require different fields. Use each contract instead of copying one fixed template.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16504">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.16504-toolbench/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2a0f6c07e30bff56">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gqa" data-paper-title="GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-gqa-9496fcce" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b644d6aec39b7b8b">Does GQA reduce Q heads or KV heads, and why does it save decode memory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agqa">GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Many query heads share fewer K/V heads while retaining different queries. Each historical position stores and reads fewer KV groups. This reduces independence compared with MHA, not history token count.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Eight queries can use two KV groups while producing eight different attention distributions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.13245-gqa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b644d6aec39b7b8b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gqa" data-paper-title="GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-16543b687401639e">Does temporarily expanding shared KV establish cache savings?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agqa">GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Logical broadcast can aid compute, but persistent KV must store fewer groups; retaining expanded copies loses savings. Check g(h) and distinguish local from original uptraining.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four Q heads sharing two groups should store two histories.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.13245-gqa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-16543b687401639e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gqa" data-paper-title="GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-58190c8080d5c2fe">Which head-count axis distinguishes MHA, GQA, and MQA?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agqa">GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MHA generally has one KV per Q, GQA shares within groups, and MQA shares globally. Query head count can remain fixed; quality and bandwidth are empirical.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Keep eight Q heads with eight, two, or one KV group.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.13245-gqa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-58190c8080d5c2fe">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gqa" data-paper-title="GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/compression-and-cache/">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-36f4e474bbcb6a45">Why share fewer K/V heads among more queries?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agqa">GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Queries keep distinct directions while grouped history lowers cache and read bandwidth. It interpolates between per-head MHA and single-group MQA.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four query heads can share two stored KV histories instead of four.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.13245-gqa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-36f4e474bbcb6a45">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:critic" data-paper-title="CRITIC" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-critic-11dab3d3" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1766e55c41f638fd">Why can external tool feedback reveal persistent errors that rereading an answer misses?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acritic">CRITIC</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Self-critique may inherit the original model&#x27;s assumptions. Search facts or code outputs provide independently observable constraints. Evidence guides revision in a loop. Tools can fail or return nothing; no feedback is not verification, and success must not be fabricated.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A wrong product may still look right to the model. A calculator result provides a concrete contradiction for revision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11738">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.11738-critic/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1766e55c41f638fd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:critic" data-paper-title="CRITIC" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-72d92522b177ffce">What feedback does the local real-traceback loop cover?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acritic">CRITIC</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It writes a defective patch, runs unittest, edits from observed feedback, reruns, and records commands and exit codes each round. This verifies controlled code feedback and iteration, not search engines, toxicity classifiers, or a general LLM critic. Running tests does not validate all paper tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A second patch turning a failed test into a pass verifies this code instance, not open-domain QA or harmlessness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11738">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.11738-critic/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-72d92522b177ffce">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:critic" data-paper-title="CRITIC" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4d28a5a81f959747">What evidence does code execution provide for critique versus web retrieval?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acritic">CRITIC</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Execution shows outputs or exceptions for a specific input. Web retrieval supplies external text whose source and support must be assessed. Both extend self-evaluation, with different limits: untested code can still fail, and a search hit need not support the answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Division by zero proves one run failed. A related web result still needs its actual passage read, not just its title.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11738">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.11738-critic/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4d28a5a81f959747">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:critic" data-paper-title="CRITIC" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-bafd7c35b893a5b8">Why does CRITIC try to find and fix errors after the model has already written an answer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acritic">CRITIC</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Drafts can contain factual, reasoning, or code errors despite confidence. CRITIC gathers external checks for critique and revision. Observable evidence helps, but tools have limited coverage and edits can add errors. Evaluate checks and final outcomes separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Execute code on a boundary input, observe an exception, and revise. Rereading the same explanation gives no equivalent evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11738">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.11738-critic/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bafd7c35b893a5b8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:slic-hf" data-paper-title="SLiC-HF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fc913597b1af1378">Why keep supervised cross-entropy when SLiC-HF already has a preference margin?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aslic-hf">SLiC-HF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Relative ranking does not prevent overall language drift. Cross-entropy preserves reference response likelihood, combining calibration and generation learning. Off-policy data do not remove coverage, length or source differences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Suppressing bad answers can satisfy ranking even while good answers get worse; supervision retains good generation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10425">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.10425-slic-hf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fc913597b1af1378">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:slic-hf" data-paper-title="SLiC-HF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1991e69bbbffe205">Why can SLiC-HF use pairs collected by another model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aslic-hf">SLiC-HF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The objective can score fixed responses and doesn&#x27;t need current-policy samples. Keep sources and same-prompt pairing. Local candidate calculations are not the paper&#x27;s T5 and human evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Old summaries can be scored by the current policy if labels still belong to those summaries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10425">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.10425-slic-hf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1991e69bbbffe205">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:slic-hf" data-paper-title="SLiC-HF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-da985f94e4904b1e">How does SLiC-HF&#x27;s hinge margin differ from DPO&#x27;s reference-relative one?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aslic-hf">SLiC-HF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The hinge directly constrains sequence likelihood differences alongside supervision. DPO contrasts log ratios relative to a frozen policy. Both baseline and loss shape differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Once the hinge margin is met, ranking penalty can stop; reference-relative preference is different.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10425">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.10425-slic-hf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-da985f94e4904b1e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:slic-hf" data-paper-title="SLiC-HF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-slic-hf-5def3201" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c231dcb6386ca8e">Why combine sequence calibration and supervised loss in SLiC-HF?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Aslic-hf">SLiC-HF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Ranking makes preferred likelihood exceed rejected likelihood. Supervision learns trusted content rather than succeeding only by suppressing bad replies. Both train the generator directly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Separate good from bad summaries while learning the good summary itself.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10425">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2305.10425-slic-hf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c231dcb6386ca8e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:doremi" data-paper-title="DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-doremi-7bfdfa8e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-82c48593bd66c5dc">Why emphasize excess loss rather than maximum raw loss in DoReMi?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adoremi">DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raw loss mixes irreducible difficulty and underfitting. Subtract reference loss and use group DRO on a small proxy to derive target mixture. This is relative to the reference and data, not a preference for all high-entropy domains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A has loss 5 vs reference 4.9; B has 3 vs 2. B&#x27;s larger excess can get more weight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10429">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.10429-doremi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-82c48593bd66c5dc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:doremi" data-paper-title="DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a08f39c27b1ec847">Why normalize α across domains after each update?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adoremi">DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Exponential updates yield relative weights, not probabilities; normalization sums to one. Keep the same reference. Local two-domain unigram work is not a Pile 280M-to-8B transfer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Relative weights 2 and 3 become 0.4 and 0.6.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10429">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.10429-doremi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a08f39c27b1ec847">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
