<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:doremi" data-paper-title="DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-395b5c5a3e6e732d">How do dynamic DoReMi weights differ from uniform sampling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adoremi">DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Uniform probabilities stay fixed. DoReMi exponentiates reference-relative excess-loss updates and renormalizes, responding to underfitting rather than raw loss alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A high loss from an intrinsically hard domain may not imply a large excess.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10429">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.10429-doremi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-395b5c5a3e6e732d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:doremi" data-paper-title="DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/training-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/training-budget/">Foundation models / Training budgets: data mixtures, objectives, and optimizers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6091e34a90a5668b">Why learn target-model mixtures with a small proxy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adoremi">DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Repeated large runs are costly. Small-proxy group DRO adjusts weights from excess loss, then target training uses that mixture. Transfer needs verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Estimate reference-relative gaps cheaply before allocating large-run data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10429">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.10429-doremi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6091e34a90a5668b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:tree-of-thoughts" data-paper-title="Tree of Thoughts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-tree-of-thoughts-32a1f51e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8b8a8b99244ced83">How does searching a tree of thoughts differ from generating several complete answers at once?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atree-of-thoughts">Tree of Thoughts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Intermediate thoughts are states that can be evaluated and expanded separately. Search can retain early alternatives, prune dead ends, and backtrack. Complete answers are often compared only at the end, paying repeatedly for bad prefixes. ToT still depends on value estimation and width/depth budgets; a tree does not make its evaluator correct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: An arithmetic problem has three possible initial decompositions. Check which preserve feasible remaining values before expanding, rather than finishing a full answer for obviously impossible ones.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.10601-tree-of-thoughts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8b8a8b99244ced83">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:tree-of-thoughts" data-paper-title="Tree of Thoughts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-2f4d0f638f26d58e">Does the local workflow-coherence value represent GPT-4 self-evaluation quality?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atree-of-thoughts">Tree of Thoughts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A small PlanBench uses deterministic workflow coherence, a fixed beam, and backtracking to test thought-tree control flow, not GPT-4 or Game of 24. Counts of nodes and backtracks show that search happens. A perfect score does not establish an open-ended language value function.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A rule can flag an action that violates a precondition. That does not prove a large model can reliably score the future promise of a creative-writing fragment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.10601-tree-of-thoughts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2f4d0f638f26d58e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:tree-of-thoughts" data-paper-title="Tree of Thoughts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-f19cba5da4346653">How do BFS and DFS spend limited ToT search budgets?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atree-of-thoughts">Tree of Thoughts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>BFS retains multiple states at one layer, making it easy to compare alternatives at similar progress but requiring a broad evaluated frontier. DFS goes deep on one path and backtracks, keeping a narrower frontier but potentially wasting depth on a bad branch. Width, depth, and pruning thresholds depend on evaluation reliability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: With three opening moves, BFS explores one step from each. DFS may follow the first to the end before trying the second.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.10601-tree-of-thoughts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f19cba5da4346653">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:tree-of-thoughts" data-paper-title="Tree of Thoughts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/planning-and-search">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/planning-and-search/">Agents / Planning and search: what should happen next?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0e3e4144da090e88">Why is ToT suited to reasoning that requires trying paths and backing out of dead ends?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atree-of-thoughts">Tree of Thoughts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Local choices affect later feasibility. One uninterrupted answer can carry a bad choice to the end. ToT represents expandable intermediate states, retaining directions, judging progress, and backtracking. This requires states that can be meaningfully evaluated; search does not supply a reliable judgment rule by itself.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: If a partial expression cannot reach the target number, change the previous grouping instead of regenerating the entire solution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2305.10601-tree-of-thoughts/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0e3e4144da090e88">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:tiger" data-paper-title="Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-41bf45ff5bebea3c">Why share semantics via residual SID instead of random hierarchy, and still use a collision token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atiger">Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Coarse centers and residual refinement can group related items, while finite codebooks still collide. A unique suffix resolves identity. Matched random IDs isolate hierarchy from semantic hierarchy; semantic IDs need not win.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Gardening books can share a prefix and split by subject or final collision suffix.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05065">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.05065-tiger/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-41bf45ff5bebea3c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:tiger" data-paper-title="Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-97a2c69cd47c2932">Does local TIGER rank with a score proxy or complete code probability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atiger">Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sum token log probabilities over valid item codes, without score fusion. Match codebooks/collisions in training and decoding; exclude invalid paths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Omitting a level changes the complete item&#x27;s generation probability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05065">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.05065-tiger/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-97a2c69cd47c2932">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:tiger" data-paper-title="Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-1e524d9ba84a0a5f">How does a collision token differ from the semantic prefix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atiger">Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It disambiguates item identity when several items share a semantic code. An arbitrary unique suffix is not a new semantic level.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two similar videos can share three levels but require distinct final tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05065">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.05065-tiger/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1e524d9ba84a0a5f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:tiger" data-paper-title="Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/generative-retrieval-reasoning/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Generative retrieval and reasoning-based recommendation</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-tiger-7436853d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-602316de33d0b529">Why quantize content into multilevel Semantic IDs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Atiger">Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Short discrete codes share meaning and support autoregressive generation. Content and quantization quality limit generalization, and codes must map to valid items.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Similar items share early codes and differ at fine levels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05065">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2305.05065-tiger/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-602316de33d0b529">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:llava" data-paper-title="Visual Instruction Tuning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-llava-9b58a1f9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0ba55b5e7a12c6c3">Why is projecting visual features to the LLM width insufficient for following visual instructions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Allava">Visual Instruction Tuning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Wisconsin-Madison / Microsoft Research / Columbia University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Matching shape does not align meaning. The connector learns a visual-to-language interface, and instruction supervision teaches how to answer questions conditioned on images. Projection alone does not confer recognition, localization, or multiround responses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A cat image can enter as a vector, but QA training is needed to answer “Where is it?”</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2304.08485-llava/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0ba55b5e7a12c6c3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:llava" data-paper-title="Visual Instruction Tuning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f05675cd47b434ea">Does the local two-layer projector&#x27;s negative result refute LLaVA&#x27;s instruction tuning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Allava">Visual Instruction Tuning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Wisconsin-Madison / Microsoft Research / Columbia University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The local run fixes a small patch encoder, classification head, and budget, and compares a linear projector with a two-layer MLP. It does not generate GPT-4 instructions or train LLaVA-13B. Extra connector capacity did not help this configuration, not all tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A decline in small clothing classification says nothing directly about large-model multiround image dialogue.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2304.08485-llava/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f05675cd47b434ea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:llava" data-paper-title="Visual Instruction Tuning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-f7c311ba118b0143">How does LLaVA instruction supervision differ from CLIP&#x27;s dual-encoder contrastive training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Allava">Visual Instruction Tuning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Wisconsin-Madison / Microsoft Research / Columbia University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>LLaVA learns conditional answer tokens from images and questions. CLIP brings paired images and texts together in a shared embedding space for matching. Retrieval scores are not instruction-generation quality, and architecture alone does not establish superiority.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Answering why two people hold umbrellas is conditional generation; selecting a supplied matching caption is a different output contract.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2304.08485-llava/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f7c311ba118b0143">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:llava" data-paper-title="Visual Instruction Tuning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-dfa5b553021f92af">What does LLaVA&#x27;s visual projector do between image and answer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Allava">Visual Instruction Tuning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Wisconsin-Madison / Microsoft Research / Columbia University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It maps image-encoder features into visual tokens that the language model reads alongside questions and conversation history. It connects the interfaces; multimodal instruction training, not shape alone, teaches instruction following.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A width-matching projection maps encoder features to LM size, but the model still must learn which features address the user&#x27;s question.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2304.08485-llava/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dfa5b553021f92af">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:raft" data-paper-title="RAFT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e3b8808917c40363">How does reward selection followed by maximum likelihood differ from direct policy gradients?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Araft">RAFT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · HKUST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rank sampled replies with the reward model and supervise selected text; scores determine selection, not per-action gradient weights. Resample with the next policy. Judge bias and missing candidates persist; local tests cover the iteration state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Learn the highest-rated candidate summary; absent good summaries can&#x27;t be chosen and judge errors can be copied.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06767">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2304.06767-raft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e3b8808917c40363">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:raft" data-paper-title="RAFT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cd03d4197adb8876">How isolate RAFT selection from evaluation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Araft">RAFT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · HKUST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Log reward model and rollout version, select among same-prompt candidates then update policy. No test answers for sorting. Local candidates aren&#x27;t a real generator or reward model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Training on choices made with test correctness invalidates held-out gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06767">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2304.06767-raft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cd03d4197adb8876">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:raft" data-paper-title="RAFT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-fc21318c02d86430">How does reward enter RAFT differently from PPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Araft">RAFT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · HKUST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>RAFT uses reward to select texts and then applies maximum likelihood. PPO uses advantages and probability ratios directly in policy objective. Selection and continuous weighting differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A high score can decide archive admission without proportionally increasing CE.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06767">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2304.06767-raft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fc21318c02d86430">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:raft" data-paper-title="RAFT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/data-and-budget">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/data-and-budget/">LLM post-training / Data and budgets: where to spend the next unit of compute</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-raft-fe9d648c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4b34e16004065fe4">Why keep generating fresh RAFT candidates from current policy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Araft">RAFT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · HKUST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed SFT data can&#x27;t follow improvement. Resample, rank by reward and supervise better behavior next round. Coverage still limits which outputs can be chosen.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Improved summarization can generate better candidates for later training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06767">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2304.06767-raft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4b34e16004065fe4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rrhf" data-paper-title="RRHF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c84c0f92798e6391">Why still apply SFT to the best answer after ranking responses?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arrhf">RRHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba DAMO Academy</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The hinge only fixes ordering conflicts and can stop giving a useful generation signal once sorted. SFT raises high-quality content likelihood. External rewards and length normalization do not guarantee factual correctness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Even with three answers ranked correctly, the best may be rare; its SFT term can still increase likelihood.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.05302">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2304.05302-rrhf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c84c0f92798e6391">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rrhf" data-paper-title="RRHF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5bdec3da01bf0a15">Why isn&#x27;t RRHF p_i raw probability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arrhf">RRHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba DAMO Academy</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It is length-normalized response log probability. The hinge compares this order within one prompt with consistent reward direction. Candidate tests do not reproduce full 7B training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Using decimal probabilities in place of mean logp changes margins and gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.05302">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2304.05302-rrhf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5bdec3da01bf0a15">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rrhf" data-paper-title="RRHF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5870e025a2c47fef">What do best-response SFT and RRHF ranking each add?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arrhf">RRHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba DAMO Academy</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Ranking corrects relative order; SFT directly raises best-response likelihood. Ranking alone can succeed by suppressing alternatives. The combination isn&#x27;t a universal optimum.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A good answer should be learned, not merely score above a bad one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.05302">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2304.05302-rrhf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5870e025a2c47fef">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rrhf" data-paper-title="RRHF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/post-training/preference-and-alignment/">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rrhf-c28f5ad3" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-25f8a4e90ddf8a40">Why use a full ordering of multiple same-prompt answers in RRHF?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=post-training%3Arrhf">RRHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba DAMO Academy</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multi-source responses provide more relative comparisons than one pair. Match length-averaged log likelihood to reward order and supervise the best answer. Ranking quality depends on labels/reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Good, middling and poor responses supply several orderings, not one winner pair.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.05302">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../post-training/2304.05302-rrhf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-25f8a4e90ddf8a40">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:generative-agents" data-paper-title="Generative Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-generative-agents-beb05f66" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-5c25df77a18e7bbd">Why shouldn&#x27;t an important old event automatically replace more query-relevant memory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Agenerative-agents">Generative Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Importance captures long-term significance, relevance measures current fit, and recency models decay. Reflection abstracts several important events, but actions still need current state. Using one dimension alone can repeat major events or focus only on recent chatter.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Moving home was important, but last night&#x27;s restaurant confirmation better answers today&#x27;s dinner-location question.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2304.03442-generative-agents/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5c25df77a18e7bbd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:generative-agents" data-paper-title="Generative Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-77326fa7f7760be0">Do local reflection triggers include a social evaluation of 25 LLM personas?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Agenerative-agents">Generative Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Controlled EvoMem tests three-score retrieval, cumulative-importance triggers, and planning dependencies without a Smallville map, real personas, or human credibility judgments. Reflection counts and proxy costs show mechanism execution, not believable relationships or coordination.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A threshold producing one rule-based reflection does not show models spreading invitations or arranging a party.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2304.03442-generative-agents/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-77326fa7f7760be0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:generative-agents" data-paper-title="Generative Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-86aad2b622fd5b5f">What questions do reflection and planning answer in everyday behavior simulation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Agenerative-agents">Generative Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reflection forms higher-level interpretations from experiences, such as relationship or habit inferences. Planning schedules what to do next using goals, memory, and time. Inferences are not events, and plans are not executed results. Separation makes both evidence and actual behavior traceable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Inferring that a neighbor likes gardening is reflection. Deciding to invite them to buy seeds this afternoon is planning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2304.03442-generative-agents/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-86aad2b622fd5b5f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:generative-agents" data-paper-title="Generative Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/memory-and-skills/">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f33684b6de1a3530">How does reflection differ from recording a single observation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Agenerative-agents">Generative Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Observations are concrete events. Reflection draws higher-level inferences across important memories for retrieval and planning. Inferences can be wrong and are not primary evidence. Keep observations traceable and plans grounded in current state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Several helpful acts may suggest someone is cooperative. That is an abstraction, not a new observed event, and should retain support.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2304.03442-generative-agents/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f33684b6de1a3530">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:camel" data-paper-title="CAMEL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-camel-640cbec7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-03d873922f3e2ffc">Why is inception prompting with roles, goals, and boundaries more than naming two models?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acamel">CAMEL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · King Abdullah University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Prompts define responsibilities, permitted requests, and cooperation. Alternating messages advance a common task under constraints. Renaming without capability or boundary differences can produce duplicates rather than collaboration. A social trace does not prove goal achievement; check deliverables separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: One role specifies implementation and the other proposes solutions without changing the overall goal. Mutual praise does not move the task forward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17760">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17760-camel/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-03d873922f3e2ffc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:camel" data-paper-title="CAMEL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1991aa1d4d0cf319">Does the local collaboration state machine match the full paper&#x27;s multi-agent instruction-following scope?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acamel">CAMEL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · King Abdullah University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It tests role messages, state updates, and budget without full large-model social traces or benchmarks. Scripted lines can verify handoffs but not autonomous cooperation or general open-task success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two templated replies show alternation works, not that models maintain role and goal boundaries on unfamiliar tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17760">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17760-camel/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1991aa1d4d0cf319">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:camel" data-paper-title="CAMEL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8dda7e7980ef7bf0">What does alternating two-role cooperation trade off against one complete model response?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acamel">CAMEL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · King Abdullah University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Dialogue can clarify and divide reasoning, but adds turns, communication, and error propagation. Models sharing biases cannot validate one another by agreement. Evaluate task outcomes and total cost rather than natural-sounding social messages.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: An executor can ask for missing input. If both roles misread the goal, more turns only extend the mistake.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17760">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17760-camel/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8dda7e7980ef7bf0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:camel" data-paper-title="CAMEL" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-707d4c87b3c8e6c6">Why does CAMEL study role collaboration instead of only a single model answer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acamel">CAMEL</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · King Abdullah University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Some tasks need requests, actions, and feedback over time. Two constrained roles can produce a longer collaboration process and data. Dialogue length and role division do not prove quality; roles can misunderstand goals, repeat, or drift. Inspect outcomes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: One role requests analysis and another implements with feedback. Repeating the request across turns does not complete the analysis.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17760">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17760-camel/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-707d4c87b3c8e6c6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:self-refine" data-paper-title="Self-Refine" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-self-refine-16be87c4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-439d518e3a48ecee">Why generate explicit feedback separately when the same model writes both draft and feedback?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aself-refine">Self-Refine</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Explicit feedback converts unmet constraints into actionable edits, avoiding mere random resampling. Generation, feedback, and refinement play distinct roles, and stopping still depends on the model. No extra training does not make feedback correct, and repeated polishing is not independent fact-checking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A draft omits units. Feedback to add units to each number gives a concrete target that &#x27;write it better&#x27; does not.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17651-self-refine/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-439d518e3a48ecee">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:self-refine" data-paper-title="Self-Refine" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d41641b7b845502f">Does stopping under a deterministic local critic demonstrate reliable real-LLM self-evaluation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aself-refine">Self-Refine</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A controlled critic verifies generation, feedback, revision, and stopping states, without a general LLM or the seven original benchmarks. Stopping verifies the contract, not reliable recognition of factual correctness on open tasks. Local perfect scores cannot stand in for human preferences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A rule can stop once text length is sufficient even when facts are wrong. Real self-assessment can be satisfied too early and needs independent evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17651-self-refine/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d41641b7b845502f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:self-refine" data-paper-title="Self-Refine" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-aafa2deef3b0dbdb">Compared with Reflexion&#x27;s cross-trial episodic memory, what loop does Self-Refine emphasize?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aself-refine">Self-Refine</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Self-Refine revises the current draft through feedback. Reflexion saves failure experience in bounded memory for a later trial. They can be combined but use different state. Refinement does not automatically form long-term memory, and repeated rewriting is not parameter RL.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Revising one email three times is Self-Refine. Saving &#x27;check recipients first&#x27; for tomorrow&#x27;s email involves cross-trial memory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17651-self-refine/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aafa2deef3b0dbdb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:self-refine" data-paper-title="Self-Refine" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f58bee1c1db1b73e">Why treat an output as a draft that can be improved against specific requirements in Self-Refine?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aself-refine">Self-Refine</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Open-ended generation may require correctness, completeness, clarity, and style; one attempt may meet only some. Self-Refine generates, diagnoses shortcomings, and revises without extra parameter training. The loop needs actionable feedback, and mistaken feedback can make later drafts worse; more rounds do not imply better quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A correct first explanation lacks an example. Point out the gap before revising; &#x27;make it better&#x27; may not identify what to change.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17651-self-refine/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f58bee1c1db1b73e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hugginggpt" data-paper-title="HuggingGPT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-hugginggpt-c07a7bb7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a9a80e3694f3511f">Why obey subtask dependencies instead of calling all multimodal experts simultaneously?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahugginggpt">HuggingGPT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A later expert may require actual outputs from detection, recognition, or transcription. Build a DAG, select compatible experts, run in topological order, then synthesize. Similar names do not imply compatible interfaces. Parallelize independent work, not dependencies.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Translate only after receiving real speech transcription. Starting translation concurrently and guessing the transcript breaks provenance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17580">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17580-hugginggpt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a9a80e3694f3511f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hugginggpt" data-paper-title="HuggingGPT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-974376ffc686eefe">Do the local capability registry and dependency edges run downloaded expert models?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahugginggpt">HuggingGPT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Local tool descriptions replace the model catalog to check matching and topological execution. No hundreds of Hugging Face checkpoints or ChatGPT calls ran. Edge counts verify flow, not cross-modal quality or real costs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A detection node&#x27;s rule-generated output can reach the answer node without establishing actual vision recognition.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17580">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17580-hugginggpt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-974376ffc686eefe">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hugginggpt" data-paper-title="HuggingGPT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-070cfaf4dcda6378">What does the language controller do versus a specialist multimodal model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahugginggpt">HuggingGPT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The controller interprets requests, selects specialists, and schedules subtasks. Specialists process vision or audio and the controller synthesizes results. Correct routing does not ensure correct predictions, and individual predictions do not guarantee a correct final answer. Verify selection, I/O, and interpretation separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A controller schedules image recognition before speech generation. The image and speech models execute their roles; the controller does not acquire their parameters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17580">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17580-hugginggpt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-070cfaf4dcda6378">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hugginggpt" data-paper-title="HuggingGPT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-898d4e2f2bf49825">Why does HuggingGPT use expert model descriptions as a searchable capability catalog?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahugginggpt">HuggingGPT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The controller matches subtasks to model-card descriptions and invokes experts instead of implementing all vision and speech itself. Descriptions guide selection, not guarantee capability. Verify versions, input/output types, and availability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Object recognition calls detection; audio-to-text calls ASR. Their media and output contracts differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17580">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.17580-hugginggpt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-898d4e2f2bf49825">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:reflexion" data-paper-title="Reflexion" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-reflexion-b837a66e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-bb3bffbeb91462b9">Why is verbal reinforcement not reinforcement-learning updates to model parameters?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Areflexion">Reflexion</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Feedback becomes natural-language experience in bounded episodic memory. The next attempt sees a different context without gradient updates to weights. Reflection can communicate more than binary success but can be wrong. An Evaluator must still judge execution rather than treating reflection&#x27;s claims as learning evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Remember &#x27;check the file path before editing&#x27; after failure. Reading that note changes behavior next round even with identical weights.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.11366-reflexion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bb3bffbeb91462b9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:reflexion" data-paper-title="Reflexion" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cba650900339d0a3">Why interpret the mini-suite score of 0.9 separately from isolated ToolRoute results?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Areflexion">Reflexion</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The mini-suite deterministically fails the first attempt in each family and then reuses feedback, with fixed reflection templates and evaluator. ToolRoute is a different tool environment without a reference-policy interface. Neither is HumanEval pass@1. Bounded append and failure retention can be checked, but scores cannot rank across protocols or replace the paper.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One deliberately failed task in each of twelve families sets the aggregate rate, unlike natural model errors across 120 independent coding problems.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.11366-reflexion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cba650900339d0a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:reflexion" data-paper-title="Reflexion" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e6913428acdd0141">What does actionable reflection add over saving a binary failure reward?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Areflexion">Reflexion</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Binary reward only says the attempt failed. Reflection proposes a cause and actions to try or avoid, supplying actionable context. That inference may be wrong and needs actual next-trial feedback. Do not place the hidden reference plan into reflection and credit later success to autonomous learning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>&#x27;Failure&#x27; does not locate the problem. &#x27;The date parameter needs ISO format&#x27; is useful, but must come from a visible error rather than a gold route.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.11366-reflexion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e6913428acdd0141">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:reflexion" data-paper-title="Reflexion" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/harness-and-self-improvement/">Agents / Harnesses and self-improvement: which layer changes?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-2a78cc6a61444ea4">Why does Reflexion retain failure lessons between attempts rather than just resample?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Areflexion">Reflexion</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Repeatedly trying the same task by resampling may repeat errors. Reflexion converts execution evaluation into readable experience so feedback survives across trials. Storing a lesson does not establish accuracy or transfer. Distinguish external reward from text reflection; neither automatically updates model weights with RL.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the first search stalls on an irrelevant page, reflection can advise checking sources and expanding the query. Restarting without the lesson can follow the same route.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.11366-reflexion/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2a78cc6a61444ea4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:art" data-paper-title="ART" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-art-62b00229" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-16afeb1e858f4dd5">Why pause at a tool marker and resume after execution instead of generating a whole program with results at once?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aart">ART</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pausing conditions later text on real tool returns rather than imagined outcomes. Retrieved reasoning/tool examples reduce manual prompts, but the runner must detect markers and inject observations. Frozen weights do not prevent tool feedback changing context and future output.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Execute a database query at its marker, then summarize the three returned rows rather than claim ten and add an unrun query.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09014">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2303.09014-art/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-16afeb1e858f4dd5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:art" data-paper-title="ART" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-9e15636c7c6d5f1c">How does the local tool-signature task bank differ from program generation by a frozen LLM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aart">ART</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Local tests check small-library retrieval, per-tool pause/resume, and updates without a frozen large model or BIG-Bench/MMLU. Pause counts show branches ran, not model-generated program semantics. Proxy costs are not paper tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Three pauses from a structured template test the runner, not automatic programming for arbitrary natural language.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
