<h2 id="qa-f15afaaf211da371">Is choosing between two local trajectories by evidence coverage equivalent to live browsing and a reward model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Awebgpt">WebGPT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Local checks retain browse actions, citation constraints, and candidate selection without live web, GPT-3 training, or a human preference model. Controlled coverage cannot be renamed human win rate, TruthfulQA, or real web fact verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Selecting a preset trace with broader evidence tests rejection sampling, not the full system without real pages and preference scoring.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09332">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2112.09332-webgpt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f15afaaf211da371">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:webgpt" data-paper-title="WebGPT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-849870cabbf2c4b0">What roles do behavior cloning and human-preference rejection sampling play?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Awebgpt">WebGPT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Cloning learns search, browsing, and answering from demonstrations. A preference model ranks and selects among candidate trajectories. Selection does not create facts, and can incur judge bias and sampling cost. Best-of-64 is not a single-call efficiency comparison.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Choosing one of 64 responses may improve preference scores while paying for multiple browsing and generation runs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09332">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2112.09332-webgpt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-849870cabbf2c4b0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:webgpt" data-paper-title="WebGPT" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/tools-and-collaboration">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/agent-research/tools-and-collaboration/">Agents / Tools and collaboration: turning plans into inspectable actions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cc127a045c60084f">Why does WebGPT include browsing and source support in long-form QA rather than rely on memory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=agent-research%3Awebgpt">WebGPT</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Open questions can need current facts and multiple sources. Browsing collects evidence for cited answers, and human feedback rates quality. Retrieved text still needs interpretation. Citation count neither proves support for individual claims nor covers all material facts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Comparing two policies requires both primary descriptions. One related link cannot support every figure in the paragraph.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09332">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../agent-research/2112.09332-webgpt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cc127a045c60084f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:alibi" data-paper-title="Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-alibi-69e595a8" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d919373883619f72">Without position vectors, how does ALiBi tell how far apart tokens are?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aalibi">Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It subtracts a distance-proportional bias from each head&#x27;s attention logits. Distant tokens need a stronger content match, and slopes vary by head. The rule extrapolates without a fixed-length table, but that does not guarantee arbitrary-length retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal content scores at distances 2 and 20 favor the closer token; a distant answer can still win with a stronger match.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2108.12409-alibi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d919373883619f72">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:alibi" data-paper-title="Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e0295b696e351666">Can ALiBi&#x27;s distance penalty replace causal masking?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aalibi">Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Bias changes preferences among visible positions, while the mask excludes future ones. Broadcast each head&#x27;s slope and keep causality. Small local models do not establish the paper&#x27;s large-scale gain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Token 3 cannot read token 4 even though their distance is one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2108.12409-alibi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e0295b696e351666">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:alibi" data-paper-title="Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e857b141de1beae3">Where do linear bias and position embeddings act?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aalibi">Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Position embeddings modify token inputs before Q/K/V projections. ALiBi does not learn position vectors; it modifies per-head matching logits directly. These are distinct information paths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The same content vectors can have different logit penalties at different distances.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2108.12409-alibi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e857b141de1beae3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:alibi" data-paper-title="Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-accc8fac0a859481">Why does ALiBi address training short and testing long?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aalibi">Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Position mechanisms fitted only to training lengths can fail at greater distances. ALiBi computes a distance penalty directly in logits. The positional rule extrapolates; long-context accuracy is empirical.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After training on 512 words, compute distances for word 800 without looking up a learned 800th position.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2108.12409-alibi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-accc8fac0a859481">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rope" data-paper-title="RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-rope-baa4b020" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9430b8ac22a0b9f9">Why do absolute Q/K rotations yield relative position in RoPE dot products?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arope">RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhuiyi Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The first rotation&#x27;s transpose cancels the shared absolute phase, leaving displacement n−m. Q/K subspaces rotate, not values. Evaluability at larger positions does not guarantee trained retrieval extrapolation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Moving positions 3 and 8 to 13 and 18 preserves distance 5 and their relative phase.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2104.09864-rope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9430b8ac22a0b9f9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rope" data-paper-title="RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-fcc3c0bb705d3c12">Can RoPE rotate only Q or only K?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arope">RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhuiyi Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Relative displacement requires both R_m and R_n. Pair channels correctly and continue absolute positions through incremental decode.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A single input token at position 100 still uses rotation 100, not zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2104.09864-rope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fcc3c0bb705d3c12">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rope" data-paper-title="RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-22c3fb74dae17ab4">How does RoPE differ from adding absolute embeddings?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arope">RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhuiyi Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Absolute embeddings modify representations additively. RoPE rotates Q/K so the inner product can express a relative rotation. These are different operations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Shifting both segments equally preserves RoPE&#x27;s relative phase.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2104.09864-rope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-22c3fb74dae17ab4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rope" data-paper-title="RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/context-and-state/">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-821e31f5f271e6be">Why rotate two-dimensional Q/K subspaces?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arope">RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhuiyi Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Position determines rotation angle, so dot products depend on relative phase and content without learning one vector per position.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Identical content at distances 2 and 20 can produce different scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2104.09864-rope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-821e31f5f271e6be">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:clip" data-paper-title="Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-clip-b03c09f0" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-48eaa29686fc2e90">Why does CLIP use both image-to-text and text-to-image contrastive learning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aclip">Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The same batch supplies two classification problems: find each image&#x27;s paired text and each text&#x27;s paired image. Both directions shape the shared similarity space. Other in-batch pairs provide negatives, but overall matching scores do not establish fine-grained factual accuracy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Cat and dog images pair with their respective descriptions, and both retrieval directions should rank each matching pair first.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2103.00020-clip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-48eaa29686fc2e90">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:clip" data-paper-title="Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-54de2a460ec3a509">Why normalize each vector before computing CLIP&#x27;s similarity matrix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aclip">Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Normalization makes dot products track direction instead of letting vector norms inflate scores; temperature controls sharpness. Matching pairs are on the diagonal, and the two directional losses use the matrix and its transpose. Not every pairing is a positive.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Doubling an image vector should not make it more correct for every text. With unit normalization only a direction change alters cosine similarity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2103.00020-clip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-54de2a460ec3a509">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:clip" data-paper-title="Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d51dbad1f172823e">How do CLIP&#x27;s class text embeddings differ from autoregressive label generation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aclip">Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>CLIP compares similarities among supplied class texts and returns a choice or ranking within the candidates. An autoregressive model predicts a label token sequence that requires generation and parsing. CLIP&#x27;s descriptions are input prototypes, not generated targets, so this interface does not provide open-ended captioning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Given “a photo of a cat” and “a photo of a dog,” CLIP compares their scores without generating “This is a cat.”</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2103.00020-clip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d51dbad1f172823e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:clip" data-paper-title="Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/multimodal-models/alignment-interfaces/">Multimodal models / Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a637592f066a62d1">Why can CLIP do zero-shot classification without retraining a classifier head?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aclip">Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · OpenAI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate encoders normalize image and class-description vectors and compare them in a shared space. The descriptions are class prototypes and can be replaced to define new labels. This depends on pretraining and does not guarantee arbitrary new concepts or fine-grained relationships are recognized.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Compare a shoe image with descriptions such as “a shoe” and “a coat,” then choose the higher similarity without training another linear head.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2103.00020-clip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a637592f066a62d1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:switch-transformer" data-paper-title="Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-switch-transformer-9afbb109" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-5ef6fd08ba273212">Why does top-1 Switch still need load balancing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswitch-transformer">Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Brain</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Top-1 caps experts per token but may concentrate traffic, bottlenecking winners and starving other experts. The auxiliary term combines actual dispatch proportions and mean router probabilities. More parameters do not imply proportional throughput.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One of eight experts receiving 90% of tokens can overload despite one FFN per token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2101.03961-switch-transformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5ef6fd08ba273212">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:switch-transformer" data-paper-title="Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cc5971522b46bfce">What do f_i and mean p_i count in Switch&#x27;s load term?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswitch-transformer">Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Brain</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>f_i is actual dispatch frequency; mean p_i is average router probability. Preserve the chosen expert&#x27;s gate. Local code does not cover capacity overflow or cross-device all-to-all.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>High dispatch and probability may correlate but are separate statistics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2101.03961-switch-transformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cc5971522b46bfce">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:switch-transformer" data-paper-title="Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d0d41032af3ea7f6">How does true top-1 dispatch differ from computing all outputs then one-hot masking?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswitch-transformer">Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Brain</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sparse dispatch executes selected experts only. Dense masking can match outputs while paying every expert&#x27;s cost. Inspect actual execution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Computing four experts and discarding three is not one-expert compute.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2101.03961-switch-transformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d0d41032af3ea7f6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:switch-transformer" data-paper-title="Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/foundation-models/conditional-compute/">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f3ee5dc08bd3f4dc">How does Switch increase parameters without using all experts per token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswitch-transformer">Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Brain</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Replace the FFN with experts and dispatch each token to one. This grows capacity without computing all expert branches, although routing and communication remain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four experts can be available while one runs per token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2101.03961-switch-transformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f3ee5dc08bd3f4dc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ple" data-paper-title="Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE): A Novel Multi-Task Learning Model for Personalized Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3abbb3ea731757ca">Why does PLE distinguish shared and private experts beyond MMoE&#x27;s task-specific gates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aple">Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE): A Novel Multi-Task Learning Model for Personalized Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MMoE mixes differently but all experts receive multiple tasks&#x27; gradients. PLE reserves private capacity alongside shared experts and extracts common and task-specific information layerwise. This changes information and gradient paths at extra capacity and routing cost; verify whether regressions actually decline.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Share category interest while purchase-private experts learn affordability and click-private experts learn headline appeal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ple" data-paper-title="Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE): A Novel Multi-Task Learning Model for Personalized Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-433f6282251197a2">Why restrict each PLE task gate to its private experts and shared experts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aple">Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE): A Novel Multi-Task Learning Model for Personalized Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>This is the CGC separation contract. Accessing another task&#x27;s private group changes the topology. Verify expert identities, masks, actual gradients, and next-layer channel layout rather than trusting variable names.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Concatenating all experts without a mask can preserve output shape but let click read purchase-private features.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/3383313.3412236">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/recsys2020-ple-ple/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-433f6282251197a2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ple" data-paper-title="Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE): A Novel Multi-Task Learning Model for Personalized Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4cfe1ebe206d5bfb">Why isn&#x27;t PLE just increasing MMoE expert count?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aple">Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE): A Novel Multi-Task Learning Model for Personalized Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>More shared experts still accept all tasks&#x27; gradients. PLE changes access and gradient topology with private groups and layered fusion, not just parameter count. Match budgets and do not generalize a local two-task comparison to every conflict.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Ten additional shared experts can still transmit click interference to purchases; a purchase-private group blocks that route.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/3383313.3412236">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/recsys2020-ple-ple/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4cfe1ebe206d5bfb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ple" data-paper-title="Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE): A Novel Multi-Task Learning Model for Personalized Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0451f6496f52aa1f">Why can average task AUC hide PLE&#x27;s seesaw effect?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aple">Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE): A Novel Multi-Task Learning Model for Personalized Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One task can improve while another regresses and the average obscures the loser. Report each objective under the same joint training. This differs from measurement noise and does not require identical gains across tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Click AUC gains two points and purchase loses one; average AUC rises without both improving.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/3383313.3412236">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/recsys2020-ple-ple/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0451f6496f52aa1f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dcn-v2" data-paper-title="DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a5fba110bcfcd1e9">Why does each DCN-V2 cross layer multiply the current transform by the original input x₀?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adcn-v2">DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The original anchor creates traceable higher-order combinations as depth increases instead of relying solely on implicit MLP interactions. Matrix crosses increase expressivity; low-rank factors and expert gating control cost. Compression can reduce capacity and must be tested with the deep path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Cross user and category first, then multiply by the original time feature to form a third-order interaction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.13535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2008.13535-dcn-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a5fba110bcfcd1e9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dcn-v2" data-paper-title="DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-80771f1fac3afa44">Which layers provide x0 and xl in DCN-V2?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adcn-v2">DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>x0 is always the cross stack&#x27;s original input and xl its current state; replacing x0 with xl changes the cross. Map each low-rank expert back to original width before multiplication and normalize gates over experts. Matching residual shapes does not verify the operator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Layer two still multiplies the original user and item vectors rather than squaring the previous state, despite matching shapes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.13535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2008.13535-dcn-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-80771f1fac3afa44">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dcn-v2" data-paper-title="DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-46f4f5f89cf26086">What is the capacity-compute trade-off between DCN-V2 low-rank expert mixing and a full cross matrix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adcn-v2">DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>U and V factor the large matrix through a smaller subspace. Multiple gated experts add input-dependent flexibility but also storage and routing. A single low-rank expert limits representable directions; parameter savings do not imply equal end-to-end latency savings because embeddings and other modules still cost time.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Project thousands of dimensions to dozens and back, with separate expert crosses. Too little rank can lose rare, important relationships.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.13535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2008.13535-dcn-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-46f4f5f89cf26086">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dcn-v2" data-paper-title="DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-31f19cb8fdc20457">Why does depth control the order of explicit crosses in DCN-V2?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adcn-v2">DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each layer elementwise multiplies a transform of current state by the original input, building higher orders while residuals retain lower ones. This gives traceable polynomial interaction paths, unlike generic MLP fitting. Rank, width, and training still constrain effective expressivity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A user age–category interaction can gain another original feature at the next layer without losing its lower-order residual.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.13535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2008.13535-dcn-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-31f19cb8fdc20457">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sim" data-paper-title="Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ff2b1a817c0aa800">Why use GSU then ESU instead of scoring lifelong history directly?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asim">Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Most history is irrelevant per candidate. Cheap GSU narrows it, then ESU attends precisely to selected behavior. Fine matching cannot recover evidence omitted by coarse retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If category filtering excludes old lens interactions, later camera attention cannot see them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05639">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2006.05639-sim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ff2b1a817c0aa800">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sim" data-paper-title="Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-24ca72f5435a3fec">How prevent future leakage in SIM top-k history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asim">Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>GSU searches only pre-request history, separate from the target label. ESU sees selected entries only. MovieLens verifies mechanism, not production or online A/B.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not add the next actual click before searching history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05639">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2006.05639-sim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-24ca72f5435a3fec">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sim" data-paper-title="Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e023b625f1151b67">How does candidate-related selection differ from one user vector?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asim">Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different candidates retrieve different evidence. A shared user vector compresses once and is easy to cache. Quality and cost still need measurement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Shoes and books can activate different historical interests for one user.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05639">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2006.05639-sim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e023b625f1151b67">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sim" data-paper-title="Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-sim-df73a28d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-3e6a146e9f258a78">Why run GSU search before ESU attention?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asim">Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Lifelong histories are long. Cheap candidate-related retrieval narrows them before fine matching, rather than always taking recent events.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A camera candidate can retrieve older photography behavior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05639">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/2006.05639-sim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3e6a146e9f258a78">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bst" data-paper-title="Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-bst-730383cc" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a856ffcdedab0d96">How does BST jointly attending over a candidate and history differ from DIN using a candidate to weight history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abst">Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>DIN mainly learns candidate-to-action activation. BST also enables interactions among past actions and embeds the candidate jointly, allowing context to change an action&#x27;s meaning. This costs more sequence computation and can limit reuse across candidates; compare matched budgets and history windows.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A camera click might be incidental, but later lens and tutorial views reinforce photography intent. A different candidate can change this jointly encoded state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.06874">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1905.06874-bst/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a856ffcdedab0d96">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bst" data-paper-title="Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f764ff81a314536c">Why not cache BST&#x27;s candidate-conditioned state as a user embedding shared by all candidates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abst">Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A candidate participating in self-attention can write into hidden history states; substituting it changes downstream inputs. Without an isolation mask, caching is valid only for the specific dependency conditions. The local candidate-aware Transformer versus DIN is not a demonstration of shared user-side caching.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A state computed for shoes can emphasize shoe history and bias a movie score. A shared cache must stop before candidate information is written.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.06874">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1905.06874-bst/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f764ff81a314536c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bst" data-paper-title="Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-54c96f178108af99">What does BST&#x27;s self-attention add over fixed history pooling, and at what cost?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abst">Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed pooling uses predetermined or simplified action weights and can miss combinations. BST learns pairwise contextual dependencies, with sequence-length-related computation and possible re-encoding for each candidate. Flexibility alone is not a win; compare matching data, budgets, and candidate protocols.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A camera view followed by a lens view can reflect a different purchase stage than a camera view alone. Attention can combine them but costs more with thousands of events.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.06874">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1905.06874-bst/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-54c96f178108af99">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bst" data-paper-title="Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a525ddf7b84c2c8a">Why include BST&#x27;s candidate token in history encoding rather than concatenating it only in the final MLP?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abst">Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Attention with the candidate lets history representations adapt early and learns both behavior-to-behavior and target-to-history relations. Late concatenation only interacts with an already compressed representation. The result is candidate-conditioned, not universal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Hiking shoes can amplify a related camping and hiking history, while a camera should refocus the encoding on photography.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.06874">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1905.06874-bst/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a525ddf7b84c2c8a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dien" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-dien-3d6c73b7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6b9b05c208996f59">How does DIEN multiplying target relevance into a GRU update gate differ from final history pooling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adien">Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Auxiliary prediction learns per-step interests, and candidate attention modulates each state update, letting relevant events revise memory while suppressing irrelevant changes. Late pooling cannot undo earlier overwrites. More recurrent computation need not help short histories.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>For a lens recommendation, a random food-ad click should weakly update a strong photography state rather than overwrite it before final pooling.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.03672">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1809.03672-dien/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6b9b05c208996f59">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dien" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-fcaef89988ef9b8e">How should DIEN auxiliary next-event supervision avoid confusing training labels with test futures?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adien">Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use next events as training labels while extraction inputs stop at current time and negatives follow training rules. Do not feed a held-out event into the GRU at evaluation. Target gating must update recurrent state step by step, not merely weight the final vector.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Predict event three from position two during training; feeding event three when evaluating that prediction leaks the answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.03672">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1809.03672-dien/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fcaef89988ef9b8e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dien" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-50f77630c64f3a37">When does candidate information enter DIEN compared with DIN target attention?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adien">Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>DIN weights history at aggregation, whereas DIEN multiplies relevance into each recurrent update gate, controlling retained and new state throughout evolution. Extra computation and training are not guaranteed improvements; the local gain did not reproduce.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A lens view can revise recurrent state immediately for a camera candidate; late weighting only reads what survives existing compression.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.03672">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1809.03672-dien/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-50f77630c64f3a37">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dien" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-9c333f1e60e9ad6d">Why separate interest extraction and target-related evolution in DIEN?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adien">Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The first stage extracts predictive interest states from behavior with auxiliary supervision. The second uses candidate relevance to control their update strength for the target. This avoids equating raw clicks with interests and remains sensitive to auxiliary negatives and noisy histories.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Camera and lens views establish photography interest, which matters more for a travel camera than for a novel.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.03672">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1809.03672-dien/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9c333f1e60e9ad6d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sasrec" data-paper-title="Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9e5caa204add37ff">How does SASRec balance recent and distant interests without reading future?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asasrec">Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Content attention accesses several earlier behaviors beyond fixed-order Markov neighbors, without RNN recurrence. Position representations preserve order and causal masks restrict reads. Next item is supervision only, and attention can still read irrelevant history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Recall old sci-fi interest despite recent comedy, while position three cannot read item four.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1808.09781-sasrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9e5caa204add37ff">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sasrec" data-paper-title="Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7b580fbe795a484e">How preserve SASRec embeddings and negative objective?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asasrec">Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tie input item embeddings with output weights and use per-position positive and sampled-negative pairwise BCE, not catalog CE. Mask padding and future positions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Never sample the true positive as its own negative.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1808.09781-sasrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7b580fbe795a484e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sasrec" data-paper-title="Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-128c509fca314590">How does causal next-item prediction differ from masked item recovery?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asasrec">Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Causal training uses only history; masked recovery can use both neighbors. Right context legal for recovery is future leakage in next-item prediction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Recovering A,[MASK],C may read C; predicting B after only A may not.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1808.09781-sasrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-128c509fca314590">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sasrec" data-paper-title="Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/history-ranking-backbones/">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-sasrec-6f67bc6e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7d35ae6cc7ed04c8">How does SASRec shift inputs and next-item targets?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asasrec">Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Position i reads history through i and supervises the following item, without exposing future events. Exclude padding; each sequence yields several prefix tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Use A→B and A,B→C; the representation predicting B cannot read C.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../reproductions/1808.09781-sasrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7d35ae6cc7ed04c8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:mmoe" data-paper-title="Modeling Task Relationships in Multi-task Learning with Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="../paths/recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality/">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-mmoe-a1bda9df" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ad97f0b0fdf40ae7">Why can shared experts with task-specific gates in MMoE reduce shared-bottom negative transfer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ammoe">Modeling Task Relationships in Multi-task Learning with Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
